t: How to Win Friends and Influence People
s: A 1936 classic of practical advice on dealing with people, from remembering names to listening and avoiding criticism.
w: HN suggests it for sales, public speaking and social awkwardness, since the core advice is to be genuinely interested in others.
ab: For people wanting better social and professional skills
Short chapters with timeless principles and anecdotes
Old-fashioned tone and examples

q.t: Be genuinely interested in other people and they will like you.

t: Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid
s: A Pulitzer-winning exploration of self-reference, recursion and consciousness through the work of Gödel, Escher and Bach.
w: HN cites it as a sprawling, mind-expanding classic on recursion, logic and meaning, often the book that got people into computer science.
ab: For readers who enjoy puzzles, logic and big ideas
Dialogues, wordplay and formal systems
Very long; demanding in parts

q.t: Very much relevant to anybody who found this interesting

t: Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software
s: A guided tour of how computers work, building from Morse code and telegraphs up through logic gates, processors and software.
w: HN's go-to first book for understanding computers from the bottom up, recommended as a gentle but rigorous grounding before assembly or C.
ab: For curious programmers who never learned how hardware works
Starts with telegraphs and relays, builds up to a CPU
Non-technical pacing; some find early chapters slow

q.t: Great read, and helped me understand exactly what you're referring to, understanding classical computers down to the metal.

s: A classic on usability and human-centered design, explaining why everyday objects confuse people and how affordances, mappings and feedback fix it.
w: HN treats it as required reading for anyone building interfaces or products, praised for teaching visibility, mapping and constraints.
ab: For developers, designers and product people building anything users touch
Plain-language principles with many door and stove examples
Some examples feel dated; ideas still hold

q.t: which I firmly believe should be required reading for anyone thinking about building anything

t: The Pragmatic Programmer: From Journeyman to Master
s: A collection of practical tips on programming craft, from tooling and debugging to automation and taking responsibility for your code.
w: HN regularly names it as a must-read on professional habits and tools for working programmers.
ab: For developers wanting good day-to-day habits
Short tips on tools, debugging and craft
Some tools and examples are dated; 20th anniversary edition exists

q.t: That book is all about tools and methods that a self-taught programmer should

s: Daniel Kahneman's survey of how the mind makes judgments, contrasting fast intuitive thinking with slow deliberate reasoning, and the biases that result.
w: HN recommends it for understanding decision-making and cognitive biases, though some priming studies have not replicated.
ab: For anyone curious about biases and decision-making
Covers heuristics, framing and loss aversion
Some cited studies failed to replicate

q.t: I highly recommend this book by Nobel Prize winner Daniel Kahneman

s: A classic on managing software teams, arguing that people, office environment and focus matter more than technology.
w: HN cites it for evidence that interruptions and open offices hurt programmers, and recommends it to anyone managing technical teams.
ab: For engineering managers and anyone who runs teams
Research-backed essays on workspace, teams and quality
Written in the 1980s; some details are dated

q.t: DeMarco and Lister nail everything you've ever thought about working in an office.

t: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs
s: The MIT introductory computer science text teaching abstraction, recursion, interpreters and language design using Scheme.
w: HN treats it as a legendary but polarizing classic: loved for changing how people think about programming, found tough by others.
ab: For programmers wanting to rethink how they program
Builds interpreters and evaluators in Scheme
Polarizing; demanding for beginners

q.t: both PG and some Peter Norvig give you permission to read it

s: A playful question-and-answer introduction to recursive thinking and functional programming, taught in Scheme.
w: HN recommends it as an entertaining way to learn recursion, easier than SICP, and a good gateway to Lisp.
ab: For programmers wanting to learn recursion and Lisp
Q&A format with whimsical illustrations
Unusual style that some find confusing

q.t: It's short (but don't read it all in one sitting), entertaining, and will teach you some important concepts.

s: Research-based look at the six principles of persuasion, such as reciprocity, scarcity and social proof, and how people use them.
w: HN recommends it for spotting and resisting manipulation tactics, and for anyone doing sales, marketing or negotiation.
ab: For anyone in sales, marketing, product or negotiation
Six persuasion principles backed by studies and anecdotes
Parts feel like common sense once explained

q.t: It's one of those great books whose lessons you carry with you many years later.

t: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance: An Inquiry into Values
s: A philosophical novel-memoir about a father and son's motorcycle trip across America, exploring the meaning of Quality and the divide between technical and romantic thinking.
w: HN readers treat it as a thinking person's book for hackers: a long meditation on quality, craft, and technology that comes up in debates over open versus closed systems.
ab: For makers and engineers who like philosophy mixed with a road trip
Reflective narrative with a long philosophical thread on Quality
Slow and abstract in places; more philosophy than motorcycle repair

q.t: A very interesting read for hackers.

by: Brian W. Kernighan, Dennis M. Ritchie
s: The original C reference and tutorial by the language's creator, known as K&R, covering ANSI C.
w: HN calls it the standard way to learn C: short, clear and sufficient on its own.
ab: For anyone learning C or wanting the canonical reference
Concise tutorial with exercises
Covers C89 only; no modern C features

q.t: Pair it with excellent notes by Steve Summit [2], and you don't need any other book to master C.

t: The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering
s: Classic essays on managing large software projects, including Brooks's law that adding people to a late project makes it later.
w: HN treats it as a perennial classic whose lessons about team size, communication and project scope still apply.
ab: For engineers and managers of software projects
Short essays on staffing, design and project management
Based on 1960s IBM experience

q.t: I'm reading the book right now, it's great.

s: Frank Herbert's 1965 science fiction epic of desert planet Arrakis, politics, ecology and prophecy.
w: HN readers treat it as the sci-fi book to recommend: an epic world mixing politics, mysticism and ecology. Commenters also reread the sequels and draw lessons about overcoming fear.
ab: For readers wanting epic, politically dense science fiction
Sequels get more philosophical and divisive
Often described as a book that needs no introduction on HN

q.t: The Dune series by Frank Herbert is by far one of the best works of fiction ever written.

s: A psychiatrist's memoir of surviving Nazi concentration camps and the logotherapy he developed around finding purpose in suffering.
w: HN recommends it as a short, accessible book on perseverance and purpose, and quotes the line about the space between stimulus and response.
ab: For anyone seeking perspective on suffering and purpose
Short and readable, a few hours
Heavy subject matter drawn from Holocaust experiences

q.t: Anyone interested in learning about human perseverance would do well to spend a couple hours reading Viktor Frankl's Man's Search for Meaning.

t: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!: Adventures of a Curious Character
s: Richard Feynman's memoir of stories from his life as a physicist, safecracker, bongo player and prankster.
w: HN regularly recommends it as an entertaining collection of anecdotes about curiosity, problem solving and not taking authority seriously.
ab: For anyone who likes funny stories and curiosity
Short anecdotes on physics, pranks and learning
Self-told, so details are embellished

q.t: I highly recommend both of Feynman's memoirs

t: Code Complete: A Practical Handbook of Software Construction
s: A comprehensive handbook on software construction covering design, naming, testing, debugging and code quality.
w: HN calls it a solid, practical reference on writing maintainable code, especially for newer developers.
ab: For developers wanting a broad craft reference
Covers construction practices and research-backed advice
Long; some material feels dated

q.t: Code Complete has pretty good bang per page, especially if you are beginner.

s: A short book on the reliable subset of JavaScript, steering readers away from the language's confusing features.
w: HN praised it as a slim, opinionated guide to writing clean JavaScript, focused on style and code organization.
ab: For developers who want clean old-style JavaScript habits
Very slim; focused on language design, not DOM
Pre-ES6; modern syntax is missing

q.t: Particularly because it's purely about style and code organization, and not about the best way to get consistent DOM access

t: The War of Art: Break Through the Blocks and Win Your Inner Creative Battles
s: A short book on 'Resistance', the force behind procrastination and creative blocks, and how professionals push through it.
w: HN recommends it for beating procrastination on important projects, praising its blunt reframing of resistance as something to fight daily.
ab: For makers, founders and writers who procrastinate
Short, punchy chapters on resistance and the professional mindset
Mystical language that some find heavy-handed

q.t: No book has helped me overcome procrastination more than Steven Pressfield's

t: The Elements of Computing Systems: Building a Modern Computer from First Principles
s: The book behind the Nand2Tetris course: build a working computer from logic gates up to an operating system and game.
w: HN recommends it for learning how computers work end to end, paired with the free nand2tetris courseware.
ab: For programmers wanting to build a computer from NAND gates
Hands-on projects with free online software tools
Simplified toy architecture, not a real CPU

q.t: Buy the book, download the courseware for free, and learn how computers work from NAND gates up.

t: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
s: A sweeping history of the human species from the cognitive revolution to the modern age, covering agriculture, religion, and empires.
w: A popular HN suggestion for readers curious about early humans and human development. Commenters say it made concepts such as multiple human species click.
ab: For general readers who like big-picture history
Readable overview of human history
Broad claims; some historians dispute details

q.t: I recommend anyone who's interested in early humans and human development to read the book Sapiens

t: Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution
s: Steven Levy's history of the early hacker culture from MIT's model railroad club to home computers and game programmers.
w: HN suggests it as the classic account of hacker culture and the early computer era, though some call it narrow and dated.
ab: For readers curious about early hacker culture
Stories of MIT, Homebrew Club and early game makers
Narrow focus and somewhat dated

q.t: considering it's in one of the best books about this history

s: A guide to the principles behind databases, distributed systems and data pipelines, covering storage, replication, partitioning and transactions.
w: HN recommends it as the best overview of distributed data systems, approachable but deep, useful for any backend engineer.
ab: For backend engineers and system designers
Covers storage engines, replication, partitioning, transactions
Long and dense; concepts over code

q.t: The book gives you a great overview of designing data systems

t: Founders at Work: Stories of Startups' Early Days
s: Interviews with founders of early tech startups about how their companies began and nearly failed.
w: HN recommends it as inspiration and examples of how real startups began, told by founders themselves.
ab: For aspiring founders wanting real origin stories
Interviews with early-era tech founders
Anecdotal rather than prescriptive; stories are from the 2000s

q.t: I really enjoyed all of the stories in Founders at Work

t: The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable
s: An essay-style book arguing that rare, unpredictable events dominate history and markets, and that people persistently underestimate them.
w: HN cites Taleb when threads turn to prediction, risk and randomness, and it often shows up on statistics and startup reading lists. Commenters usually pair it with Fooled by Randomness.
ab: For readers interested in risk, uncertainty and forecasting
Entertaining but opinionated and repetitive in places
Taleb's tone and claims divide readers

q.t: Nassim Nicholas Taleb also addresses this topic in some depth in his book

t: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
s: Douglas Adams's comic science fiction novel following Arthur Dent across the galaxy after Earth is demolished.
w: A go-to recommendation for funny, light reading. Commenters say Adams's humor stayed with them for years and shaped how they write and think.
ab: For readers who want comedic, absurdist sci-fi
First of a five-book series
Short and easy to read and re-read

q.t: Douglas Adams' humour had a (very) lasting impression on me

s: Gregory Hays's modern English translation of Marcus Aurelius's private Stoic notes to himself, with an introduction.
w: HN commenters name the Hays translation as the one to read. They say it keeps the informal, notes-to-self feel and reads easily, and cite it as a daily reminder to focus on what you control.
ab: For first-time readers of Stoic philosophy
Modern, plain-English translation with a helpful introduction
Aphoristic; best read a few passages at a time

q.t: the Hays edition captures this informal nature. It makes for an easy and delightful read.

t: The Soul of a New Machine
s: A Pulitzer Prize-winning account of a team at Data General racing to design a new minicomputer in the late 1970s.
w: HN's most-named book about what building hardware under pressure feels like. Commenters say it is a page-turner about team politics, and one says it made them cry for its passion for the craft.
ab: For engineers who want a story about building a product
Set in Data General in 1979; not in Silicon Valley
Reads like a novel; light on technical detail

q.t: Soul of a New Machine made me cry and, especially if you do low level stuff or hardware, is one of the best books

s: Ayn Rand's 1957 novel about industrialists withdrawing from a collectivist society, presenting her Objectivist philosophy.
w: A perennial favorite among HN readers who say it shifted their worldview and taught them to stand by their ideas. Even admirers note Rand's characters are unrealistic.
ab: For readers interested in Objectivism and individualism
Very long, philosophical and polarizing
Characters are archetypes rather than realistic people

q.t: Atlas Shrugged gave me a different perspective and changed a lot of viewpoints.

t: Masters of Doom: How Two Guys Created an Empire and Transformed Pop Culture
s: The story of id Software founders John Carmack and John Romero and the creation of Doom and Quake.
w: HN recommends it as a fast, gripping read about game development and id Software, with lessons for any software team.
ab: For programmers and gamers curious about id Software
Narrative of Carmack, Romero and the Doom era
Journalistic and dramatized rather than technical

q.t: I highly recommend it to all software folks, even if you're not a gamer.

t: The Dream Machine: J.C.R. Licklider and the Revolution That Made Computing Personal
s: A history of computing and the internet told through J.C.R. Licklider, who shaped ARPA research and interactive computing.
w: HN recommends it as an overlooked, well-researched history of early networking, human-computer interaction and the people behind the internet.
ab: For readers curious about how personal computing and the internet began
Biography plus the wider story of ARPA and cybernetics
Long, with a lot of names and institutions

q.t: It's a very well written book and gives great insight into the pre-web era of networking

s: A former FBI hostage negotiator's negotiation tactics for business and daily life.
w: HN recommends it as a readable negotiation book. Commenters like the FBI stories and say it complements Getting to Yes.
ab: For anyone who negotiates salary or deals
Tactical empathy and mirroring techniques
Some tactics are pop-psychology

q.t: there is the excellent "never split the difference" book

t: Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder
s: Taleb's book on systems that get stronger under stress and volatility, and on building lives, businesses and institutions that benefit from shocks.
w: HN cites it in talks about risk, prediction failure and resilience, where Taleb's point is to stop forecasting and build things that survive or gain from the unexpected. Opinions on his style are mixed.
ab: For readers interested in risk, resilience and decision-making
Introduces ideas like fragilista and the barbell strategy
Long, combative and repetitive; claims are argued rather than tested

q.t: Taleb's emphasis in his latest book is on avoiding the naive attempt to predict the unpredictable.

t: Don't Make Me Think: A Common Sense Approach to Web Usability
s: A short, illustrated guide to web usability that explains how people scan pages and how to make sites self-evident.
w: HN recommends it as the quick, readable intro to usability for developers and designers who want to make better interfaces.
ab: For developers and designers new to usability
Short, funny and heavily illustrated
Web examples date quickly; principles still apply

q.t: It's more of a usability book, but it covers some visual aspects to design.

t: Why We Sleep: Unlocking the Power of Sleep and Dreams
s: A neuroscientist's popular account of why sleep matters, covering memory, health, dreams and the costs of sleep loss.
w: HN posts it whenever sleep comes up, praising it as approachable and persuasive about taking sleep seriously.
ab: For anyone curious about sleep science
Popular-science style, with advice on sleep habits
Some claims are considered overstated by critics

q.t: It's pop-sciency in style but more nuanced and well-supported than most pop science books I've read.

s: Neal Stephenson's novel linking WWII codebreaking with a modern-day startup and data haven.
w: The always-recommended novel for hackers, and the answer when someone asks for fiction about startups. One calls it a favorite, though slow compared to a news briefing.
ab: For readers who like cryptography and startup-flavored fiction
Interwoven WWII and dot-com era storylines
Very long and digressive

q.t: Startups and science fiction... that book is a favorite of mine.

s: Lenovo's lightweight business ultrabook in the ThinkPad line, popular for running Linux.
w: Developers praise it as light, fast, with a good keyboard and trouble-free Linux, with some calling it the best developer machine. A few early Linux driver and display quirks come up.
ab: For developers wanting a light laptop that runs Linux well
Praised keyboard and TrackPoint nub
Early generations needed some Linux tweaking

q.t: Lenovo X1 Carbon. I've been using Linux on it for over 4 years now, with zero complaints.

s: A cyberpunk novel about a pizza-delivering hacker in a virtual Metaverse and a mind-virus that threatens both worlds.
w: A staple of HN lists of books that changed your life and favorites. It coined the metaverse for many techies and is often paired with Stephenson's command-line essay.
ab: For readers who like fast cyberpunk with tech ideas
Satirical, inventive world-building
Dated 1992 tech; uneven ending

q.t: BOOK - Snow Crash by Neal Stephenson

t: The Four Steps to the Epiphany
s: The founding text of customer development, laying out a process for finding customers and a repeatable business model before scaling.
w: HN recommends it to technical founders who need structure for sales and customer discovery, and it influenced the Lean Startup.
ab: For founders validating a new product or market
Detailed process, checklists and case studies
Dense, textbook-like writing

q.t: It puts a comforting amount of structure around the sales process

t: The Idea Factory: Bell Labs and the Great Age of American Innovation
s: A history of Bell Labs and the scientists who invented the transistor, information theory and much else, and the organization that enabled it.
w: HN recommends it for the people behind the transistor and information theory and for lessons on how to build a lab that produces real innovation. It comes up in every Bell Labs and R&D thread.
ab: For readers interested in research culture and the history of electronics
Mixes biographies with the story of the institution
Mostly the pre-1980 era; little on Unix or later years

q.t: If you have not, you should read The Idea Factory.

t: How to Read a Book: The Classic Guide to Intelligent Reading
by: Mortimer J. Adler, Charles Van Doren
s: A 1940 classic, revised in 1972, that teaches systematic levels of reading, from inspection to analytical and comparative reading of difficult books.
w: HN readers treat it as the book about reading well, recommended in speed-reading and learning threads. People say it changed how they absorb non-fiction and wish they had learned its method in college.
ab: For anyone who wants to get more out of dense non-fiction
A step-by-step method for active, analytical reading
Some sections on literature and philosophy lists feel dated

q.t: should be the first book gift you ever give. It changed my life.

s: A popular science classic presenting evolution from the gene's point of view and introducing the term meme.
w: HN commenters credit it with changing how they understand life and evolution, and point people to it for the origin of the word meme.
ab: For anyone curious about evolution and the logic of genes
Accessible writing; the 30th anniversary edition adds notes
Some ideas have been refined since 1976

q.t: I understood the world a whole lot better after reading The Selfish Gene

t: A Guide to the Good Life: The Ancient Art of Stoic Joy
s: A modern introduction to Stoic philosophy that adapts its techniques for dealing with anxiety, desire and adversity to daily life.
w: HN recommends it as an accessible entry to Stoicism for anxious or driven people, a practical mindfulness alternative.
ab: For readers new to Stoicism and practical philosophy
Techniques like negative visualization and voluntary discomfort
Light on original texts; some find it simplified

q.t: It's got a lot of the Buddhist elements of learning to accept the present while also focusing on achievement.

t: Programming Collective Intelligence: Building Smart Web 2.0 Applications
s: A hands-on introduction to machine learning for the web, with Python examples of recommendations, clustering, search and classification.
w: HN recommended it as a practical, example-driven intro to machine learning and recommendation algorithms.
ab: For programmers who want applied ML with working code
Python examples for recommendations, clustering and ranking
Written in 2007 (Python 2); modern libraries have replaced the code

q.t: It serves as a practical introduction to several different machine learning algorithms.

s: An anthropologist's history of debt, money and obligation across 5,000 years, challenging the standard barter story of money.
w: HN readers recommend it as a thought-provoking alternative history of money, though some dispute its claims.
ab: For readers curious about the origins of money and credit
Anthropological and historical approach to economics
Political perspective; some claims are contested

q.t: Its a very interesting and though provoking read thus far.

t: The E-Myth Revisited: Why Most Small Businesses Don't Work and What to Do About It
s: A business book arguing that small-business owners should build systems and processes instead of working in the business, told through a pie-shop story.
w: HN recommends it to founders starting a business, for the idea of building a repeatable system that runs without you.
ab: For founders and small-business owners
Pie-shop parable about systemizing a business
Cheesy storytelling and sales-y style

q.t: on how to start a business that is a system you own rather than a business that owns you.

t: Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience
s: A psychologist's study of flow, the state of deep absorption that makes activities enjoyable, and how to cultivate it.
w: HN cites it when discussing focus, work satisfaction and creative output, and readers say it changed their day-to-day lives.
ab: For anyone interested in focus, motivation and satisfying work
Research-backed account of the flow state
Academic and somewhat repetitive

q.t: a book that has had tremendous effects on my day to day life.

s: Apple's thin, lightweight laptop line, cheaper than the Pro models.
w: Often called the default choice for web developers: light, affordable and capable enough for everyday coding, even running Linux. Some older Airs drew complaints about a low-resolution screen.
ab: For web developers wanting a light, inexpensive laptop
Runs macOS well and can also run Linux
Older models had weak screens and limited upgradability

q.t: For web developers, I feel like the Air is almost the default option.

by: Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson et al.
s: The standard university textbook on algorithms and data structures, with rigorous proofs and pseudocode (CLRS).
w: HN calls it the bible and reference for breadth, best if you have a math background; some find Skiena friendlier.
ab: For CS students and engineers wanting a full algorithms reference
Rigorous proofs, pseudocode, broad coverage
Heavy and dry; readers with weaker math prefer Skiena

q.t: and you have a strong math background, then CLRS is the book to get

s: A hard science fiction novel about first contact with an alien intelligence, with vampires, consciousness and the Chinese room.
w: HN regulars recommend it as a must-read for hard sci-fi fans. Commenters cite interesting characters, philosophical questions and its free online release, though one noted minor narrative issues.
ab: For hard sci-fi readers interested in consciousness
Free online under a Creative Commons license
Dense, bleak and philosophical

q.t: Watts poses some very interesting philosophical questions along the way.

t: Nonviolent Communication: A Language of Life
s: A communication method built on observations, feelings, needs and requests, aimed at resolving conflict and empathy.
w: HN recommends it for changing how people speak with colleagues and family, a compact book on word choice and hidden assumptions.
ab: For people who want to communicate and resolve conflict better
Four-step method with dialogues
Some find the technique stilted and jargon-heavy

q.t: A great resource about choice of words and the internal assumptions we make when we communicate in certain ways.

t: The Phoenix Project: A Novel About IT, DevOps, and Helping Your Business Win
by: Gene Kim, Kevin Behr, George Spafford
s: A novel about an IT manager forced to rescue a failing company project, used to illustrate DevOps, flow and lean ideas.
w: HN recommends it as an easy, story-driven introduction to lean and DevOps thinking, a companion to The Goal. It sticks with people for ideas like limiting work in progress and the overloaded key engineer.
ab: For managers and engineers new to DevOps and lean ideas
Fiction format makes concepts easy to remember
Some find the characters and plot simplistic

q.t: I'd recommend the Phoenix Project - very easy read.

s: A study of why well-run established companies fail when disruptive technologies arrive.
w: HN calls it required reading for entrepreneurs and managers, and cites it when discussing why big companies ignore small new markets.
ab: For founders, managers and strategists
Explains disruptive versus sustaining innovation
Some case studies are decades old

q.t: As far as I am concerned, required reading for every entrepreneur, manager and executive today.

s: Jared Diamond's argument that geography and environment explain why some societies came to dominate.
w: HN recommends it for its sweeping ideas on why some groups did better than others. Commenters love it while noting it is not perfect.
ab: For readers of big-picture history
Environmental, not racial, explanations
Critics call it too deterministic

q.t: It's not perfect but the author throws in so many great ideas as to why certain groups did better than others.

t: The Art of Computer Programming, Volumes 1-4A Boxed Set
s: Donald Knuth's multi-volume encyclopedia of algorithms and their mathematical analysis, in MIX/MMIX assembly.
w: HN treats it as the ultimate algorithms reference and deep-dive, though not for beginners and very math-heavy.
ab: For experienced programmers wanting depth and rigor
Exhaustive coverage and exercises
Dense math; not for beginners

q.t: I'm surprised Donald Knuth's Art of Computer Programming only got 1 upvote.

s: Apple's high-end MacBook laptop line, used by many developers as a primary machine.
w: HN developers name it, alongside the ThinkPad, as one of only two serious dev laptops. Commenters say the hardware is great and use it everywhere from couch to clamshell desk setups with external monitors.
ab: For developers who want a polished Unix laptop with great hardware
Works as a portable machine or docked with monitors and keyboard
Prices are high and specs vary a lot by model year

q.t: There are really only two: the MBP and the ThinkPad.

s: Isaac Asimov's classic science fiction series about a scientific effort to shorten a galactic dark age.
w: Beloved classic recommended as endlessly rereadable. One commenter suggests sticking to the original trilogy since later sequels weaken it.
ab: For readers who like big-idea sci-fi
Original trilogy is the strongest part
Prose and characters feel dated compared to modern sci-fi

q.t: All are so much fun to read over and over again.

t: On Writing Well: The Classic Guide to Writing Nonfiction
s: A classic guide to clear nonfiction writing, covering simplicity, clutter, style and writing about people and places.
w: HN recommends it for anyone who writes, from blog posts to documentation, for its focus on clarity and cutting clutter.
ab: For anyone writing essays, docs or articles
Short chapters on clarity and simplicity
Journalistic tone; less about technical writing

q.t: a book I highly recommend for anyone interested in doing any kind of writing.

t: The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement
s: A business novel about a plant manager who saves his factory by learning the Theory of Constraints, focusing on bottlenecks and throughput.
w: HN recommends it as the classic fictional lesson in systems thinking, constraints, and operations, applicable to software work and the companion to The Phoenix Project.
ab: For engineers and managers interested in bottlenecks and flow
Told as a novel, so the ideas stay memorable
Manufacturing setting; the story shows its age

q.t: both of which use fictional narratives to illustrate best engineering practices in the context of saving a (fictional) business

t: Deep Work: Rules for Focused Success in a Distracted World
s: A book arguing that the ability to focus without distraction is increasingly valuable, with practical rules for scheduling and protecting deep concentration.
w: HN's go-to answer for distraction, internet addiction and focus threads. Readers like that it backs its claims with evidence rather than reading as productivity fluff, though some admit they struggled to keep up the habits.
ab: For knowledge workers and programmers who want to focus better
Concrete routines like scheduled internet time and shutdown rituals
Habits are hard to sustain; some sections feel padded

q.t: I recently read this book and I can't recommend it enough.

s: Hermann Hesse's short 1922 novel about a young man's spiritual search in ancient India.
w: Commenters list it as an outstanding book that changed how they see the world; one has gifted many copies. It is often paired with Hesse's Steppenwolf.
ab: For readers drawn to spiritual and reflective fiction
Short and approachable
Often cited as life-changing

q.t: I think the book changes the way you see the world.

t: The Cuckoo's Egg: Tracking a Spy Through the Maze of Computer Espionage
s: Clifford Stoll's true story of tracing a 75-cent accounting error to a German hacker selling secrets to the KGB in the 1980s.
w: HN recommends it as a gripping true tale of early network intrusion and an excellent read for security-minded programmers.
ab: For readers who like security stories and computer history
True account of tracking a 1980s hacker
Dated technology; the story still holds up

q.t: really blew my mind when I read it back in 2005.

s: A practical guide to adding tests and safely changing existing code that has none, with techniques for breaking dependencies.
w: HN's standard answer for inheriting a messy codebase: it shows how to get untested code under test and refactor incrementally.
ab: For engineers maintaining large untested codebases
Catalog of dependency-breaking techniques with examples
Examples in C++, Java and C#; some are dated

q.t: Best book I’ve read on the topic, highly recommended

t: The Power of Habit: Why We Do What We Do in Life and Business
s: A popular science book explaining the cue-routine-reward habit loop, with stories from companies, sports and individuals about changing habits.
w: HN recommends it as the readable introduction to habit formation, drawing on years of academic research on psychology and willpower. It is the answer to threads about forming good routines.
ab: For anyone who wants to understand and change habits
Story-driven, with practical habit-loop framework
Lighter on rigor than academic sources; some anecdotes disputed

q.t: The Power of Habit, great book, just finished it.

t: Show-Stopper!: The Breakneck Race to Create Windows NT and the Next Generation at Microsoft
s: A journalist's account of the Microsoft team led by Dave Cutler building Windows NT in the early 1990s.
w: HN recommends it as an engaging story of the NT project and Dave Cutler's intense leadership style.
ab: For readers who like software project war stories
Profiles Dave Cutler's NT team
Dramatized in places; early 1990s Microsoft

q.t: if even half of the anecdotes in Showstoppers are true then Dave Cutler is indeed a force of nature

s: William Gibson's 1984 cyberpunk novel about a washed-up hacker hired for a dangerous cyberspace heist.
w: Cited as a cool, foundational cyberpunk novel by HN readers who remember enjoying it and call it life-changing; its 1984 publication date impresses them.
ab: For readers who like cyberpunk and hacker culture
Dense, stylized prose
Coined the idea of cyberspace long before the web

q.t: I remember enjoying Neuromancer by William Gibson

s: A techno-thriller about a dead programmer's autonomous software that reshapes society.
w: HN recommends it as a near-future thriller that is technically credible. It gets cited whenever threads discuss bots, autonomous corporations or weaponized cars.
ab: For fans of tech thrillers
Sequel is Freedom
Plot gets cited in HN debates about autonomy

q.t: while technically futuristic isn't stupid, definitely check out Daemon

t: Skunk Works: A Personal Memoir of My Years at Lockheed
s: Ben Rich's memoir of leading Lockheed's Skunk Works, covering projects like the U-2, SR-71 and F-117 stealth fighter.
w: HN recommends it as inspiring first-hand engineering history on how a small team built groundbreaking aircraft.
ab: For engineers drawn to stories of small elite teams
First-hand accounts of the U-2, SR-71 and F-117
Memoir: self-flattering in places

q.t: the book Skunk Works is a great read (and also a great audio book)

s: Orson Scott Card's 1985 novel about a gifted child trained at a military space school to fight an alien war.
w: HN readers recall it as a formative childhood read, often giving or recommending it. One says it instilled a sense of agency at a young age.
ab: For teens and adults who like military sci-fi and strategy
A quick, gripping read
Sequels vary in reception

q.t: Reading Ender's Game as a child instilled a sense of agency at a young age.

s: Taleb's book on how luck is mistaken for skill in markets and life.
w: HN readers often recommend it before The Black Swan. Commenters call it a very good set of cautionary tales mostly from Wall Street.
ab: For anyone interested in probability and luck
Anecdotal rather than mathematical
Taleb's tone is abrasive

q.t: It's more of a set of cautionary tales, mostly pulled from Wall Street

t: So Good They Can't Ignore You: Why Skills Trump Passion in the Quest for Work You Love
s: Cal Newport's argument that career satisfaction comes from building rare skills, not following your passion.
w: HN recommends it as a framework for thinking about careers: build skills first and passion follows.
ab: For people questioning 'follow your passion' advice
Career capital framework with examples
Repeats its central idea

q.t: I highly recommend this book, which provides a super good framework to think about the situation you're in

s: Dell's compact 13-inch ultrabook, including the Developer Edition sold with Ubuntu preinstalled.
w: Recommended as a compact developer laptop with first-party Linux support; owners say it mostly just works with Ubuntu. Others warn about heat, so-so battery life and poor recent keyboards.
ab: For developers who want a small laptop that runs Linux
Dell is one of few makers shipping Ubuntu preinstalled
Some owners report heat, mediocre battery and weak keyboards

q.t: Mostly they just work and are fine for coding if you don't need a lot of oomph.

t: Getting Things Done: The Art of Stress-Free Productivity
s: David Allen's task management method built on capturing everything and reviewing it regularly.
w: HN's go-to productivity method; commenters pair it with tools like OmniFocus. One says they tried it for seven years before giving up while keeping some ideas.
ab: For people overwhelmed by tasks
Capture, clarify, review workflow
Can be heavy; some drop it

q.t: Try GTD, aka David Allen's "Getting Things Done".

t: The Code Book: The Science of Secrecy from Ancient Egypt to Quantum Cryptography
s: A popular history of codes and ciphers from ancient times through Enigma to public-key cryptography, written for general readers.
w: HN's usual beginner introduction to cryptography and code-breaking. Commenters praise Singh for making dry subject matter fascinating and for explaining why naive ciphers are easy to crack.
ab: For curious readers new to cryptography
History and stories more than math or code
Not a practical guide to modern crypto engineering

q.t: His specialty is taking very dry subjects and writing about them in a way that makes them fascinating.

s: George Orwell's 1949 dystopian novel about totalitarian surveillance, propaganda and thought control.
w: Commenters say it turned them against authoritarianism and think every citizen should read it. It is the book many HN readers say stuck with them from youth.
ab: For readers interested in surveillance and authoritarianism
A short, dark classic
Often paired with Animal Farm and Brave New World

q.t: Every citizen should read it, on my opinion.

s: J.R.R. Tolkien's epic fantasy trilogy following the quest to destroy the One Ring.
w: A formative favorite for many commenters, who say it captured their imagination as kids and reread it yearly. It frequently appears in lists of books that changed lives.
ab: For fans of epic, richly built fantasy
Slow, descriptive in places
Often reread as a yearly tradition

q.t: Lord of the Rings captured my imagination so profoundly as a kid there's no way it didn't change my life.

t: Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship
s: A handbook of principles and examples for writing readable, maintainable code, with a long refactoring case study.
w: HN recommends it for naming and readability, though some note the author is divisive and some advice is dogmatic.
ab: For newer developers learning readable code
Naming, functions and refactoring examples in Java
Opinionated; some advice debated by HN

q.t: is a great read and discusses good naming in exhaustive and occasionally alarming depth.

t: Predictably Irrational: The Hidden Forces That Shape Our Decisions
s: A behavioral economics book that uses experiments to show how people make systematically irrational choices about money, prices and decisions.
w: HN recommends it as an entertaining intro to cognitive biases and loss aversion, with ideas that carry over to marketing and sales. A commenter warned that the studies lack statistical significance, and later replication problems back this up.
ab: For readers new to behavioral economics
Lively experiments with everyday decisions
Several findings have not replicated; treat as anecdotes

q.t: It covers exactly this subject and makes for fascinating reading.

s: A practical algorithms text focused on designing solutions, with a large catalog of problems and war stories.
w: HN calls it more readable than CLRS and great for interviews and learning how to approach real problems.
ab: For self-taught programmers and interview prep
Readable explanations plus a catalog of problems
Less formal proof coverage than CLRS

q.t: if you read this book, it'll blow your mind and have you off to the races trying a hundred fascinating things

s: A hard sci-fi novel about digital copies of minds and the Dust Theory of existence.
w: Recommended as mind-bending hard sci-fi and a favorite on mind emulation.
ab: For hard sci-fi readers.
Heavy ideas on consciousness.
Dense.

q.t: He really takes sci-fi ideas to unpredictable yet believable conclusions. It is real hard sci-fi.

s: A survival novel about an astronaut stranded on Mars who uses engineering and science to stay alive until rescue.
w: HN's go-to fun read about space. Commenters call it impossible to put down and say it shows the technical difficulty of Mars and space missions.
ab: For readers who like problem-solving and hard-ish sci-fi
Fast and humorous
The movie adaptation is also well regarded

q.t: The book was a wild read, and does a tremendous job showing the myriad difficulties humanity must overcome in order to colonize Mars.

t: Three Felonies a Day: How the Feds Target the Innocent
s: A civil-liberties lawyer's argument that vague federal statutes mean ordinary people unknowingly commit multiple felonies daily.
w: HN cites it whenever privacy or prosecution comes up: the law is so broad that almost anyone could be charged, so enforcement is really a matter of discretion.
ab: For readers worried about overcriminalization and prosecutorial discretion
Case studies of ordinary people caught by vague federal laws
US-centric and strongly advocacy-minded

q.t: It discusses the selective enforcement of vague statutes and the incredible number of said statutes.

s: A Neal Stephenson novel about a nanotech-age girl raised by an interactive primer.
w: HN cites it often when discussing AI tutors and education.
ab: For sci-fi readers
Hugo winner
Dense

q.t: That looks like a good genre fit for my son's tastes

s: A short introduction to systems thinking covering stocks, flows, feedback loops and leverage points.
w: HN recommends it as a compact catalog of common system patterns, useful for engineers, policy and permaculture thinking.
ab: For people who want to model complex systems
Feedback loops, delays and leverage points
Abstract in places; few worked equations

q.t: It's a catalog of common system patterns and how they behave

t: The Intelligent Investor: The Definitive Book on Value Investing
s: Benjamin Graham's classic on value investing, margin of safety and investor temperament, with modern commentary added by Jason Zweig.
w: HN recommends it as the foundation for understanding investing and for how Buffett learned. The revised edition is praised for adding a chapter of modern interpretation after each of Graham's chapters.
ab: For long-term investors who want first principles
Revised edition adds commentary in each chapter
Original 1949 examples are dated; not financial advice

q.t: Each of Graham's chapters is followed by another chapter of interpretation/reflection on his advice in a modern context.

t: Venture Deals: Be Smarter Than Your Lawyer and Venture Capitalist
s: A guide to venture financing terms, covering term sheets, valuation, equity and negotiating with investors.
w: HN recommends it to founders raising money for its plain explanation of term sheets, valuation and investor rights.
ab: For founders about to raise or negotiate venture funding
Clause-by-clause explanation of term sheets
US venture focus; check updated editions

q.t: I just finished reading it, and found it extremely informative.

t: Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy
s: A self-help guide to cognitive behavioral therapy techniques for depression and anxiety, with exercises for challenging negative thinking.
w: HN readers credit it with helping them manage depression and negative thought patterns, and recommend it as an accessible intro to CBT.
ab: For people dealing with low mood or negative self-talk
Practical CBT exercises you can do yourself
Not a substitute for professional care

q.t: covers this, and ways to deal with it in a very accessible and straightforward way.

t: The Making of the Atomic Bomb
s: A Pulitzer Prize-winning history of the science and engineering behind the first nuclear weapons, from the discovery of fission to Hiroshima.
w: HN recommends it to anyone in a technical field for its precise account of how scientists, engineers and government worked together. One commenter calls it the best hard sci-fi book ever written.
ab: For readers interested in physics and history of science
Over 800 pages, detailed and well written
Heavy on personalities and physics; long read

q.t: is a fantastic book for anybody in a technical field.

t: Dealers of Lightning: Xerox PARC and the Dawn of the Computer Age
s: The story of Xerox PARC, where the graphical interface, Ethernet and laser printing were invented before the PC era.
w: HN recommends it as one of the best histories of computing, covering the people and ideas at PARC and how Xerox failed to capitalize.
ab: For readers curious about the origins of the GUI and networking
Profiles the PARC researchers and their culture
Long; dense with names and company politics

q.t: it's one of the two best history of computing books i've read

t: The Linux Programming Interface: A Linux and UNIX System Programming Handbook
s: A comprehensive reference to Linux and UNIX system programming, documenting system calls, the C library interfaces and how they behave.
w: HN's standard recommendation for learning low-level Linux programming. Commenters like that it documents all system call interfaces in detail and say it is worth its high price for relevant work.
ab: For systems programmers working in C on Linux or UNIX
Over 1,500 pages; best used as a reference
Not for the kernel itself; covers user-space API

q.t: I've really enjoyed the book The Linux Programming Interface by Kerrisk as a guide for learning some of these types of low level concepts.

t: Seven Languages in Seven Weeks: A Pragmatic Guide to Learning Programming Languages
s: A tour of seven programming languages, including Ruby, Io, Prolog, Scala, Erlang, Clojure and Haskell, each in a short chapter.
w: Recommended for people who want to explore different programming paradigms and try Clojure or Prolog for the first time. A commenter says it was fun even though he did not write anything great.
ab: For experienced programmers wanting a taste of other paradigms
One short chapter per language, with exercises
Language versions have moved on since 2010

q.t: I didn't write anything great, but it was a lot of fun to play with new ideas.

t: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, 3rd Edition
by: Randal E. Bryant, David R. O'Hallaron
s: A textbook that explains how hardware, machine code, memory, linking and networking affect the programs that developers write, with labs.
w: HN calls CS:APP the book for anyone interested in low-level systems and recommends knowing its material to be a better engineer. One commenter warns to buy the North American edition, not the global edition.
ab: For programmers who want to know what the machine does
Covers x86-64, caches, linking, concurrency and networking
Pricey; buy the North American edition, not the global edition

q.t: CS:APP is hands down THE book that every person interested in the low-level stuff in computer systems should own.

t: The Checklist Manifesto: How to Get Things Right
s: A surgeon and New Yorker writer shows how simple checklists cut errors in medicine, aviation and construction, and how to design them well.
w: HN brings it up whenever a thread is about preventable error, from medical mistakes to outages and incident postmortems. It is the go-to reference for why humble checklists beat expert memory.
ab: For engineers, ops people and managers who want fewer avoidable mistakes
Case studies from surgery, aviation and building projects
Short, anecdote-driven, and light on how to build your own

q.t: The Checklist Manifesto is a great book on this topic

s: A Hugo-winning Chinese hard sci-fi novel about first contact, set against the Cultural Revolution and a virtual-reality game, first in the Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy.
w: It is the go-to answer on HN when someone asks for great modern sci-fi, and commenters bring up its Dark Forest idea whenever Fermi's paradox comes up.
ab: For hard sci-fi fans who like big ideas
Translated well; the first book of a trilogy
Characters are thin to some; slow start before the big ideas

q.t: which I would highly recommend (it originally came out in Mandarin, but it has a great translation)

s: A short philosophical work distinguishing finite games played to win from infinite games played to keep playing, applied to life, culture, and power.
w: HN readers recommend it as a book-length idea that is a metaphor for life and strategy. Commenters call it the last word on games and often cite it with startups and business.
ab: For readers who like compact philosophy and strategy ideas
Aphoristic, dense chapters
Abstract and metaphorical; styles vary in clarity

q.t: the James Carse book, "Finite and Infinite Games" is the last word on all games!

s: A collection of essays on practical algorithm design, problem solving and engineering trade-offs, with worked problems and exercises.
w: HN lists it among the classic books on thinking about code, praised as a book of ideas to play with rather than just problems. Solutions are iteratively improved with clear reasoning.
ab: For programmers who enjoy puzzles and clever solutions
Short, essay-style chapters with exercises
Examples and tooling date from the 1980s and 1990s

q.t: Programming Pearls is a fairly well known, well regarded book

t: The Mom Test: How to Talk to Customers & Learn If Your Business Is a Good Idea When Everyone Is Lying to You
s: A short guide to customer interviews that teaches founders how to ask questions that produce honest, useful answers instead of polite praise.
w: HN's top pick for validating a startup idea or collecting user feedback. Readers say the first pages changed how they talk to customers, and it is the usual answer to threads about asking users about pain points.
ab: For founders and product people running customer interviews
Quick read with concrete do and don't questions
Author's book was first self-published; short on advanced techniques

q.t: The first few pages blew my mind. It was a great read all the way through.

t: The Millionaire Next Door: The Surprising Secrets of America's Wealthy
by: Thomas J. Stanley, William D. Danko
s: A study of American millionaires, finding that most live frugally, build wealth steadily and avoid flashy spending.
w: HN recommends it to debunk the flashy-rich stereotype and to show that wealth usually comes from saving and frugality.
ab: For people learning how ordinary households build wealth
Survey data on millionaire habits
Repetitive in places; data is decades old

q.t: this is an excellent book (a classic really)

t: The 4-Hour Workweek: Escape 9-5, Live Anywhere, and Join the New Rich
s: A lifestyle and business book about automating income, outsourcing tasks and designing a life of mini-retirements and remote work.
w: HN recommends it in threads about remote work, time management and escaping a day job, with IT workers saying its ideas fit them. It also draws pushback; skeptics argue against following its approach.
ab: For people who want remote work or a side business
Covers outsourcing, automation and lifestyle design
Several tactics are dated; hype and a salesy tone put some off

q.t: Great advice for time management, works well for IT positions.

s: A Charles Stross novel of the technological singularity across three generations.
w: HN cites it for reputation economies and corporate AI.
ab: Sci-fi readers
Dense
Free online

q.t: My favorite use of shell corporations in fiction so far is in Accelerando

s: Dan Simmons's 1989 science fiction novel, structured as pilgrims' tales on the way to the Time Tombs; first of the Hyperion Cantos.
w: Repeatedly named among the best sci-fi on HN, valued for interwoven stories and an emotional finale. The whole four-book Cantos series gets recommended.
ab: For readers who like literary, multi-story space opera
Four-book series; the first two feel like one story
Rich in literary allusions

q.t: Hyperion (Dan Simmons) and Three Body Problem (Liu Cixin) stand out from all the SF I've read

t: The Information: A History, a Theory, a Flood
s: A history of information from talking drums to Shannon's theory and the modern data flood.
w: HN suggests it as a great read on the history of information and computing, including Babbage and Lovelace. One commenter said it was the book they wanted to write.
ab: For curious readers of science and tech history
Covers Shannon, Babbage, and more
Long and wide-ranging

q.t: is the book that I wanted to write and then I found out it existed

t: The Emperor of All Maladies: A Biography of Cancer
s: A history of cancer and the people who fought it, from ancient times to modern research.
w: HN recommends it as the best way to understand cancer for non-specialists. Commenters say it gave them a solid grasp of the history and biology, though it is a bit depressing.
ab: For general readers curious about medicine
Narrative history plus science
Heavy subject matter

q.t: I would highly recommend "The Emperor of All Maladies" for anyone seeking a more solid understanding of cancer.

t: The Power Broker: Robert Moses and the Fall of New York
s: A Pulitzer Prize-winning biography of Robert Moses, the unelected official who reshaped New York's roads, parks and neighborhoods for decades.
w: HN's classic for understanding urban planning and political power. Commenters call it a fantastic read about how Moses shaped the city and starved public transit in favor of highways.
ab: For readers interested in cities, politics and power
Over 1,200 pages; takes months
Detailed, sometimes slow

q.t: This book is very long, but a good way to spend a few months for anyone interested in urban planning.

s: Eric Ries's method for building startups through rapid experiments, validated learning and pivots.
w: HN readers recommend it to developers moving toward product or founding. One says to run, not walk, to get it; another found the pivot idea radical.
ab: For first-time founders and product people
Build-measure-learn loop
Often oversimplified in practice

q.t: If you haven't red the book The Lean Startup by Eric Ries, run, don't walk to get it.

t: A Random Walk Down Wall Street
s: A classic argument for index fund investing and market efficiency, with a history of bubbles.
w: The usual HN recommendation for passive investing. Commenters say it taught them the fundamentals and often pair it with the Bogleheads community.
ab: For beginner investors
Case for low-cost index investing
US-centric and edition-dependent

q.t: This book is enormously valuable to me, and I wholeheartedly recommend it to everyone

t: A Short History of Nearly Everything
s: Bill Bryson's popular science tour of how we came to know about the universe, Earth and life.
w: Recommended as an excellent popular science introduction to nearly everything, and one that pushed a commenter into research. Often listed alongside other approachable science nonfiction.
ab: For curious readers wanting a readable overview of science
Light in tone but wide in scope
Some science has moved on since 2003

q.t: Excellent popular science intro to, well, nearly everything.

t: Command and Control: Nuclear Weapons, the Damascus Accident, and the Illusion of Safety
s: A history of US nuclear weapons safety failures, built around a 1980 Titan II missile accident in Arkansas.
w: HN recommends it as a gripping, terrifying account of how close accidents came to disaster, with lessons for engineering safety.
ab: For readers interested in safety, engineering failure and nuclear history
Alternates a 1980 missile accident with weapons history
Disturbing; long

q.t: which I just finished and thoroughly enjoyed/was terrified by.

s: Dostoevsky's 1880 novel about three brothers and the murder of their father, exploring faith, doubt and morality.
w: A staple on HN reading lists, re-read by fans who single out the chapter The Grand Inquisitor. People pick it up after seeing it referenced everywhere.
ab: For readers ready for dense Russian philosophical fiction
Long, with heavy religious and moral debate
Translation choice matters

q.t: The chapter "The Grand Inquisitor" is the cream of the cream.

t: Factfulness: Ten Reasons We're Wrong About the World--and Why Things Are Better Than You Think
s: Hans Rosling's argument that people hold outdated, pessimistic views of the world, with ten instincts that distort our thinking and data to correct them.
w: HN readers recommend it as a fact-based corrective to pessimism, with the Four Levels of Global Income idea cited as a better way to talk about countries.
ab: For anyone who wants data-backed views of global progress
Ten thinking traps with global statistics
Optimistic framing; some find it simplistic

q.t: The late Dr. Hans Rosling's Factfullness is a great read.

t: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software
by: Erich Gamma, Richard Helm et al.
s: The Gang of Four catalog of 23 object-oriented design patterns, each with motivation, structure and sample code in C++ and Smalltalk.
w: HN calls it the classic on software design, usually listed next to Refactoring. Commenters say it is dry and academic, and some use it more as a shared vocabulary than a how-to.
ab: For OO programmers who want a shared design vocabulary
Catalog format is dense and reads like a reference
Examples in C++ and Smalltalk; some patterns are outdated

q.t: The bible of all developers is the Gang Of Four

t: The Dictator's Handbook: Why Bad Behavior Is Almost Always Good Politics
by: Bruce Bueno de Mesquita, Alastair Smith
s: A political science book arguing that leaders of any regime keep power by rewarding the small group whose support they need, per selectorate theory.
w: HN cites it when threads ask why leaders do things that seem bad for their countries. Readers call it insightful and a clear account of the incentives dictators and elected leaders face; CGP Grey's video summarizes it.
ab: For readers curious about power, incentives and politics
Explains selectorate theory with real-world examples
Simplified model; some critics find it overly cynical

q.t: a book I cannot recommend enough, extremely insightful especially in the context of this election

s: A collection of bit-manipulation tricks, arithmetic algorithms and low-level programming techniques for fast code.
w: HN recommends it whenever bit twiddling comes up: a fun reference of clever tricks that people actually use in real work.
ab: For systems programmers and compiler-minded readers
Bit tricks, integer arithmetic and division by constants
Dense and math-heavy; niche for most application work

q.t: I know that I've used more than a few of the tricks in my day-to-day work.

t: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success
s: A psychologist's book on fixed versus growth mindsets, arguing that how people think about ability shapes learning, effort and achievement.
w: HN recommends it in threads about perfectionism, praised kids and fear of failure. Readers say it clarified how praise for being smart can make people avoid risk, and it is a quick read.
ab: For parents, teachers and high achievers who avoid challenges
Quick, readable book with plenty of examples
Growth mindset research has had mixed replication results

q.t: I recommend it, it's amazing how hackable your mind is.

t: The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark
s: Carl Sagan's defense of scientific skepticism against pseudoscience and superstition, including his Baloney Detection Kit.
w: HN cites it when pseudoscience, snake oil or ghosts come up. Commenters recommend it for explaining the scientific method and especially the Baloney Detection Kit chapter.
ab: For readers who want a toolkit for skepticism
Includes the Baloney Detection Kit
Accessible popular-science tone

q.t: If only everyone read Carl Sagan's The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark[0], or at least the Baloney Detection Kit part.

s: A humorous sci-fi novel in which a software engineer's mind is uploaded after death and becomes a self-replicating space-probe AI exploring the galaxy.
w: HN readers recommend it as a fun, funny story about uploaded minds and space probes, often suggested alongside threads on Fermi's paradox and Lena.
ab: For sci-fi fans who like humor and software-engineer protagonists
First book in the Bobiverse series
Light and fun rather than deep; the title is silly

q.t: An awesome sci-fi story about a software developer who wakes up in the 22nd as a computer program

s: A rigorous, proof-based introduction to calculus and real analysis, famous for its challenging problem sets.
w: HN recommends it for self-learners who want real mathematical rigor, best if comfortable with logic and proofs.
ab: For motivated self-learners who want a rigorous treatment
Proofs and hard problems, close to intro real analysis
Challenging; not a plug-and-chug textbook

q.t: I would recommend this book to anybody who wants to brush up on calculus after studying it before.

t: The Beginning of Infinity: Explanations That Transform the World
s: A physicist's argument that good explanations drive knowledge and progress, spanning epistemology, science, computation and optimism.
w: Recommended as a starting point for thinking about how knowledge is created. Commenters connect it to computation and to optimism about solving problems.
ab: For readers who like big-picture ideas on knowledge
Dense and contrarian in places
Optimistic, Popperian worldview

q.t: Like many I've been influenced by "The Beginning of Infinity" by David Deutsch in this regard.

t: Crucial Conversations: Tools for Talking When Stakes Are High
by: Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny et al.
s: A communication guide on handling high-stakes, emotionally charged conversations at work and at home.
w: HN readers point to it whenever conflict, confrontation or a difficult boss comes up. It is a learnable toolkit rather than theory, and several say it changed how they handle tense meetings.
ab: For anyone who dreads confrontation or manages people
Concrete skills for staying calm and getting to shared understanding
HN calls it a bit dry

q.t: provides guidance on some very straightforward to pick up skills which are unimaginably important in business and personal relationships

s: A short 1946 primer that argues good economics means tracing the long-run and secondary effects of policies on all groups, not just the visible ones.
w: A frequent first recommendation for newcomers to economics because it is short and teaches second-order thinking. Commenters call it a classic, though one thread questions its free-market slant.
ab: For readers new to economics wanting a short intro
Clear arguments about unintended consequences of policy
Written from a free-market viewpoint; the examples are dated

q.t: one of those perfect little books that can greatly expand your world view in one night.

t: Zero to One: Notes on Startups, or How to Build the Future
s: Peter Thiel's startup book, adapted from Blake Masters' notes of his Stanford course, on building monopolies and creating new technology.
w: Appears on HN founder reading lists and gets cited as a popular startup book. Reaction in comments ranges from interest in its ideas to cynicism about its marketing.
ab: For founders thinking about original businesses
Short essays on monopoly, secrets, and competition
Contrarian claims; HN split on its value

s: Jeff Hawkins's theory that the neocortex works by predicting patterns, and what that means for building intelligent machines.
w: HN recommends it as a thought-provoking take on how the brain works, and several readers credit it with changing how they think about intelligence.
ab: For readers curious about brains and AI
Memory-prediction theory for general readers
2004 neuroscience; some ideas are speculative

q.t: Hawkins presents a compelling theory of how the human brain works and how we can finally build intelligent machines

t: Stories of Your Life and Others
s: Ted Chiang's debut short story collection, including the title story that became the film Arrival.
w: Commenters call it some of the most thought-provoking science fiction around, and one of the best single-author SF collections. A few note the stories are a little uneven.
ab: For readers who like idea-driven, intellectual science fiction
Eight stories, including Story of Your Life and Tower of Babylon
Some stories are weaker than others

q.t: Probably the best SF collection by a single author I've ever read.

t: Where Wizards Stay Up Late: The Origins of the Internet
s: A narrative history of how ARPANET, the precursor of the internet, was conceived and built by a small group of engineers at BBN and elsewhere.
w: HN's default recommendation for the story of ARPANET, posted whenever a pioneer dies or an internet history thread appears. One reader found it far more interesting than the subject suggested.
ab: For anyone curious about how the internet began
Focus is people and personalities, not technical depth
Covers ARPANET era; the later web is out of scope

q.t: I found it to be _much_ more interesting than I expected from the subject material. Highly recommended.

t: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
s: Ben Horowitz's advice on running a startup through hard times.
w: HN recommends it for hard startup situations. Commenters call it a goldmine for new managers.
ab: For founders and CEOs
Candid stories
Not a how-to

q.t: is a bit of a goldmine for someone in your shoes

t: The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger
s: The history of the shipping container and how it transformed global trade, ports and labor.
w: HN recommends it as a fascinating account of standardization and how an ordinary invention reshaped the world economy.
ab: For readers who like stories of standards and logistics
Covers Malcom McLean, unions, ports and global trade
Some sections get detailed on business and labor

q.t: It is an excellent read which explains how the container came to be

s: A book on designing efficient immutable data structures for functional languages, with analysis and implementations in ML and Haskell.
w: HN calls it the definitive book on persistent functional data structures, recommended for anyone implementing or using a functional language.
ab: For functional programmers and language implementers
Design and amortized analysis of persistent structures
Code in ML and Haskell; academic style

q.t: This book is more or less the definitive book on functional persistent data structures.

t: How to Solve It: A New Aspect of Mathematical Method
s: A classic short guide to mathematical problem solving, offering a four-step method and heuristics for tackling unfamiliar problems.
w: HN recommends it as a general problem-solving book for programmers and mathematicians, helpful for interviews and puzzles.
ab: For students, programmers and puzzle solvers
Four-step method plus a dictionary of heuristics
1945 examples; terse in places

q.t: which is apparently a popular general purpose problem solving book

t: 1491: New Revelations of the Americas Before Columbus
s: A survey of recent archaeology arguing the pre-Columbian Americas were more populous, complex and managed than once believed.
w: A frequent HN recommendation for anyone curious about the Americas before European contact. Commenters call it a great, eye-opening read on dense populations, managed landscapes and the effect of disease.
ab: For history and anthropology fans
Covers population, agriculture, and landscape management
Get the adult edition, not the young readers one

q.t: The book _1491_ is a great read to learn more about what the Americas were like before the European arrival.

s: A novel in which a telepathic gorilla teaches a narrator about civilization, agriculture and humanity's relationship with the planet.
w: HN readers press it on people who want to question modern civilization's narrative, saying it might change your view on how humans live and why.
ab: For readers interested in ecology and critiques of civilization
Philosophical dialogue in novel form
Preachy for some; ideas are debatable

q.t: and see if it changes your view.

s: A detailed manual to the squat, deadlift, press, bench press and power clean, with a novice linear progression program.
w: HN recommends it as the book for learning barbell lifting form and starting a simple strength program. A reader credits it with fixing joint aches from years of other sports, and another with improving posture.
ab: For beginners who want to start lifting with a barbell
Detailed technique coaching for five core lifts
Rigid, opinionated approach; assumes access to a gym with a rack

q.t: Starting Strength is an excellent book for getting started with lifting.

t: Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code
s: A catalog of refactorings with step-by-step mechanics for improving code structure without changing behavior.
w: HN names it among the most important programming books, saying it teaches how to safely evolve code.
ab: For working developers maintaining real code
Catalog of named refactorings with mechanics
First edition uses Java; later edition uses JavaScript

q.t: In my view it is the single most important programming book in existence.

t: The Righteous Mind: Why Good People Are Divided by Politics and Religion
s: A social psychologist explains moral foundations theory and why people of different political and religious views reason from different intuitions.
w: HN recommends it to understand people on the other side of the political divide and to debate with less friction. Commenters like the focus on tribal instincts and implicit values behind arguments.
ab: For readers who want to understand political disagreement
Introduces six moral foundations and tribal psychology
Haidt's framework is debated by other researchers

q.t: this book is awesome. It'll show you how to find common ground and understand implicit values behind arguments.

t: Expert C Programming: Deep C Secrets
s: A humorous, detailed look at C's quirks and pitfalls, covering declarations, linking, memory and the language's history.
w: HN recommends it as the book to read after K&R, to go deeper into how C really works.
ab: For C programmers wanting to go beyond the basics
Quirks, pitfalls and war stories with humor
Dated in parts; pre-C99 era

q.t: Every C programmer should have this on their bookshelf!

s: The foundational scripture of Christianity, in Hebrew and Christian canons, in many translations.
w: Recommended as required reading for understanding Western literature and philosophy, and as a text some HN readers go through every year. Others advise reading the original religious texts before commentaries.
ab: For readers wanting the source of much Western literature and thought
Many translations exist, so pick one suited to you
Long and varied: law, poetry, history and letters

q.t: I read through the bible every year and each time it shapes my thinking.

s: Neal Stephenson's 2008 novel set on a world where monastic scholars live apart from society, mixing philosophy, math and adventure.
w: HN readers call it one of the best novels they've read, say it changed how they think, and some reread it. Commenters like its comforting cloistered society.
ab: For readers who like ideas-heavy sci-fi and philosophy
Starts slowly with invented vocabulary
Long; payoff builds after the first fifty pages

q.t: Seriously one of the best novels I've ever read.

s: Keith Johnstone's notes on improvisation, status and spontaneity in theatre.
w: HN recommends it for its sections on status and social interaction. Commenters say it is more than a theatre book, and call it eye-opening for anyone who struggles socially.
ab: For anyone interested in social dynamics
Exercises on status and spontaneity
Theatre-oriented in places

q.t: It may seem like a book on improvisational theater, but is more a collection of notes on interaction between people.

s: A practical textbook covering analog and digital circuit design, with real components, tips, and design examples.
w: HN regards it as the standard electronics book and one of the greatest pieces of non-fiction, though dense. Readers say electronics only started to make sense after it. One buyer warned of a poor-quality copy.
ab: For programmers and hobbyists moving into hardware design
Very dense; best with a project and some math
Check seller; one reader received a poor-quality copy

q.t: For me, electronics only started to make sense after this book:

t: The Better Angels of Our Nature: Why Violence Has Declined
s: A long argument, with data, that violence has declined over centuries, and an account of the forces Pinker thinks explain it.
w: HN cites it as the answer to doom about the state of the world, praised for its stats and facts over anecdotes. Commenters use it in debates on peace, trade and long-term trends.
ab: For readers who want a data-driven view of human progress
Hundreds of charts and statistics on violence
Methods and conclusions have drawn academic criticism

q.t: The Hacker News community should like it as it focuses on the stats and facts rather than anecdotal stories the media slings.

t: Coders at Work: Reflections on the Craft of Programming
s: Long interviews with 15 well-known programmers about how they learned, think, debug and design software.
w: HN recommends it for candid, detailed interviews with respected programmers about their craft, in the same vein as Founders at Work.
ab: For programmers curious how masters think and work
Detailed interviews with Knuth, Armstrong, Allen and others
Opinions vary; some interviews are dated

q.t: Each of the interviews are pretty detailed, down to nitty-gritty, often mundane details

t: How to Prove It: A Structured Approach
s: An introduction to mathematical proofs and logic that teaches how to read and write rigorous proofs, needing only high school math.
w: HN recommends it as the right first step before upper-level math, and often as the better starting point than denser texts. Readers say it teaches how to do mathematics, not just read it.
ab: For self-learners who want to get comfortable with proofs
Needs only high school math; exercises throughout
Book of Proof by Hammack is a free alternative

q.t: If you don't understand proofs, don't read any more maths books until you've read

s: David Foster Wallace's sprawling 1996 novel about addiction, entertainment and a tennis academy, famous for its length and footnotes.
w: Frequently named as a re-read favorite and a rite-of-passage challenge. HN readers mention it as an ambitious, difficult book to tackle, sometimes lumped with other famously hard novels.
ab: For patient readers who enjoy long, experimental novels
Over 1,000 pages with endless footnotes
Often called hard to grasp, but rewarding to fans

q.t: A few on my "re-read every few years" list

by: William Strunk Jr., E. B. White
s: A short American English writing guide on usage, composition and plain style, first written in 1918 and revised by E. B. White.
w: HN recommends it as the quick, practical book on clear and concise writing. Commenters suggest it to developers writing documentation or anyone who barely has time to read a style guide.
ab: For anyone who wants clearer, tighter prose
Very short, with rules and examples
Some rules are contested by modern linguists; 1918 origins

q.t: if you want to know how to write, and barely have time to make breakfast, The Elements of Style is the book for you.

t: Crossing the Chasm: Marketing and Selling High-Tech Products to Mainstream Customers
s: A marketing classic on how technology companies move from early adopters to the mainstream market, focusing on one beachhead segment.
w: HN names it as the standard text on technology adoption and focus when startups struggle to grow past early users. Readers say its patterns still show up in modern startup stories.
ab: For founders and product people selling tech to businesses
Introduces the adoption lifecycle and beachhead strategy
Examples are from the 1990s and enterprise-flavored

q.t: I highly recommend Crossing the Chasm by Geoffrey Moore.

t: Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software
s: A software design book on modeling complex business domains with ubiquitous language, bounded contexts and aggregates.
w: HN recommends it for organizing large code bases around the domain, though it is long and dry.
ab: For engineers building complex business software
Patterns like aggregates, repositories and bounded contexts
Long and dry; examples are in Java

q.t: is long and pretty dry, but it's immediately practical and opened my mind to how object-oriented design is supposed to work.

s: Leo Tolstoy's epic novel of Russian families during the Napoleonic wars.
w: HN readers say it shows how little human nature changes, and that you can empathise with every character. Fans reread it repeatedly and recommend the Pevear and Volokhonsky translation.
ab: For readers committed to a very long classic
Dense, with a huge cast of characters
Translation matters; Pevear and Volokhonsky is recommended

q.t: the more everything changes the same humans stay. 200 years old and yet you can empathise with every character

s: Paulo Coelho's allegorical novel about an Andalusian shepherd who travels to Egypt in search of treasure and his destiny.
