q.t: If you have yet to read it and have any interest in the psychology of happiness

s: A history of the telegraph and the nineteenth-century network of operators, cables and inventors around it.
w: HN recommends it for the parallels between telegraph networks and the internet, down to chat rooms and information overload. Commenters call Standage an engaging writer.
ab: For readers who like technology history
Light, readable popular history
Short on technical depth

q.t: The first internet was really the telegraphy network. It even had chat rooms.

s: Robert Anton Wilson's book on the eight-circuit model of consciousness and how people can reprogram their mental imprints.
w: Recommended in lists of books that changed how people think, for its idea of seeing your own mind as constructing your reality. Related reading for those interested in psychedelics.
ab: For readers curious about unconventional models of mind
Practical exercises for changing mental habits
Counterculture style, not mainstream science

q.t: "Hacking" reality, your mind, alternate viewpoints of reality

s: Mikhail Bulgakov's satirical novel in which the devil visits Soviet Moscow, intercut with a retelling of Pontius Pilate.
w: HN readers rank it among their best-loved novels; one read it in Russian and couldn't put it down. It also appears on lists of famously inventive, hard-to-grasp literature.
ab: For readers who enjoy surreal, satirical fiction
Interlaced storylines and Russian references
Translation quality varies

q.t: It was the first book I started reading I could not put down until the end.

t: Logicomix: An Epic Search for Truth
s: A graphic novel following Bertrand Russell's search for the foundations of mathematics, with Frege, Hilbert, Wittgenstein and Gödel.
w: Recommended as a fun, educational way into the history of logic and the foundations of math, including as a comic to read with kids.
ab: For anyone curious about logic and mathematics history
Graphic novel, quick and approachable
A narrative, not a math course

q.t: which is aslo very highly recommended - a comic about logic, Godel, and the foundations of mathematics

t: How to Talk So Kids Will Listen & Listen So Kids Will Talk
s: A parenting communication guide with practical techniques and cartoon examples for handling feelings, cooperation, discipline and conflict with children.
w: HN parents recommend it whenever kid behavior comes up. Commenters call it invaluable and life-changing, and say it improved how they talk with adults as well.
ab: For parents and teachers of young children
Concrete scripts and exercises
Pairs well with Unconditional Parenting

q.t: This book has been life-changing with regards to my relationship with my 3-year-old.

t: Elon Musk: Tesla, SpaceX, and the Quest for a Fantastic Future
s: A biography of Elon Musk by Ashlee Vance, drawing on interviews with Musk, family, and colleagues, covering Tesla, SpaceX, and his early life.
w: HN readers recommend it as a fascinating look at the man and his companies, and cite it when discussing SpaceX or Tesla history. It comes up often in Musk threads.
ab: For readers interested in Tesla, SpaceX, and Musk
Narrative biography with many first-hand interviews
Published in 2015; later events are not covered

q.t: Fascinating life of both the man and his companies if you are interested

s: Niccolò Machiavelli's 1532 treatise on gaining and holding political power.
w: Cited as a timeless guide to power, read alongside Art of War and The Book of Five Rings. One recommends the edition annotated by Napoleon.
ab: For readers interested in power and politics
Short and public domain
Cynical ideas worth reading in context

q.t: The Prince by Niccolò Machiavelli. Specially the edition annotated by Napoleon Bonaparte itself.

t: Behave: The Biology of Humans at Our Best and Worst
s: Robert Sapolsky's wide-ranging account of why humans behave as they do, tracing actions back through neurobiology, hormones, genes, evolution and culture.
w: A repeat entry on HN 'books that changed how I think' lists. Commenters pair it with Sapolsky's free Stanford lectures and use it as a reference on how biology shapes behaviour.
ab: For readers interested in neuroscience, behaviour and free will
Long and densely packed with research
Free lecture course companion by the author

s: Neal Stephenson's 2015 hard sci-fi novel about humanity's race to survive after the Moon breaks apart.
w: HN readers call it fantastic, grounded near-future science fiction with accurate engineering, and some reread it, calling it an inspiration for their thinking.
ab: For hard sci-fi and space engineering fans
Long, with detailed technical exposition
Third act splits opinion

q.t: Everything is near-future sci-fi and as grounded and accurate as possible.

s: A proof-based linear algebra textbook that develops the theory through vector spaces and linear operators while avoiding determinants until late.
w: HN's favorite rigorous linear algebra text. Commenters like that it avoids matrix and determinant computation and builds mathematical reasoning, though some call it less applied.
ab: For readers comfortable with proofs and abstraction
Determinant-free approach to eigenvalues
Less focused on computation and applications

q.t: This is my favorite introductory textbook on linear algebra which goes to great lengths to avoid matrix and determinant computations

t: The Principles of Product Development Flow: Second Generation Lean Product Development
s: A dense book applying queueing theory, batch size and work-in-progress limits to product development and engineering management.
w: HN recommends it for understanding why queues, batch sizes and WIP limits matter in software projects, even though it is dense. Commenters call it the best text on managing development flow.
ab: For engineering managers and process designers
Quantitative; explains queues and batch size economics
Hard to read; many dense principles

q.t: incredibly difficult book to read (i.e. lots of good but dense information) but it explains well the underlying principles

s: A hard science-fiction novel about a lone astronaut who wakes up on a ship with no memory and must save Earth.
w: Cited by HN readers as a fun hard sci-fi read, including for its take on intelligent life evolved under high pressure.
ab: For fans of The Martian and hard sci-fi
Fast-paced and puzzle-driven
Spoilers abound in discussion, so go in blind

s: A fourteen-book epic fantasy series begun by Robert Jordan and completed by Brandon Sanderson, following Rand, Mat and Perrin against the Dark One.
w: Commenters call it among the best fantasy series they've read, and a common reread. HN readers like the scale of its world and the way its main characters develop.
ab: For patient readers who want a huge, immersive series
Fourteen long books; a big time commitment
Completed after Jordan's death by Sanderson

q.t: I started the Wheel of Time series and am currently through book 3 and I am loving it.

t: The Rent Is Too Damn High
s: A short ebook arguing that restrictive zoning and limited construction are the main drivers of high urban housing costs.
w: HN uses it as the quick explainer for housing affordability: build more density and rents fall. Commenters call it a short read.
ab: For readers curious about zoning, YIMBY arguments and housing
Roughly a 30-minute read
US urban focus; written in 2012 so statistics are old

q.t: Everyone should read the author's e-book (it's a really short ~30 min. read).

s: A short book on practical programming covering style, debugging, testing, performance, and portability, by two Unix and Go veterans.
w: HN readers call it very good and an excellent read. It is often recommended as a starting point for becoming a better programmer.
ab: For programmers who want better habits at any level
Short chapters on style, testing, and debugging
Examples in C and Java; 1999 vintage

q.t: I think "The Practice of Programming" was and is very good.

s: A short book of thought experiments about simple imagined vehicles whose wiring produces complex, seemingly intelligent behavior.
w: Recommended as a short, witty book on how complex behavior arises from simple parts, and used in AI and robotics courses.
ab: For readers curious about emergent behavior and AI
Short with subtle humor
A thought-experiment book, not a textbook

q.t: It's a wonderful and short book with some subtle humor

t: The Dawn of Everything: A New History of Humanity
s: A challenge to the standard narrative of early human societies.
w: Recommended as a favorite and for archaeology detail.
ab: Reframes prehistory
Archaeology
Contested

q.t: It's one of my favorite books of my life now - I think more people need to read this.

s: A visually rich, conversational introduction to the Gang of Four design patterns with Java examples.
w: HN's friendly alternative to the dry Gang of Four book. Commenters suggest it for novices and say its content has aged better than its cover.
ab: For beginners learning object-oriented design
Java examples; patterns apply broadly
Quirky layout and some dated style

q.t: Might I suggest Head First Design Patterns [1] as a good introductory alternative that won't sap his will to live.

s: J. K. Rowling's seven-book fantasy series about a young wizard at Hogwarts school and his fight against Voldemort.
w: HN commenters name it as a comfort read and a childhood favourite they reread or listen to on long drives. One says it shaped them as a kid.
ab: For readers of all ages who want a familiar comfort series
Also popular as an audiobook for road trips
Seven books; read in order

q.t: Harry Potter - JK Rowling (re-read it all when the last book came out)

s: Vernor Vinge's 1992 space opera, first of the Zones of Thought series, in which the galaxy's physics varies by region and a godlike intelligence is unleashed.
w: A staple of HN sci-fi lists from a computer-scientist author. Readers like the big ideas and say it is fun, not dry.
ab: For fans of idea-driven space opera
First in the Zones of Thought series; read in order
Its 'Deepness in the Sky' prequel is also loved

q.t: read it in order. Which would mean starting with A Fire Upon the Deep, which is excellent.

t: The Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing and Thinking
s: A consulting classic on structuring business writing and arguments by leading with the main point and grouping supporting ideas beneath it.
w: HN recommends it for writing clear proposals and persuasive documents, and for learning concise, structured communication in senior roles. A summary notes it favors short, unqualified language.
ab: For engineers, consultants and managers who write reports
Teaches answer-first structure and logical grouping
Business-writing focus; dry and formula-driven

q.t: Recommended reading, especially for anyone whom consults or writes proposals.

s: Informal talks by Zen teacher Shunryu Suzuki on zazen meditation and practice, with an emphasis on a beginner's open mind.
w: HN meditation beginners are pointed to it as a good intro to practicing, described as a transcript of a Zen master's talks that is not religious in tone.
ab: For anyone starting meditation or curious about Zen
Short talks in plain language
Zen in tone; not a how-to manual

q.t: Check out Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind for a good book on practicing meditation.

s: Franklin's unfinished memoir of his rise from printer's apprentice to statesman, including his methods of self-improvement and the Junto club.
w: HN readers recommend it as practical, still-relevant advice on self-improvement and entrepreneurship. The Junto club and Franklin's habit-building get singled out.
ab: Free in the public domain, so many read it online
Short, practical self-improvement advice told as a life story
18th-century prose, but commenters say it aged well

q.t: Here’s another vote for Ben Franklin’s autobiography. It’s full of remarkably good advice and aged very well.

t: The Shallows: What the Internet Is Doing to Our Brains
s: An argument that constant internet use is rewiring our brains for skimming and distraction at the expense of deep reading and concentration.
w: HN recommends it in threads about attention spans, distraction and the effect of the internet on thinking. Readers call it a must-read for IT people and say its points still apply today.
ab: For readers worried about their attention and online habits
Mixes history of media with brain-plasticity research
Written in 2010; some science has moved on

q.t: I would recommend reading The Shallows: What the Internet Is Doing to Our Brains.

t: Inspired: How to Create Products Customers Love
s: A guide to product management from a former eBay and Netscape product executive, covering discovery, product teams, and how to build products customers want.
w: When anyone on HN asks for a book on product management, this is the usual answer, praised as concise and useful for how product, design, and engineering fit together.
ab: For new and aspiring product managers and founders
Practical lessons on product discovery and team roles
The 2008 edition is dated; a newer edition covers tech product teams

q.t: It's short, well written and covers several visions (product, engineering, etc).

s: The narrative account of Shackleton's 1914 Antarctic expedition, in which the ship was crushed by ice and the crew survived for months.
w: Called a must-read and one of the greatest adventure books by commenters, and brought up whenever Shackleton or lost expeditions come up.
ab: For readers who like survival and exploration stories
Gripping narrative based on crew diaries and interviews
Grim at times, including the war aftermath

q.t: It was one of the greatest adventure books I've ever read

s: Robert Kiyosaki's pop personal-finance book contrasting two father figures' attitudes to money, with a focus on assets versus liabilities.
w: Some HN commenters credit it as their first introduction to thinking about investments and assets. Others dismiss it as shallow and note the author's own business results are vague.
ab: Beginner-friendly intro to the assets vs. liabilities idea
Light on specifics; critics call it an easy sell
Several fans say they no longer endorse all of its advice

q.t: I had never really thought about investments before, or the difference between assets and liabilities.

s: First book of the Kingkiller Chronicle, in which the innkeeper Kvothe recounts his own legendary life as a gifted arcanist and musician.
w: Frequent pick among HN's fantasy readers for its prose and story that doesn't over-explain. One commenter warns the trilogy's final book has been delayed for a decade.
ab: For readers who want lyrical, character-driven epic fantasy
First of an unfinished trilogy; the third book was long delayed
Reads as a complete, satisfying first volume

q.t: Wonderful fantasy that treats the reader as an adult and doesn't over explain.

t: Dreaming in Code: Two Dozen Programmers, Three Years, 4,732 Bugs, and One Quest for Transcendent Software
s: A journalist follows Mitch Kapor's Chandler project, a personal information manager that struggled for years, and tells the story of why software is so hard to build.
w: HN brings it up as the cautionary story of a well-funded software project that failed, a good read for anyone who has watched a software project drift.
ab: For programmers and managers who have seen projects go wrong
Narrative of the Chandler project and its lessons
About a 2000s project; no code or technique

q.t: Great read, and shows how difficult it was and is to compete with office.

t: The Perfectionists: How Precision Engineers Created the Modern World
s: A history of precision engineering, from Wilkinson's cannon-boring and steam engines to modern chip lithography and gravitational-wave detectors.
w: Readers call it an enjoyable history of how precision came to be, from steam-cylinder boring onward, and recommend it to anyone who liked a related HN post.
ab: For readers who like engineering history and metrology
Narrative style rather than technical detail
Covers centuries, so each era gets limited depth

q.t: Simon Winchester wrote an enjoyable book about the history of precision

s: A test-driven, language-agnostic guide to building a ray tracer from scratch, with test cases that let you write it in any language.
w: HN recommends it as a fun way to learn computer graphics and a new programming language at once. The test-first structure and language independence come up repeatedly.
ab: For programmers who want a hands-on graphics project
Language-agnostic; you supply your own implementation
Each chapter is driven by tests, so you can check progress

q.t: I used Jamis Buck's book The Ray Tracer Challenge[1] as a fun kind of way to learn the language

s: Argues that metaphor shapes how we think and speak, not just poetic language.
w: Cited as an interesting book on the idea that our conceptual system is largely metaphorical; one commenter thinks they take it too far.
ab: For readers interested in language and cognition
Influential cognitive linguistics text
Some find its claims overextended

q.t: Super interesting book, for anybody interested in those kinds of things!

t: Against the Gods: The Remarkable Story of Risk
s: A history of how humans came to understand probability, statistics and risk, from antiquity to modern finance.
w: Recommended as a fascinating historical perspective on probability and statistics over millennia. Commenters like the chapters on figures like the Bernoullis and its account of how risk management developed.
ab: For readers curious about the history of probability and finance
Narrative history, not a math text
Published 1996; post-2008 developments are absent

q.t: for a fascinating, historical perspective on people's growing understanding of probability and statistics over the last few millennia.

s: Pixar co-founder Ed Catmull's account of how the studio built a culture and management process that sustains creative work.
w: HN readers rate it among the best books on management and creative culture, and give it as a gift. Commenters also like the Pixar history woven through.
ab: For managers and founders who run creative teams
Mixes Pixar history with management lessons
Some parts are more story than playbook

q.t: It's one of the best books I've read on business/management and personal development.

t: Accelerate: The Science of Lean Software and DevOps
by: Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble et al.
s: A research-based study of which practices make software delivery teams perform well, including the four key metrics.
w: HN cites it for data over opinion on delivery performance. Commenters point to its deployment metrics and warn that 100% utilization hurts, though one says it is less of a revelation now.
ab: For engineering managers and DevOps teams
Survey-based evidence and metrics
Findings are widely adopted now

q.t: I prefer studies over anecdotes and found this

t: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up: The Japanese Art of Decluttering and Organizing
s: Marie Kondo's method for decluttering a home by keeping only items that spark joy and organizing the rest.
w: Appears on HN lists of books that changed people's thinking. Commenters say it cut housework and helped their mental health, though one warns it is a bit silly.
ab: For people overwhelmed by clutter
Step-by-step method for decluttering and folding
Some find the tone quirky or silly

q.t: we found a marked sustained decrease in housework attributed to a reduction in time required for tidying, washing and sorting

s: A trilogy (Quicksilver, The Confusion, The System of the World) of historical fiction spanning 17th-18th century Europe, science, money and intrigue.
w: Fans of Cryptonomicon treat it as a huge, rewarding epic that takes a year to finish; some prefer the audiobook. One commenter would skip it, so expect a divisive slog.
ab: Three long volumes, 3000+ pages in total
Prequel-ish to Cryptonomicon's world, heavy on history and science
Some readers bounced off the print version

q.t: It was 3000+ pages all told, and I LOVED it.

s: Napoleon Hill's 1937 self-help classic distilling thirteen principles of success from interviews with wealthy men of his era.
w: HN readers list it with other classic wealth-and-mindset books and say it changed their thinking or is a good gift. One adds the caveat that its insights are simplistic.
ab: For readers interested in mindset-style self-help classics
Free online as it is in the public domain
Dated and simplistic, per commenters

q.t: Amazing, though maybe simplistic, insights.

t: Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr.
s: A detailed biography of John D. Rockefeller, tracing his rise from poverty to founding Standard Oil and becoming a philanthropist.
w: HN readers list it among the best biographies of self-made business figures, and some use it to challenge the usual monopoly story about Standard Oil.
ab: For readers of business history and biography
Thorough and long; over 700 pages
Offers a sympathetic view of Rockefeller to some readers

q.t: Titan, a Rockefeller Sr. biography by Ron Chernow, is great book.

s: Robert Pirsig's follow-up to Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, developing his Metaphysics of Quality through a river voyage.
w: HN readers name it a lesser-known sequel worth reading for those who loved Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, and one said it gave the most food for thought in a year.
ab: For readers who enjoyed Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
Philosophy wrapped in a narrative
Less accessible than the first book

q.t: Lila is not as well known, but it's fun to read if you really enjoyed ZMM.

s: A surreal novel interleaving a teenage runaway's story with that of an old man who can talk to cats.
w: HN readers recommend it as a fine, strange place to start with Murakami, appreciating its dreamlike themes on creativity.
ab: Magical-realist novel with parallel storylines
Considered a good first Murakami book
Surreal, ambiguous plot

q.t: Kafka on the Shore is a great starting book.

s: Michael Lewis's memoir of his years as a bond salesman at Salomon Brothers in the 1980s, covering Wall Street culture and the rise of mortgage bonds.
w: A staple HN recommendation for understanding Wall Street culture and why bankers are paid so much. Commenters call it a good look at the system and a prequel to the 2008 crisis.
ab: For readers curious about Wall Street culture
Funny, readable memoir from the 1980s
Dated details; the bond market has changed

q.t: In order to understand why bankers get such massive bonuses it would probably be good to read this first

t: The Elements of Statistical Learning: Data Mining, Inference, and Prediction
by: Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani et al.
s: A graduate-level textbook covering supervised and unsupervised learning, with emphasis on statistical foundations such as regression, trees, boosting and support vector machines.
w: HN commenters list it among the standard machine learning textbooks to learn from, though they note it assumes prior knowledge. Beginners are usually pointed to its easier companion, An Introduction to Statistical Learning.
ab: For readers with a math and statistics background learning ML
Rigorous coverage of classical statistical learning methods
Free PDF exists; predates deep learning

q.t: These are both good options:

t: The Obstacle Is the Way: The Timeless Art of Turning Trials into Triumph
s: A modern, example-filled introduction to Stoic ideas about turning adversity into advantage.
w: Offered as an easy entry into Stoicism, though one commenter warned the author is a PR guy and others prefer Seneca and Marcus Aurelius first.
ab: For readers new to Stoicism
Pop-philosophy style with anecdotes
Original sources like Meditations go deeper

q.t: is also a good one on the Stoic philosophy, could serve as in introduction to Meditations

s: A guide to the Zettelkasten note-taking method for writing, learning and thinking.
w: Recommended as the book to read for understanding Zettelkasten, with notes in your own words and interlinks.
ab: For students, writers and researchers who take notes.
Explains Luhmann's slip-box method.
Method over tools.

q.t: There's a whole book on that ('How to Take Smart Notes'), which I highly recommend

s: First book of Brandon Sanderson's Mistborn trilogy, a heist-flavoured epic fantasy set in a world of ash where some people can burn metals for powers.
w: HN readers call it one of the best fantasy series, praising its unique magic system, tight plotting and a surprising ending. It's a common gift for people new to fantasy.
ab: Good entry point for newcomers to fantasy
Detailed, logical magic system
First of a trilogy; several sequels exist

q.t: It has a unique magic system and is very well written.

by: Jim Blandy, Jason Orendorff, et al.
s: O'Reilly's in-depth guide to the Rust programming language, covering ownership, traits, concurrency and async with explanations of the reasoning behind each feature.
w: HN Rust learners name it the book that made concepts click, especially for C/C++ veterans and experienced programmers. The async chapter gets specific praise.
ab: For experienced programmers learning Rust after the Rust Book
Comprehensive but takes dedicated effort
Good coverage of async, with clear explanations

q.t: To me, this was the book that made everything click

s: A Hugo Award winning novel in which the stars vanish behind a mysterious barrier around Earth.
w: Called a highly entertaining novel about the stars going out, recommended in threads on the Fermi paradox and sci-fi reading lists.
ab: For fans of big-idea sci-fi
Hugo winner
First of a trilogy

q.t: a highly entertaining science-fiction novel about the stars going out

t: Mazes for Programmers: Code Your Own Twisty Little Passages
s: A hands-on book that teaches maze-generation and solving algorithms through Ruby code.
w: Repeatedly suggested in threads asking for books that teach programming by building things, as an incremental project book.
ab: For intermediate programmers who like to learn by building
Algorithms, graphs and code
Examples in Ruby; not for absolute beginners

q.t: Some good ones I don't see yet, which I like because they very much follow the organic path you might follow doing things incrementally

s: A sociologist's analysis of why complex, tightly coupled systems produce accidents.
w: Recommended for understanding failure in complex systems, from outages to maritime and space accidents.
ab: For engineers and operators of complex systems
Case studies
Tight-coupling concept

q.t: It's basically the long-form complete version of the paper you mentioned and packed with interesting examples.

t: How to Measure Anything: Finding the Value of Intangibles in Business
s: A book on quantifying hard-to-measure things such as risk and quality, with methods for calibrated estimates and decision analysis.
w: HN readers recommend it for approaching intangible measurement with estimates and probability. Commenters mention it for showing how to answer questions that seem unmeasurable.
ab: For managers and engineers making decisions under uncertainty
Practical methods like calibrated estimation
Consulting-flavored; light on rigorous statistics

q.t: I'm a fan of the work of Douglas Hubbard, in his book How to Measure Anything

s: A widely used university textbook covering processes, memory management, file systems, I/O, and security in modern operating systems.
w: The default OS textbook that HN has pointed people to since 2009. Commenters say many engineers cut their teeth on it, and it is the standard pairing with Tanenbaum's Minix material.
ab: For self-taught programmers who want to understand how operating systems work
Broad coverage of OS concepts with a textbook structure
Large and academic; pair it with hands-on kernel projects

q.t: One book many engineers have cut their teeth on for OS would be Andrew Tanenbaum's Modern Operating Systems, 3rd ed.

t: The Elephant in the Brain: Hidden Motives in Everyday Life
s: An examination of the unconscious, self-serving motives behind everyday behavior in areas like politics, medicine, education and art.
w: HN readers use it as the go-to book for why people's stated reasons differ from their real ones. Commenters call it a fun, convincing explanation of puzzling human behavior and policy.
ab: For readers curious about self-deception and social signaling
Applies an evolutionary-psychology lens to institutions like school and medicine
Some find the thesis cynical or overextended

q.t: gives a pretty convincing explanation for some seeming puzzles across several areas of human behavior and policy

s: James Clavell's 1975 novel about an English ship's pilot who is shipwrecked in feudal Japan and becomes entangled in a struggle for power.
w: HN readers call it a captivating epic, with historical fiction about 16th-century Japan that makes a thousand pages fly by. Several name it a favourite.
ab: For readers who like long, immersive historical fiction
Roughly 1,100 pages; commenters say it reads fast
Part of Clavell's Asian Saga, but works standalone

q.t: Really great historical fiction about 16th century Japan. Quickest 1100 pages I've ever read.

s: Apple's MacBook laptop line, over the years including the polycarbonate and 12-inch models alongside the Air and Pro.
w: HN commenters over the years name MacBooks as their go-to laptop for build quality and longevity. One dissenting developer warns against them for non-Python/Ruby toolchains.
ab: Praised for lasting longer than Windows laptops
Comments span many generations from 2008 to Apple Silicon
Early models criticised for development outside web stacks

q.t: I recently purchased a 2016 Macbook. Reasoning is, they last longer.

s: A data-driven study of wealth and income inequality in the West over the last few centuries.
w: Cited in inequality and wage-stagnation debates and included on reading lists alongside Debt: The First 5000 Years.
ab: For readers interested in inequality
Long and statistics-heavy
Conclusions are debated

t: The Art of Doing Science and Engineering: Learning to Learn
s: Richard Hamming's lectures on how to do creative, important work in science and engineering, with discussion of dimensions, computing and style.
w: Linked after the You and Your Research talk and called a fun walk through ideas like the curse of dimensionality plus life lessons. It appears on Bret Victor's favourite books thread.
ab: For engineers and scientists thinking about careers
Technical and general lessons from a Bell Labs veteran
Some content is dated by technology

q.t: A fun walk through the curse of dimensionality and how your intuition can break down in higher dimensional spaces, and other life lessons

s: George Orwell's 1945 allegorical novella about farm animals who overthrow their farmer and are betrayed by their leaders.
w: HN readers hand out copies and say it shows how revolutions and power work; it's short enough to read early and stays applicable throughout life.
ab: For readers of all ages; very short
Political allegory about the Russian Revolution
Often paired with 1984

q.t: As I get older, I love seeing younger people flip out when they read it and see how applicable it is in modern life.

t: Trading and Exchanges: Market Microstructure for Practitioners
s: A textbook on how securities markets work, covering traders, dealers, order types and the trade lifecycle.
w: Programmers asking about quant finance or algorithmic trading get pointed here. Commenters say it explains the roles in a market and traces a trade from order to settlement, though it is heavy going.
ab: For engineers building or studying trading systems
Walks through placing, executing and settling trades
Textbook-dense and written pre-HFT era

q.t: To trade effectively you need to understand how the markets work

s: Douglas Hofstadter's 2007 book arguing that the self is a pattern arising from recursive loops in the brain.
w: Readers call it a fascinating exercise in thinking about thinking that changed their view of the self. One skeptic soured on Hofstadter after reading it.
ab: For readers curious about consciousness and self
Less playful than Godel, Escher, Bach
Some find the argument unconvincing

q.t: fascinating exercise in 'thinking about thinking' that radically changed my perspective on the concept of 'self'.

s: An advanced book on implementing Lisp and Scheme, covering interpreters, compilers, bytecode, macros, reflection and object systems.
w: HN recommends it for people who want to implement Lisp or Scheme, as a deeper follow-up to the usual starter lists. It is called out for covering interpretation, compilation to C and bytecode.
ab: For programmers who want to build Lisp interpreters and compilers
Covers fast interpretation, macros, reflection and objects
Advanced and dense; assumes Scheme familiarity

q.t: If you're interested in getting into the details of implementing a Lisp/Scheme interpreter and compiler, I highly recommend Lisp in Small Pieces

s: Peter Norvig's case studies in classic AI programs in Common Lisp.
w: HN recommends it as a classic on symbolic AI and Lisp. One commenter says it is outdated but a classic read.
ab: For Lisp and AI history fans
Working programs for classic AI
Pre-deep learning

q.t: Is it outdated? Absolutely, but it is a classic read.

s: A classic survey of mathematical ideas and methods, from numbers and geometry to calculus, written for an educated general reader.
w: A perennial HN pick for how mathematicians think. Commenters call it a terrific read that generations of mathematicians recommend, though one warns it will challenge you.
ab: For motivated readers who want to see real mathematics
Elementary topics treated with depth
Demanding, and the style is old-fashioned

q.t: quite good and respected, but it will challenge you

s: The 17th-century Spanish classic about a deluded gentleman who sets out as a knight-errant with his squire Sancho Panza, often called the first modern novel.
w: Named as a rewarding classic worth reading, with several recommending the Edith Grossman translation for its notes. Readers say it is worth finishing even if the ending annoys.
ab: Grossman translation praised for readability and footnotes
Long and episodic; reward comes from sticking with it
A foundational classic of world literature

q.t: If you only read one book, I suggest Don Quixote, the Grossman translation particularly

t: Language Implementation Patterns: Create Your Own Domain-Specific and General Programming Languages
s: A practical guide to building parsers, interpreters, and translators for DSLs and general languages using recurring implementation patterns, in Java.
w: HN recommends it as a practice-focused alternative to the Dragon Book. Commenters like how it ties grammar forms to code patterns, built in small steps, though it leans on ANTLR and Java.
ab: For learning to build parsers and DSLs
Examples in Java, centered on ANTLR 3
Some find pacing slow

q.t: because it illustrates how certain grammar-forms become recognizable code-patterns and control-flow.

t: No More Mr. Nice Guy: A Proven Plan for Getting What You Want in Love, Sex, and Life
s: A self-help book aimed at men who habitually seek approval, with exercises on assertiveness and relationships.
w: Commenters say it helped them become more assertive and happier socially, and recommend it to people who see themselves as too nice. One advises ignoring the parts about women.
ab: For men trying to be more assertive and stop people-pleasing
Includes exercises and a related community
Aimed mainly at heterosexual men; some find that limiting

q.t: one book that really helped me be assertive, certain, spontaneous, and happy in the social arena

s: Daniel Keyes's novel, told as progress reports, about a man with an intellectual disability whose intelligence is temporarily raised by an experimental surgery.
w: Commenters call it deeply moving and still affecting after rereads. HN readers praise its form (progress-report narration) and say it made them reconsider how they treat others.
ab: For readers who like emotional, idea-driven science fiction
Told through diary-style progress reports that shift with the narrator's mind
Some prefer the original short story to the novel

q.t: I read Flowers for Algernon for the first time as an adult and it really touched my soul.

s: Arthur C. Clarke's 1973 novel about humans exploring a huge, silent alien spacecraft passing through the solar system.
w: Described by HN readers as an inspiring hard-SF classic and a gift worth giving. Commenters admit it is slow in places.
ab: For readers who like idea-driven, exploration-style sci-fi
Pacing is slow; light on characters
Followed by sequels, though fans mostly rate the original

q.t: It can be fairly slow at times but it's such an inspiring read.

t: Healing Back Pain: The Mind-Body Connection
s: Dr. Sarno's argument that most chronic back, neck, and joint pain comes from unconscious emotional tension rather than structural damage.
w: Many HN commenters say reading it ended long-running back, knee, or wrist pain, and they push it on anyone in chronic pain, while others admit the scientific case is not strong.
ab: For people with chronic pain that doctors can't explain
Self-help approach: reading and reframing, no equipment or treatment
Controversial; scientific evidence is limited, so use alongside medical advice

q.t: Literally within a week of reading that book my knee pain was gone

s: Dr. Sarno's argument that much chronic back pain and RSI is psychosomatic and can be treated by understanding emotions.
w: HN readers with RSI and back pain credit it with curing them. Commenters say it may change your life, and if not it can't harm.
ab: For chronic pain sufferers
Mind-body theory of pain
Controversial; not mainstream medicine

q.t: If you're suffering from back pain, or carpal tunnel syndrome, or such ailments, read this book, it might change your life!

s: Stephen King's seven-book fantasy and western series about Roland Deschain's quest toward a mysterious tower, linking many of King's other works.
w: Commenters list it as a favourite series and finish it as a long project. Several name it among King's best.
ab: For King fans who like fantasy/western crossovers
Seven main books plus an extra volume; uneven in places
Ties into many of King's other novels

q.t: Dark Tower by Stephen King - do I need to say more?

t: Sophie's World: A Novel About the History of Philosophy
s: A novel in which a teenager receives letters about the history of philosophy from the pre-Socratics to the modern day.
w: Recommended as an easy first pass through the history of philosophy, including for kids and as a weekend read.
ab: For beginners wanting a story-based tour of philosophy
Covers thinkers chronologically
Simplifies; not a substitute for primary texts

q.t: The book "Sophie's World" does a great intro here and it a really great weekend read.

t: The Annotated Turing: A Guided Tour Through Alan Turing's Historic Paper on Computability and the Turing Machine
s: Charles Petzold's walk through Alan Turing's 1936 computability paper, with commentary and background for non-specialists.
w: HN recommends it as the accessible way to read Turing's paper. Commenters say it works without a deep pure math background and covers computability well.
ab: For programmers curious about computability
Walks through Turing's original paper line by line
Some math effort still required

q.t: the excellent and surprisingly accessible The Annotated Turing[0], which I can highly recommend

s: A hard science fiction novel about software-based humans and their descendants exploring the universe after Earth faces catastrophe.
w: HN readers say it reshaped how they think about consciousness and identity. Fair warning: Egan writes very hard sci-fi, and his characters can be a little flat.
ab: For fans of hard, idea-driven sci-fi
Heavy on physics and math concepts
Characters are a weaker point

q.t: No other book has caused such a seismic shift in how I think about consciousness, personhood, continuity of self

t: The Humane Interface: New Directions for Designing Interactive Systems
s: Jef Raskin's argument for user interfaces built around human cognition, covering modeless design, zooming interfaces, and quasimodes, from the creator of the Macintosh project.
w: A perennial pick on HN for UX thinking. Commenters call it a classic that makes you reconsider how we interact with computers, and one bought two Canon Cats after reading it.
ab: For UI and UX designers and thoughtful programmers
Principles of interface design rooted in cognitive psychology
Some ideas and examples are decades old

q.t: For anyone who hasn't read it, Jef Raskin's The Humane Interface is a great book.

t: Revolution in the Valley: The Insanely Great Story of How the Mac Was Made
s: Andy Hertzfeld's collection of first-hand anecdotes from the original Macintosh team, compiled from his folklore.org site.
w: HN regulars treat it as the insider account of the original Mac, told by an engineer who was there. Readers say the anecdotes are funny enough to derail a workday.
ab: For anyone interested in Apple and early personal computing
Short, self-contained stories rather than a single narrative
Written from one engineer's memory, so a partial viewpoint

q.t: my at-home productivity is all time low. I crack up every time remembering

s: Kurt Vonnegut's 1959 satirical science fiction novel about the richest man on Earth, a journey across the solar system and the search for meaning.
w: HN readers name it a life-changing favourite, call it emotionally resonant and say it increased their empathy. A darkly funny take on meaninglessness.
ab: For readers who like satirical, philosophical sci-fi
Short and quick; a good entry to Vonnegut
Comic tone with a bleak view of free will

q.t: this book changed the way I relate to others and made me more empathetic.

t: The Art of Learning: A Journey in the Pursuit of Excellence
s: A memoir by a chess prodigy turned martial arts champion about how he learned, performed under pressure, and built mastery.
w: HN readers pass it along to people getting into competitive chess or martial arts, and a few say it shaped how they approach learning and performance generally.
ab: For anyone chasing mastery in a skill
Part memoir, part learning method
Chess and martial arts heavy

q.t: One of the books that has had the biggest influence in my life

s: A Culture novel in which a bored master game-player is sent to an alien empire whose entire society is built around a single game.
w: HN regulars suggest it as the best way into Banks's Culture series: relatively self-contained and lighter than the others. One reader found it only enjoyable.
ab: Good first book of the Culture series
Mostly standalone; no prior reading needed
Less heavy than later Culture novels

q.t: Player of Games is a good introduction to the series

t: Why We Get Fat: And What to Do About It
s: A science journalist's case that carbohydrates and insulin regulation, not calories or lack of exercise, drive fat accumulation and obesity.
w: HN brings it up in diet and keto threads as the book that argues sugar, not fat, is the problem. Fans call it a great review of past research; the hormone theory it argues is still disputed.
ab: For readers curious about low-carb and insulin theories
Argues its case through historical studies
Taubes' conclusions are contested by many nutrition scientists

q.t: The third chapter is all about why exercise isn't a good way to lose weight. It is generally a fantastic book.

s: A wireless split-style ergonomic keyboard with a domed layout, cushioned palm rest, and detached numeric keypad, sold without a mouse.
w: HN commenters with RSI or wrist pain call it a cheap, comfortable ergonomic entry point with a standard layout and a long battery life.
ab: For typists with wrist strain who want an affordable ergonomic board
Standard layout, detached numpad, wireless USB dongle
Membrane keys; avoid the grey Bluetooth variant

q.t: Eliminated my wrist pain and the little USB dongle means the battery lasts for ever.

s: Kurt Vonnegut's 1963 satirical novel about the creator of the atomic bomb, a substance called ice-nine and a made-up religion, Bokononism.
w: HN readers often name it a life-changing favourite. It is short, darkly funny, and one commenter says it describes Silicon Valley's detached geniuses accurately. One calls it good but overrated among Vonnegut's books.
ab: Short; can be read in a sitting
Dark satire on science, religion and the bomb
Some prefer Slaughterhouse-Five or Sirens of Titan

q.t: It's very short and can be read in a single sitting if one is determined.

t: The Book: On the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are
s: A short book by Alan Watts on selfhood and the illusion of the separate ego.
w: Recommended by many as a life-changing book that reframes the sense of self.
ab: For readers curious about Eastern philosophy.
Short and witty.
Not academic.

q.t: that book taught me how to deal with them better

t: Blink: The Power of Thinking Without Thinking
s: A popular book on rapid, intuitive decision-making and the thin-slicing of snap judgments.
w: Mentioned on HN as the better-known book on intuition, well written but light on references.
ab: For general readers
Easy and engaging
Some findings haven't held up; light on citations

q.t: It is very well written, but (IMHO) not as heavy as it should be on references.

s: A semi-autobiographical novel about an escaped Australian convict who builds a new life in the slums and underworld of Mumbai.
w: One of the most gushed-over novels in HN reading threads: people call it gripping, immersive and a book to press on friends and family.
ab: Long, sweeping adventure set in 1980s Mumbai
Great for readers who want a story that swallows them
Billed as 'true' but largely fictionalized

q.t: Just finished Shantaram (best book I've ever read)

t: Getting Real: The Smarter, Faster, Easier Way to Build a Successful Web Application
s: 37signals' short guide to building web software with small teams, tiny feature sets and quick iteration instead of heavy planning.
w: A long-time HN founders' staple: readers say it pulled them out of the corporate grind, and it comes first when people recommend Basecamp's books. Its advice suits small teams and goes against conventional wisdom.
ab: For small teams and solo founders building web products
Opinionated and short; many essays
Pre-2010 examples; the Basecamp Shape Up book is newer

q.t: Getting Real - got me out of the corporate grind

s: First book of Pierce Brown's sci-fi series about Darrow, a Mars miner who infiltrates the ruling caste of a colour-coded future society.
w: HN readers list it as fast, enjoyable sci-fi and recommend it to fans of fantasy and YA-style adventure. One calls it less polished than Sanderson but worth following.
ab: For readers who like fast-paced dystopian sci-fi
First of a multi-book series
Younger-adult flavour; one reader finds it less developed than Sanderson

q.t: Recently finished the Red Rising trilogy and would recommend to anybody who likes fantasy.

t: Poor Charlie's Almanack: The Wit and Wisdom of Charles T. Munger
s: A large illustrated collection of Charlie Munger's speeches and essays on investing, decision making, and mental models.
w: Recommended as the way into Munger's thinking, including his talk on elementary worldly wisdom. Commenters cite him on checklists and curiosity, and one calls it a great read.
ab: For readers who want Munger's mental models firsthand
Speeches, essays and commentary in a big coffee-table book
Bulky and repetitive in places

q.t: a big coffee table book of his speeches and essays, good for leaving on the kitchen table to read over a meal

t: Our Mathematical Universe: My Quest for the Ultimate Nature of Reality
s: A physicist's popular account of cosmology and his hypothesis that physical reality is a mathematical structure.
w: Recommended by readers who like mind-blowing physics, with one saying it goes from simple concepts to blowing your mind. Another jokes about building a religion on its ideas.
ab: For readers who like speculative physics and cosmology
Goes from simple ideas to multiverses
Its main thesis is speculative

q.t: a fantastic job of going from really simple concepts/experiments to blowing your mind

t: Seeking Wisdom: From Darwin to Munger
s: A collection of ideas from biology, psychology and investing on human biases and good thinking, inspired by Charlie Munger.
w: HN's pick for a book on human biases and mental models, often preferred over Poor Charlie's Almanack for being more structured. Commenters call it a deep read focused on cognitive biases.
ab: For readers interested in mental models and Munger
Deep, dense on cognitive biases
Was out of print at times; check availability

q.t: For those interested in a good book about human biases and thinking, check out Seeking Wisdom From Darwin to Munger.

s: A history of genetics from Mendel to CRISPR, written by an oncologist.
w: Recommended for CRISPR background and ethical discussions. One reader credits it for the first account of Rosalind Franklin they had heard.
ab: For general readers curious about genetics
Covers ethics and CRISPR
Narrative and personal, not a textbook

q.t: the entire book is also highly recommended

s: Camus's 1942 short novel about Meursault, an indifferent French Algerian who commits a senseless killing, and the absurdist worldview behind it.
w: A staple of HN 'books that changed my life' lists. Commenters like that it is short, and that it works as accessible philosophy about absurdity and meaning.
ab: Short read that suits first-time philosophical fiction readers
Pairs well with Camus's Myth of Sisyphus and The Plague
Bleak, detached tone; not a feel-good book

q.t: I've found all three very enjoyable and unexpectedly applicable to real life for being philosophical texts.

t: The Now Habit: A Strategic Program for Overcoming Procrastination and Enjoying Guilt-Free Play
s: A self-help book that treats procrastination as a coping mechanism and teaches scheduling and mindset techniques, including guilt-free leisure.
w: HN's go-to answer for chronic procrastination threads. Commenters say it is a quick read whose advice, especially on allowing real rest, is effective and sustainable.
ab: For chronic procrastinators and the self-employed
Quick read with practical scheduling methods
Self-help style; not a replacement for treating depression

q.t: It's a quick read, and at least in my case the advice is effective and sustainable.

s: A ten-volume epic fantasy series by Steven Erikson, starting with Gardens of the Moon, known for its scale, ancient history and refusal to explain itself.
w: HN fans call it mind-blowing and unusually thoughtful about politics and philosophy, and a book you must commit to. One reader found it impenetrable and gave up.
ab: For readers who want huge, demanding epic fantasy
Ten long books; the opening is famously hard to follow
Expect little hand-holding or exposition

q.t: Malazan just blew my mind. One of the best things I've ever read.

t: Mathematics: From the Birth of Numbers
s: A single-volume encyclopedic history and exposition of mathematics from counting and arithmetic through algebra, geometry, and calculus, written by a Swedish surgeon.
w: HN readers who feel traditional math teaching failed them recommend it as a readable path through the whole subject, with history that explains why things are the way they are.
ab: For self-learners wanting a broad, readable tour of math
Large book, over 1,000 pages, covering history and technique
Not a quick read; a reference to dip into

q.t: It's better than anything I've read from any mathematician

s: A 1984 introduction to Unix tools, shell programming and the filesystem and signal APIs, by two Bell Labs authors.
w: Often paired with K&R as the book that taught a generation to think in Unix. Commenters are surprised how well its lucid writing has aged and like its project-driven chapters.
ab: For anyone who wants the Unix philosophy at its source
Shell, pipes, and C system programming in small projects
Examples predate modern Unix and window systems

q.t: I read it over 20 years later and was astonished at how well it had aged.

s: A practical, plain-language guide to vipassana meditation covering technique, distractions, physical pain and what to expect while practicing.
w: HN's default recommendation for learning meditation. Commenters say it is direct, simple to follow and covers practical problems like distraction and pain; it is often paired with The Mind Illuminated.
ab: For beginners to meditation
Free online edition exists
Buddhist framing, not a secular science book

q.t: It's direct, to the point, and addresses many topics such as distractions, pain during practice, exactly how to prepare

s: A nine-novel space-opera series by James S. A. Corey, starting with Leviathan Wakes, set in a colonised solar system on the edge of war.
w: HN readers recommend it as fast, entertaining near-future space opera, and the audiobooks as particularly good. One notes it gets repetitive around the fourth book.
ab: For fans of political, grounded space opera
Nine novels plus novellas; audiobooks well-liked
TV adaptation exists but the books go further

q.t: I listened to The Expanse and First Law audiobooks and can highly recommend both of them.

t: C Interfaces and Implementations: Techniques for Creating Reusable Software
s: A book that builds a library of reusable C modules (lists, tables, memory management) to show how to design clean APIs in C.
w: HN recommends it as the book to work through after K&R to write safe, reusable C. Commenters like its well-documented library and its API design lessons, and tptacek's recommendation is cited.
ab: For C programmers who have finished K&R
Complete working library with explanations
Written in 1996; no modern C standards or tooling

q.t: It's a fantastic book to work through after finishing K&R for anyone wanting to learn how to write safe and reusable C code.

s: The standard university algorithms textbook (CLRS), covering sorting, graphs, dynamic programming and analysis with rigorous proofs and pseudocode.
w: Cited constantly as the default algorithms text and the book universities actually assign. HN suggests working through it for a real CS foundation, balancing intuition and theory.
ab: For self-learners and students wanting rigor
Big, dense reference; expect to work the exercises
Pseudocode only, not tied to any language

q.t: If you're looking for a comprehensive review including both intuition and theory, I'd be remiss if I didn't recommend CLRS

t: The Making of Prince of Persia: Journals 1985-1993
s: Jordan Mechner's published journals from creating Karateka and Prince of Persia, covering game development, Hollywood ambitions, and his family life.
w: HN game developers recommend it as an inspiring, enjoyable look at making a classic game. Commenters call it amazing even if you have never played the game.
ab: For game developers and retro-computing fans
First-person journal entries from 1985 to 1993
A journal rather than a polished narrative

q.t: They are enjoyable reads, and I highly recommend them.

s: A geometric, picture-driven treatment of complex analysis that builds intuition with diagrams rather than algebra.
w: Held up as the beautiful math book where geometry replaces symbol pushing. Commenters call it wonderful and accessible for anyone wanting new insight into complex numbers.
ab: For people who want an intuitive, visual grasp of complex analysis
Hundreds of hand-drawn figures and geometric proofs
Still real math; expect to work through problems

q.t: if you are interested in new insights about complex numbers and analysis from a geometric POV, this book is wonderful

s: A critique of rewards, bonuses and praise arguing that they undermine intrinsic motivation.
w: HN recommends it in threads on bonuses, gamification and education.
ab: For managers and teachers designing incentives
Provocative, one-sided
Some research is contested

q.t: Punished by rewards is an interesting book on the same lines.

s: A university algorithms textbook organized around design techniques with worked problems.
w: HN readers prefer it to CLRS for its narrative and readability. Commenters call it more direct and more enjoyable for a first serious pass at algorithms.
ab: For students after an intro algorithms course
Clear narrative and design-technique focus
Requires some mathematical maturity

q.t: It is a really enjoyable read and has a nice narrative that I think other algorithm books are lacking.

s: The standard university cell biology textbook.
w: HN recommends it as the standard text. Commenters call it indispensable.
ab: For serious biology learners
Comprehensive
Heavy and expensive

q.t: It's an indispensable book for anyone studying or interested in cell biology and molecular genetics.

s: An O'Reilly book by Flickr's lead engineer on architecting, scaling, and optimizing web applications, covering caching, databases, and deployment.
w: HN commenters in the 2000s pointed to it as the accessible classic on web scalability, drawn from Henderson's real work building Flickr.
ab: For web developers learning how to scale an application
Practical lessons from Flickr's early growth
Written in 2006 with LAMP-era examples; dated tools

q.t: If scalability is relevant to your product, this is an accessible classic

t: Crypto: How the Code Rebels Beat the Government, Saving Privacy in the Digital Age
s: A history of the 1970s-1990s cryptography movement, from public-key encryption and PGP to the crypto wars over export controls and the NSA.
w: HN names it the definitive account of how strong cryptography went public, a gripping history for anyone interested in privacy, the NSA, or hacker culture.
ab: For readers interested in the history of cryptography and privacy
Story-driven, with no technical crypto methods taught
Covers events through about 2000

q.t: Great book if you enjoy computer history or interested in infosec.

s: Jerry Kaplan's first-person account of founding GO Corporation, a pen-computing startup, and how it failed.
w: Recommended as a book-length cautionary tale of an early tablet company and the pitfalls startups still repeat. One commenter says anyone doing a startup should read it, another points to it for how Microsoft operated.
ab: For founders who like war stories about failure and hubris
Covers GO Corp and its early tablet computer
Mid-1990s setting, but the lessons about big-company dynamics hold

q.t: Hell, anyone doing a startup needs to read it anyway.

t: The Blank Slate: The Modern Denial of Human Nature
s: Steven Pinker's argument that human nature is shaped by biology as well as culture.
w: HN cites it in debates about nature versus nurture. Some commenters say research has moved on since it was published, so treat it as a starting point.
ab: For readers interested in nature vs nurture
Popular science argument, not neutral survey
Published in 2002; some science superseded

s: A military science fiction novel in which 75-year-olds join the colonial defense forces and get new young bodies to fight alien species.
w: A frequent pick in HN sci-fi lists as fun, fast, accessible space adventure. Readers say the first few books in the series are the strongest.
ab: Easy, entertaining read for casual sci-fi fans
First of a multi-book series
Later sequels reportedly weaker

q.t: John Scalzi's Old Man's War series is really enjoyable.

s: A memoir by neurosurgeon Paul Kalanithi, written as he faced a terminal lung cancer diagnosis, about mortality and meaning.
w: HN readers recommend it as a haunting, moving book and warn you to come prepared emotionally. It comes up repeatedly as a most memorable read of the year.
ab: For readers drawn to medical memoir and reflections on death
Short and quick to read, but emotionally heavy
Recommended alongside Atul Gawande

q.t: Haunting, beautiful, moving and perfect.

by: Sam Ruby, Dave Thomas et al.
s: The Pragmatic Programmers' long-running guide to building web apps with Ruby on Rails, built around a tutorial store app.
w: Early HN recommendation for learning Rails, praised as very helpful. Later notes point out the edition and licensing caveats and suggest learning Ruby first.
ab: For learning Rails 4 era apps
Has been through several editions; check version
Learn some Ruby first

q.t: Agile Web Development with Rails was very helpful

t: A People's History of the United States
s: Howard Zinn's history of the US told from the viewpoint of Native Americans, slaves, workers, women and the poor rather than its political leaders.
w: HN readers recommend and gift it as a counterweight to textbook history, covering what school leaves out. Several flag its clear left-leaning slant.
ab: For readers who want US history from the bottom up
Openly one-sided and politically charged, per commenters
Often given as a gift

q.t: A People's History of The United States by Howard Zinn. Given it at least 5 times.

s: Ted Chiang's second short-story collection of nine thoughtful science fiction stories on free will, time, machine minds and parallel worlds.
w: HN readers recommend it as a quick, high-payoff sci-fi collection with warm characters rather than chess-piece plots. It is routinely paired with Chiang's earlier Stories of Your Life and Others.
ab: For readers who want idea-rich, short sci-fi
Stories can be read in short sittings
Pairs well with Stories of Your Life and Others

q.t: I really loved Exhalation by Ted Chiang. Too often sci-fi feels cold, and detached with characters that feel akin to chess pieces

s: A Manning book on advanced JavaScript techniques by jQuery creator John Resig, covering functions, closures, prototypes and cross-browser code.
w: HN recommended it, when it was in early access, as the best resource on advanced JavaScript. It was written long before modern ES6+.
ab: For intermediate to advanced JavaScript programmers
Written by the creator of jQuery
Original edition predates modern JavaScript

q.t: John Resig (creator of jQuery) is in the process of writing a great book

s: Gary Taubes' critique of mainstream nutrition research arguing that refined carbohydrates, not dietary fat, drive obesity and metabolic disease.
w: A regular HN recommendation in diet threads, praised as a well-researched review of the literature that prompted some readers to experiment with low-carb eating. The science remains contested.
ab: For readers questioning conventional diet advice
Dense literature review with a strong thesis
Contested; nutrition science has moved on since 2007

q.t: read Good Calories, Bad Calories for a well researched book on why this is

t: The Art of the Metaobject Protocol
s: A book on the CLOS metaobject protocol, showing how Common Lisp's object system can be customized and extended.
w: Commenters say it deserves a mention whenever object systems come up and highly recommend it. It is paired with Lisp in Small Pieces for people exploring Lisp internals.
ab: For Lisp programmers curious about object-system design
Authors include Kiczales and Bobrow, who shaped CLOS
Dense and tied to Common Lisp

q.t: If you haven't had the chance to read "The Art of the Metaobject Protocol" [0], I highly recommend it.

s: A 1969 sci-fi novel in which a team of psychic-cancelling operatives struggle in a world where reality itself seems to regress and decay.
w: Named by PKD fans as their favourite of his books: mind-bending, a story that made readers question the reality of their surroundings.
ab: Short, trippy PKD classic
Reality-bending plot
Good starting point for Philip K. Dick

q.t: No book has made me question the reality of my surroundings like Ubik by Philip K Dick.

t: The Inner Game of Tennis: The Classic Guide to the Mental Side of Peak Performance
s: A classic on the mental side of performance, teaching how to quiet self-criticism and trust your body, using tennis as the example.
w: HN recommends it when anxiety, being hard on yourself, or mental game in sports and work come up. Commenters call it a classic on the psychology of performance.
ab: For anyone whose self-doubt hurts performance
Tennis is the example; ideas apply broadly
Short and conversational

q.t: If you connect with this idea, you may want to check out the book The Inner Game of Tennis:

t: I Will Teach You to Be Rich
s: A personal finance guide built around automating savings, investing in index funds and not sweating small expenses.
w: Recommended to young earners for its automation advice and practical basics. A few say the title and tone are off-putting.
ab: For people starting out with money management
Practical, action-oriented steps
Hype title; author joined HN threads

q.t: is one of the best personal finance books I've read.

t: Ghost in the Wires: My Adventures as the World's Most Wanted Hacker
by: Kevin Mitnick and William L. Simon
s: Kevin Mitnick's memoir of his years as a hacker and social engineer, evading the FBI while breaking into major corporate systems.
w: HN readers call it a suspenseful, humorous and inspiring true story that pulled some into hacking and social engineering.
ab: Gripping hacker memoir with a likeable narrator
Strong on social engineering anecdotes
Mitnick's own account, so one-sided

q.t: I can't believe no one recommended this. The guy literally evaded the FBI using technology.

t: How Buildings Learn: What Happens After They're Built
s: Stewart Brand's study of how buildings change over time, showing how adaptable structures outlast fashionable ones.
w: HN software people recommend it for ideas about maintenance, adaptation, and software lifecycles. One commenter has given away around ten copies.
ab: For architects, software engineers, and systems thinkers
Many photos and examples of buildings changing
Ideas map well to software architecture

q.t: Highly recommend it. I've lost track of how many copies (10?) I've given as gifts to friends.

t: The Effective Engineer: How to Leverage Your Efforts in Software Engineering to Make a Disproportionate and Meaningful Impact
s: A guide to high-leverage practices for software engineers, covering prioritization, onboarding, technical debt and team effectiveness.
w: HN recommends it as a practical book on growing as an engineer. Commenters say it distills tribal knowledge about how engineering works from mid-level to early senior roles.
ab: For mid-level engineers growing toward senior roles
Collects practices from Silicon Valley companies
Less new for experienced seniors

q.t: This book surprised me by how good it is -- it distills a lot of tribal knowledge about how software engineering works

s: Thomas Pynchon's 1973 postmodern novel set around the V-2 rocket program at the end of World War II.
w: Named by HN readers as a favourite and a life-shaping read, and as a 'platonic ideal' of the postmodern novel. Commenters agree it is hard going but rewarding.
ab: For readers who like dense, sprawling postmodern fiction
Not an easy read; hundreds of characters and digressions
Often listed alongside Infinite Jest and Ulysses as a challenge

q.t: Not the easiest read but immensely rewarding.

t: The Clean Coder: A Code of Conduct for Professional Programmers
s: Uncle Bob's book on professionalism for programmers: estimates, saying no, testing and time management.
w: HN recommends it for early-career programmers who want to behave as professionals. Commenters say it goes beyond code to the social side of the job.
ab: For junior developers
Covers professionalism and discipline
Author's opinions are polarizing

q.t: It goes beyond code to what it takes to be a software professional.

t: The Startup Owner's Manual: The Step-by-Step Guide for Building a Great Company
s: A large how-to for founders based on customer development, with checklists for finding a business model and validating it with customers.
w: HN cites it as the in-depth version of Steve Blank's 'get out of the building' approach. One commenter finds it much more thorough than The Lean Startup; it also appears on validation reading lists.
ab: For founders who want a detailed customer development process
Hundreds of pages of steps and checklists
Large and dry; lean-startup summaries cover the core

q.t: seems much more thorough than Lean Startup

s: A post-apocalyptic classic following a monastic order that preserves scientific knowledge through centuries after nuclear war.
w: Regularly cited as a recommended SF classic and an all-time favourite on HN reading lists, often paired with Anathem.
ab: Classic of post-apocalyptic science fiction
Told in three parts across thousands of years
Religious themes run through it

q.t: One of my alltime favourite books.

t: How to Change Your Mind: What the New Science of Psychedelics Teaches Us About Consciousness, Dying, Addiction, Depression, and Transcendence
s: A journalist's survey of psychedelic history and the revival of research, mixing science, history and his own experiences.
w: HN commenters recommend it as an accessible, well-written primer on psychedelics and their return to medicine and neuroscience, with the author's personal trips adding a skeptic's view.
ab: For curious readers new to psychedelic science and history
Narrative style that reads quickly
Covers some medical risks lightly; not a guide to use

q.t: It is a really nice, easy to read primer on the topic, and his experience with psychedelics.

s: A split, programmable, ergonomic mechanical keyboard sold assembled by ZSA, based on the open-source ErgoDox design.
w: Users report better ergonomics, less back and wrist pain, and a keymap configurator they love. Pricy with a learning curve, but worth it to many.
ab: Split design for wrist and back comfort
Fully remappable with layers and modes
Pricey; typing relearning takes about a month

q.t: I finally settled on the ErgodoxEZ and it feels great.

t: Hackers & Painters: Big Ideas from the Computer Age
s: A collection of Paul Graham essays on programming as a creative craft, startups, wealth, Lisp and the culture of hackers.
w: As the founder's own book it is a staple of HN reading lists, recommended as a classic by readers who liked his essays. Many point to it as the reason they looked at Lisp.
ab: For programmers curious about startups and the hacker mindset
Essays also available free on paulgraham.com
Some pieces are dated; opinions are strong and sometimes contested

q.t: Hackers and Painters: Big Ideas from the Computer Age from PG is a classic

s: Steinbeck's novel of an Oklahoma family forced west to California during the Dust Bowl.
w: Cited as a classic to read alongside discussions of inequality and economic displacement.
ab: Classic American novel
Literary fiction, bleak themes
Widely assigned in schools

q.t: They complement each other, and this post, very well.

s: Apple's true wireless earbuds with active noise cancellation, a transparency mode and tight integration with iPhones and other Apple devices.
w: HN buyers list them as a favourite purchase, praising the noise cancellation and the upgrade over standard AirPods. A flight comparison finds Bose over-ear better for engine noise, while a commenter notes occasional Bluetooth glitches.
ab: Good noise cancelling in a pocketable earbud
Best with Apple devices
Over-ear Bose or Sony beat them for flight noise

q.t: The original ones were awesome, but these ones are even better. Absolute game changer.

s: Homer's ancient Greek epic poem of Odysseus's ten-year journey home from the Trojan War.
w: Called a clear winner by HN readers, with Emily Wilson's recent translation singled out as fantastic, even for those who have already read it.
ab: For readers wanting the foundational epic
Translation choice changes the experience; Emily Wilson recommended
Often read alongside the Iliad

q.t: especially if you've already read it, this translation is fantastic.

t: Practical Vim: Edit Text at the Speed of Thought
s: A book of 121 self-contained tips for editing text efficiently in Vim, organized by task.
w: Called an excellent read that covers a lot of ground and is easy to jump around. Another commenter notes it is highly regarded.
ab: For Vim users who want to get faster
Tips are standalone; read in any order
Written for Vim, not Neovim-specific features

q.t: Practical Vim is an excellent read

s: George Orwell's 1949 dystopian novel about a totalitarian state with constant surveillance, doublethink and rewritten history.
w: HN readers cite it as a formative book that seeded distrust of government and surveillance. Others compare it with Fahrenheit 451 and Camus as a pairing.
ab: A classic dystopia that is cited as freshly relevant
Short, bleak, and politically charged
Kindle edition once removed from devices, a famous HN story

q.t: it helped seed (or at least exacerbate) a strong sense of distrust for government and its agents.

t: Bad Samaritans: The Myth of Free Trade and the Secret History of Capitalism
s: An economist's argument that rich countries developed through protectionism and then urged free trade on poorer ones.
w: Recommended for explaining how South Korea and other economies developed with tariffs, subsidies and IP borrowing. Commenters call Chang's books approachable.
ab: For readers curious about development economics
Challenges free-trade orthodoxy
Argumentative; other economists disagree

q.t: I highly recommend the book, Bad Samaritans [1] as it shows that all developed countries followed a similar pattern of IP theft and protectionism.

s: Hermann Hesse's 1927 novel about Harry Haller, a middle-aged intellectual torn between his human and wolfish natures, in a surreal portrait of alienation.
w: HN readers put it among Hesse's must-reads alongside Siddhartha and the Glass Bead Game. Commenters describe it as a surreal, semi-autobiographical novel about depression, existentialism and recovery.
ab: For readers who like introspective, philosophical novels
Surreal and dark in its second half
Often paired with Siddhartha as an easier entry

q.t: It's supposedly about the author himself in 1920s Germany, also about depression, existentialism, and recovery

s: A short philosophical essay arguing that bullshit differs from lying because the bullshitter does not care whether what they say is true.
w: HN uses it as the reference for bullshit as a technical term, and recommends it for explaining how BS attacks the concept of truth itself.
ab: For readers interested in truth, rhetoric, and honesty
Very short, a quick read
Brief essay; more of a thought experiment than a theory

q.t: BS attacks the very concept of truth as such

s: A popular physics book on space, time and the nature of reality.
w: Recommended as a starting point for physics newcomers and for clear explanations of space and time.
ab: For curious people wanting physics without heavy math.
Covers relativity, quantum mechanics and cosmology.
Some views are dated.

q.t: Brian Greene's 'Fabric of the Cosmos'[1] has some great explanations of space and time and their relationship.

t: The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat
s: Neurologist Oliver Sacks' collection of case studies of patients with unusual neurological conditions.
w: HN readers recommend it as an amazing collection that changes how you think about brains.
ab: For general readers
Case studies
Humane

q.t: It's an amazing book full of stories just like in this article

s: A young-adult techno-thriller about teenagers who fight back against a surveillance state after a terrorist attack on San Francisco.
w: Hackers love it as a fast, idealistic novel about civil liberties, crypto and tinkering. Several finished it in one sitting, though one reader found it only okay.
ab: For readers who like tech-and-freedom stories
Marketed as young adult but reads fine for adults
Plot is breezy; one commenter called it merely OK

q.t: I could not put it down, and read it in one sitting.

s: An illustrated satire in which archaeologists in the year 4022 excavate a buried motel and misinterpret every object.
w: HN posts it whenever archaeology guesswork comes up, as a funny reminder of how future people may misread what we leave behind.
ab: For fans of satire and archaeology humor
Short, illustrated and quick to read
Written in 1979, so some references are period

q.t: imagines a 41st-century archaeologist attempting to interpret a 20th-century motel (and getting it hilariously wrong)

s: Gilbert Strang's linear algebra textbook, written to accompany his MIT 18.06 course, emphasizing intuition and applications.
w: Praised for clarity and pairing with the free MIT OpenCourseWare lectures. One commenter notes some one-star reviews, mostly from readers who found it unsuited to a rigorous first course.
ab: For self-learners, engineers, and machine learning students
Intuitive explanations with applications, matching the MIT lectures
Less rigorous than proof-based texts

q.t: Strang presents the subject so clearly and intuitively that you feel like an expert on the subject after reading each chapter.

s: A guide arguing charisma is a learnable skill built on presence, power, and warmth, with practical techniques for managing body language and mindset.
w: A frequent HN suggestion for people who want to be more socially effective. Readers call it one of two go-to books on the subject and rated it highly enough to buy a physical copy.
ab: For introverts and technical people who want to improve social skills
Exercises and techniques you can practice
Some advice is pop psychology

q.t: On audio book and immediately bought a physical copy.

t: The Design and Implementation of the FreeBSD Operating System
by: Marshall Kirk McKusick, George V. Neville-Neil
s: A detailed walk through the architecture and kernel internals of FreeBSD, written by core developers.
w: The recommended pick for learning how a real Unix kernel works. Commenters call it possibly the best applied OS book and praise its explanation of UFS and Unix internals.
ab: For systems programmers and kernel curious readers
Real kernel code, filesystems and networking
Dense and expensive

q.t: It's possibly the best "applied" OS book.

t: The Sense of Style: The Thinking Person's Guide to Writing in the 21st Century
s: A cognitive scientist's modern style guide that explains good prose using linguistics and psychology and corrects common writing habits.
w: HN recommends it as the alternative to Strunk and White, a longer, more focused guide whose advice fits the way software people think about structure.
ab: For people who write at work, from documentation to papers
Practical advice backed by linguistics and psychology
Longer than The Elements of Style; some skip the grammar chapters

q.t: It is full of practical advice.

t: The Prize: The Epic Quest for Oil, Money & Power
s: A sweeping history of the oil industry from the 1860s through the Gulf War, covering its business, geopolitics and wars.
w: Called a stellar history of oil, long but captivating. Commenters point to its chapters on oil in World War II and say it made them interested in history.
ab: For readers curious about oil, geopolitics and business history
Long and detailed
Updated through the early 1990s

q.t: The Prize by Daniel Yergin is a stellar history of the oil industry from 1800s-1990s

t: Learned Optimism: How to Change Your Mind and Your Life
s: A founding positive psychology text on learned helplessness and explanatory style, with techniques for replacing pessimistic thought patterns with optimistic ones.
