w: HN commenters recommend it to people struggling with depression, negativity, or low self-esteem, praising Seligman's research and CBT-style methods.
ab: For readers dealing with pessimism, low mood, or helplessness
Research-backed exercises based on cognitive therapy
Self-help, not treatment; seek professional help for serious depression

q.t: I suggest reading Martin Seligman's Learned Optimism. I found it pretty eye opening.

t: The New Jim Crow: Mass Incarceration in the Age of Colorblindness
s: A legal and sociological argument that mass incarceration and the war on drugs function as a system of racial control in the United States.
w: HN commenters recommend it when race, policing and the drug war come up. They call it a great overview and a helpful resource on the history of incarceration.
ab: For readers interested in criminal justice reform
Thesis is argued strongly and is debated
Mix of law, history and statistics

q.t: for a great overview of the subject I highly recommend The New Jim Crow: Mass Incarceration in the Age of Colorblindness

s: A surreal novel in which a man's search for his missing cat and wife pulls him into a dreamlike web of history, war memories and strange encounters.
w: HN readers call it a standout Murakami, a trip of unconventional plotting that people reread and give as gifts. Several name it the book that most affected them in a given year.
ab: For readers who enjoy surreal, open-ended literary fiction
Long and slow-burning; not plot-driven in a conventional way
Some readers say it is a good first Murakami

q.t: It was the first Murakami book I read, and I've read plenty since. Wonderful.

s: A tip-by-tip guide to Vim's editing model, organised as short recipes covering modes, motions, registers, the dot command and more.
w: Repeatedly named by HN as the book to read after you can navigate Vim. Commenters say it explains the 'why' behind techniques and made them more effective in the editor.
ab: For people who already know basic Vim and want to improve
Short, self-contained tips rather than a long tutorial
Author's free Vimcasts screencasts are a good companion

q.t: I'm 100% in vim these days and more effective in it than in my old primary editor PyCharm.

t: The Way of Kings (The Stormlight Archive)
s: Brandon Sanderson's ongoing epic fantasy series set on the storm-swept world of Roshar, beginning with The Way of Kings.
w: HN fantasy readers praise the worldbuilding, the "hard fantasy" magic system that works like a puzzle, and well-written characters who deal with mental health. Many name it a favorite of the decade.
ab: For readers who like long, plotted epic fantasy with rules-based magic
Each volume is huge, and the series is still unfinished
Part of the larger Cosmere universe, but standalone to start

q.t: My favorite current series is "The stormlight archive". The world building is very good.

s: A short, illustrated introduction to the molecules and machines inside living cells, with Goodsell's watercolor illustrations.
w: Recommended as a fantastic introduction to how proteins and cells work at their own scale, and for its illustrations. Commenters suggest it after videos of molecular animation.
ab: For curious laypeople who want intuition about cell biology
Heavily illustrated by the author
Brief and introductory

q.t: Machinery of Life is a fantastic introduction to an intuition for what proteins and the mechanics of their scale.

s: C. S. Lewis's case for Christian belief and ethics, developed from his wartime radio talks.
w: Recommended by Christian commenters as strong theology and a favorite book, and linked as a root of belief.
ab: For readers curious about Christian apologetics
Accessible argument written for lay readers
Religious viewpoint; arguments are contested

q.t: If you want really good theology I would recommend Mere Christianity by C.S. Lewis

t: Shop Class as Soulcraft: An Inquiry into the Value of Work
s: A philosopher-turned-motorcycle-mechanic argues for the value of skilled manual work and against the push to turn everyone into knowledge workers.
w: HN commenters recommend it to readers of Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance and in threads about caring about craft.
ab: For people drawn to craftsmanship and hands-on work
Mixes memoir with philosophy
Good companion to Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance

q.t: A lovely book that is worth a read.

s: Carl Sagan's sweeping tour of the universe, the history of science and humanity's place in the cosmos, companion to his TV series.
w: A frequent favorite on HN, credited with sparking love of physics and science and shaping views on life's big questions; one reader says it blew their mind as a kid.
ab: Classic popular-science writing on astronomy
Great gateway to physics and curiosity
Published 1980; some science has since moved on

q.t: Cosmos - helped me fall in love with Physics, and the sciences.

by: Andrew S. Tanenbaum, Albert S. Woodhull
s: A textbook that teaches operating systems using the full source of MINIX.
w: HN suggests it for learning OS design by reading real code. Commenters call the Minix book an amazing resource and note it influenced Linus Torvalds.
ab: For students and OS hobbyists
Includes complete MINIX source
Older edition; MINIX is a teaching system

q.t: aka the Minix book, is an amazing resource

t: Turing's Cathedral: The Origins of the Digital Universe
s: A history of John von Neumann's IAS computer project and the birth of the digital universe.
w: Called the best of its kind by one reader, and recommended for von Neumann's wartime work and the IAS machine. It is often listed with The Information.
ab: For readers curious about von Neumann and early computers
Covers the IAS machine and its purposes
More about people and ideas than technical details

q.t: "Turing's Cathedral: The Origins of the Digital Universe" is the best I've read.

s: A philosophical science fiction novel about scientists studying a mysterious ocean planet whose intelligence defies human understanding.
w: Recommended as a sci-fi classic about how hard it would be to communicate with or comprehend a truly alien mind. One reader notes a new direct Polish-to-English translation.
ab: Slow, philosophical first-contact novel
Prefer the direct Polish-to-English translation
Short and often reread

q.t: It feels more relevant now than ever and there is now a direct Polish->English translation.

t: In Defense of Food: An Eater's Manifesto
s: A short book arguing for eating real food in sensible amounts rather than following nutrition fads, summed up as eat food, not too much, mostly plants.
w: HN readers quote its seven-word rule and recommend it for cutting through shifting diet advice. It is repeated as a simple heuristic for what to buy.
ab: For anyone confused by changing nutrition advice
Easy to read, with practical rules of thumb
Popular argument, not a rigorous nutrition text

q.t: there's a great heuristic for walking out of your local supermarket carrying food

s: Pixar co-founder Ed Catmull's account of building and running a creative company.
w: Recommended as a leadership book. The Pixar brain trust idea inspired a code-review comment.
ab: For leaders of creative teams
Pixar stories
Management lessons

q.t: wrote a great book about building and running creative businesses in general, and Pixar in particular

s: A classic introduction to general semantics showing how words shape thinking, covering connotation, abstraction levels and clear language use.
w: HN commenters recommend it for how it changes the way you read arguments and word choices. One says reading it changed their life, and another calls it more entertaining than it sounds.
ab: For readers who want to think and write more clearly
Covers connotation, abstraction and propaganda techniques
Mid-century examples; some feel dated

q.t: Honestly, reading that changed my life.

t: The Fifth Discipline: The Art and Practice of the Learning Organization
s: A management classic introducing systems thinking and the idea of the learning organization.
w: Appears in HN reading lists on systems thinking and organizational learning, usually alongside Donella Meadows.
ab: For managers interested in systems thinking and organizations.
Introduces mental models and shared vision.
Business-book style; Meadows is suggested as an easier systems entry.

s: A 14-inch business laptop from 2018 with a classic ThinkPad keyboard and a dual-battery hot-swap design, popular for Linux.
w: HN people like it as a Linux workhorse with excellent keyboard, upgradeable RAM up to 64GB, and hot-swappable batteries. Many still use it years later.
ab: Great keyboard and Linux support
Dual-battery, upgradable RAM and SSD
2018 hardware; used units are the norm now

q.t: Runs amazing with linux and the keyboard is a huge upgrade from my 2016 MBP.

s: Kahlil Gibran's 1923 collection of poetic essays on love, work, joy, sorrow and death, spoken by a wise man leaving a city.
w: HN readers list it as a short, beautifully written book they reread, and a book that shaped their thinking. One says it's worth it if you like the style.
ab: Short, poetic prose on life's big themes
Spiritual tone suits readers of Siddhartha or Zen texts
Style is flowery and divides some readers

q.t: The Prophet - Kahlil Gibran (Recommended if you like the style)

t: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, 7th Edition
by: James F. Kurose, Keith W. Ross
s: A university networking textbook that starts at the application layer and works down through transport, network and link layers.
w: Called the best textbook on computer networking, bar none, and a good fit for web developers coming without a CS degree. One reader says it is exhaustive and long.
ab: For developers learning networking fundamentals
Top-down order starting from familiar applications
Long, with about 900 pages

q.t: It is the best textbook on computer networking, bar none.

s: Surgeon Atul Gawande examines aging, dying and what matters at the end of life.
w: Recommended as enlightening and surprisingly enjoyable despite the sobering subject.
ab: For anyone thinking about aging or end of life
Narrative nonfiction
Emotional topics

q.t: absolutely enlightening and surprisingly enjoyable to read, despite the sobering topics

s: A guide to product and learning design built on helping users become skilled and capable, instead of selling features.
w: HN recommends it to people building products, onboarding and docs. Commenters say it is insightful and practical on what users feel and experience, and is the core of making good products.
ab: For product managers, designers and developers
Focus on user skill over product features
Less about UI details than user psychology

q.t: I found the Badass users book to be very insightful and practical

t: The Road to Reality: A Complete Guide to the Laws of the Universe
s: Roger Penrose's 1,100-page tour of the mathematics and physics of the universe, from basic geometry to quantum field theory and cosmology.
w: HN math fans suggest it as the single book that shows how math underlies physics, praising its depth while warning it is dense and takes a long time.
ab: For math or physics readers who want serious depth
Covers math from basics to advanced physics
Dense and long; the reader needs math background

q.t: this book has proven to me to be the most enlightening mathematics text I've ever read

t: Rise of the Warrior Cop: The Militarization of America's Police Forces
s: A journalist's history of how American police forces adopted military tactics and equipment, from SWAT teams to no-knock raids.
w: HN brings it up in policing and civil-liberties threads as the thorough account of how militarization happened. Commenters call it an excellent read and point to Balko as the writer who covered it best.
ab: For readers interested in policing and civil liberties
Mix of history, case studies and policy analysis
US-focused; published 2013, so recent events are missing

q.t: If you're interested in how this kind of thing happens (and alarmingly how often it happens), this book is an excellent read

s: A textbook on type systems and programming language theory, using typed lambda calculus with implementations.
w: Recommended as the most useful and accessible book on type theory. Commenters say it is dense but rewarding, and that you can evaluate its examples by hand.
ab: For language implementers and type theory learners
Typed lambda calculus with proofs and implementations
Dense; wants careful reading

q.t: I think it's the most useful + accessible book on type theory out there.

t: Becoming a Technical Leader: An Organic Problem-Solving Approach
s: Weinberg's book on how technical people grow into leaders, covering problem solving, motivation and organization.
w: Recommended to developers moving into lead roles as a book that shows why technical people struggle with leadership.
ab: For developers moving into leadership
Not only for formal tech leads
Written in 1986; some examples show age

q.t: A lot of eye-opening insights in: Becoming a Technical Leader

s: A hands-on guide to building two complete interpreters for a scripting language, one in Java and one in C, with all the code explained.
w: HN regards it as the friendliest path into compilers and interpreters, easier than the dragon book, with clean code you can follow along with. Readers keep returning to implement variations.
ab: For programmers curious how languages are built
Walk through a tree-walk interpreter and a bytecode VM
Also free to read online by the author

q.t: Would recommend this to people curious about compilers/Interpreters over the dragon book.

s: An undergraduate-level history of mathematics that teaches the subject through its historical development, from Greek geometry to modern algebra and topology.
w: HN commenters suggest it for learning real math while following its history, and note the accompanying lectures by N J Wildberger.
ab: For people with undergraduate math who like historical context
You do math as you go, not just read stories
Textbook-style and dense in places

q.t: which goes through the history of maths while actually _doing_ some maths at undergraduate level

s: Scott Aaronson's lectures-turned-book linking computational complexity, quantum mechanics, logic and philosophy.
w: HN recommends it as an amazing, well-written book for anyone interested in math, physics or theoretical computer science. Commenters call Aaronson possibly the best technical author around.
ab: For curious people with some math background
Wide-ranging, witty, and opinionated
Not a quantum programming tutorial

q.t: it is an amazing book. Highly recommended for anyone interested in math, physics, theoretical computer science, quantum computing or just good science writing

s: A comprehensive reference to JavaScript and its core APIs.
w: HN recommends it as a reliable reference for learning JavaScript. Commenters call it a great book, though some prefer The Good Parts for experienced programmers.
ab: For learners and reference
Very thorough
Large; edition matters

q.t: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide' by David Flanagan is a great book.

s: Selected letters from the Roman Stoic philosopher Seneca to Lucilius on how to live well, face death and handle wealth and anger.
w: HN readers call it a compass and the philosophy book they actually enjoyed, with one saying it's their bible as an atheist. It shows up in must-read lists next to Meditations.
ab: For readers new to Stoicism who want practical wisdom
Short letters can be read in any order
Pairs well with Marcus Aurelius's Meditations

q.t: As an atheist, Seneca's Moral letters to Lucilius is my bible. My compass when life gets hard.

s: A Soviet-era science fiction novel about stalkers who scavenge dangerous alien artifacts from restricted Zones; the basis of Tarkovsky's film Stalker.
w: Called a classic that has not dated, tight and haunting, and beloved enough to have inspired later films and games.
ab: Short, atmospheric Russian sci-fi classic
Inspired the film Stalker and the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games
Loosely sci-fi; more mood than gadgets

q.t: Tight and well written, not dated at all.

s: First book of the Nexus trilogy: a near-future thriller about a nano-drug that lets human minds link together and run software.
w: HN readers enjoy it as great transhumanist sci-fi about nanotech and brain augmentation, with one calling it a favourite modern series. One notes later prose is meh.
ab: Near-future thriller about mind-linking technology
First of a trilogy (Crux, Apex follow)
Prose is not the strongest point

q.t: Rereading it at the moment, my favourite modern sci-fi series by far.

s: A short fable about a seagull who wants to fly for the love of flying and rises beyond the flock's limits.
w: Readers on HN call it a short, inspiring story that shaped their outlook; one says it made them realize being different is a superpower.
ab: Very short, quick inspirational fable
Allegory about pursuing mastery and independence
Sentimental; some find it spiritual self-help in disguise

q.t: Made me realize being different is a superpower.

by: Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson
s: A conspiracy satire trilogy of counterculture sci-fi.
w: Listed as a book that changed how people think, and a lighter read.
ab: For fans of cult sci-fi.
Satirical conspiracy.
Weird.

t: The Signal and the Noise: Why So Many Predictions Fail - but Some Don't
s: A survey of forecasting in fields from baseball to politics, weather, and finance, arguing for probabilistic, Bayesian thinking.
w: HN recommends it as an approachable guide to prediction and probability, handy whenever someone claims to forecast markets or crises with confidence.
ab: For readers interested in forecasting and Bayesian thinking
Case studies from weather, sports, economics, and politics
Some chapters, such as climate and GDP, drag

q.t: Nate Silver's The Signal and the Noise [1] is excellent.

s: Jane Austen's 1813 comedy of manners about Elizabeth Bennet, her four sisters, and her tangled relationship with the proud Mr Darcy.
w: HN readers name it a comfort book and one that sticks as modern. Commenters like the human characters and the humour, with a nod to the romance.
ab: For readers who want a witty, light classic
Social-comedy romance set in Regency England
Sharp observations about pride, class and character

q.t: It's a surprisingly modern book, very much worth reading if you don't mind the romance.

s: The first book of the Silo series: a post-apocalyptic story about humanity living in an underground silo where leaving is a death sentence.
w: A popular dystopian pick (Wool, Shift, Dust) and a notable self-publishing success. One reader was deeply disappointed, so reactions vary.
ab: Dystopian mystery set inside an underground silo
Wool, Shift and Dust make up the original trilogy
Not everyone loves it

q.t: I really liked the Wool series, Wool, Shift, Dust.

s: A dialogue introducing Adlerian psychology.
w: Recommended for anxiety and self-help threads.
ab: For those facing anxiety.
Dialogue format.
Not a clinical treatment.

q.t: The Courage To Be Disliked by Ichiro Kishimi and Fumitake Koga was a book I enjoyed that might help your sister.

t: Flatland: A Romance of Many Dimensions
s: An 1884 satirical novella about a square living in a two-dimensional world who discovers the third dimension.
w: HN calls it mind-bending, amusing and still useful for thinking about higher dimensions; one reader needed to go slowly. It also satirizes Victorian society.
ab: Short Victorian classic for math lovers
Satire of social class and gender
Some Victorian attitudes feel dated

q.t: I had to read Flatland slowly, but I would definitely describe it as mind bending.

s: A survey of the software architecture of professional game engines, from math and rendering to animation, physics, audio, and tools, written by a Naughty Dog engineer.
w: HN's go-to for anyone entering game development. Several commenters read it cover to cover and call it readable for an 800-page textbook and an excellent introduction.
ab: For programmers entering game development or curious about engines
Wide coverage of engine subsystems with practical detail
Long; a survey rather than a deep dive on any one topic

q.t: It's extremely readable for an 800 page textbook (I actually read it cover to cover)

s: A comic-form analysis of how comics work, covering visual storytelling, iconography, time and the relationship of words and pictures.
w: Recommended to designers and programmers as a source of thinking about visual communication and UX, not just comics. Commenters call it fantastic and enlightening.
ab: For designers, UX people and anyone curious about visual storytelling
Written as a comic itself
Focus is on comics, though lessons generalize

q.t: If anyone hasn't read Understanding Comics, it's a fantastic book.

s: Cringely's wry account of how the personal computer industry grew.
w: HN recommends it for anecdotes about founders and the early industry. Commenters call it required reading, more for historical perspective than anything else.
ab: For computing history fans
Anecdotes about founders
Written in 1992

q.t: This is required reading for anyone on HN

t: The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses
s: A game design book organized around 100 'lenses', questions designers can use to examine a game from different angles.
w: Called the bible of game design and the most valuable book on one reader's shelf, thanks to its lenses. Commenters quote it when discussing toys and fun.
ab: For game designers and developers building games
Lenses as practical checklists of questions
Broad rather than deep on any single topic

q.t: To me, this is the most valuable book I have on my bookshelf.

t: Essentialism: The Disciplined Pursuit of Less
s: A book on identifying what is most important and cutting out everything else, to focus effort on fewer, higher-impact things.
w: Widely listed in HN reading lists, often alongside Deep Work, as a good prompt to focus on less. One reader found it repeats itself a lot.
ab: For overcommitted people wanting to prioritize
Good ideas; one reader found it repetitive
Pairs well with Deep Work

q.t: Good ideas and content, repeats a lot

s: A Pulitzer Prize-winning 1973 work arguing that much human behavior and culture is a defense against awareness of our own mortality.
w: A repeat name in HN favorite-book lists, with readers saying it completely changed how they see life and society. One notes its discussion of homosexuality is outdated.
ab: Heavy psychology/philosophy of death anxiety
Pulitzer winner, widely cited
Some sections feel dated

q.t: Completely changed how I view life and the world around me.

s: James Joyce's 1922 modernist novel following one day in the lives of Leopold Bloom and Stephen Dedalus in Dublin.
w: HN lists it as the canonical 'hard' novel: people name it as most challenging or mind-bending, and several keep returning to it for a second attempt. It is respected more than easy-loved.
ab: For readers who want a serious literary challenge
Dense, allusive stream-of-consciousness; many readers admit missing large parts
Reread attempts are common, so expect to work at it

q.t: I just started Ulysses for the second time, see if I get further this time.

t: Bose QuietComfort 20 Acoustic Noise Cancelling Headphones
s: Wired in-ear noise-cancelling earphones with an inline battery module, made by Bose.
w: HN commenters recommend them for open offices and travel, saying they block steady noise and quieter conversations well. They are also praised as comfortable, with a secure fit.
ab: For commuters, flyers and open-office workers wanting strong ANC
Wired with a non-replaceable battery module
Discontinued model; battery may age

q.t: Let me introduce you to the best pair of headphones for travel that I own

t: The Geography of Nowhere: The Rise and Decline of America's Man-Made Landscape
s: A critique of American suburban sprawl, car-centered planning and ugly modern architecture, and an argument for walkable places.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a clear analysis of why American towns look the way they do, even while calling Kunstler a bit of a crank.
ab: For readers interested in urban planning and why sprawl feels soulless
Covers postwar suburbs, zoning and architecture
Opinionated and polemical; Kunstler's later predictions were widely criticized

q.t: That book completely opened up my thinking about how the elements in a city relate to each other

s: A posthuman sci-fi thriller in which a man with erased memories joins an experiment re-creating Earth's 'dark age' society.
w: Stross fans on HN list it as really great sci-fi and a close second to Accelerando.
ab: Post-singularity thriller by Charles Stross
Stand-alone novel
Dense with transhumanist ideas

q.t: Just finished The Glasshouse by Charles Stross, really great sci-fi

s: Edited transcripts of Feynman's Caltech course on computation, covering computer architecture, theory of computation, and the physical limits of computing.
w: Recommended as an unusual first-principles tour of computation through Feynman's eyes, which helped some readers connect the ideas from a CS degree.
ab: For curious readers with some CS or physics background
Covers reversible computing and quantum computing basics
Has been hard to find; editions vary

q.t: there was a book that hit at the right place and time: Feynman Lectures on Computation.

t: The Daily Stoic: 366 Meditations on Wisdom, Perseverance, and the Art of Living
s: A daily reader with 366 short Stoic passages and commentary, one per day of the year.
w: Recommended as an approachable daily introduction to Stoicism that readers say has helped them tremendously.
ab: For daily reflection, not a systematic study
Each entry takes under two pages
Pop version of Stoicism

q.t: One thing that has helped me tremendously is The Daily Stoic

t: Programmers at Work: Interviews with 19 Programmers Who Shaped the Computer Industry
s: A 1986 collection of in-depth interviews with 19 early software pioneers, including Bill Gates, Andy Hertzfeld and Dan Bricklin.
w: HN recommends it as a companion to Coders at Work. Commenters value the detailed, often mundane look at how early programmers thought, calling it timeless.
ab: For readers curious about the early personal computer era
Interviews with Gates, Hertzfeld, Bricklin and others
Out of print for years; may cost more

q.t: it's a timeless and fascinating look at the minds of Bill Gates, Andy Hertzfeld (apple/mac), Dan Bricklin (visicalc)

s: Martha Wells's series of short sci-fi novellas narrated by a security android that has hacked its own governor module and mostly wants to watch TV serials.
w: HN readers recommend it as short, snappy and gripping, with one warning that you will lose sleep finishing it. It shows up on favourites lists from 2021 through 2025.
ab: Start with All Systems Red
Short novellas, easy to read in one sitting
Funny, character-driven sci-fi

q.t: short enough and gripping enough that it is very hard not to trade a night of sleep

s: Adam Smith's 1776 foundational work of political economy on the division of labour, markets and the nature of national wealth.
w: Cited on HN as an essential economics classic, one that is more nuanced than its reputation. Readers call it heavy but rewarding.
ab: For readers who want to read economics' founding text first-hand
Long and slow in places; many read only the first book
Smith is often misrepresented, commenters say

q.t: Very old, very heavy, but very eye opening. A must read for anyone interested in economics.

t: How to Design Programs: An Introduction to Programming and Computing
s: An introductory programming textbook that teaches a systematic design process using Racket.
w: Recommended as a more accessible alternative to SICP for beginners. It is also a common pick in lists of where to point newcomers to programming.
ab: For beginners and teachers wanting a structured method
Teaches design recipes in Racket
Less ambitious than SICP

q.t: HTDP (How to Design Programs) is more accessible than SICP

t: Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned: The Myth of the Objective
s: An argument from AI research that setting objectives can block innovation, and that searching for novelty finds more interesting results.
w: HN commenters recommend it to explain why chasing a fixed goal fails in complex settings like innovation, learning and research. They also tie it to novelty search in AI.
ab: For researchers, founders and curious AI readers
Short and idea-driven
Thesis is applied broadly beyond AI

q.t: Talks about how optimization doesn't lead to optimal goals in complex environments (e.g. life).

t: Dreamland: The True Tale of America's Opiate Epidemic
s: A journalist's account of how pill-mill prescribing and Mexican black-tar heroin sellers fueled the American opioid epidemic.
w: HN commenters offer it as the definitive history of the opioid epidemic, in any thread about OxyContin, Purdue or drug policy.
ab: For readers wanting the story behind the opioid crisis
Covers both the pharma marketing and the street-level sellers
Narrative journalism, US-focused, published 2015

q.t: Sam Quinones wrote a rather definitive history of the opioid epidemic in America.

t: Radical Candor: Be a Kick-Ass Boss Without Losing Your Humanity
s: A management book built on a framework of caring personally while challenging directly, with advice on giving and receiving feedback.
w: HN commenters point new managers and founders to it as soon as they start hiring or running 1:1s. It gives a simple vocabulary for honest feedback that people find immediately usable.
ab: For new engineering managers and founders hiring their first team
Practical framework for feedback, 1:1s and difficult conversations
Corporate-coach tone; some find the examples Silicon Valley-centric

q.t: I'd highly recommend reading Radical Candor by Kim Scott.

s: The first novel of Kim Stanley Robinson's Mars trilogy, following the first colonists as they terraform Mars and clash over its future.
w: HN readers call the trilogy packed with ideas about the next century and praise its hopeful outlook for humanity. It is a go-to long-form hard sci-fi pick, including for audio.
ab: For fans of realistic, science-heavy colonization fiction
Trilogy: Red Mars, Green Mars, Blue Mars
Slow, detailed pacing; one reader called finishing it a slog

q.t: These books gave me a very hopeful outlook for humanity's future.

t: Colossus: The Secrets of Bletchley Park's Code-breaking Computers
s: A collection of essays on the Colossus machines built at Bletchley Park, with technical detail on Flowers, Tutte and the codebreaking.
w: Recommended for the technical history of Colossus, including Tommy Flowers and Bill Tutte. One commenter warns it is a multi-author collection so quality varies.
ab: For readers of WWII and early computing history
Includes schematics and technical detail
Essay collection; uneven in places

q.t: The book talks about Tutte and Flowers and how they went about building the world's first true computer.

s: Kent Beck's short book that teaches test-driven development by building two worked examples, with patterns for writing tests first.
w: Recommended as the original, clearest explanation of TDD. One commenter read many tutorials without getting it until this book; others quote it to settle arguments about what TDD originally meant.
ab: For developers new to TDD or wanting its original form
Two worked examples plus a catalog of patterns
Examples are dated; the practice remains debated

q.t: I read many tutorials and several books on TDD but never quite got it until I read Kent Beck's Test Driven Development By Example

t: Waking Up: A Guide to Spirituality Without Religion
s: Sam Harris's book arguing for meditation and the illusory nature of the self, approached through science and philosophy rather than religion.
w: HN readers recommend it for scientific and philosophical reasoning about the self and mindfulness, and as a life-changing read on mind and consciousness. It has detractors who dismiss Harris and his program.
ab: For skeptics curious about meditation and consciousness
Mix of neuroscience, philosophy and personal practice
Harris is divisive; some dismiss his guided program

q.t: Scientific and philosophical reasoning for why the self is an illusion.

t: The Computational Beauty of Nature: Computer Explorations of Fractals, Chaos, Complex Systems, and Adaptation
s: A book that explores fractals, chaos, cellular automata, neural networks and adaptation through computer experiments.
w: Suggested repeatedly as a book worth checking out for people interested in complexity and generative art. One reader calls it wonderful to own in print and inspiring for generative art.
ab: For programmers interested in fractals, chaos and complex systems
Combines exposition with code-based explorations
Published in 2000; examples feel dated

q.t: It's a wonderful book to own as a physical copy, and the contents are very inspiring for generative art.

t: The Game: Penetrating the Secret Society of Pickup Artists
s: A journalist's memoir of going undercover in the pickup-artist community and what he learned about dating and social dynamics.
w: HN commenters suggest it for shy people as a lesson in social dynamics and as entertaining reading. It also shows up in lists of books that changed lives.
ab: For readers curious about dating and social skills
Memoir format, entertaining, with some lurid episodes
Some of the tactics are manipulative and widely criticized

q.t: It's superficially about how to pick up women, but a lot of it is actually about how to understand social life

t: On Food and Cooking: The Science and Lore of the Kitchen
s: A 900-page reference that explains the chemistry and physics behind ingredients and cooking techniques, from eggs and meat to vegetables and dairy.
w: HN engineers put it first on any list of food science, comparing it to an O'Reilly book on cooking, a guide to why recipes work.
ab: For curious cooks who want to know why techniques work
Very detailed science of foods and processes
Large and technical; reference rather than recipes

q.t: If you're curious enough to read a 900 page book containing very accurate information about the specific processes that occur when preparing most foods

t: iWoz: Computer Geek to Cult Icon
s: Steve Wozniak's memoir about inventing the personal computer and co-founding Apple.
w: HN readers recommend it as a fun look into Woz's mind, especially for engineers.
ab: For engineers and Apple history fans
Told in Woz's voice
Personal, not a corporate history

q.t: It's a really interesting look into Woz's mind and his life.

s: Clarke's 1953 novel of benevolent aliens who arrive on Earth and guide humanity toward an uncertain transformation.
w: HN readers cite it as a mind-changing science fiction classic, praising its sweep of time and its themes of endings and human destiny.
ab: For fans of classic big-idea science fiction
Short, with a time scale covering generations
Some 1950s tech and social assumptions

q.t: I know it's fiction but it left me speechless.

s: A survey of the Unix design philosophy and its culture, covering rules of modularity, simplicity and composition with case studies.
w: HN cites it for its statements of the Unix philosophy, and links the free online version and the Unix koans. One quoted review calls the author self-promoting.
ab: For programmers curious about Unix design and tradition
Free online edition is available alongside the print copy
Raymond's self-congratulation and dated tooling are common complaints

q.t: The Unix philosophy is bottom-up and not top-down. It is pragmatic and grounded in experience.

t: Radical Markets: Uprooting Capitalism and Democracy for a Just Society
by: Eric A. Posner, E. Glen Weyl
s: Two economists propose market-based reforms such as quadratic voting and common ownership self-assessed taxes to address inequality and monopoly.
w: HN commenters point to it for concrete, workable policy ideas, such as quadratic voting and common ownership. Some disagree with parts of it, but it gets cited as a provocative way to rethink markets.
ab: For readers interested in market design and mechanism design
Proposals include quadratic voting and self-assessed property taxes
Many ideas are speculative; critics doubt practicality

q.t: The book has a lot of other cool reasonably doable ideas.

t: Born a Crime: Stories from a South African Childhood
s: Comedian Trevor Noah's memoir of growing up mixed-race under apartheid in South Africa, told through funny and moving personal stories.
w: Recommended repeatedly as an entertaining, thought-provoking memoir that teaches the nuances of apartheid. Many specifically recommend the audiobook, which Noah narrates himself.
ab: For readers wanting an accessible, funny memoir with real history inside
The audiobook narrated by the author is widely praised
Good pick for people who do not usually read much

q.t: Highest possible recommendation. Everyone I've urged to read it has loved it.

s: Arthur C. Clarke's 1968 novel of a mission to Jupiter and the intelligence of the computer HAL, written alongside Kubrick's film.
w: HN readers name it among their favorite sci-fi, as a fun reread, and it's often suggested when people ask about fiction on artificial intelligence.
ab: For classic science fiction readers
Companion to the Kubrick film that explains more
Written in the 1960s; the science is dated

q.t: I first read it when I was 12, in 1968, the year that both the movie and book came out.

s: A guide to building an investment portfolio.
w: Recommended as a classic for investing beginners.
ab: For new investors
Portfolio basics
Classic

q.t: Two classics are The Four Pillars of Investing and The Bogleheads' Guide to Investing

t: Prisoners of Geography: Ten Maps That Explain Everything About the World
s: A journalist's short guide to how mountains, rivers, coastlines and climate shape the foreign policy and power of Russia, China, the US and other regions.
w: HN readers rate it a quick, fun and mind-expanding introduction to geopolitics that explains why nations act the way they do and how geography drives economic success.
ab: For readers wanting an accessible primer on geopolitics
Ten chapters, each on one region, with maps
Simplified at times; geography as destiny is debated

q.t: looking at the present through analysis of the past and the geography that influences it

s: Carl Sagan's 1985 novel about a scientist who detects a signal from an alien civilization and the global response.
w: A favorite sci-fi pick on HN, with readers calling it emotionally intense and sometimes life-changing, and a story that ties the present to future promise. The movie is called a fair adaptation.
ab: For readers who like serious, science-grounded first-contact stories
Combines science, faith and politics
Not a light read; slower than the film

q.t: One of my absolute favorites. It's such an intense book emotionally.

s: A plastic plunger-style coffee press that brews a single cup quickly with paper filters.
w: HN's favorite cheap coffee gadget: faster and easier to clean than a french press and better tasting. Recommended as an under-$100 buy.
ab: For people wanting a cheap, quick coffee maker
Easy cleanup, great for travel
Makes one cup at a time

q.t: Faster and easier cleanup than a french press and tastes better than pretty much every other method IMHO

t: A Pattern Language: Towns, Buildings, Construction
s: A catalog of 253 interlocking design patterns for towns, buildings and rooms, written as a shared language anyone can use.
w: Programmers cite it as the origin of design patterns and a lesson in how design shapes daily life. People recommend it for city planning, homes and thinking about design.
ab: For anyone curious about architecture, cities or design thinking
Big reference book you dip into, not read straight
Some patterns reflect 1970s assumptions

q.t: It's full of fascinating insights into the ways functional design interacts with our lives

s: Hermann Hesse's last novel, set in a future intellectual order whose members play a game synthesising all arts and sciences; Nobel Prize-winning author.
w: HN readers call it incredible and mind-exciting, and one read it at 14. It's appreciated for portraying a life lived for pure intellectual values, though one commenter didn't like it.
ab: For readers drawn to philosophical, idea-driven fiction
Slow and cerebral; not plot-driven
Hesse's other novels, like Siddhartha, are easier starting points

q.t: Read when I was about 14. I just remember the way it excited my mind.

by: Andrew S. Tanenbaum, David J. Wetherall
s: A standard university textbook on computer networking, covering layers from physical to application.
w: Called the standard text and a classic in threads about learning networking, often paired with Kurose and Ross.
ab: For students and self-learners of networking
Thorough layer-by-layer coverage
Large; older editions lag on modern protocols

q.t: the standard text book on computer networks is Tanenbaum

by: Alfred V. Aho, Brian W. Kernighan
s: The original book on AWK by its creators, covering the language and examples such as a small relational database and parsers.
w: HN calls it among the best programming books in any language. Commenters praise its concision and impressive examples, and say it is worth reading even if you never use AWK.
ab: For Unix users and anyone who loves tight technical writing
Under 200 pages with worked projects
Covers the original AWK, not GNU extensions

q.t: is one of the best programming books, on any language, in my opinion. Worth reading even if you don't use awk.

t: The Big Short: Inside the Doomsday Machine
s: Michael Lewis's narrative of the few investors who bet against the subprime mortgage market before the 2008 financial crisis.
w: HN readers recommend it as a gripping insider story of the mortgage collapse, centered on Michael Burry. It surfaces whenever people debate whether the crisis could be predicted.
ab: For anyone curious about the 2008 financial crisis
Character-driven, entertaining narrative
Simplifies some financial mechanics for storytelling

q.t: please PLEASE read The Big Short by Michael Lewis, in which he tells the entire, fascinating story of Michael Burry

t: Range: Why Generalists Triumph in a Specialized World
s: David Epstein's case that broad experience and delayed specialization often beat early narrow focus in sports, careers, and creativity.
w: Recommended as the counterpoint to Tiger-parent and early-specialization advice. Commenters say it is entertaining and informative, though not an academic text.
ab: For people choosing between specializing and exploring
Stories and research on learning and careers
Popular, not academic; cherry-picked examples

q.t: Everyone should read "Range By David Epstein"

s: Lenovo's 14-inch 2012 business laptop, the generation after the T420, with chiclet keyboard and good Linux support at low used prices.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a cheap used Linux dev laptop, often by upgrading the older T420. Fans say it runs everything a developer needs once a SSD is added.
ab: Cheap second-hand for Linux developers
Chiclet keyboard; older T420 keyboard can be swapped in
Dated hardware; battery and screen are weak

q.t: Ive been really happy with my T430, works great with linux, every function button mapped to a command in Mint.

s: A Socratic Q&A-style introduction to relational and logic programming with miniKanren, written in the style of The Little Schemer.
w: HN Lispers recommend it as a mind-bending intro to logic programming, from the authors of miniKanren. It continues the Little Schemer series style.
ab: For those comfortable with Scheme and recursion
Teaches miniKanren-style relational programming
Unusual dialogue format takes getting used to

q.t: The whole series is great! I especially enjoyed _The Reasoned Schemer_

s: Space opera in which a starship AI, now trapped in a single human body, pursues revenge inside a vast empire; first of the Imperial Radch trilogy.
w: HN sci-fi threads list it as a fresh take on space opera that swept the Hugo, Nebula and Clarke awards. Readers like the unusual narration and the AI-in-a-body premise, though one calls it good but not great.
ab: For sci-fi readers who want something unlike typical space opera
First of three books: Sword and Mercy follow
Unusual handling of gender and a non-linear narrator can take adjusting

q.t: a very, very good sci fi series which is unlike any other sf I've ever read

s: Haldeman's 1974 Hugo-winning novel about a soldier fighting an interstellar war where time dilation leaves him decades out of step with home.
w: A frequent entry on HN sci-fi lists, praised as possibly the best science fiction one commenter read; it uses time dilation and Vietnam-era alienation.
ab: For readers of military sci-fi with a thoughtful edge
Allegory for Vietnam; short novel
A different book of the same title by Dexter Filkins covers Iraq

q.t: Possibly the best science fiction I ever read!

t: The Hidden Life of Trees: What They Feel, How They Communicate
s: A German forester's popular account of how trees live in communities, share resources through fungal networks, and respond to their surroundings.
w: HN readers bring it up in threads on fungi, forests, and nature, recommending it as a warm, accessible look at connections between trees, insects, and fungi.
ab: For nature lovers and casual science readers
Lyrical, accessible look at forest ecology
Not a pure science book; some claims lean anthropomorphic

q.t: I highly recommend (not a pure science book) Hidden Life Of Trees

s: Josh Kaufman's overview of core business concepts, condensing ideas from hundreds of business books into short explanations of value creation, marketing, sales and finance.
w: HN readers recommend it as a clear crash course in business basics for technical founders and call it simple enough to re-listen once or twice a year.
ab: For engineers and founders who want business fundamentals
Broad survey rather than a deep dive
Often cited alongside The E-Myth and Deep Work

q.t: So simple and clear. I listen to it once or twice a year.

s: Susanna Clarke's 2020 short fantasy novel about a man living in an endless house of statues, tides and halls, who slowly pieces together who he is.
w: HN readers recommend it as an inventive, gorgeous-prose escape, with one comparing it to a lightweight House of Leaves. It turns up on best-of lists from 2021 through 2025.
ab: Short, strange and atmospheric; best read blind
Mystery plot with a gentle tone
Different in style from Clarke's Jonathan Strange

q.t: Piranesi was a comforting other worldly read that really helped with escapism.

t: How Not to Die: Discover the Foods Scientifically Proven to Prevent and Reverse Disease
s: A diet and health book arguing that whole-food, plant-based eating can prevent and reverse leading causes of death, with extensive references.
w: HN commenters who want diet advice grounded in studies point to it, along with the author's nutritionfacts.org site. They like the heavy referencing and balance of science with plain explanations.
ab: For readers wanting evidence-cited nutrition guidance
Strongly advocates a plant-based diet
Nutrition science is contested; meat debates came up in threads

q.t: If you're looking to make dietary choices based on the results of high-quality dietary studies, my goto is

t: Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests
s: A guide to test-driven development with mock objects, showing a project built test-first.
w: HN recommends it as the book behind the mockist TDD school. Commenters say few people know it and that it answered their TDD questions.
ab: For developers learning TDD
Worked example of test-first design
Java-focused, mock-heavy style

q.t: almost nobody is aware of this book [1] and the entire school of TDD it spawned.

s: A coming-of-age novel set in the Depression-era South, told by a young girl whose lawyer father defends a Black man falsely accused of rape.
w: A classic repeatedly named by HN commenters for its timeless themes of race, class and morality, and as a simple, refreshing read.
ab: Classic often assigned in school
Themes of racism, class and justice
Told through a child's eyes

q.t: The timeless beauty and innocence of the book remains unparalleled.

t: SQL Antipatterns: Avoiding the Pitfalls of Database Programming
s: A catalog of common database design and SQL mistakes, each with the problem, why it fails, and a better alternative.
w: Recommended to people learning SQL and database design as a practical guide to common mistakes. One reader says it had the largest impact on how he thinks about databases.
ab: For developers who write SQL or design schemas
Each chapter pairs a mistake with a fix
Not a SQL tutorial; assumes basics

q.t: SQL Antipatterns is the book that had the largest impact on my thinking

s: Solzhenitsyn's three-volume account of the Soviet forced-labour camp system, mixing history, testimony and his own experience.
w: HN readers call it harrowing and mentally formative, and mark it as a must-read for understanding Soviet history. One says it changed their politics.
ab: For readers who want first-hand Soviet history
Three volumes; heavy going emotionally
A frequent 'must read' in history lists

q.t: The books that caused me the most mental change were the three volumes of the Gulag Archipelago.

s: A spare post-apocalyptic novel following a father and his young son walking through a burned America toward the coast.
w: A recurring favorite on HN reading lists, praised as really good and unforgettable; one parent says it is brutal to read.
ab: Bleak, powerful post-apocalyptic novel
Short and spare, but emotionally heavy
Especially intense for parents

q.t: I just finished The Road by Cormac McCarthy a couple of weeks ago. It's really good.

t: Avogadro Corp: The Singularity Is Closer Than It Appears
s: A techno-thriller about an email-assistant AI that gains autonomy inside a tech company.
w: HN readers mention it when news echoes its plot, praising it as an entertaining AI read.
ab: For fans of near-future AI fiction
First in a series
Plausible tech-thriller

q.t: It's a great book where someone basically develops Crystal except it can compose messages too.

s: A broad electronics reference and tutorial covering components, circuits, analog and digital design, microcontrollers and projects, with practical examples.
w: HN's frequent first suggestion for people learning electronics. Commenters like that it starts from basics yet stays comprehensive, balancing practice with explanation.
ab: For beginners and hobbyists wanting a broad electronics reference
Real-world examples and problem solving, with theory included
Large, heavy book; The Art of Electronics goes deeper

q.t: I generally recommend this book for people getting started, because it teaches them how to solve specific problems with real examples.

t: A Song of Ice and Fire
s: An epic fantasy series of political intrigue, war and shifting loyalties across the continent of Westeros; the source of the TV show Game of Thrones.
w: HN commenters call it a must-read, immersive even for people who don't usually like fantasy, and say the books beat the TV show. Some note it gets slow and repetitive.
ab: Long, immersive fantasy series
Better than the TV adaptation, per fans
Slow stretches and an unfinished series

q.t: I never really liked fantasy but this series is wonderful.

t: Business Model Generation: A Handbook for Visionaries, Game Changers, and Challengers
s: A visual handbook introducing the Business Model Canvas for designing and testing business models.
w: Called mandatory reading for thinking about business models, and listed alongside Steve Blank's books and The Lean Startup. Commenters praise its design and say to read it before building something.
ab: For founders deciding what to build and for whom
Introduces the Business Model Canvas with examples
Visual and quick to skim; lighter on execution detail

q.t: It's thorough, fun to read and beautifully designed.

s: A collection of short essays on how behavior, emotion and luck shape people's relationship with money, rather than math or technical knowledge.
w: HN recommends it as a balanced, readable look at the emotional side of saving, investing and risk, and a good starting point before learning about investing. Several people call it a game-changer.
ab: For anyone who earns, saves or spends money, no finance background needed
About 20 short, story-driven chapters
Behavioral focus; not a how-to for picking investments

q.t: Psychology of Money from Morgan Housel was a game-changer. Highly recommend.

s: Apple's slim wireless keyboard with scissor-switch keys, rechargeable battery and a compact layout designed to sit flat on a desk.
w: HN commenters like its small, low-profile layout and keep using it even when they own mechanical keyboards. Short key travel suits fast typing.
ab: Compact, low-profile and wireless
Short key travel; some prefer it to mechanical boards
Less suited to people who want tactile switches

q.t: Apple Magic Keyboard Wireless. It's small and light and has decent travel.

s: An in-depth look at Clojure's idioms and the thinking behind functional programming on the JVM.
w: Called excellent but not for beginners; HN suggests it for people who already know some Clojure and want the philosophy and idioms.
ab: For intermediate Clojure programmers
Covers the why, not just the syntax
Pair with a beginner book first

q.t: Clojure: The Joy of Clojure. Not for beginners, but it's excellent.

t: The Dip: A Little Book That Teaches You When to Quit (and When to Stick)
s: A short book arguing that winners quit fast on dead ends and push through the hard stretch before success.
w: HN keeps pointing people at it when they ask whether to abandon a struggling project or keep going.
ab: For founders and side-project builders deciding to quit
Very short read
Light on specifics; one commenter was not impressed

q.t: There's a surprisingly good book by Seth Godin (sorry!) called The Dip about this dilemma.

s: A short, readable introduction to the axiomatic foundations of set theory by Paul Halmos, covering ordinals, cardinals and the axiom of choice.
w: HN names it as the best set theory book one commenter read, aimed at people heading into math who do not wish to specialize in set theory.
ab: For students who want a first look at axiomatic set theory
Compact and lightly written, around 100 pages
Not a deep treatise on advanced set theory

q.t: The best set theory book that I read was

s: A noir detective novel about a murder in two rival cities that occupy the same physical space, where citizens must "unsee" the other city.
w: HN readers pitch it as a mind-bending premise that changes how you look at borders and perception, wrapped in an engaging murder mystery. It comes up constantly in 'books that changed you' threads.
ab: For readers who like high-concept speculative fiction with a crime-novel spine
A standalone novel, so no series commitment
Best entered knowing little; HN says go in blind

q.t: The premise is great, the characters are fun, the plot will keep you engaged.

s: Zelazny's 1967 Hugo-winning novel in which colonists use technology to pose as Hindu gods, until one of them rebels as a Buddha.
w: HN sci-fi fans name it an underrated classic and one they re-read, praising Zelazny's economical, vivid prose. One says it deserves to be far better known.
ab: For readers who like mythic sci-fi and sharp prose
Mixes Hindu and Buddhist mythology with sci-fi
Zelazny's Amber series is the fantasy alternative

q.t: I don’t think this book is as half as well known in the Sci-fi genre as it should be.

t: Freakonomics: A Rogue Economist Explores the Hidden Side of Everything
by: Steven D. Levitt and Stephen J. Dubner
s: A popular economics book applying incentive-based analysis to everyday puzzles from crime and cheating to parenting and names.
w: Many HN readers credit it with changing how they think about incentives and sparking a lasting interest in economics. One reader found it a disappointment.
ab: Light, readable entry point to economic thinking
Pop-science style, not a rigorous textbook
Some claims have been challenged since publication

q.t: Great book about how and why people respond to incentives.

t: The Web Application Hacker's Handbook: Finding and Exploiting Security Flaws
s: A practical manual of web vulnerabilities, attack techniques and testing methodology.
w: The default HN pick for web security. Commenters say every page shows attacks you hadn't considered and like its practical instructions and checklist.
ab: For web developers and pen testers
Hands-on attack techniques with a checklist
Written around 2011 so some tooling is dated

q.t: Awesome book covers EVERYTHING with practical instructions + a comprehensive checklist.

s: A sales method built on research into thousands of sales calls, centered on Situation, Problem, Implication and Need-payoff questions for large, complex deals.
w: Recommended as the rare sales book grounded in research rather than scripts, especially for big B2B deals where listening and asking good questions beats pushing.
ab: For engineers and founders learning to sell to organizations
Research-based question framework for complex, high-value sales
Dated 1980s examples; theory over scripts

q.t: It's almost the only sales book based on real research.

s: A beginner-friendly discrete mathematics textbook covering logic, proofs, sets, counting, and graphs, with many worked problems and answers in the back.
w: HN self-learners suggest it as a gentle start to discrete math and proof-writing that assumes no prior knowledge, though its textbook price annoys people.
ab: For self-learners building math foundations for computer science
Assumes little background, with many exercises
Expensive new; older editions are cheaper

q.t: I really like this book, it start with the very basics

t: Blind Man's Bluff: The Untold Story of American Submarine Espionage
s: A history of secret U.S. Navy submarine spying missions during the Cold War, including cable tapping and tracking Soviet subs.
w: HN commenters bring it up for stories of submarine espionage, comparing it to Skunk Works and recommending it whenever a thread touches undersea cables, spy ships, or Cold War reconnaissance.
ab: For Cold War and military-technology fans
Narrative accounts of submarine intelligence operations
Some details are dated or based on declassified sources

q.t: Absolutely amazing stories about submarine espionage, stealth fighters but underwater.

s: Christopher Alexander's theory of architecture and the quality without a name, the basis of pattern languages.
w: Recommended as the philosophy behind patterns, and the source for software design patterns.
ab: For designers and software engineers.
Philosophy behind pattern language.
Dense.

q.t: This is the book that explains the philosophy and thinking behind all those patterns, and where I personally found the vast majority of his insight.

t: What Every BODY Is Saying: An Ex-FBI Agent's Guide to Speed-Reading People
s: A former FBI counterintelligence agent explains how to read nonverbal cues such as feet, hands, and facial expressions, and how to establish a baseline for each person.
w: HN recommends it as a practical guide to body language, valued for the baseline method and for changing how readers notice people and what they themselves signal.
ab: For readers curious about nonverbal communication and social awareness
Practical examples from the author's FBI interviewing career
Body-language reading is imperfect; treat as cues, not proof

q.t: Excellent read and be forewarned that you'll start seeing other people in a very different light.

t: First, Break All the Rules: What the World's Greatest Managers Do Differently
s: A management book based on Gallup interviews with over 80,000 managers, arguing that great managers play to individual strengths rather than fixing weaknesses.
w: HN commenters list it among the books for first-time managers and cite its finding that people leave managers, not companies. It is quoted on promotions and on why bosses get chosen badly.
ab: For first-time managers and team leads
Built on large Gallup survey data
Advice to play favorites and focus on strengths is debated

q.t: One of the most powerful sections for the book for me was

s: Apple's small desktop computer, sold without display, keyboard or mouse.
w: Recommended as a simple, compact machine for desks, media servers and home servers, and lately for local AI. Complaints focus on high prices for higher-specced RAM.
ab: For a compact desktop or home server
Display and peripherals not included
Upgrading RAM and storage costs extra

q.t: If you want something simple and standalone that just works, buy a MacMini and a DAS.

t: Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning
by: Peter C. Brown, Henry L. Roediger III et al.
s: A research-based book on effective study methods such as retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving.
w: HN recommends it in every thread about learning better. Commenters like that it backs techniques like self-quizzing and spaced repetition with actual studies, and point to it as the book version of those ideas.
ab: For students and self-learners
Evidence-backed study techniques with examples
Overlaps with spaced repetition material you may know

q.t: which details effective, proven methods to improve memorisation and learning

s: A guide to object-oriented design using Ruby.
w: Recommended as a great book for designing maintainable OO code.
ab: OO design
Ruby
Clear

q.t: It teaches you how to build OO applications that are pleasant to maintain. I highly recommend it.

s: Fitzgerald's 1925 short novel of wealth, obsession and the American dream, narrated by Nick Carraway in Jazz Age Long Island.
w: HN readers list it among favorite and most re-read novels, praising the prose and how reading and discussing it changed one dyslexic reader's reading habits.
ab: For readers wanting a short, polished American classic
Quick read at under 200 pages
Public-domain editions are widely available

q.t: The prose in Gatsby is so good.

t: The Snowball: Warren Buffett and the Business of Life
s: The authorized biography of Warren Buffett, tracing his life and investing career with Buffett's cooperation.
w: HN calls it by far the best biography of Buffett and an instructive life story for entrepreneurs and investors, showing how extreme his decades of full investment were.
ab: For readers who want to understand Buffett's life and character
Long, detailed and personal
Authorized, so occasionally flattering

q.t: This is by far the best biography on the man.

s: Robert Greene's study of how great masters in many fields reached their level, laying out apprenticeship, creative breakthroughs and practice.
w: HN readers repeatedly list it as a guide to reaching mastery in any field, one of the closest things they've found to a blueprint, though one avoids calling it life-changing.
ab: Profiles masters across history
Practical stages: apprenticeship to mastery
Popular-psychology style; examples chosen to fit the thesis

q.t: Gives you a guide on how to attain a level of mastery in a domain of knowledge.

t: The Drunkard's Walk: How Randomness Rules Our Lives
s: A popular-science history of probability and statistics showing how chance shapes success, careers, and events we explain after the fact.
w: HN recommends it as an approachable way to see how randomness and regression to the mean explain winning streaks, firings, and success stories without needing heavy math.
ab: For general readers who want probability intuition without equations
Real-world examples from sports, business, and science history
Light on rigorous math; a popular introduction

q.t: very interesting look at the math without getting too caught up in the math.

s: A deep guide to how regex engines work and how to write fast, correct patterns, centered on Perl.
w: The classic regex book. People say it made them genuinely good at regular expressions, even if it is not language specific.
ab: For developers who use regex seriously
Covers engine internals and optimization
Perl-flavored; edition is old

q.t: This helped me master regular expressions

t: The Old Man and the Sea
s: Hemingway's short novel about an aging Cuban fisherman's epic struggle to catch a giant marlin.
w: A brief classic on HN reading lists, read in one evening and praised for its gorgeous take on struggle and suffering.
ab: Short; can be read in an evening
Simple prose with deep themes
A classic of American literature

q.t: a gorgeous tale that brings to life the beauty of struggle and suffering.

s: A history of two competing visions for feeding and sustaining humanity: Borlaug's technological optimism versus Vogt's call for limits and conservation.
w: HN readers urge anyone interested in climate and technology debates to read it as a balanced meditation on tech versus restraint. One says it eased their climate anxiety.
ab: Explores tech versus conservation approaches to climate
From the author of 1491
Narrative history about Borlaug and Vogt

q.t: I absolutely cannot recommend The Wizard and the Prophet enough.

t: Ideas That Created the Future: Classic Papers of Computer Science
s: A collection of about fifty classic computer science papers with an introduction by Lewis before each one explaining its context.
w: Suggested as the way into the original computer science literature, because each paper comes with commentary. Commenters also point to the Harvard course it grew out of.
ab: For readers who want to explore foundational papers with guidance
Each paper has an introduction by Harry Lewis
Some papers are hard going

q.t: There is an introduction to each that helps explain the paper and its context.

t: When Genius Failed: The Rise and Fall of Long-Term Capital Management
s: The story of how hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management, run by Nobel laureates and star traders, collapsed in 1998 and nearly took the financial system with it.
w: The standard answer when anyone asks about LTCM or leveraged strategies blowing up. Commenters describe it as excellent and recommend it strongly whenever the fund's collapse comes up.
ab: For readers curious about finance, risk, and market blowups
Narrative history of one fund's rise and collapse
Journalistic rather than technical about the trading

q.t: I finally read it last year and it's excellent.

s: A fictionalized biography of speculator Jesse Livermore, told as stories of trading in bucket shops and on Wall Street in the early 1900s.
w: HN commenters call it one of the most recommended trading books ever and required reading for market history. They say its lessons about crowds and speculation still apply.
ab: For traders and anyone interested in market history and psychology
Readable story, not a trading manual
The annotated edition adds helpful commentary

q.t: It could have been written yesterday or a thousand years ago.

s: A near-future thriller set in a drought-stricken American Southwest where water rights are fought over by ruthless agents and corporations.
w: People bring it up whenever water scarcity, Phoenix or the Colorado River comes up, calling it prophetic and a Chinatown-meets-Mad Max read.
ab: Climate-fiction thriller set in Phoenix
Gritty and violent in tone
Pairs well with Chinatown and Cadillac Desert

q.t: The water knife becomes more prophetic every day

by: Daniel P. Friedman, David Thrane Christiansen
s: A MIT Press introduction to dependent types in the Little Schemer question-and-answer style, using a small Pie language.
w: HN recommends it as a fun, approachable introduction to dependent types, a friendlier on-ramp than Agda, Coq or Lean documentation. It is the newest of the Little series.
ab: For programmers curious about dependent types and proofs
Playful dialogue format, with a small Racket-based language
Not a practical guide to production languages

q.t: is a pretty good introduction to this topic.

t: Clean Architecture: A Craftsman's Guide to Software Structure and Design
s: Uncle Bob's guide to software architecture, covering design principles, component boundaries and dependency rules.
w: Recommended as an exploration of building systems, often alongside Clean Code and Domain-Driven Design.
ab: For developers wanting architecture ideas
Opinionated; read critically
Light on code examples

q.t: Uncle Bob has been talking about this for years, but it's a really good exploration of how to build systems.

t: Turn the Ship Around!: A True Story of Turning Followers into Leaders
s: A submarine captain's account of handing decision-making authority down the ranks and building a leader-leader culture.
w: Managers hand it to new managers as the antidote to micromanagement; HN readers cite it for pushing decisions to the people with the information.
ab: For new and aspiring managers
Short chapters built on a real Navy story
Military setting may feel remote for some teams

q.t: One of the best books I've found on this topic

s: Ten science-fiction novels set in the Culture, a post-scarcity, anarchist galactic civilization run by benevolent AI Minds; starts with Consider Phlebas.
w: A perennial answer to 'best sci-fi' threads. HN readers love Banks's style and the post-scarcity setting, and say once you start you will not be able to put it down.
ab: For fans of space opera and big ideas about utopia
Novels are mostly standalone; many start with Player of Games
Some entries are dark and violent

q.t: Love his style, love the setting, and love the stories.

s: Axelrod's study of the iterated prisoner's dilemma.
w: Recommended for the argument that cooperation is rational.
ab: Game theory
Classic
Narrow

q.t: is a great book that basically makes the case that cooperation is rational as long as there is the promise of more interaction

s: J.D. Salinger's 1951 novel narrated by teenager Holden Caulfield as he wanders New York City and rails against 'phoniness'.
w: A classic that HN commenters name among books they love and reread; some say it speaks to a teenager's disillusion, while others only mention it as high-school reading.
ab: Classic coming-of-age novel
Strong teenage voice; polarizing
Often assigned in school

q.t: the Holden Caulfield in me who couldn't tolerate all the phoniness around

t: Calculus, Vol. 1: One-Variable Calculus, with an Introduction to Linear Algebra
s: Apostol's rigorous calculus textbook covering one-variable calculus with proofs, plus an introduction to linear algebra.
w: HN math fans name Apostol as the best calculus series for learning deeply, a classic to reach for when you want rigor and proofs, not formulas.
ab: For learners who want a proof-based calculus
Rigorous treatment of limits, integration, and linear algebra
Expensive new; hard going without math maturity

q.t: If you're looking to learn calculus really well, or just brush up, these are the ones.

t: Collapse: How Societies Choose to Fail or Succeed
s: Jared Diamond examines why past societies such as Easter Island and the Norse in Greenland collapsed and what environmental choices lie behind success and failure.
w: HN commenters cite it as an exceptional, well-referenced look at environmental limits and societal collapse. It comes up in debates about population, sustainability and island civilizations.
ab: For readers interested in environmental history and sustainability
Case studies from Easter Island to modern Rwanda
Some historians dispute individual case studies

q.t: is an exceptional book on the subject, with facts and references for every claim and anecdote

s: Heinlein's 1959 military sci-fi novel about a soldier in a future infantry fighting an alien species, with controversial views on citizenship.
w: Often called an indispensable sci-fi classic, and readers note the book is very different from the movie. Its politics are debated.
ab: Classic military science fiction
Very different from the film
Politically controversial

q.t: Just read this a couple weeks ago, highly recommended.

t: Serious Cryptography: A Practical Introduction to Modern Encryption
s: Explains modern cryptographic primitives, protocols and common failure modes in practical terms, with minimal math and code examples.
w: HN security folks, including tptacek, list it among the best books on cryptography: accessible, practical on primitives and what goes wrong when they are misused.
ab: For engineers who use crypto and want to use it correctly
Light on math; not a proofs textbook
Pair with Real World Cryptography for protocols

q.t: It's one of the best and most accessible crypto books that have recently been written.

t: The Four Agreements: A Practical Guide to Personal Freedom
s: A short self-help book offering four principles for personal conduct, rooted in Toltec wisdom.
w: Recommended by a few commenters as a short book about relationships. One says its four agreements became a personal mantra that improved his interactions.
ab: For readers wanting a short self-help book on relationships
Four simple principles, quick read
Spiritual framing; light on evidence

q.t: the four agreements have become a mantra for me in almost all the relationships I have.

s: A comprehensive biography of Albert Einstein, covering his scientific discoveries, personal life and politics.
w: Repeatedly listed as one of the best books people read in a given year; one calls it an amazing journey and another praises how humane Einstein appears. It also works well as an audiobook.
ab: Accessible biography for non-physicists
Covers both science and personal life
Long; audiobook version is popular

q.t: That's an amazing journey into the

t: Seven Concurrency Models in Seven Weeks
s: A Pragmatic Programmers book surveying seven approaches to concurrency, including threads, actors, CSP and data parallelism, with hands-on examples.
w: Offered whenever someone wants a high-level overview of concurrency approaches; commenters call it pretty good and a pleasant surprise. It doesn't cover Node.js or Go specifically.
ab: Survey of concurrency models, not a deep dive
Good for developers wanting the big picture
Doesn't cover Node.js or Go directly

q.t: Seven Concurrency Models in Seven Weeks is pretty good

s: R. V. Jones's first-hand account of British scientific intelligence in World War II, including the Battle of the Beams against German radio navigation.
w: Commenters call it a spectacular, in-depth story of how technical and scientific intelligence decided battles, and say it stays relevant to anyone building technology under pressure.
ab: For readers of WWII history and technology history
First-person account from the scientist who led the counter-effort
In-depth and detailed, so not a quick read

q.t: There is a spectacular book about the Battle Of the Beams written by R. V. Jones

t: How Will You Measure Your Life?
s: Clayton Christensen applies business theories to personal life, covering career, relationships and integrity.
w: Called an incredibly good book for big life decisions and a help in introspection about why life matters. Also cited for a Dell outsourcing example.
ab: For readers weighing career and life choices
Business theory applied to personal decisions
Self-help framing may not suit everyone

q.t: This book is an incredibly good book for making this kind of decision

t: Vagabonding: An Uncommon Guide to the Art of Long-Term World Travel
s: A guide to taking extended trips around the world on a budget, and a philosophy of travel and simple living.
w: HN's go-to book for people planning long-term, cheap world travel. Commenters say it goes beyond logistics to a philosophy of living with less.
ab: For anyone planning a long trip or career break
Mixes practical tips with philosophy
Some logistical advice predates smartphones

q.t: deeper than that is a philosophy about going without things you don't need and connecting with people more authentically.

t: The True Believer: Thoughts on the Nature of Mass Movements
s: Eric Hoffer's 1951 study of why people join mass movements and fanatical causes, and what such movements share regardless of ideology.
w: HN readers call it the classic, concise guide to mass movements, useful for understanding politics and ideology across the spectrum. It's called easy to read and full of aphorisms.
ab: For readers trying to understand political and social movements
Short and aphoristic
Written in 1951; its generalizations are debated

q.t: You will see applications for the principles in this book in all aspects of society and politics.

t: In Search of Stupidity: Over 20 Years of High-Tech Marketing Disasters
s: An insider's account of marketing blunders that sank early PC software companies such as MicroPro and Ashton-Tate.
w: Recommended for early PC industry history and learning what made software companies fail.
ab: For fans of software industry history
Case-study format
Covers 1980s and 90s

q.t: It's an amazing look at the history of microcomputers and the ensuing software market

t: Emotional Intelligence: Why It Can Matter More Than IQ
s: Daniel Goleman's popular account of emotional intelligence and why it affects success at work and in life.
w: Cited as the foundational book on emotional intelligence and recommended to people struggling with interpersonal skills, no psychology background needed.
ab: For readers who want to improve interpersonal skills
Accessible without a psychology background
Popular-science treatment; some claims have been challenged

q.t: It was definitely a worthwhile read

s: A novel about a man who repeatedly relives his life from his forties, each time making different choices.
w: Recommended as a Groundhog Day on a lifetime scale about happiness. One person gifts it and suggests going in without reading plot summaries.
ab: For readers who like time-loop stories with emotional depth.
Explores regret and what makes a life well spent.
Best read without spoilers.

q.t: It's ground hog day, but on a lifetime scale. The search for happiness and what it means to be happy.

t: Let My People Go Surfing: The Education of a Reluctant Businessman
s: The Patagonia founder's memoir and business philosophy on running a company with environmental responsibility, quality and a humane workplace.
w: HN says every entrepreneur should read it as a manifesto about what a business can be, and cites the Patagonia story of growth, layoffs and focus on repair.
ab: For founders who want a values-driven company
Memoir and business philosophy in one
Patagonia-specific; limited operational detail

q.t: Every entrepreneur should read this book as it's a great manifesto about what a business can be.

t: Who Is Fourier? A Mathematical Adventure
s: A quirky illustrated course from basic arithmetic through trigonometry, calculus, and Fourier series, written by a language-learning collective.
w: HN readers rediscovering math call it an unusual gem that makes Fourier analysis intuitive, starting from basic algebra.
ab: For adults relearning math or wanting intuition for Fourier series
Starts with basic arithmetic and builds to Fourier transforms
Unusual style that some find odd; not a rigorous textbook

q.t: I was tremendously surprised by this unusual gem of a book.

s: Bastiat's 1850 essay arguing that law should protect person, liberty, and property rather than be used for plunder.
