w: HN readers cite it as an extremely good, short classic of political philosophy, readable in a weekend and listed among books that shaped their views. Mostly libertarian-leaning fans.
ab: For readers interested in classical liberal and libertarian thought
Short, about 75 pages
Public domain; many cheap editions

q.t: Weighing in at 75 pages, you can read this 176 year old classic in a weekend.

t: Computer Organization and Design: The Hardware/Software Interface
by: David A. Patterson, John L. Hennessy
s: The standard computer architecture textbook, covering instruction sets, datapaths, pipelining and memory, with MIPS, ARM and RISC-V editions.
w: HN's default recommendation for learning how CPUs work. Commenters say you can't go wrong with it for teaching assembly and processor design, and it is a standard systems architecture course text.
ab: For learning CPU and hardware fundamentals
Pick MIPS, ARM or RISC-V edition
Textbook pace; pairs with Code or Nand2Tetris beforehand

q.t: you can't go wrong with Patterson and Hennessy's Computer Organisation and Design.

s: The definitive reference to C++ by its creator, updated for C++11 with about 1,300 pages on the language and standard library.
w: Recommended as the book on C++ written by its creator, and the fourth edition is the one to get because it reflects modern practice.
ab: For people who want the authoritative reference, not a tutorial
Huge and heavy; read in pieces
Newer standards have moved on since C++11

q.t: The 4th edition of Stroustrup's classic was updated to reflect modern practices.

s: A 14-inch 2018 ThinkPad ultrabook with an Intel 8th-generation CPU, a hot-swappable battery setup and optional discrete graphics.
w: HN developers recommend it as a thin, well-built Linux and Windows laptop with one of the best keyboards, good Linux support and a cheaper alternative to the X1 Carbon. One owner warns about a keyboard failure on the T490s.
ab: For developers wanting a light, Linux-friendly ThinkPad
Choose the model without discrete GPU for cooler running
2018 hardware; buy used and check battery health

q.t: It has one of the best keyboards on any laptop I have used.

t: Bargaining for Advantage: Negotiation Strategies for Reasonable People
s: A Wharton professor's guide to negotiation that helps readers identify their own style, set goals, and prepare, using case studies and research.
w: HN's favorite negotiation book for years: commenters call it the very best they have read and a more practical follow-up to Getting to Yes.
ab: For anyone negotiating salary, deals, or contracts
Practical frameworks plus research and cases
Academic in tone

q.t: The very best negotiations book I have ever read.

s: Herman Miller's mesh ergonomic office chair, a long-running classic often bought used.
w: HN owners say it is worth the price, comfortable for hours and durable; one still uses a 2002 chair daily. Others prefer the Steelcase Leap, and buying second-hand is common advice.
ab: For people who sit at a desk all day
Expensive new; used units are common
Some find office-style chairs tiring regardless

q.t: I have an Aeron; before I had it my back started to hurt, so I picked one up -- IMHO it's worth the price.

t: 12 Rules for Life: An Antidote to Chaos
s: A self-help book of twelve life principles drawing on psychology, mythology and religion.
w: Recommended to young people looking for direction and quoted for individual lessons; commenters often tell readers to set aside what they have heard about the author.
ab: For readers seeking life advice grounded in psychology
Mixes practical advice with long mythological digressions
Polarizing author; some find it preachy

q.t: set aside all that you may have heard about the author and sincerely read

t: Homo Deus: A Brief History of Tomorrow
s: A sequel to Sapiens in which Harari speculates on how data, AI and biotechnology might reshape humanity's goals and beliefs.
w: Frequently listed among favorite reads of the year, often alongside Sapiens, with one reader calling it life-changing. A few note it is trendy and speculative.
ab: Best read after Sapiens
Big-picture speculation rather than hard evidence
Wide-ranging, easy to read popular history

q.t: Homo Deus by Yuval Noah Harari was quite the life changing book.

s: A techno-thriller about an online game hijacked by ransomware, pulling a game company founder and his family into a chase involving hackers, gold farmers and terrorists.
w: Stephenson fans regularly list it among their enjoyable reads, praising it as quite good fun that suits a Valley audience. It is a mainstream thriller rather than his densest work.
ab: Fast-paced thriller with MMO and hacker themes
Long novel, easy to read compared to his other work
Works as a standalone

q.t: Neal Stephenson's REAMDE was quite good

t: A Mind at Play: How Claude Shannon Invented the Information Age
s: A biography of Claude Shannon, the father of information theory, covering his life, inventions and playful side.
w: Recommended as the new biography of Shannon, including his toys and roulette machine.
ab: For fans of information theory history
Covers Shannon's inventions
Biography, not technical

q.t: Just yesterday I finished up a biography of Claude Shannon that I recommend to anyone that ones to learn more.

s: Kuhn's influential account of how science progresses through paradigm shifts rather than steady accumulation.
w: Frequently invoked on HN to explain stagnation and breakthroughs in fields like physics. A primary text people tell you to read directly.
ab: For anyone curious how science really changes
Short, influential, academic prose
Origin of the term paradigm shift

q.t: is worth the read

s: A book on automating build, test and deployment.
w: HN recommends it as the primer on continuous delivery. Commenters call it a great primer.
ab: For teams adopting CD
Pipeline patterns
Older tooling

q.t: Really wish I would have grabbed this years ago, great primer on what (for me) is a confusing topic.

s: Victor Hugo's 1862 epic novel of redemption, justice and revolution in nineteenth-century France, following the convict Jean Valjean.
w: HN readers call it wonderful and well worth the length, noting it covers love, redemption, justice and rebellion. They warn it rambles and is a slog in parts.
ab: For patient readers who want a sweeping classic
Very long, with digressions; read the unabridged book
The book is richer than the musical

q.t: Hugo really gives his characters space to develop and for you to care about.

by: Gerald Jay Sussman and Jack Wisdom
s: A MIT Press text that teaches differential geometry for physics using a Scheme-based computational notation, a companion to Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics.
w: Recommended to people who want to learn advanced mathematics by programming it, in the same spirit as SICP. Readers note it is free to read as open access and 'especially beautiful'.
ab: For physics-minded programmers comfortable with Scheme
Companion to Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics
Advanced math; expect to work through it

q.t: It builds up the theory of differential geometry using Scheme

s: The first Culture novel: a shapeshifting mercenary is caught up in a vast war between the utopian Culture and the religious Idirans.
w: HN sci-fi fans recommend it as the gateway into Banks's Culture universe. One reader found it well written but far longer than necessary.
ab: First book in the Culture series, though others also start fine
Space-opera war story with big ideas
Considered long and meandering by some

q.t: It's my favorite sci-fi universe of any book, movie, or game.

s: Le Guin's 1969 science-fiction novel about an envoy to a planet whose people have no fixed gender, exploring politics, loyalty and perception.
w: HN readers call it a shockingly original classic and a favorite Le Guin, a book that showed them other ways of knowing and being. It won both the Hugo and Nebula awards.
ab: For readers who like thoughtful, social science fiction
Standalone novel from the Hainish Cycle
Slow, anthropological pacing

q.t: Both taught me there are more ways of knowing (and being) than my scientific brain had realized.

t: The Cambridge Handbook of Expertise and Expert Performance
by: K. Anders Ericsson, Neil Charness et al.
s: An academic compilation of research chapters on how experts develop skill, including the work behind the 10-year and deliberate practice ideas.
w: HN cites it as the primary source behind the 10,000 hours idea. Commenters recommend going to it directly, warning it is academic rather than light reading.
ab: For readers who want the research behind deliberate practice
Many authors, many fields of expertise
Dense academic papers, not popular science

q.t: It is not lightweight entertainment reading, but it's the real deal.

s: Voltaire's 1759 satirical novella following the naive Candide through absurd misfortunes that mock philosophical optimism.
w: A short, funny classic that HN readers say made them laugh out loud and shaped their sense of humor and worldview.
ab: Very short satirical classic
Mocks blind optimism
Great first 'old book' for many

q.t: It was the first book I read for school that made me laugh out loud

t: C Programming: A Modern Approach, 2nd Edition
s: A thorough C textbook that teaches the language, including C99, through clear explanations, exercises, and guidance on organizing larger programs.
w: The most-recommended book for learning C properly on HN, praised as well suited to self-study and honest about pitfalls. Commenters call it hefty but worth it.
ab: For beginners and self-learners who want solid C fundamentals
Exercises, clear explanations, and notes on pitfalls
Long; some find it heavy going

q.t: I cannot recommend "C Programming: A Modern Approach" [1] enough.

s: A former HR executive's guide to how companies really treat employees and how to protect your career.
w: HN recommends it for the view that HR protects the company, not you.
ab: For employees facing layoffs or conflicts
Cynical but practical
Written for U.S. employment

q.t: if you work for a company, you really owe it to yourself to read Corporate Confidential.

s: Gerald Weinberg's classic study of the human side of programming: teams, egos, motivation and how programmers work.
w: Recommended for its observations on programmer behavior and teams that commenters say remain accurate decades later, such as warning about people trying to become indispensable.
ab: For programmers and managers interested in the human side of software
Written in 1971, with later commentary added
Examples come from the punch-card era

q.t: Written in 1971, and still completely relevant.

t: The Knowledge: How to Rebuild Civilization in the Aftermath of a Cataclysm
s: A thought experiment guide on how to restart civilization's key technologies after a collapse.
w: Given as a gift and recommended in threads about rebuilding technology. One commenter says it would be worth kingdoms in such a situation.
ab: For readers fascinated by how technology builds up
Covers agriculture, materials, medicine and more
Broad rather than deep

q.t: This book, for instance, would be worth kingdoms in such a situation

s: Homer's ancient Greek epic poem about the final weeks of the Trojan War and the wrath of Achilles.
w: HN readers put it on lists of must-read classics and mind-bending books, usually next to the Odyssey. Comments are brief; it is cited as foundational reading.
ab: For readers who want the foundational Western epic
Translation matters; pick one that reads well
Often paired with the Odyssey

q.t: If I had to choose myself : Homer (The Iliad and the Odyssey)

s: A biography of Leonardo da Vinci drawing on his notebooks.
w: Given as a present and called a beautiful and interesting book.
ab: For biography fans
Based on notebooks
Long

q.t: The biography of Leonardo da Vinci, a beautiful and interesting book

t: Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos: With Applications to Physics, Biology, Chemistry, and Engineering
s: An introductory textbook on nonlinear differential equations, bifurcations, chaos and fractals with applications across science.
w: HN's pick for a first book on dynamical systems. Commenters call it the best intro to nonlinear differential equations and say it changed how they saw applied math.
ab: For students who know basic calculus and differential equations
Clear, intuitive and application-driven
Covers chaos, bifurcations, fractals

q.t: the best intro book on non linear diff eq I have ever come across.

s: Nietzsche's philosophical novel in which the prophet Zarathustra preaches the Overman, eternal recurrence and the death of God.
w: HN readers list it in 'best philosophical books' and 'changed how I think' threads and call it an influential must-read. It is often paired with other works in reading lists.
ab: For readers ready to engage with Nietzsche's ideas in poetic form
Translations differ; choose one carefully
Aphoristic and difficult, not a beginner's textbook

q.t: "Thus Spoke Zarathustra" - Nietzsche (French Translation) - 5/5 An absolute Must read.

t: The Toyota Way: 14 Management Principles from the World's Greatest Manufacturer
s: An account of Toyota's management philosophy and lean manufacturing principles, organized around 14 principles.
w: HN treats it as the canonical source on Toyota's philosophy and lean thinking. Commenters point to it when lean startups, quality and the five whys come up.
ab: For managers and engineers curious about lean
Goes beyond manufacturing tactics to culture
Corporate-book style; some repetition

q.t: For those of you willing to pay for a canonical source on Toyota's philosophy, I heartily recommend The Toyota Way:

t: Software Engineering at Google: Lessons Learned from Programming Over Time
s: An O'Reilly book describing Google's engineering culture, practices and tools for keeping a large codebase maintainable over decades.
w: A few commenters suggest it for learning how big teams build software over time, though others mostly link it and ask for reviews. Treat HN's endorsement as modest.
ab: For engineers curious about large-scale practices
Describes Google's culture, tooling and testing
Some advice may not suit small teams

q.t: Have you considered the SWE book?

s: Over-ear passive hearing protection earmuffs.
w: HN recommends cheap earmuffs for blocking office noise. Commenters say they work for focus and also deter interruptions.
ab: For open offices
Passive, no electronics
Not comfortable for all-day wear

q.t: Hunting earmuffs are useful if you don't want to actually listen to music.

s: Stephen Hawking's popular introduction to cosmology, covering black holes, the Big Bang and the nature of time for general readers.
w: A staple of science reading lists on HN; commenters credit it with changing their view of the universe and making life feel more precious. One doesn't rank it among the very best.
ab: Easy popular introduction to cosmology
Some science has moved on since 1988
Short and non-mathematical

q.t: Makes my life feel ephemeral and therefore more precious

t: Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind
s: A marketing classic on how products claim a distinct place in the minds of prospects, with examples of strong and weak positioning.
w: HN founders recommend it when discussing messaging and 'X for Y' pitches. Commenters call it the best book on positioning, with dated anecdotes but solid concepts.
ab: For founders and marketers working on messaging
Short, example-driven chapters
Anecdotes are from the 1970s and 80s

q.t: This is the best book I've read on positioning.

t: Conceptual Mathematics: A First Introduction to Categories
by: F. William Lawvere, Stephen H. Schanuel
s: A gentle, exercise-driven introduction to category theory that assumes only high-school math, covering sets, maps, and categories.
w: HN programmers wanting category theory without prerequisites suggest it as an unusually accessible start, praised for being friendly enough for high-school students and for self-study.
ab: For beginners and programmers curious about category theory
Written for self-study with many exercises
Not oriented to programming or Haskell

q.t: Conceptual Mathematics is a good introduction to category theory (which is all about objects and morphisms) and especially well suited for self-study

t: The High Cost of Free Parking
s: An urban-planning classic arguing that minimum parking requirements and underpriced curb parking distort cities, raise costs and encourage driving.
w: HN cites it in zoning and urbanism threads as the standard explanation of why free parking is costly and how pricing helps.
ab: For readers interested in cities, zoning and transport
Argues for pricing curb parking and ending minimums
Long and academic; the thesis is repeated

q.t: A must read classing for anyone interested in this topic

t: Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art
s: A journalist investigates ancient and modern breathing practices and the research on how breathing affects health, sleep and stress.
w: HN commenters bring it up whenever breathing, Wim Hof or the vagus nerve come up. They like the mix of personal narrative and research and say it changed their practice.
ab: For anyone curious about breathwork, nasal breathing or stress control
Part personal story, part research summary
Popular-science style; some claims are less rigorous than the tone suggests

q.t: Highly recommend reading James Nestor's Breath

t: The Tipping Point: How Little Things Can Make a Big Difference
s: Malcolm Gladwell's popular book on how ideas, products and behaviors spread like epidemics once they pass a threshold.
w: Recommended in lists of startup books and used as shorthand for tipping point behavior in startup and growth discussions.
ab: For readers curious about how trends spread
Popular social science with many anecdotes
Some claims are simplified and not all have held up

q.t: it also talks about this same issue and is all around a great read

s: A hard space-opera novel set in a galaxy of relics from an extinct alien civilization, and the first of Alastair Reynolds' Revelation Space series.
w: HN sci-fi readers praise its creative worldbuilding and twisting plot, and often list it alongside Hyperion and the Culture. It is called an immersive read with a xenoarchaeology angle.
ab: For fans of hard space opera and big-universe worldbuilding
Series entry point; several sequels follow
Dark, intricate plotting

q.t: really creative world-building in a galactic society and an engaging, twisting plotine.

s: A catalog of patterns for enterprise application design, including unit of work, identity map, domain model and ORM approaches.
w: Recommended for learning software architecture and ORM concepts, and cited as the source for business logic living in the model.
ab: For developers designing business applications and ORMs
Pattern catalog covering persistence and domain logic
Examples from the 2000s Java and .NET era

q.t: Fowler is a great resource for this

t: What Do You Care What Other People Think?: Further Adventures of a Curious Character
s: Richard Feynman's second memoir of anecdotes, including his account of serving on the Challenger disaster commission.
w: HN recommends it as the excellent sequel to Surely You're Joking. Commenters especially like the in-depth account of how the Challenger commission's Appendix F came to be written.
ab: For Feynman fans after the first memoir
Includes the Challenger investigation
Anecdotal rather than technical

q.t: is also excellent, and includes his account of serving on the commission that investigated the Challenger disaster.

s: Comic sci-fi short stories about two robot inventors, Trurl and Klapaucius, that play with language, math and philosophy.
w: HN readers call it the most hilarious science fiction they have read and a favorite of programmers and mathematicians. Several recommend the Michael Kandel English translation.
ab: For readers who like witty, philosophical sci-fi fables
Wordplay-heavy; translation matters, per one HN reader
Short stories, easy to dip into

q.t: It's the most hilarious science fiction I've read.

s: The sequel to The Little Schemer, teaching functional programming in Scheme through question-and-answer dialogue, covering letrec, continuations and state.
w: HN recommends it as the follow-up to The Little Schemer, saying the pair lift your ability to write higher-order functional code. People who worked through all the exercises praise it.
ab: For programmers who liked The Little Schemer and want more
Interactive Q&A style with many exercises
Quirky format; read the first book first

q.t: they really up one's ability to write higher order functional (and pure functional) code

t: UNIX: A History and a Memoir
s: Kernighan's personal account of Unix's creation at Bell Labs and the people and culture around it.
w: HN recommends it as a fun, personal tour of how Unix came about and what Bell Labs was like. Commenters say it helped them understand the tools they still use today.
ab: For Unix fans and computing history readers
Covers both the technology and the personalities
A memoir, not a technical manual

q.t: by Kernighan is a really fun read

t: Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain
s: A drawing instruction book built on exercises that train you to see shapes and edges as they are rather than as symbols.
w: HN keeps recommending it to adults who want to learn to draw, saying its exercises teach seeing. One commenter warns that its dated neuroscience should be skipped past.
ab: For adults who want to learn realistic drawing
Step-by-step exercises with before and after examples
Right-brain/left-brain framing is outdated

q.t: if you are interested in learning to draw, read this book

s: An 1874 adventure novel about five castaways who use ingenuity and engineering to survive on an uncharted island.
w: HN readers recall it as a childhood favorite, praising its realism and optimistic engineer's spirit; one has reread it a dozen times.
ab: Classic castaway adventure of building from scratch
Verne's celebration of science and engineering
Victorian pacing; long technical passages

q.t: inspired by its radiant optimism about engineering advances extracting men from peril

t: Power, Sex, Suicide: Mitochondria and the Meaning of Life
s: A popular science book on how mitochondria shaped the evolution of complex life, sex, aging and cell death.
w: HN commenters call it fascinating and cite its arguments that complex multicellular life may be rare. One notes the science may be outdated.
ab: For curious readers wanting accessible cell biology and evolution
Covers energy metabolism, the origin of eukaryotes and aging
Published in 2005; newer research has moved on

q.t: a great argument that complex multicellular life is extremely rare in the universe

s: Ted Nelson's 1974 counterculture manifesto on personal computing and hypertext, printed back-to-back with Dream Machines.
w: Recommended as a fantastic, iconic read from the person who coined hypertext. Commenters suggest buying a copy because the first read is short and fun.
ab: For readers of computing history and early hypertext ideas
Quirky, hand-drawn pages from the 1974 era
Idiosyncratic layout; not a technical manual

q.t: Ted's book is fantastic, Computer Lib and Dream Machines.

s: Rudin's compact graduate-level textbook on real analysis, known as Baby Rudin.
w: Listed among the books to cover the main areas of higher math, alongside Spivak. Commenters warn it has big gaps in exposition and is not ideal for a first exposure.
ab: For math students after a rigorous real analysis text
Terse proofs, challenging exercises
Hard for self-study; not a first exposure

q.t: I'd recommend the following three books to similarly cover the three main areas of higher mathematics (analysis, algebra, and topology):

s: A near-future climate novel that follows a global agency tasked with protecting future generations, opening with a catastrophic heat wave in India.
w: HN readers call it a gripping glimpse of how climate change and policy responses like carbon coin might unfold, and say it gets into your head. One finds it less fun than other climate fiction.
ab: For readers interested in climate policy told through fiction
Opening heat-wave chapter is harrowing
Structured as essays and vignettes, not a conventional plot

q.t: Fantastic glimpse into what our future may hold.

s: Carnegie Mellon professor Randy Pausch's reflections on life and childhood dreams, written after a terminal cancer diagnosis.
w: Recommended as inspiring and eye-opening, including by someone who had already watched the lecture and still got more from the book.
ab: Short, personal and easy to read
Expands on the famous lecture
Emotional; centers on his terminal illness

q.t: I had already watched the lecture on YouTube and thought I wouldn't get much from the book but I was wrong.

s: A 15-inch 2017 Dell mobile workstation with an optional 4K display and 97Wh battery, sold with Ubuntu preinstalled as a developer edition.
w: HN developers recommend it as the Linux-friendly cousin of the XPS 15, running Arch and Ubuntu without trouble, with a good backlit keyboard. Battery life with discrete graphics is shorter than the XPS 13.
ab: For developers wanting a powerful 15-inch Linux laptop
Developer Edition shipped with Ubuntu
2017 hardware; buy used and check battery

q.t: I use a Dell Precision 5520 as my daily driver and have been very impressed.

t: The Moral Animal: Evolutionary Psychology and Everyday Life
s: A popular introduction to evolutionary psychology, using Darwin's life and modern research to explain human behavior, relationships and morality.
w: Cited when HN discusses human nature, sex and morality as the readable evolutionary psychology book. Commenters point to it as evidence that science now studies morality.
ab: For readers curious about evolutionary psychology
Uses Darwin's biography to illustrate the ideas
From 1994, so parts of the research are dated

s: Dell's line of high-end business laptops and mobile workstations with professional graphics, ECC options and Ubuntu-supported configurations.
w: HN developers recommend Precision laptops as strong non-Apple development machines, available with Ubuntu preinstalled and cheaper refurbished. They can cost as much as MacBooks, and one commenter says the keyboard and power wear out by year two.
ab: For developers wanting a powerful Windows or Ubuntu workstation laptop
Refurbished units are a good-value option
Expensive new; durability comments are mixed

q.t: the Dell Precision line (the business workstation-replacement line) is exceptional for development

s: Chad Fowler's collection of short career-advice chapters for software developers on becoming remarkable, staying relevant and marketing yourself.
w: HN names it a quick, nugget-filled career book, recommended with The Pragmatic Programmer and Clean Coder. One reader found it disappointing, like a series of blog posts.
ab: For developers thinking about career direction
Short chapters; reads like blog posts to some
Second edition of 'My Job Went to India'

q.t: are both excellent books on making a career out of writing software.

s: A beginner's guide that builds a simple Python neural network from scratch to recognize handwritten digits, with a gentle explanation of the needed math.
w: HN readers recommend it to anyone who sees neural nets as magic, because it uses minimal math, gentle calculus, and working code to explain backpropagation.
ab: For programmers new to neural networks
Builds a one-hidden-layer Python network on handwritten digits
Basic networks only; not deep learning or modern frameworks

q.t: I had my own neural nets working before I touched a framework, and it demystified what would have otherwise seemed like black magic.

t: The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking
s: An argument that bitcoin is sound money, tracing the history of money and criticizing central banking and inflation.
w: HN bitcoin fans give it as the quick, readable case for bitcoin's scarcity and role as reserve asset. It is advocacy rather than neutral analysis.
ab: For readers wanting the pro-bitcoin economic argument
Short history of money, gold and central banking
Partisan; skeptics dispute its economics

q.t: For a relatively quick read with an alternative perspective, check out The Bitcoin Standard

t: Eloquent JavaScript, 3rd Edition: A Modern Introduction to Programming
s: An introduction to programming through JavaScript, covering language fundamentals, browser and Node.js projects, and the art of controlling complexity.
w: HN names it the go-to JavaScript book for beginners and lower-intermediate readers, with enough rigor for a good base. Its literary tone suits creative people new to coding, and the author hosts it free online.
ab: For beginners and developers wanting a solid JavaScript foundation
Free to read online; print copy available
Move on to You Don't Know JS for depth

q.t: I love giving this to creative people who are interested in coding.

s: A Culture novel with two interwoven timelines following a mercenary agent, famous for its structure and a devastating twist ending.
w: HN readers praise it as a master class in interwoven narrative with a nice twist, and many list it among favorite fiction books. One reader found it left a bad taste.
ab: For readers who like complex, non-linear science fiction
Can be read without prior Culture books
Contains dark, violent material

q.t: Use of Weapons by Iain M Banks - master of the interwoven narrative

s: Richard Dawkins's argument for atheism and critique of religion, covering evolution, morality and belief.
w: Frequently named in HN reading lists as gripping non-fiction. One commenter called it blunt and mean but convincing, another says it made them an arrogant atheist.
ab: Strong, polemical case against religion
Blunt tone; some readers find it abrasive
Popular among nonfiction readers

q.t: Very blunt and mean. But also convincing...

t: The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich: A History of Nazi Germany
s: William Shirer's 1960 comprehensive history of Nazi Germany, written by a journalist who reported from Berlin during the rise of the regime.
w: HN names it a classic and one of the most comprehensive works on Nazi Germany, chilling but rereadable, and a common gift for history fans. Readers value the firsthand perspective of a western reporter who was there.
ab: For readers wanting a sweeping narrative of the Third Reich
Very long; written in the 1960s
Later scholarship has refined some of its claims

q.t: The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich was chilling but I'd read it again.

t: Rapid Development: Taming Wild Software Schedules
s: A 1996 guide to software project management that catalogs schedule risks, best practices and estimation approaches for development teams.
w: HN lists it as an overlooked McConnell book alongside Code Complete and Software Estimation, recommended as an encyclopedia of project management. Commenters note that it predates Scrum and Agile.
ab: For team leads and managers who estimate software projects
Encyclopedia of practices, risks and schedule tactics
Pre-Agile (1996); some advice is dated

q.t: Although it's 20 years old, it has some good ideas in it.

t: Mathematical Notation: A Guide for Engineers and Scientists
s: A compact reference that explains the symbols and conventions used across mathematics, so readers can decode formulas in papers and textbooks.
w: HN readers who struggle to read math in papers recommend it as a Rosetta stone for notation. It is repeatedly called helpful and reasonably priced.
ab: For engineers and programmers reading math-heavy papers
A lookup guide to symbols and conventions
A glossary, not a path to learning the math itself

q.t: I've been able to walk through papers that I never would have understood without this rosetta stone.

s: Paul Hawken's 1988 guide to starting and running a small company, drawn from his experiences founding natural foods and other businesses.
w: HN founders call it one of the best books on starting a business, with timeless advice like bootstrapping and treating sales staff well, anticipating ideas that 37signals later made popular.
ab: For bootstrappers and small-business founders
Down-to-earth lessons on self-funding and customers
Dated references; stories come from the 1980s

q.t: hands down one of the best books on starting a business I have read.

s: A 1995 novel told through diary entries by Microsoft employees who leave to start a company, capturing 1990s tech culture and relationships.
w: HN brings it up as a quaint snapshot of a moment in tech and as a reminder that life is more than work, from people who miss that era.
ab: For readers nostalgic for 1990s tech culture
Epistolary, quirky novel
Strong period feel; some will find it dated

q.t: That was an amazing moment in time and I miss it.

s: Robert Caro's multi-volume biography of Lyndon B. Johnson, tracing his rise from Texas Hill Country poverty through Congress to the presidency.
w: HN treats it as the definitive study of how political power is gained and used in the US. Fans say they reread the whole series and call it the best books they have read.
ab: For readers who want deep, narrative political history and biography
Several large volumes; a big time commitment
Described as dense but gripping

q.t: The best books I've ever read. I effectively re-read them all every year or two.

t: Debugging: The 9 Indispensable Rules for Finding Even the Most Elusive Software and Hardware Problems
s: A short book of nine general rules for debugging software and hardware systematically.
w: Called the best general-purpose debugging book and one person's number-one recommendation for engineers. Commenters like that it is short and applies to any technology problem.
ab: For developers and engineers who want a debugging method
Short and readable
Not language specific; light on tools

q.t: It's short and sweet and applies to any technology problem.

s: A compact introduction to Haskell and functional programming by a University of Nottingham professor.
w: Suggested on lists of functional programming books and for monadic parsing.
ab: For Haskell beginners
Concise and clear
Not a deep practical guide

q.t: If someone is interested in Functional Programming, here are the books which I highly suggest everyone to read

s: David Wong's Manning book explaining the cryptography used in real systems, from TLS to key management, for practitioners.
w: Recommended on HN, including by Thomas Ptacek, as a readable, applied intro that doesn't drown you in math. Note the author also posted about it himself.
ab: For developers wanting applied crypto without heavy math
Covers modern protocols and pitfalls
Pair with Serious Cryptography

q.t: I've read Real World Cryptography and greatly enjoyed it.

t: The Old New Thing: Practical Development Throughout the Evolution of Windows
s: A collection of Raymond Chen's essays on Windows history, design decisions and backward-compatibility quirks.
w: Recommended for stories of why Windows works the way it does, including how much effort went into backward compatibility.
ab: For Windows developers and history fans
Anecdote-driven; read in short bursts
Blog posts are free, the book collects them

q.t: was a huge part of ensuring that everything was backwards compatible

s: A modular, repairable laptop from Framework with swappable ports, upgradeable memory and storage, and good Linux support.
w: HN commenters suggest it as the Linux option for people not buying a MacBook, valuing repairability and x86 compatibility. Reviews warn to check the current generation, and some are waiting on a matte screen.
ab: Modular and user-repairable; good for Linux users
Comments say to check reviews for the current generation
Battery life concerns mentioned by some

q.t: I would get a machine like Framework laptop with Linux.

s: Apple's touchscreen tablet line, used with the Apple Pencil for drawing and with apps for reading.
w: HN commenters name it as a source of calm drawing, reading PDFs, and apps like Procreate, and as the preferred device for young kids or non-technical parents.
ab: For reading, sketching and note-taking
Best with Apple Pencil and good apps
Locked-down OS limits some uses

q.t: I can access the ever-elusive flow state by drawing/sketching/coloring

s: A short experimental novel in which Marco Polo describes fantastical cities to Kublai Khan, each one a meditation on memory, desire and civilization.
w: HN readers recommend it as a poetic, layered little book about complexity, memory and storytelling, short enough to read quickly but hard to describe. It shows up in lists of favorite fiction.
ab: For readers who like poetic, idea-driven fiction
Very short, structured as a series of city vignettes
No conventional plot, which some find abstract

q.t: so layered that I actually have a hard time describing it

s: A dystopian novel about an employee at a powerful internet company whose push for total transparency erodes privacy.
w: HN recommends it as a cautionary tale about surveillance and tech culture. Opinions on the writing are mixed, but commenters praise it for provoking thought about privacy and sharing.
ab: For readers interested in privacy and tech dystopia
Provocative premise, thin characters
Some HN readers found the execution weak

q.t: I give it 5 stars for provoking thoughts about hyper-connectedness, net neutrality, surveillance, over-sharing on social networks

s: The 1986-87 graphic novel in which retired costumed heroes investigate a murder amid Cold War tension, deconstructing the superhero genre.
w: HN readers recommend it as the graphic novel that proves comics can handle ethics, morality and philosophy, and many reread it every few years. It is a common gateway for people returning to reading.
ab: For readers who want serious, layered storytelling in comic form
Complete in one volume
Dense with symbolism; best read slowly

q.t: It may be a graphic novel, but the issues it raises on ethics and morality are chilling.

s: A Pulitzer-winning comic novel about the slothful, pompous Ignatius J. Reilly and his misadventures in 1960s New Orleans.
w: HN readers call it a wonderful reread and a top-five book, praising its mix of tragedy, comedy and unforgettable characters. Michael Lewis's favorite novel is also noted, though the antihero bothers some.
ab: For readers who like satirical, character-driven comic novels
The lead is an antihero some find grating
The backstory of its posthumous publication is poignant

q.t: amazing book! tragedy, comedy, insane characters, really good book!

s: Orson Scott Card's 1986 sequel to Ender's Game, in which a speaker investigates a murder on a colony world inhabited by an alien species.
w: HN sci-fi readers rank it as fascinating alien-contact fiction and, for some, even better than Ender's Game. It won back-to-back Hugo and Nebula awards with its predecessor.
ab: For readers who liked Ender's Game and want deeper, slower sci-fi
A very different tone from the first book
Card is a polarizing author; later sequels divide readers

q.t: Speaker for the Dead is even better, and my favorite science fiction novel of all time

t: Are Your Lights On?: How to Figure Out What the Problem Really Is
by: Donald C. Gause, Gerald M. Weinberg
s: Short, witty book on defining the right problem before solving it, told through stories and exercises on perception and decision-making.
w: HN recommends it as a starting point for Gerald Weinberg's writing. Fans say it profoundly changed how they approach problems, and it appears on non-technical must-read lists.
ab: For anyone who solves problems for others, engineers and consultants
Short, humorous and anecdotal
Written in 1982 but not tied to technology

q.t: I particularly recommend 'Are Your Lights On?' as a place to get started

s: Mary Shelley's 1818 Gothic novel about a scientist who creates a living being and abandons it, often called the first science fiction novel.
w: Readers say it is nothing like its pop-culture image: superb, very readable science fiction whose warning feels sharper in the age of AI.
ab: Gothic classic and early science fiction
Quite different from movie versions
Short and readable in modern editions

q.t: Superb science fiction, very readable even though written 200 years ago.

t: Unlocking the Clubhouse: Women in Computing
s: A research study from Carnegie Mellon on why fewer women than men pursue computer science, based on interviews with students over several years.
w: Whenever HN debates women in tech, commenters offer this as the actual research on the topic, showing the gap stems from early socialization and access rather than aptitude.
ab: For anyone curious why CS has a gender gap
Interview-based academic study with direct student quotes
Dated, based on 1990s CMU data; conclusions are still discussed

q.t: is an excellent book on this topic

t: The Field Guide to Understanding 'Human Error'
s: A guide to safety investigation arguing that so-called human error is a symptom of systemic trouble, not a cause, and how to learn from accidents.
w: HN recommends it, often repeatedly, in postmortem and blameless-culture discussions. It gives a vocabulary for why blaming individuals is lazy and what to ask about systems instead.
ab: For SREs, engineers and managers running incident reviews
Draws on aviation, medicine and industrial accidents
Academic in tone; newer editions exist

q.t: Please consider reading Sidney Dekker's books, The Field Guide to Understanding Human Error[1] and Drift Into Failure[2]

t: How Would You Move Mount Fuji?
s: A book on puzzle interviews at Microsoft and similar companies and the ideas behind them.
w: HN readers point to it for background on puzzle-style interviews and IQ testing. Commenters call it detailed and recommend it to anyone facing such interviews.
ab: For interview prep and history of hiring puzzles
Covers Microsoft's puzzle culture
Dated; puzzle interviews have fallen out of favor

q.t: a detailed book on the topic of IQ, puzzles, and job interviews

s: A Manning guide to the Nim programming language, covering syntax, concurrency and building real projects such as a chat app and a web app.
w: HN Nim users point newcomers to this book by a core Nim developer. Commenters say it gets you running with Nim and teaches concepts from first principles, and a free chapter is available.
ab: For programmers who want to learn Nim
Written by a core Nim team member
Targets Nim 0.x; language details have changed since

q.t: Really good book overall and helps get you up and running with Nim concepts.

s: Thomas Mann's 1924 novel about a young man who visits a Swiss sanatorium for three weeks and stays for seven years, immersed in debates about life, illness and time.
w: Readers say it stays with you for years and rewards rereading, with one calling it life-changing. It's slow on a first read.
ab: Dense, slow, philosophical German classic
Rewards patient or repeat readings
Considered Mann's top pick by some

q.t: It's an incredible book. It changed my life (really).

s: Heinlein's 1973 novel following Lazarus Long, a centuries-old man who has outlived everyone, as he looks back on his many lives.
w: Repeatedly named as a favorite and life-changing book on HN. One commenter says four people he recommended it to made it their new favorite, and others say it shaped their view of culture and freedom.
ab: For fans of classic big-idea sci-fi
Episodic, with philosophical tangents on love and society
Some readers find it scandalous; 1970s attitudes show

q.t: I've recommended it to four people and all came back with it being their new favorite book.

by: Charles W. Misner, Kip S. Thorne
s: The graduate textbook on general relativity by Misner, Thorne and Wheeler, famous for its size and geometric approach.
w: HN treats it as the bible of general relativity: huge, in print since 1973, and unparalleled in scope and depth even if its experimental sections have aged.
ab: For serious students of general relativity
Over 1,200 pages and very heavy
Experimental data are behind the times

q.t: it is still unparallelled in scope and depth today

t: The Rise and Fall of American Growth
s: An economic history of US living standards from 1870 on, arguing that the great inventions of that era drove growth that later slowed.
w: Recommended as an objective overview of the huge jump in living standards from 1870 to 1970, and as the book-length version of the stagnation argument.
ab: For readers curious why growth slowed after 1970
Long and data-heavy, with plenty of social history
Argues a contested pessimistic thesis

q.t: I would recommend Gordon's book as an objective overview of the astonishing growth in economic and quality of life terms from 1870-1970.

t: Release It!: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software
s: A book on stability patterns, such as circuit breakers and bulkheads, for building production systems.
w: Credited as the original source of the circuit breaker pattern and called an excellent proto-devops book.
ab: For engineers running production services
Stories of real outages
Examples are Java-flavored

q.t: I first read about this in the excellent book Release it!

s: A productivity book that argues for focusing on a single most important priority at a time.
w: Recommended to people overwhelmed by tasks or side projects, for its focus-on-one-thing question.
ab: For people with too many priorities
Simple, repeatable focus question
Self-help style, light on evidence

q.t: I recommend the book The ONE Thing, Gary Keller

s: A narrative history of corrosion, the people fighting rust and its cost to industry and infrastructure.
w: Recommended for being an interesting story about stainless steel and corrosion, despite the weak title.
ab: For engineering and materials fans
Narrative non-fiction
Not about the Rust language

q.t: Rust - The Longest War; is a book about this topic, very insightful read.

t: Managing Gigabytes: Compressing and Indexing Documents and Images
s: A reference on compression and full-text indexing for large collections of text and images, covering inverted indexes, coding methods, and retrieval.
w: HN search and database people plug it whenever the topic comes up as a great reference on indexing and compression. One notes it is a bit outdated.
ab: For engineers building search or compression systems
Rigorous treatment of indexes and coding
Dated in places; the fundamentals still apply

q.t: I always have to plug Managing Gigabytes whenever a discussion of computer books comes up.

by: David Money Harris, Sarah L. Harris
s: A textbook covering digital logic, hardware description languages and CPU architecture, building up to a MIPS processor.
w: Recommended as a great intro before tackling FPGAs, with Verilog/VHDL examples, and a handy way to learn MIPS assembly.
ab: For learners moving from logic gates to a working CPU
Covers both Verilog and VHDL
Older editions use MIPS; newer have RISC-V/ARM

q.t: this book is a great intro with examples in verilog/hdl

s: John Williams's 1965 novel about the quiet life of William Stoner, a Missouri farm boy who becomes an unremarkable English professor.
w: HN readers call it a slow-burn, tender portrait of an average life, and say the prose is moving enough to read in one sitting. It appears in lists of best unknown classics.
ab: For readers who enjoy quiet, character-driven literary fiction
Slow pacing; a muted tragedy
A recent revival made it better known

q.t: I recently read Stoner by John Williams. Would recommend.

t: Joe Celko's SQL for Smarties: Advanced SQL Programming
s: A reference on advanced SQL techniques and database design by Joe Celko, covering set-based thinking, normalization and tricky queries.
w: HN's classic suggestion for going beyond basic SQL. Commenters call it a book that keeps its value because SQL fundamentals and schema design have not changed much.
ab: For developers who know basic SQL
Teaches set-based thinking and schema design
Older edition examples vary by SQL dialect

q.t: I highly recommend SQL for Smarties.

t: Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan
s: Applied Bayesian statistics textbook that builds intuition for multilevel models, priors and causal inference with R and Stan code and a companion lecture series.
w: HN data people call it the most accessible intro to Bayesian statistics and an uncommonly readable stats textbook. One says it changed how they think about statistics.
ab: For analysts and programmers learning Bayesian statistics
Examples in R, Stan; the 2nd edition is newer
Free lectures online; needs some algebra

q.t: This is widely regarded as the most accessible intro textbook to Bayesian statistics.

t: The New Turing Omnibus: Sixty-Six Excursions in Computer Science
s: A collection of 66 short, accessible chapters on topics across computer science, from algorithms and complexity to AI and cryptography.
w: HN recommends it as an easy overview of computer science that isn't a textbook. Commenters say it gives a nice survey of many topics, with some chapters harder than others.
ab: For self-taught programmers filling CS gaps
Short standalone chapters
From 1993; some topics feel dated

q.t: to give a really nice overview of a bunch of topics, some chapters were a lot harder to follow than others

by: Martin Logan, Eric Merritt et al.
s: A guide to Erlang's OTP framework for building fault-tolerant, concurrent and distributed systems.
w: The book to read after learning basic Erlang, for OTP's patterns and for building robust systems. Commenters recommend it for Elixir learners too.
ab: For developers learning Erlang or Elixir who want OTP
Short read focused on robust system design
Written in 2011; OTP details have evolved

q.t: It's a reasonably short read and will make you think through what needs to happen to build a robust system

t: Goliath: The 100-Year War Between Monopoly Power and Democracy
s: A history of American monopoly power and antitrust from the Gilded Age to today's tech giants.
w: HN readers point to it as a solid history of how US monopolies formed and why antitrust faded after the 1970s, useful context for today's tech dominance.
ab: For readers curious how antitrust policy shaped modern tech giants
Narrative history spanning a century of US monopoly politics
One commenter disagrees with parts but values the core argument

q.t: his main argument was that business monopoly and democracy are in direct opposition

t: Modern Fortran: Building Efficient Parallel Applications
s: A Manning book teaching modern Fortran, including derived types, collective subroutines and building a parallel neural network.
w: HN readers recommend it as the book to read if you want to learn current Fortran, saying the others assume old-style Fortran. Several bought a copy on release.
ab: For scientists and engineers picking up modern Fortran
Covers parallel programming with coarrays
Author is active in the Fortran community

q.t: Modern Fortran by Milan Curcic seems to be a pretty good book.

s: Historical epic based on the life of Miyamoto Musashi, the 17th-century samurai who became Japan's most famous swordsman.
w: HN readers call it life-changing and inspiring, citing its themes of discipline and finding your path. Several wish they had read it earlier; one went to it after reading the Vagabond manga.
ab: For readers who want an epic samurai novel with life lessons
Over 900 pages, originally a serial
Fiction rather than a biography

q.t: Highly recommended for anyone who has discipline problems, it is really inspiring, one of the top 3 books I've read.

s: The first novel in the Aubrey-Maturin series, following Royal Navy captain Jack Aubrey and physician Stephen Maturin in the Napoleonic era.
w: HN readers re-read the series for its writing, character depth and humor rather than the sea battles. It is a 20-book commitment that fans call a lifelong companion.
ab: For readers who like long historical series
Prized for prose and characters over battles
Heavy on period naval detail

q.t: Exquisite writing, funny, interesting, deep characters and chock full of interesting philosophy and life observations.

s: Murakami's realistic coming-of-age novel about love, loss, and student life in 1960s Tokyo.
w: HN readers recommend it as a light introduction to Murakami and a book that left a strong impression in their youth. Others suggest following it with Wind-Up Bird Chronicle.
ab: For readers new to Murakami
Realistic, with none of his usual magical elements
Melancholic themes including loss and depression

q.t: Norwegian Wood made a big impression on me as a young man in my late teens.

s: An introduction to Taoism that uses Winnie-the-Pooh and friends to illustrate its ideas about simplicity and living naturally.
w: HN readers cite it as a gentle first look at Eastern philosophy that shaped how they think, calling it accessible and delightful. Some note it is a simplified, fictionalized introduction.
ab: For readers new to Taoism
Short, light, and easy to read
A simplified take, not a scholarly one

q.t: a delightful introduction into Taoism that opened my mind to eastern philosophy as a young adult

t: What I Talk About When I Talk About Running
s: Haruki Murakami's memoir about running and writing, with reflections on discipline, aging and his life as a novelist.
w: HN readers pick it as a short memoir about running and writing, and one says it was their first Murakami and a pleasing introduction to the author.
ab: For runners and writers curious about Murakami's habits
Short memoir; essay-like
More about discipline than training advice

q.t: it's my first book from H. M. and I really liked it.

s: John McPhee's profile of Theodore Taylor, the physicist who designed small nuclear weapons and worried about nuclear terrorism.
w: Called excellent by commenters; also cited for the history of plutonium sales and nuclear power subsidies.
ab: Profile of a weapons designer turned nuclear-safety campaigner
McPhee's clear reporting style
Cold War era; some details are decades old

q.t: "The Curve of Binding Energy: A Journey into the Awesome and Alarming World of Theodore B. Taylor" is excellent as well

t: Buffett: The Making of an American Capitalist
s: A biography of Warren Buffett that traces his career and the specific analyses behind his investments.
w: Recommended as the best way to learn how Buffett actually invested, via real anecdotes rather than theory. One commenter also likes it over a rival Buffett biography as an easier read.
ab: For readers who want investing lessons told through a biography
Detailed anecdotes about specific deals and analyses
Ends in the 1990s, so recent decades are missing

q.t: Nobody can invest like Buffett, but just about everyone can benefit from reading about how he did it.

s: IBM's 1980s buckling-spring keyboard, built like a tank and still used today; Unicomp makes new Model M-style keyboards.
w: HN owners love the tactile typing feel and durability, with some using units over thirty years old. Critics call it very loud and unnecessary in 2023, and say it is poor for gaming.
ab: Heavy, durable and very loud buckling-spring switches
Great typing feel, poor for gaming; lacks a Windows key
Unicomp sells new versions

q.t: the 2nd one that I will use when the 1st one breaks, which probably means never.

t: On Lisp: Advanced Techniques for Common Lisp
s: Paul Graham's book on advanced Common Lisp techniques, especially macros and bottom-up programming.
w: Treated as a classic of Lisp macro programming and cited when discussing Lisp's strengths. Mentions here are brief links.
ab: For Lisp programmers ready to learn macros and bottom-up design
Freely available online as well
Focused on Common Lisp

s: Dell's business-class laptop line, often bought used or refurbished, with good build quality and broad Linux support.
w: HN commenters recommend a used Latitude as a cheap, durable Linux laptop that is easy to upgrade. One user says Latitudes with Ubuntu beat the XPS for them.
ab: Business-grade build; cheap when bought used
Generally works well with Linux
Line spans many generations; check the specific model

q.t: Dell Latitude, HP EliteBook or Lenovo ThinkPad. All work well with Linux and have good support and/or can be purchased with additional warranty.

s: A history of human civilization told through energy sources and conversion, from foraging and farming to fossil fuels and electricity, published by MIT Press.
w: HN recommends it for understanding how energy underpins everything, from agriculture to nuclear debates. Readers call it engrossing despite being dry and data-dense, and it is cited in energy-policy arguments.
ab: For readers who want a rigorous long view of energy and history
Dense with raw data; dry in places
Expanded and revised from Smil's earlier Energy in World History

q.t: I highly recommend Energy and Civilization[1], the most engrossing dry recitation of facts I've ever read.

t: Atomic Accidents: A History of Nuclear Meltdowns and Disasters: From the Ozark Mountains to Fukushima
s: A history of nuclear accidents told by a nuclear engineer, from early reactor mishaps through Chernobyl and Fukushima.
w: HN regulars recommend it as a favorite on atomic energy. Commenters say it is well written for laypeople, engineering-minded, and surprisingly leaves readers less afraid of nuclear power.
ab: For readers interested in nuclear safety and engineering
Written for laypeople by a nuclear engineer
Covers accidents from the 1800s to Fukushima

q.t: it turned out to be FANTASTIC, would highly recommend if you have any interest in nuclear accidents or nuclear energy in general

t: The Talent Code: Unlocking the Secret of Skill in Sports, Art, Music, Math, and Just About Anything
s: A look at how skill develops through deep practice, ignition and coaching, drawing on talent hotbeds around the world.
w: Recommended as a companion to deliberate practice research. HN readers like its three-part framework for mastering new skills.
ab: For learners and coaches
Anecdote-driven with some neuroscience
Myelin claims have been questioned

q.t: The author finds places around the world that produce a lot of top talent and tells how they do it.

t: Lenovo ThinkPad Compact USB Keyboard with TrackPoint
s: A slim wired USB keyboard with a built-in TrackPoint pointing stick and the ThinkPad key feel.
w: Favored by people who want a slim keyboard with a TrackPoint so their hands never leave the home row. Not mechanical, which one commenter noted.
ab: For TrackPoint fans wanting a desktop keyboard
Slim, no number pad
Not a mechanical keyboard

q.t: I can't live without a TrackPoint because I never have to leave the home row with it!

s: A practical O'Reilly guide to managing interruptions, to-do lists and priorities, written for the constant context-switching of sysadmin and ops work.
w: Repeatedly recommended in time-management threads as a workable system that helped people take control of interrupt-driven jobs, useful beyond sysadmins too.
ab: For sysadmins, ops and anyone interrupt-driven
Takes discipline to apply the system
Author also co-wrote the classic sysadmin 'bible'

q.t: Just following it for a short time made my work & life a whole, whole lot better.

t: Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World
s: A history of Genghis Khan and the Mongol empire that argues the Mongols helped shape the modern world.
w: HN commenters point to it for a more nuanced view of the Mongols than warlord stereotypes, stressing their influence on trade and Eurasia.
ab: For readers of world history
Revisionist, positive take on the Mongols
Some historians dispute its framing

q.t: For an interesting historical perspective of the interaction, check "Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World" by Jack Weatherford

t: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
s: Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel about a bounty hunter retiring rogue androids in a ruined future Earth, the basis of the film Blade Runner.
w: HN readers list it with the best of classic sci-fi. Some say the book blew them away and is much better than the film; others prefer the movie.
ab: Differs a lot from Blade Runner; worth reading either way
Short, idea-rich classic
Strong on empathy and what it means to be human

q.t: Blew me away. So much better than the film adaptation.

t: Traffic: Why We Drive the Way We Do (and What It Says About Us)
s: A popular-science book on the psychology, engineering, and behavior behind driving, congestion, and traffic patterns.
w: Offered whenever traffic jams or driver behavior come up. HN readers call it an engaging, readable alternative to blog posts on the subject and cover traffic waves and bus findings.
ab: For curious readers interested in driver behavior and traffic flow
Anecdotes and research written for a general audience
Popular-science tone, not a technical traffic-engineering text

q.t: There's an interesting book on the topic, focusing on the way human behavior affects traffic patterns.

t: Don't Make Me Think, Revisited: A Common Sense Approach to Web Usability
s: A short, illustrated introduction to web usability that explains how people scan pages and how to design sites that need no thought.
w: HN gives it as the place to start for developers learning UX, often in reading lists beside The Design of Everyday Things. It is brief and practical.
ab: For developers and founders designing their own web UI
Quick read with many illustrated examples
Web focus; mobile and modern app patterns get less coverage

q.t: by Steve Krug is a great place to start.

t: 21st Century C: C Tips from the New School
s: A guide to modern C practice, covering tooling like git, autotools and valgrind plus libraries like GLib, SQLite, libxml and cURL.
w: HN recommends it for learning how modern C is actually written. Commenters value its focus on tooling and libraries as a follow-up to K&R, though some warn of mixed reviews.
ab: For C programmers beyond K&R
Teaches tooling and common libraries
Some HN readers found reviews mixed

q.t: This book teaches you modern C techniques and, most importantly, the tooling that modern C programmers use

s: Apple's true wireless earbuds with easy iPhone pairing, a charging case and, in later models, noise cancellation.
w: HN commenters love them for being cordless and light, and for onboarding that just works. They are generally recommended for everyday use and exercise, with over-ear headphones for heavy noise cancelling.
ab: Very light and comfortable for long wear
Seamless pairing with Apple devices
Over-ear Bose/Sony still beat them for noise cancelling

q.t: AirPods. Eliminating the cord changed my exercise and my life.

s: Lenovo's 15-inch premium ThinkPad with high-power Intel CPUs, optional discrete graphics and a 4K display, positioned between the X1 Carbon and the P1.
w: HN developers use it for years with Pop!_OS and Ubuntu, praising its build quality, keyboard and easy battery and drive replacement. It is pricey and uses a fast CPU, and one commenter has reservations about Lenovo.
ab: For developers wanting a powerful 15-inch Linux laptop
Up to 64 GB RAM and a 4K display
Pricey; heavier than the X1 Carbon

q.t: I am happy with my Lenovo X1 extreme running pop os.

s: A comprehensive graduate textbook covering machine learning from a probabilistic and Bayesian viewpoint, with graphical models, kernels, and deep learning.
w: HN lists it among the big textbooks for machine learning, with one reader calling it the best they found and others naming it a go-to reference.
ab: For graduate students and engineers who want one ML reference
Wide coverage built on probability and Bayesian methods
Big and dense; newer Murphy books update the material

q.t: is the best book I have found so far

s: A near-future science-fiction novel set in a world of ubiquitous wearable augmented reality, following a recovering poet and a tangled plot over information control and security.
w: HN likes it as an early blueprint for ubiquitous computing, AR and digital security hygiene, and an easy read with real ideas for programmers. It is also cited for its view of AI and education.
ab: For tech people who like near-future fiction about augmented reality
Written in 2006, so some tech is now reality
Idea-heavy; one reader calls it an easy read

q.t: I liked Rainbows Edge because in addition to a nifty story, it felt like a blueprint or use case for the near future.

t: Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals
s: A critique of productivity culture arguing that the average human life is about four thousand weeks and that we should accept our limits rather than try to do everything.
w: HN recommends it as the counter-argument to productivity literature, a book that helped readers rethink what they choose to do and not do. It's called more of a kick in the pants than an inspirational read.
ab: For people burned out by productivity systems and to-do lists
Philosophical and practical rather than a method
Light on tactics; not a time-management how-to

q.t: It's more of a kick in the pants than an inspirational book

t: Uvex S1933X Orange Anti-Fog Safety Glasses
s: Inexpensive orange-tinted safety glasses with anti-fog coating, used by many people to block blue light in the evening.
w: HN's cheap, blunt answer to blue-light blocking before bed. Several commenters say these $8 to $10 glasses work better than pricey options, though they look goofy.
ab: For people trying to cut evening blue light to sleep better
Cheap, durable, orange lenses that block blue light strongly
Look odd and tint everything orange

q.t: These $9 orange safety glasses have worked extremely well for me over the past few years

s: A short guide to basic graphic design and typography principles for people without design training, built around contrast, repetition, alignment and proximity.
w: HN's go-to design book for developers, praised for its quick read and the CRAP principles. It is repeatedly credited with improving visual work without a designer.
ab: For developers and founders who need to make things look decent
Quick read with before-and-after examples
Colors and fonts are dated; one commenter prefers the earlier edition

q.t: It's a quick, easy read and the concepts can really apply to any kind of visual design.

t: Big Data: Principles and Best Practices of Scalable Realtime Data Systems
s: A Manning book on designing scalable batch-and-realtime data systems, introducing the lambda architecture by the creator of Storm.
w: HN data engineers cite it as the source for the lambda architecture and recommend it as a lasting systems-thinking book, useful even if you do not have huge data. Its author appears in the thread.
ab: For engineers designing data pipelines and realtime analytics systems
Teaches principles, not a single tool
Lambda architecture has since been challenged; some examples are dated

q.t: Don't let the name Big Data make you feel this is only for people with big data needs

t: Pitch Anything: An Innovative Method for Presenting, Persuading, and Winning the Deal
s: A short book on pitching to investors using a framework drawn from neuroscience-flavored ideas about attention and status.
w: Recommended as a favorite book about the act of pitching, one commenter saying to read it cover to cover in a weekend. It is cited for its power-frame idea.
ab: For founders pitching investors or salespeople pitching deals
Short enough to read in a weekend
Leans on pop evolutionary psychology and 'frame control'

q.t: No seriously, read that book cover to cover, you can do it in a weekend.

s: First volume of The Stormlight Archive, a huge epic fantasy about war, honor and broken people on a storm-scoured world with a rigorous magic system.
w: HN readers who normally stick to tech books point to it as the fantasy to try: big worldbuilding, hard-edged magic, and characters who deal with trauma and mental health. Several re-read it.
ab: For readers who want long, immersive epic fantasy
Over 1,000 pages; the first of a long ongoing series
Slow first act, big payoff; strong character arcs

q.t: Some seriously fantastic therapy mixed into the beautiful fantasy world.

t: Cocoa Programming for Mac OS X
s: A hands-on tutorial for building Mac applications with Cocoa and Objective-C, written by Aaron Hillegass of Big Nerd Ranch.
w: HN's top pick for learning Mac development in the Objective-C era. Commenters call it the best beginning Cocoa book and one of the finest programming books.
ab: For anyone learning Cocoa and Objective-C on the Mac
Project-based chapters that build real apps
Objective-C-era material; Swift and SwiftUI changed things

q.t: The best beginning Cocoa book is "Cocoa Programming for Mac OS X"

t: Learning From Data: A Short Course
s: A concise machine learning textbook on the theory of generalization, linear models, overfitting, and validation, accompanying Caltech's online course.
w: HN recommends it as an off-the-beaten-path ML intro that explains core principles clearly without heavy math, and its Caltech lectures are free online.
ab: For beginners wanting ML theory fundamentals
Companion Caltech videos are free
Short; does not cover many modern methods

q.t: LfD encapsulates a number of really core principles in a simple text.

t: The Founder's Dilemmas: Anticipating and Avoiding the Pitfalls That Can Sink a Startup
s: A data-driven study of the people decisions founders face, including co-founders, equity splits, roles and when to bring in investors.
w: HN founders recommend it for its research base on co-founder choice and equity splits. It is repeatedly offered as a rigorous complement to startup how-to advice.
ab: For founders and early team members facing equity or co-founder decisions
Backed by a decade of data on startups
Academic in tone; US venture-style startups focus

q.t: an academic study of startups. Highly recommended.

s: A thorough introduction to Ruby the language, covering objects, classes, modules and idioms in depth.
w: Suggested as the book to learn Ruby itself before or alongside Rails. Commenters like David Black's clear writing and say it helped them after starting with Rails.
ab: For developers who want to understand Ruby itself
Covers core language features and object model
Written for Ruby 1.9; later versions have changed

q.t: David Black's writing style simply delivers.

s: Kerouac's 1957 Beat Generation novel about restless cross-country road trips, jazz, friendship and freedom in postwar America.
w: HN readers credit it with sparking wanderlust and a push to see the world. Several wish they had read it earlier, and one calls the free-form style liberating.
ab: For readers who want a book that urges travel and risk
Free-form, stream-of-consciousness prose
Some find it romanticizes aimlessness

q.t: It taught me to be mad, to live life, to get out and see the world.

s: Marcel Proust's early-20th-century multi-volume novel of memory, time, society and perception, famous for its very long sentences.
w: HN readers hold it up as a great novel about memory and attention, saying it makes them slow down and notice small details. Warnings include its length and long sentences.
ab: For patient readers who like introspective, literary classics
Seven volumes with very long sentences
Many say it is more talked about than read

q.t: reading this book is an oasis in the desert experience to me

s: A split, curved ergonomic keyboard with a cushioned palm rest and domed layout.
w: HN recommends it as a cheap, well-liked ergonomic option for avoiding RSI, with some moving up to Kinesis or ErgoDox boards later.
ab: For typists wanting relief from RSI
Wired, cheap
Discontinued; later Sculpt models replaced it

q.t: I have the 4000 and the Sculpt ergonomic for more than 5 years each.

t: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man
s: A memoir by a former consultant claiming he persuaded developing countries into debt to serve U.S. interests.
w: Recommended in threads on foreign debt and infrastructure. At least one reader is unsure how much is true.
ab: For readers curious about debt and geopolitics
Memoir with unverified claims
Accuracy disputed

q.t: I suggest reading John Perkins's "Confessions of an Economic Hit Man"

t: All of Statistics: A Concise Course in Statistical Inference
s: A compact graduate-level text covering probability and statistical inference for computer science and machine learning students.
w: HN recommends it as a dense, concise reference for the statistics behind machine learning, and it appears on many lists of essential math and ML books.
ab: For readers with calculus and some probability who want rigorous statistics
Concise coverage of inference, Bayes, and modern methods
Dense and terse; not a first statistics book

q.t: I found this gem of a book that I think many here would find interesting

s: The central religious text of Islam, revealed in Arabic and available in many translations.
w: HN commenters from the Muslim community recommend it for its poetic beauty and as a source of comfort during anxiety and depression. Several say translations do not fully capture the Arabic.
ab: For readers of world religions or those studying Islam
Translations differ; commenters say the Arabic carries the poetry
Religious scripture, with devotional recommendations

q.t: reading The Quran is always soothing and sometimes cathartic.

t: The Origin of Wealth: Evolution, Complexity, and the Radical Remaking of Economics
s: An argument that economies are complex adaptive systems best understood through evolution and complexity science rather than equilibrium theory.
w: Recommended as a great introduction to complexity economics, in contrast to equilibrium and efficient-market thinking. It shows up in reading lists for people curious about alternatives to textbook economics.
ab: For readers curious about complexity economics and agent-based models
Accessible overview aimed at general business readers
Written in 2007, before several later developments

q.t: was a great introduction to "complexity economics"

s: John Gall's humorous classic on why systems fail, also known as Systemantics.
w: HN recommends it for its witty look at system design and failure. Commenters call it brilliant, funny and thought-provoking, and quote its laws.
ab: For engineers and managers
Humorous aphorisms about systems
Some examples feel just-so

q.t: a slightly odd but unique and in-depth view of Systems design and failure

s: Derek Sivers's short account of building CD Baby and the lessons he learned about running a business his own way.
w: Recommended as a quick, inspirational read about starting a business, with a tone matching Sivers's blog.
ab: For founders and side-project makers
Short read of about an hour
More a story than a manual

q.t: reading it is probably one of the best ways you can spend an hour.

s: A detailed walkthrough of how the Linux 2.6 kernel works internally, covering memory, processes, filesystems and networking.
w: Called very hard and dense but without a better book on kernel networking. It is recommended alongside Linux Kernel Development and The Linux Programming Interface.
ab: For readers who want to learn Linux kernel internals
Covers the 2.6 kernel in implementation detail
Dense, and the kernel has changed a lot since

q.t: It's very hard and dense to read, but I don't think there's a better book out there about a networking stack implementation.

s: Edited transcripts of Noam Chomsky's Q&A sessions on US foreign policy, media, and power, with extensive footnotes.
w: HN readers call it a worldview-changing, conversational on-ramp to Chomsky, often picked over his denser books. One suggests reading the footnotes alongside it.
ab: For readers new to Chomsky's politics and media critique
Conversational Q&A format, easy to read
Footnotes are substantial and nearly double the length

q.t: I knew the United States was complicit in some nefarious things, both domestic and abroad, but wow

s: The spiritual memoir of Paramahansa Yogananda, covering his life, teachers, and introduction of Kriya Yoga to the West.
w: HN readers recommend it as an inspirational read, and note that Steve Jobs reportedly reread it many times. It shows up on lists of mind-blowing books and biographies.
ab: For readers interested in yoga and Indian spirituality
Mix of memoir and devotional teaching
Contains miracle claims; read as a spiritual text

q.t: pretty good as far as inspirational goes

t: Salt Sugar Fat: How the Food Giants Hooked Us
s: An investigative look at how large food companies engineer processed foods around salt, sugar and fat to drive consumption.
w: HN brings it up in threads on obesity, junk food and sugar. Commenters say it opened their eyes to how cereal and snack companies hooked consumers, much like tobacco firms.
ab: For readers curious about the processed food industry
Investigative journalism, not a diet plan
Names specific companies and tactics

q.t: really opened my eyes to how the cereal giants hooked kids and their parents on sugar

s: A short book distilling the Durants' lifetime of historical study.
w: Recommended and quoted for synthesizing lessons from history. One commenter notes small parts are dated.
ab: For readers wanting big-picture history
Short and quotable
Some parts dated

q.t: two historians who—after a lifetime of studying history—wrote a book trying to synthesize any lessons from their studies

t: UNIX and Linux System Administration Handbook
by: Evi Nemeth, Garth Snyder et al.
s: A comprehensive reference for administering Unix and Linux systems, covering networking, storage, users and services.
w: The standard recommendation for learning sysadmin properly. Commenters recommend it for people starting to manage their own servers.
ab: For anyone running or learning to run Linux servers
Broad reference covering many Unix variants
Distro details change; later editions update them

q.t: the Nemeth book is very good

t: This Time Is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly
s: A data-driven history of financial crises across countries and centuries, showing the same boom and bust patterns repeating.
w: HN reaches for it whenever someone claims a bubble, whether housing or bitcoin, is different. The point is that crises rhyme.
ab: For readers who want historical context on bubbles and crashes
Heavy with data and case studies
Its debt-growth findings were later challenged

q.t: History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme, and you'd be surprised just how similar this time is.

t: Dominion: How the Christian Revolution Remade the World
s: A history arguing that Christianity shaped Western moral values, from antiquity to the modern world.
w: HN commenters recommend it to people who assume modern morals are secular in origin; one calls it an excellent read.
ab: For readers interested in the history of Western values
Narrative history by a non-theologian historian
Argument will be contested by many readers

q.t: Those interested may find Dominion[0] an excellent read.

s: A short handbook of Stoic ethics compiled from the teachings of the Greek philosopher Epictetus, concerned with what is and is not in our control.
w: HN readers call it the most practical Stoic text, a short book that changed how they see their lives. It pairs with Marcus Aurelius and Seneca, and the text is free online.
ab: For readers wanting a compact introduction to Stoicism
Very short, under 100 pages
Easy to read but hard to apply

q.t: the best practical piece of stoic philosophy that I read

t: The Supermen: The Story of Seymour Cray and the Technical Wizards Behind the Supercomputer
