s: A history of Seymour Cray and the engineers at Control Data and Cray Research who built the fastest supercomputers of their era.
w: Recommended whenever Cray or supercomputer history comes up. Commenters call it a fun, very good read about the CDC 6600 era engineering culture.
ab: For readers interested in computing history and engineering culture
Personality-driven account of the first supercomputers
Covers the 1960s to 1990s; later machines are out of scope

q.t: If you haven't already done so, I highly recommend reading "The SUPERMEN" by Charles J. Murray.

t: A Farewell to Alms: A Brief Economic History of the World
s: An economic history arguing that the Industrial Revolution came from cultural and demographic changes in England, after millennia of stagnation.
w: HN commenters call it one of the more interesting books they have read, with a provocative argument about long-run living standards and why the Industrial Revolution happened.
ab: For readers interested in economic history and long-run growth
Data-heavy and sweeping in scope
Its genetic-selection argument is controversial among economists

q.t: One of the more interesting books I've read recently

t: Applied Cryptography: Protocols, Algorithms, and Source Code in C
s: Schneier's comprehensive survey of cryptographic protocols and algorithms, with C source code for many of them.
w: Commenters call it the best technical book they have read and say it is more readable than expected. People who worked on hardware crypto recommended it, and it is cited as the standard introduction.
ab: For programmers who want to understand how cryptographic protocols fit together
Explains protocols conceptually first, then algorithms and C code
Published 1996, so it predates modern primitives and practices

q.t: It's __excellent__. It's the best technical book I've ever read.

t: Search Inside Yourself: The Unexpected Path to Achieving Success, Happiness (and World Peace)
s: A Google engineer's guide to mindfulness and emotional intelligence, based on the course he developed at Google.
w: HN readers recommend it as meditation taught in a geek-friendly way, and credit it with helping with stress and scattered attention.
ab: For skeptical, analytical people curious about meditation
Practical exercises for attention and emotional awareness
Corporate-wellness flavor; some may find it light

q.t: This is very good book teaching about mediation in a geeks way

s: The classic reference on how database transactions, logging, locking and recovery are implemented.
w: Commenters say it has proven indispensable in their careers and recommend it for the storage side of database implementation. It is paired with Stonebraker's Architecture of a Database System.
ab: For database engineers and distributed-systems builders
Deep coverage of transactions, locking and recovery
Large, dense, and from 1993

q.t: proven indispensable in my career and a generally great book

s: Post-singularity heist novel starring master thief Jean le Flambeur, first of a trilogy with dense invented slang and a wild far-future Mars.
w: HN sci-fi fans praise its vivid ideas and worldbuilding, calling it full of ideas technologists will find fascinating. One says its invented language works better than any other book they have read.
ab: For readers of dense, idea-rich far-future sci-fi
Throws jargon at you with no hand-holding
Trilogy continues with The Fractal Prince and The Causal Angel

q.t: It's chock full of ideas that any technologist would find fascinating.

t: What Got You Here Won't Get You There
s: Executive coach Marshall Goldsmith describes 20 habits that hold successful people back and how to change them.
w: HN managers recommend it for moving up: it helped readers become better teammates and communicators and gain self-awareness, especially past the Director level.
ab: For managers and senior engineers moving into leadership
Focuses on interpersonal bad habits
Written for executive audiences

q.t: Once you get beyond a Director level with some mistakes, read this book

s: Apple's high-end tablet, used with the Apple Pencil and Magic Keyboard.
w: HN commenters use it for handwriting notes with GoodNotes and annotating PDFs, and as a laptop replacement at home. Developers note some webkit limitations.
ab: For handwritten notes and reading papers
Apple Pencil and keyboard are extra
iPadOS limits developer workflows

q.t: on an iPad Pro (12.9 inch) and Apple Pencil. Haven't touched paper since getting it.

s: ASUS's Zenbook line of thin ultrabook laptops, sold from 2011 as an aluminium alternative to the MacBook Air.
w: HN commenters suggest Zenbooks as a thin Linux-friendly laptop, with decent deals. Others report a dim or glare-prone screen and one developer who found Linux on theirs horrible.
ab: Thin and light, often run Linux for developers
Opinions are mixed; some report glare and driver trouble
Comments mostly cover 2011-2016 models

q.t: Check out the Asus Zenbooks. My friends have them and run Linux on them.

s: Hayek's 1944 argument that central economic planning leads toward loss of individual freedom and tyranny.
w: Often listed among classic economics and political reading, with one commenter saying it subtly shaped nearly all their political-economic views. It's flagged as a right-leaning pick, and one calls it a controversial choice.
ab: For readers curious about classical-liberal political economy
A 1944 polemic, so context matters
Frames itself against socialism; read alongside other views

q.t: has had at least a subtle influence on almost every political economic belief I hold

s: Mark Manson's dating advice book, favoring honesty and emotional connection over pickup tactics.
w: Recommended as the only dating book worth reading and for rejecting pickup culture in favor of authenticity.
ab: For men wanting honest dating advice
Emphasis on self-improvement over tactics
Aimed at a narrow audience

q.t: including IMO the only dating book you should ever read

t: The Willpower Instinct: How Self-Control Works, Why It Matters, and What You Can Do to Get More of It
s: A Stanford health psychologist's guide to the science of self-control, with exercises for resisting temptation and building focus.
w: HN commenters suggest it to people who struggle to start or stay focused on projects. One argues it will help a programmer do better work than a book on compilers.
ab: For people who procrastinate or struggle with habits
Based on a Stanford course, with weekly exercises
Some cited ego-depletion research has not replicated

q.t: will help a programmer perform better work than a book on compilers

s: A novel in Iain M. Banks's Culture series about a mysterious alien artifact that sets the god-like AI Minds of the Culture scheming against each other.
w: HN readers rate it the best or most fun Culture book, praised for its worldbuilding and the AI Minds' point of view. One reader found it a letdown, and another says its human characters are underdeveloped.
ab: For hard space-opera fans; works as an entry to the Culture
Standalone plot inside a larger series
Human characters are weaker than the Minds

q.t: The other culture novels are also good but not as fun as Excession.

t: Code Reading: The Open Source Perspective
s: A guide to reading and understanding existing code, with examples taken from large open source codebases.
w: Suggested as a dedicated book on how to read code. Opinions are mixed: some call it excellent, others lost interest or found reviews unflattering.
ab: For developers learning to navigate unfamiliar codebases
Examples from real open source projects
Mixed reviews; dated tooling

q.t: a more comprehensive text on acquiring the skill to read code is the book Code Reading

s: A Manning guide to tuning search relevance with Elasticsearch and Solr, covering analysis, scoring and building a relevance-engineering workflow.
w: Recommended by several readers as the best starting point for search relevance on Elasticsearch or Solr. The authors also plug it themselves, so weigh the independent praise.
ab: For developers building search on Solr or Elasticsearch
Focus on relevance tuning rather than basic setup
Authors promote it on HN themselves

q.t: it's a great starting point!

s: A comprehensive introduction to C++ updated for C++11, with exercises in every chapter that teach modern practices from the start.
w: HN recommends it as the thorough, didactic way to learn modern C++ from scratch, with exercises and a modern-first approach instead of a history of C.
ab: For beginners and returning programmers learning C++
Exercises in each chapter and a modern-C++ approach
Covers C++11 only; not C++14/17 or later, and it is long

q.t: it covers all the basics really well. Great resource for people new to the language.

t: The Man Who Solved the Market
s: A biography of mathematician Jim Simons and the quant hedge fund Renaissance Technologies.
w: Recommended after Simons' death. Readers like the early startup-like years of improvising data and models.
ab: For readers curious about quant finance
Story, not method
Little on Renaissance's actual models

q.t: I really enjoyed the early parts where they were solving problems in creative ways like any startup.

t: The Case Against Education: Why the Education System Is a Waste of Time and Money
s: Economist Bryan Caplan's argument that much of schooling is signaling to employers rather than building skills, with data and policy suggestions.
w: HN readers cite it in debates about college value, with one calling it a careful social science book full of data on the signaling model.
ab: For readers questioning the value of college
Data-driven argument for signaling over human capital
Provocative thesis; economists disagree

q.t: I highly recommend The Case Against Education by Bryan Caplan

t: Just for Fun: The Story of an Accidental Revolutionary
s: Linus Torvalds's memoir of creating Linux, written with David Diamond.
w: Recommended to anyone writing their own OS or curious about Linux history. Commenters pair it with the Revolution OS documentary.
ab: For readers interested in Linux and open source history
Personal account of building Linux
Light on technical details

q.t: Also worth a read: Just for Fun

t: The PayPal Wars: Battles with eBay, the Media, the Mafia, and the Rest of Planet Earth
s: An insider account of PayPal's early years, from its email payments pivot through fraud fights and the eBay rivalry to its IPO.
w: HN startup readers cite it for the inside look at the Thiel, Musk and Levchin era, including the Unix versus Windows clash. One commenter calls it informative but not well written.
ab: For founders and fans of early internet startup history
Detailed stories on fraud, growth tactics and the eBay fight
Prose is uneven, per HN; the author was a PayPal executive

q.t: which is quite a fascinating read with lots of insight

t: Python for Kids: A Playful Introduction to Programming
s: A beginner's book that teaches Python to children by building simple games and drawings with turtle graphics and Tkinter.
w: Suggested when people ask for programming books for kids, since it covers making a couple of different 2D games. One commenter pairs it with Scratch books for younger children.
ab: For kids and parents starting with Python
Builds simple 2D games
Some HN readers prefer free books like Invent with Python

q.t: It covers how to make a couple different 2D games.

t: Start with Why: How Great Leaders Inspire Everyone to Take Action
s: Simon Sinek's argument that organizations succeed by communicating their purpose before their product.
w: Recommended by founders who found it helpful, though one commenter says you can skip the book and watch his TED talk.
ab: Leadership and purpose framework
Core idea fits in a talk
Some find it repetitive

q.t: helped me figure out why I am running my business

t: The New New Thing: A Silicon Valley Story
s: Michael Lewis's portrait of Jim Clark, founder of SGI, Netscape and Healtheon, and Silicon Valley's boom.
w: Recommended as a primer on Jim Clark and Silicon Valley culture, with a summer-reading suggestion.
ab: For Silicon Valley history fans
Narrative profile of Jim Clark
Written at the late-90s peak

t: Other Minds: The Octopus, the Sea, and the Deep Origins of Consciousness
s: A philosopher-diver's exploration of octopus and cuttlefish intelligence and what it says about the evolution of minds.
w: HN cites it whenever octopus intelligence comes up. Commenters call it a fascinating, very accessible book on octopuses and cuttlefish, and a good source on cephalopod evolution.
ab: For readers curious about animal intelligence
Accessible blend of biology and philosophy
Draws on the author's diving observations

q.t: a fascinating and very accessible book about the octupus and cuttlefish

t: The Case for Mars: The Plan to Settle the Red Planet and Why We Must
s: An aerospace engineer lays out the Mars Direct plan for sending humans to Mars with existing technology and living off the land.
w: HN commenters recommend it for the technical case that Mars missions are feasible with current technology. It is routinely cited as the source of the Mars Direct idea.
ab: For space enthusiasts and engineers curious about Mars mission design
Detailed Mars Direct mission architecture
Written by an advocate; optimistic on costs and timelines

q.t: you'll be surprised what else is possible on Mars with current technology

t: The User Illusion: Cutting Consciousness Down to Size
s: A popular-science book arguing that consciousness processes only a tiny fraction of the information our senses take in, drawing on information theory and psychology.
w: HN commenters recommend it for exploring consciousness and the bandwidth limits of the mind. They quote its figures on how few bits per second conscious attention can handle.
ab: For readers interested in consciousness, information theory and cognition
Links physics, psychology and philosophy
Some figures are dated and debated

q.t: is a great read if you're interested in exploring consciousness

t: Database Internals: A Deep-Dive into How Distributed Data Systems Work
s: A guide to how storage engines and distributed databases work, covering B-trees, LSM trees, replication and consensus.
w: Recommended alongside Designing Data-Intensive Applications and CMU's database course for learning how databases work internally.
ab: For engineers wanting to understand storage engines and consensus
Technical; assumes programming background
Pairs well with Andy Pavlo's lectures

q.t: The book referenced on the blog post seems interesting

t: Kitchen Confidential: Adventures in the Culinary Underbelly
s: Anthony Bourdain's 2000 memoir of his years working in New York restaurant kitchens, and a frank look at professional cooking culture.
w: Recommended as an entertaining, easy beach read and the best portrait of restaurant kitchen life, from people who have worked in them. Some HN readers also note its lessons about managing teams under pressure.
ab: For anyone curious about restaurant life or who likes blunt memoirs
Fast, funny read with strong voice
Written in 2000, so some restaurant-world details are dated

q.t: 'Kitchen Confidential' by Anthony Bourdain comes the closest to describing life in a restaurant kitchen in a very entertaining way.

s: A 12.1-inch business laptop from 2008 with a Core 2 Duo, one of the last ThinkPads designed under IBM-era standards and a Libreboot favorite.
w: HN likes it for its build quality, Linux compatibility and keyboard, and as a Libreboot-friendly machine you can upgrade with RAM and an SSD. A dissenter reports plastic breaking and a cheap feel.
ab: For retro-ThinkPad fans and libre-firmware enthusiasts
Libreboot-flashed units are sold by specialist shops
Very old hardware: slow, low-res screen, battery replacements needed

q.t: Personally, I am running a ThinkPad X200 since 2008 with nearly no software problems.

s: Milan Kundera's 1984 philosophical novel of love, infidelity and political repression in 1968 Prague, interleaving four characters' lives.
w: HN readers recommend it as a beautiful, heartbreaking story that mixes philosophy, psychology and humor, and one that stays with you on rereading. It shows up in lists of fiction worth reading earlier.
ab: For readers who enjoy philosophical literary fiction
Realistic, unromantic take on relationships
Set in Cold War Czechoslovakia

q.t: A beautiful story, told with equal parts philosophy, psychology, and humor

s: Dostoevsky's 1864 short novel narrated by a bitter, isolated former civil servant, a landmark of existential and psychological fiction.
w: HN readers call it a book they reread often and think everyone should read; people name it among the books that shook them most. It's free in the public domain.
ab: For readers curious about existential and psychological literature
Short and readable, but unsettling
Available free through Project Gutenberg

q.t: The first should be read by everyone though

s: A posture guide with eight illustrated techniques for sitting, standing, walking, and sleeping to relieve back, neck, hip, and knee pain.
w: HN sufferers of back pain from sitting recommend it repeatedly, saying the diagrams helped them fix pain and posture. One commenter admits the presentation and science are imperfect.
ab: For desk workers with back pain or poor posture
Illustrated, step-by-step posture techniques
Methods are unconventional; science is thin

q.t: it has ended my back pain and given me awareness of my body.

s: Simon Singh's popular account of the 350-year quest to prove Fermat's Last Theorem, culminating in Andrew Wiles's proof.
w: Recommended as a great, accessible book on how Wiles solved the problem, readable without advanced math.
ab: For general readers curious about math
Narrative, little technical detail
Light on actual proof details

q.t: Great book. Highly recommend you give it a read!

s: A 12.5-inch ThinkPad from 2017 with a removable battery plus internal battery, a water-resistant keyboard and a full set of ports.
w: HN developers recommend it as a light, durable Linux laptop with an excellent keyboard, very long battery life and a hot-swappable battery. It's also a cheap used purchase, sometimes around $300.
ab: For Linux users wanting a lightweight, repairable ThinkPad
Dual-battery design allows hot-swapping
Older hardware: buy used and check battery condition

q.t: Excellent Linux support, zero issues even on day 1

t: Illusions: The Adventures of a Reluctant Messiah
s: Short philosophical fable about a pilot who meets a barnstorming messiah and learns that reality is shaped by choices and beliefs.
w: A frequent HN comfort and life-changing short book, valued for its message about choices, identity and what you can and cannot control. Readers re-read it and pair it with Jonathan Livingston Seagull.
ab: For readers who like short, inspirational parables
Quick read of about 130 pages
Sentimental and spiritual in tone

q.t: An amazing book about choices. And what you can and cannot control in your life.

t: Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd Edition
s: A graduate-level classical mechanics text that expresses Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics as executable Scheme programs, by the authors of SICP-era computing.
w: HN recommends it for learning classical mechanics through code, listing it with Taylor's Classical Mechanics and The Theoretical Minimum. It is open access under Creative Commons, and ports to Clojure exist.
ab: For programmers and physicists who like to compute as they learn
Free open-access online edition
Assumes comfort with Scheme and calculus; not a gentle intro

q.t: the books that I settled on as providing a good introduction to classical mechanics

t: Cadillac Desert: The American West and Its Disappearing Water
s: A history of water development in the American West, covering dams, politics, and engineering that shaped California and nearby states.
w: HN calls it the definitive history of California water. Commenters recommend it as an accessible, sometimes infuriating chronicle whenever drought or water rights come up.
ab: For readers interested in infrastructure, politics, and the West
Narrative history with engineering and political drama
Written in 1986; recent events not covered

q.t: The definitive history of water development in California is this book

s: A short ebook that walks you through writing a simple ray tracer in C++, the first of a three-part minibook series.
w: HN's favorite quick, fun project for learning graphics. Commenters recommend it as the easy entry point to ray tracing and a satisfying small C++ project.
ab: For programmers new to computer graphics
Produces a rendered image in a weekend
Series continues with The Next Week and The Rest of Your Life

q.t: If you want fun miniproject may I suggest Peter Shirley's excellent mini-raytracing bookseries

t: Free to Choose: A Personal Statement
s: Milton and Rose Friedman's popular defense of free markets and limited government, tied to a PBS series.
w: Recommended as a fundamental, readable economics book, often paired with The Shock Doctrine for balance. Appears in YC's winter reading list thread.
ab: For readers wanting the free-market case from Friedman
Plain-language and example-driven
Strongly ideological, from one school of thought

q.t: I found Milton Friedman's "Free To Choose" fundamental and very readable.

s: Oscar Wilde's only novel, about a young man whose portrait ages while he stays youthful and corrupt.
w: Commenters cite it as beautifully written classic fiction that stays with you. One reads it as a story of the alter-egos we build to hide our worst sins.
ab: For fans of classic gothic and literary fiction
Short, quotable, and witty prose
Public-domain, so many cheap editions

q.t: The Picture of Dorian Gray (by Oscar Wilde) is just so beautifully written.

t: Devil Take the Hindmost: A History of Financial Speculation
s: A history of financial bubbles and speculation from tulip mania through the 1990s.
w: Recommended whenever a bubble is mentioned, including bitcoin and railway manias.
ab: For readers who like financial history
Narrative history
Published 1999; modern bubbles missing

q.t: If you want a great book on the history of financial speculation,

s: A classic guide to mnemonic memory techniques, including peg lists, the memory palace, and remembering names and numbers.
w: Recommended as the best-known Harry Lorayne book and a practical, older guide to memory techniques. One reader calls it life-changing, and it is suggested alongside Moonwalking with Einstein.
ab: For people who want to learn mnemonic memory systems
Covers lists, names, numbers and more
Takes practice; the 1970s tone shows

q.t: Also would recommend books by Harry Lorayne (The Memory Book is the most well known).

s: A readable survey of major Western philosophers from Plato to John Dewey, with their lives and ideas.
w: The default answer when someone asks where to start with philosophy: readable and broad. One commenter notes it dates from 1926 and skips later figures like Wittgenstein.
ab: For newcomers wanting a readable overview of philosophy
Covers Plato through Dewey and Santayana
Written in 1926; no Wittgenstein

q.t: Considered a classic and one of the best introductions to philosophy

s: A short book in which Sam Harris argues that free will is an illusion.
w: HN cites it in discussions of determinism and the brain, and recommends it to people on philosophy.
ab: For readers interested in determinism and neuroscience
Very short
Philosophers dispute the conclusion

q.t: Sam Harris' Free Will and Moral Landscape are totally worth reading.

s: The life story of Malcolm X, told to Alex Haley, from his rough youth through prison, the Nation of Islam, and his break with it.
w: HN readers say it changed their view of him and of empathy generally, with one saying it should be required reading in US high schools. One finds it repetitive at times.
ab: For readers interested in civil rights history
Candid personal transformation story
Can feel repetitive in places

q.t: It should be required reading for high school students in the United States.

s: Chesterton's 1908 defense of Christian belief, written as a personal account of how he arrived at orthodoxy.
w: HN readers list it among books that changed them and call it one of the finest works of Christian philosophy of the 20th century. It is free on Project Gutenberg.
ab: For readers curious about Christian apologetics and wit
Free public-domain text
Written in an early-1900s style

q.t: something not to be missed if you are looking for one of the finest works of christian philosophy in XX century

t: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
s: Joseph Campbell's comparative study of world myths and the common hero's journey pattern behind them.
w: HN readers say it opened their eyes to metaphor and structure in stories, with one warning it will ruin fiction for you by exposing the pattern.
ab: For writers and readers of myth and storytelling
Dense academic style in places
Its single monomyth theory is debated

q.t: It opened my mind to understand metaphors and analogies in literature.

s: Tom Wolfe's satirical history of modern architecture, tracing how Bauhaus and its European followers shaped the glass-and-steel boxes of American cities.
w: HN recommends it as a short, funny explanation of why modern buildings look the way they do, and a critique of modernist architecture that applies to flat design.
ab: For design and architecture fans open to a polemic
Short, witty, and opinionated
One-sided critique by Wolfe; not a neutral history

q.t: A great dive into why every damn sky-rise seems to be nothing but glass panels. Short read too.

by: Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio, et al.
s: A comprehensive graduate-level textbook on deep learning covering applied math background, deep networks, and research topics, also available free online.
w: A fixture on HN machine learning reading lists, praised as readable and broad, with practical tips. The free web version is why many point to it.
ab: For readers with math basics who want a full ML foundation
Three parts: math background, practice, research topics
Predates transformers and modern large language models

q.t: covers a broad set of modern topics, and has pragmatic tips for real use cases.

t: The Long Way to a Small, Angry Planet
s: The first book of the Wayfarers series: a crew-driven space opera about a ragtag ship digging tunnels through space.
w: Readers say it is touching and character-driven, with fantastic worldbuilding and questions about AI. Others warn the plot meanders, but call it a great way to get back into fiction.
ab: Warm, character-focused space opera
First of the Wayfarers series
Plot meanders; light on action

q.t: If you forgot how to read fiction, The long way to a small angry planet will put you back on track no time.

s: A detachable 2-in-1 Windows tablet with a keyboard cover, pen support and a 3:2 screen.
w: HN developers like it as a light, portable machine that runs Windows 10 with WSL and has a comfortable keyboard cover. Several note Linux can be made to work.
ab: For developers who want a very portable Windows machine with WSL.
Detachable tablet with keyboard cover and pen-friendly screen.
Mentioned caveats: Linux support takes effort, webcam support lacking for one user.

q.t: I am loving my Surface Pro. Great build quality, extremely portable, 8+ hours of battery life, detachable, writable screen

t: The Red Queen: Sex and the Evolution of Human Nature
s: Matt Ridley's popular account of how sexual selection and the evolutionary arms race shape human nature and behavior.
w: Suggested in HN threads about evolution and sexual selection as a good popular science read. One commenter highly recommends it for anyone interested in the topic.
ab: For general readers curious about evolutionary biology
Accessible popular science with many examples
Published in 1993; some claims are dated

q.t: If you guys are interested in this stuff, I highly recommend "The Red Queen" by Matt Ridley.

s: An argument that large, diverse, independent groups often make better judgments and predictions than individual experts.
w: HN commenters point to it for why groups can outperform experts, including in prediction markets and polls. They also use it to warn about conditions such as independence that must hold.
ab: For readers interested in prediction and group decisions
Lays out conditions for crowd accuracy
Popular treatment; some cases are anecdotal

q.t: please go read James Surowiecki's book of the same name.

s: A collection of short chapters on 99 common cognitive biases and thinking errors, with examples.
w: Recommended as an accessible book on avoiding thinking errors, though one reader says spotting biases in daily life is still hard.
ab: For readers new to cognitive biases
Short chapters, easy to read
Light on depth and sources

q.t: 99 cognitive biases with memorable examples and stories.

s: A 2011 15.6-inch mobile workstation laptop with Core i7 quad-core CPU, up to 32GB RAM, Quadro graphics and room for several drives.
w: HN developers keep a used W520 as a dock-it-and-forget-it dev machine: sturdy, upgradeable, great keyboard, works well on Linux. One user warns the Optimus/Nvidia dual-GPU setup is painful.
ab: For tinkerers who want a cheap, upgradeable used workstation
Battery life is poor, and dual-GPU switching can trouble Linux
Old hardware; sold used or refurbished only

q.t: the last workstation version with the better keyboard and the speed to feel comparable to current laptops

t: Evicted: Poverty and Profit in the American City
s: An ethnographic look at eviction and housing instability in Milwaukee, following tenants and landlords.
w: HN readers name it among the best books on poverty and housing, and one commenter notes it also shows how landlords profit from the system.
ab: For readers interested in housing and poverty
Immersive, story-driven reporting
US-specific; emotionally heavy

q.t: anyway I found it fascinating and worth recommending here

s: A science-fiction horror novel about a secret agency fighting antimemes, ideas that erase themselves from memory, expanded from the author's SCP Foundation stories.
w: HN sci-fi readers call it the best idea of a year's reading and say it pulled them back into reading. It started online as free SCP fiction, and a print edition exists.
ab: For readers who like cosmic horror and idea-driven science fiction
Originally free to read at qntm.org; buy it to own a copy
One reader finds the pacing odd, though the central idea wins praise

q.t: You can read it over here, for free. Or buy a physical copy (which I did, and was very happy to)

t: The DevOps Handbook: How to Create World-Class Agility, Reliability, and Security in Technology Organizations
s: A practical guide to DevOps principles and practice.
w: Recommended as the companion to The Phoenix Project and a better-grounded alternative to Agile cargo-culting.
ab: For engineering managers
Practical case studies
Management-speak

q.t: there are a couple of great books that dig more into this kind of thing.

t: Digital Apollo: Human and Machine in Spaceflight
s: History of the Apollo guidance computer and the debate between pilots, engineers and automation over how much control astronauts should have over the spacecraft.
w: HN brings it up in threads on spaceflight software, automation and who controls a spacecraft. Commenters call it fascinating and easy reading on the early space program, though one reader rated it only 2.5 of 5.
ab: For readers interested in Apollo, NASA and human-versus-machine control
Focuses on the pilot-versus-automation debate, not code details
One reader found it underwhelming

q.t: is probably the one that makes the best light / easy reading

s: Brené Brown's book on shame, vulnerability, and courage, and how embracing vulnerability changes work, parenting, and relationships.
w: HN readers say it reshaped how they think about shame, anxiety, and trust, and one credits it with changing how he runs his business.
ab: For managers and people struggling with shame or perfectionism
Based on the author's research on vulnerability
Popular self-help tone rather than academic

q.t: Daring Greatly by Brené Brown revolutionized my understanding of anxiety, guilt, shame, vulnerability, courage and trust.

t: The Design of the UNIX Operating System
s: A 1986 textbook explaining the algorithms and data structures of the System V Unix kernel, including the buffer cache, file system, processes, and I/O.
w: HN commenters recommend it as the classic for understanding how Unix kernels work internally, and several say it taught them more than their OS courses.
ab: For people wanting to understand OS internals through Unix
Clear kernel algorithms: buffer cache, inodes, and processes
Dated: based on System V of the 1980s, not modern Linux

q.t: I learned more about OS from this book than any academic material used at the university

s: Alan Watts's introduction to the history and ideas of Zen Buddhism for Western readers.
w: Recommended as a good starting point for Zen, with one reader saying it changed how they view the world. It comes up in threads about Stoicism, Taoism and eastern philosophy.
ab: For newcomers curious about Zen and Taoist ideas
Covers the history and philosophy of Zen
Written in the 1950s; later scholarship differs on some points

q.t: The Way of Zen by Alan Watts is really good. I learned a lot and it helped me view the world differently.

t: High Performance Web Sites: Essential Knowledge for Front-End Engineers
s: A short O'Reilly book of 14 rules for making web pages load faster, written by a former Yahoo and Google performance lead.
w: HN commenters call it the definitive treatment of front-end performance and say following it makes a material difference. Some note it is older but largely still relevant.
ab: For front-end developers wanting faster page loads
Short, rule-based and easy to apply
Written in 2007; HTTP/2 and modern bundlers change some advice

q.t: Get it immediately and do what he says. In my experience, the differences are very material.

t: Structures: Or Why Things Don't Fall Down
s: A friendly, non-mathematical introduction to structural engineering and the physics of why buildings, bridges and animals stand up.
w: One of the most persistent plugs on HN, with a commenter joking they should limit how often they recommend it. Called a good book on the philosophy of engineering.
ab: For curious readers with no engineering background
Intuitive explanations using everyday examples
Written in 1978; materials science has progressed

q.t: I should probably enforce a limit on the number of times I'm allowed to plug this book on HN every year

s: Dr. Jason Fung argues obesity is a hormonal problem driven by insulin and advocates intermittent fasting.
w: Pushed hard in weight-loss threads as the science-backed alternative to diet fads.
ab: For anyone struggling with weight
Surveys diets and studies
Contested claims, mixed expert views

q.t: Please, please, please read the Obesity Code by Dr. Jason Fung

s: Maugham's 1915 semi-autobiographical novel following Philip Carey from a lonely childhood through medical school, love and the search for the meaning of life.
w: HN readers rank it among the greatest novels they have read, often tied with Brothers Karamazov. They praise it as a compelling story of a life and a take on life's meaning.
ab: For readers who want a long, character-driven classic
Semi-autobiographical coming-of-age
Public-domain; many editions

q.t: tie between Of Human Bondage by W.Somerset Maugham or The Brothers Karamazov by Dostoevsky

s: Cyberpunk noir in which minds can be stored and moved between bodies, and an ex-soldier is hired to solve a rich man's murder.
w: HN sci-fi fans list it as a fun body-swapping cyberpunk noir and for thinking about digital consciousness. It often appears in lists of favorites and audiobook picks.
ab: For readers of cyberpunk and hard-boiled detective fiction
Violent and graphic
First of a trilogy about Takeshi Kovacs

s: Nabokov's novel in the form of a 999-line poem with a deranged scholar's commentary that slowly reveals its own story.
w: HN readers name it among the best books they have read, praising the language and meta-literary play. A non-native reader finds it challenging but entertaining.
ab: For readers who enjoy puzzle-like literary fiction
Unusual poem-plus-commentary format
Dense prose; can be hard for non-native English readers

q.t: I finally read Nabokov's Pale Fire. It is far and away the best book I have ever read.

s: A Pulitzer Prize-winning novel interweaving the lives of nine people drawn together by trees and forest activism.
w: HN readers call it incredible and mind-shifting, saying it changed how they look at trees. One calls it one of the best things read in a lifetime.
ab: For readers who like ecological, character-driven fiction
Interwoven stories across decades
Long, slow-burn narrative

q.t: One of the best things I've read this decade, perhaps this lifetime.

s: The complete short fiction of Jorge Luis Borges, in Andrew Hurley's translation, including The Library of Babel and The Garden of Forking Paths.
w: Recommended to HN readers who like math and ideas, for stories about infinity, libraries and labyrinths. Commenters call Borges a genius and say he shapes how you read fiction.
ab: For readers who like ideas, mathematics and puzzles in fiction
Short stories, complete in one volume
Dense and dreamlike; stories are short

q.t: IMO you won't really understand the nature and limitations of fiction until you've read JLB.

s: A narrative history of mathematics that teaches the subject from ancient astronomy and geometry up to calculus.
w: Repeatedly suggested to people who feel bad at math or want to learn from first principles, because it builds ideas in the order humans discovered them.
ab: For adults restarting math from the beginning
Teaches through history rather than drills
Written in the 1930s, so the prose is dated

q.t: It goes through the history of math, how it was discovered and used, from ancient Egypt (geometry) to the 1600s (Calculus)

s: Douglas Adams and zoologist Mark Carwardine travel the world to see endangered animals.
w: Called possibly Douglas Adams' best book, a funny and moving look at endangered species.
ab: For Adams fans and nature readers
Funny and moving
Written 1990s; some species updates

q.t: Those that liked this, will probably also enjoy what I consider maybe Douglas Adam's best book

t: The Man Who Knew Infinity: A Life of the Genius Ramanujan
s: A biography of the self-taught Indian mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan and his collaboration with G. H. Hardy in Cambridge.
w: HN commenters point to it whenever Ramanujan comes up, as the readable account of his strange gifts and short life, which was also made into a film.
ab: For anyone curious about Ramanujan or mathematical history
Narrative biography rather than a math text
A 2015 film adaptation exists

q.t: there's a great book called "The Man who Knew Infinity"

s: Sinclair's 1906 muckraking novel following a Lithuanian immigrant family in Chicago's meatpacking district, exposing brutal working conditions and corruption.
w: HN readers say it is more than a food-safety exposé: a gripping story of immigrant struggle that showed one reader how regular people lived. It appears on lists of books that shook people's views.
ab: For readers of social-realist classics
Grim and harrowing; the novel ends with a political argument
Gives a view of 1900s American working life

q.t: Grapes of Wrath stayed with me for a very long time. The Jungle too.

s: A playful, game-driven introduction to programming in Racket, a Scheme-family language, with comic-style illustrations.
w: Often suggested as a fun first book for Racket or Lisp, and for kids. One commenter contrasts it with How to Design Programs: that one fits a classroom, this one is about fun.
ab: For beginners and curious kids learning Lisp-style languages
Builds small games to teach core ideas
Lighter than How to Design Programs

q.t: i feel the easy intro to racket will stand you in good stead

s: Wittgenstein's short early work on logic, language, and the limits of what can be said, written in numbered propositions.
w: HN readers list it among mind-blowing books and call it the philosopher's philosopher. It is usually paired with his later Philosophical Investigations.
ab: For readers drawn to logic and philosophy of language
Short but extremely dense and aphoristic
Often read alongside Philosophical Investigations

q.t: Considered to be the philosopher's pholosopher!

s: Philip K. Dick's 1977 novel about an undercover narcotics agent losing his identity to a drug that splits his mind.
w: HN readers repeatedly list it among their favorite science fiction, with one calling it better than Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?. It is a staple on sci-fi recommendation lists.
ab: For readers who like dark, personal science fiction
Drug addiction and identity are central themes
Also a 2006 animated film

q.t: A Scanner Darkly - Philip K. Dick (even better)

s: Emerson's 1841 essay on individualism, nonconformity and trusting your own mind over social convention.
w: A short classic that HN readers list with Meditations and Montaigne as texts that challenge one's sense of self. Commenters recommend it for its challenge to conformity.
ab: For readers of philosophy and self-improvement classics
A short essay, often collected in Emerson anthologies
19th-century prose; best read slowly

q.t: Both offer some pretty significant challenges to one's notion of self.

s: Steinbeck's 1945 short novel about the eccentric residents of a rundown sardine-cannery street in Monterey, California.
w: HN readers love it as a short, witty read full of characters, and at least two reread it every year, finding more insight into the human condition each time.
ab: For readers wanting a quick, warm classic
Episodic vignettes about down-and-out friends
Short and gentle on plot

t: Behind Closed Doors: Secrets of Great Management
s: Pragmatic Bookshelf management book, told as a story, on one-on-ones, feedback, and managing teams, aimed at new technical managers.

ab: For new managers and tech leads, especially from engineering
Short, story-driven, and practical
Basic if you already manage a team

q.t: this one is pretty good and short

by: David Freedman, Robert Pisani et al.
s: An intro statistics textbook that teaches concepts through real data and clear explanations instead of formulas.
w: The go-to recommendation for a conceptual intro statistics book. Commenters like its real data, its exercises and that older editions work.
ab: For beginners wanting to understand statistical thinking
Uses real data in examples and exercises
Concept-first; light on software

q.t: All exercises use real data as cases, I learned a lot more from them!

s: A broad, readable introduction to algorithms, complexity and the limits of computing for a general technical audience.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a computing book that doesn't read like a textbook, and one gets it as a suggested bedside read.
ab: For readers wanting a wide view of computer science
Reads more like a narrative than a textbook
Not a hands-on programming book

q.t: The book Algorithmics: The Spirit of Computing doesn't read like a textbook to me, and it's quite interesting.

t: The Joy of X: A Guided Tour of Math, from One to Infinity
s: A popular-math tour of ideas from numbers and geometry through calculus and infinity, written for a general audience.

ab: For general readers who want math without heavy formulas
Short chapters, accessible tone
Not a textbook; won't teach you problem-solving

q.t: Related and a great read

t: How I Found Freedom in an Unfree World
s: Harry Browne's 1973 libertarian self-help book on living by your own choices and finding personal freedom within social and economic constraints.

ab: For readers wanting a personal philosophy of independence
Practical advice on choices, money and living on your own terms
Libertarian slant and 1970s examples; you may disagree with parts

s: A popular math book of applied problems from wartime mathematics, codebreaking and everyday puzzles.
w: Recommended as a well-written, challenging general-audience introduction to applied math.
ab: For math hobbyists
Applied stories
Moderately challenging

q.t: an amusingly written yet intellectually challenging introduction to applied maths for the general audience.

s: The classic sociology text on how new ideas and technologies spread, introducing early adopters and laggards.

ab: Origin of the adopter categories
Case studies on how ideas spread
Academic textbook feel

ab: For general readers curious about neuroplasticity
Story-driven case histories
Written in 2007; some claims have been challenged since

s: Neil Gaiman's 2001 novel in which an ex-con named Shadow becomes caught up in a war between old gods and new ones in America.

ab: For readers who like mythology-meets-modern-America fantasy
Long-winded in places
Also a TV series

q.t: which I quite enjoyed until near the end where it got a little too crazy.

t: The Tangled Web: A Guide to Securing Modern Web Applications
s: A guide to browser security that explains how web technologies work, their quirks, and how to defend applications.
w: Frequently recommended for web security. Commenters like its opening history of how the web's hacks accumulated and call it one of their favorite web security books.
ab: For web developers who want to understand browser security
Explains why browsers behave the way they do
2011 publication; some details are outdated

q.t: he wrote one of my favourite books on web (browser) security

t: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team: A Leadership Fable
s: A business fable about a struggling executive team that lays out five dysfunctions, from absence of trust to inattention to results.
w: Shows up on many manager and founder reading lists. One reader called it the only leadership book you need.
ab: For new managers and startup leaders
Fable format; quick and easy to read
Framework is simple; some find it oversimplified

q.t: The only one you need

t: An Elegant Puzzle: Systems of Engineering Management
s: A handbook of engineering management covering teams, org design, career growth and technical strategy, drawn from the author's blog essays.
w: HN managers say you can dive into whichever section matches your problem rather than reading cover to cover. Interesting as a practical handbook.
ab: For engineering managers and aspiring ones
Reference-style; read chapters as needed
Based on a well-known engineering management blog

q.t: It's a bit of a handbook and you don't necessarily have to read it cover to cover

s: An archaeologist's theory that societies collapse when increasing complexity yields diminishing returns, with case studies of Rome and the Maya.

ab: For readers interested in societal collapse and complexity
Academic argument with archaeological case studies
Dense and theoretical in places

q.t: I recommend reading "The Collapse of Complex Societies" by Joseph Tainter [0].

s: A collection of worked examples that derive efficient functional algorithms in Haskell through equational reasoning.

ab: For readers who already know Haskell
Each chapter derives an algorithm step by step
Not a language tutorial

q.t: is a fantastic book if you are interested in some more equational reasoning, I highly recommend it.

t: Start-up Nation: The Story of Israel's Economic Miracle

w: HN's standard reference when Israel's tech scene or national startup ecosystems come up. Commenters call it a great read and a deeper exploration of the topic.
ab: For readers curious about startup ecosystems
Focuses on military service and culture
Written around 2009; some claims are criticized

q.t: would be useful for anyone who wants a little deeper exploration of the topic

t: Surveillance Valley: The Secret Military History of the Internet
s: A history arguing that the internet and Silicon Valley grew out of military and intelligence surveillance projects.

Journalistic and polemical rather than neutral

s: Behind-the-scenes account of Twitter's founding and the clashes among its founders.

ab: For startup and tech-history fans
Narrative nonfiction
Some details disputed

q.t: Definitely would recommend, even for entertainment value, but definitely for the SV lore

t: Scale: The Universal Laws of Growth, Innovation, Sustainability, and the Pace of Life
s: A physicist's look at scaling laws in organisms, cities and companies.

ab: For curious generalists
Covers cities and companies
Uneven in places

s: A humorous classic on why systems fail, with laws such as complex systems that work evolve from simple ones.

ab: Humorous systems laws
Useful for engineers
Aphoristic

ab: For developers choosing between database types
Introductory, not deep on any one database
Original edition is from 2012; check the newer one

s: An analysis of why some East Asian economies grew rapidly, centered on land reform, manufacturing policy and finance.

Country case studies
Narrow to East and Southeast Asia

Works well with WSL for Unix-style dev
Expensive; some early reliability issues

s: A nephrologist's guide to intermittent, alternate-day, and extended fasting, covering the science, practical protocols, and risks.

ab: For readers curious about intermittent or extended fasting
Practical protocols and explanations by a clinician
Consult a doctor first; extended fasting carries real risks

First-person account from the flight director
Written from Kranz's perspective

Maps of trigger points
Not a substitute for care

Written by the tool's creator
Tied to ANTLR 4 specifically

Popular, narrative style

s: A concise algorithms textbook.

ab: Concise
Exercises
Hard

Kernighan-style clear prose with many worked examples
Predates modules and generics

Ethnography of machine gamblers
Academic in tone

Skeptical
Business books

Sequel to 1491
Narrative popular history

Accessible writing
Debated causes

Companion to the free Coursera course
Written for a younger audience

Original edition is dated on computing

Practical
Some findings contested

Journalistic review of diet science
