Focuses on textbooks, not a full history
Argues from a critical, revisionist angle

q.t: it hits on just this, being the "heroification" of American leaders.

t: The Storm Before the Storm: The Beginning of the End of the Roman Republic
s: A narrative history of the Roman Republic's decline, from the Gracchi to Sulla, by the creator of the History of Rome podcast.
w: Recommended as a great read leading into the Sulla era and the rise of Caesar, from fans of Duncan's podcast.
ab: For readers who liked the History of Rome podcast.
Covers the decades leading up to Caesar.
Narrative, accessible history.

q.t: is a great read as well. I was genuinely saddened when I finished it.

t: Distributed Services with Go: Your Guide to Reliable, Scalable, and Maintainable Systems
s: A Pragmatic Bookshelf project book in which you build a distributed event-sourcing service in Go, from a commit log through networking to deployment.
w: HN readers recommend it as a learn-by-building book on distributed systems, loaded with tests, and helpful for understanding a key-value store. One reader notes it is dense and mostly code listings.
ab: For Go developers who want to build a distributed service step by step
Mostly code listings, so dense
Author appears in the HN thread to promote it

q.t: Distributed Services with Go is a great learn-by-building book for distributed systems

s: A classic essay collection on what mathematicians do, covering mathematical culture, proof and the philosophy of mathematics.
w: HN readers suggest it for a view of math as a human, cultural pursuit. One says high-school math is enough to enjoy it.
ab: For anyone curious about math culture and philosophy
Accessible to non-mathematicians, richer with more math
Originally from 1981; it is not a textbook

q.t: High school math is enough to enjoy it, but the more math you have, the more you'll get out it.

s: A split, ortholinear, programmable mechanical keyboard with thumb clusters and tenting, successor to the ErgoDox EZ.
w: Users like its configurability and firmware compared to Kinesis, and say the split layout helps ergonomics. Adjustment takes weeks, and not everyone is happy with it.
ab: Fully programmable via ZSA's web configurator
Split, tentable layout for ergonomics
Takes about two months to adapt

q.t: the firmware and configurability is so much better than what I was used to from Kinesis

t: Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
s: A book on the Good Judgment Project, showing how a group of ordinary people made accurate forecasts by using probabilistic thinking and constant updating.
w: Cited whenever people argue about prediction, pundits, or bets. HN readers suggest it as the book on forecasting research and how good forecasters think.
ab: For anyone who wants to make better predictions
Research-backed habits for probabilistic thinking
Some examples are tied to geopolitics

q.t: Try Superforecasting by Philip Tetlock.

s: A 9.7-inch e-ink Kindle with a large screen and free 3G, aimed at PDFs and documents.
w: HN people point to it as the large-screen e-ink option for PDFs and technical reading, and a few owners say they are happy with it.
ab: For readers who want a big e-ink screen for PDFs
9.7-inch e-ink display, 3G connectivity
Old hardware (2009 design), now dated

q.t: You can get the Kindle DX if you want a larger screen. I have one and am very happy with it.

s: A cone-shaped pour-over coffee dripper with spiral ribs and a large single hole, used with paper filters to brew one cup or more.
w: HN coffee drinkers pick it as a cheap, compact, plastic-free alternative to a coffee maker or Aeropress, and the basis of a daily ritual. It works with fresh-ground beans and a gooseneck kettle.
ab: For people who want to brew better coffee by hand
Needs paper filters and a way to pour slowly
Technique and grind matter more than gear

q.t: V60 pour over set. Takes less space than a coffee maker and is cheap.

t: Delivering Happiness: A Path to Profits, Passion, and Purpose
s: Zappos CEO Tony Hsieh's memoir and business book on building the company around culture, customer service and happiness.
w: HN readers call it great and an easy read about making people happy while staying entrepreneurial, and helpful if you are building a business. Some say it is not fantastic.
ab: For founders interested in company culture and customer service
Part memoir of Hsieh's earlier ventures and the Zappos story
Written in 2010; the Zappos story has since moved on

q.t: Delivering Happiness by Tony Hsieh has had a great impact on me.

s: Larry Niven's 1970 Hugo-winning novel about an expedition to explore a vast artificial ring built around a distant star.
w: A recurring HN sci-fi pick: commenters like the megastructure concept and call it a lighter, more plausible big-object story than something like a Dyson swarm. It is often listed beside Foundation and Rendezvous with Rama.
ab: For fans of classic hard sci-fi and big ideas
Written in 1970; some dated characterization
Followed by several sequels

q.t: the ringworld concept is by far my favorite

t: The Myth of the Rational Voter: Why Democracies Choose Bad Policies
s: An economist argues that voters hold systematically biased beliefs about economics and that democracies therefore adopt bad policies.
w: HN commenters recommend it as an evidence-backed look at why voting does not produce good policy. It is cited in political and economic arguments and called a favorite by some.
ab: For readers interested in political economy and public choice
Uses survey data on economists versus voters
Contrarian thesis; many disagree with its conclusions

q.t: One of my favorite books. Helps to know a bit of public choice theory.

s: Introductory text on writing and understanding proofs, available free as a PDF.
w: Recommended as a nice introduction to proofs and formalism, free from the author.
ab: For learning to write proofs
Free PDF available
Includes problem sets

q.t: Book Of Proof by Richard Hammack is a nice introduction to proofs and formalism.

t: Phantoms in the Brain: Probing the Mysteries of the Human Mind
s: Neurologist V. S. Ramachandran's case studies of patients with brain damage, such as phantom limbs and delusions, and what they reveal about how the brain works.
w: HN readers rank it among the mind-bending books that changed their view of perception and consciousness. One says it changed their perspective on pretty much everything.
ab: For anyone curious about the brain and perception
Case-based and engaging popular neuroscience
Written in 1998; some interpretations have been challenged

q.t: Blew my mind (pun intended) and changed my perspective on pretty much everything forever.

s: A collection of short profiles of the daily routines of writers, composers, artists and scientists.
w: Recommended as a great small book on the habits of creative people, especially writers. One commenter disagrees and finds the routines boring and repetitive.
ab: For writers and makers curious about routines
Short entries, easy to dip into
Some find the entries repetitive

q.t: It's a really great small book that goes in detail through the daily routines of many authors and artists.

t: Agile Web Development with Rails, 3rd Edition
by: Sam Ruby, Dave Thomas, et al.
s: The Pragmatic Bookshelf's tutorial guide to Ruby on Rails, building a shopping-cart application step by step.
w: In the early Rails years HN pointed new learners to it as one of the better books around, though some switched to the Rails guides and API docs after starting with it.
ab: For historical interest in early Rails; this edition covers old Rails
Tutorial built around a shopping-cart app
Superseded by newer editions

q.t: Agile Web Development with Rails was one of the better books that were around when I first started learning Ruby/Rails.

t: Modernist Cuisine: The Art and Science of Cooking
s: A multi-volume encyclopedia of cooking techniques and food science, with extensive photography and cutaway images, produced by a team led by Nathan Myhrvold.
w: HN mentions it as an impressive, science-minded cooking bible and a maximum kitchen reference. Commenters also joke about the $500 price tag and its big footprint.
ab: For serious cooks and food-science nerds
Huge, lavishly photographed reference with technical detail
Very expensive and large; best as a reference set

q.t: helped me learn about the MAXIMUM viable kitchen.

t: Disciplined Minds: A Critical Look at Salaried Professionals and the Soul-Battering System That Shapes Their Lives
s: A critical look at how professional training selects for obedience and political conformity, particularly in science and academia.
w: HN brings it up in discussions of PhDs, careers and workplace conformity. Commenters call it an important book on why bosses rarely tolerate independent thought.
ab: For people questioning academia and professional culture
Polemical, with a left-leaning critique
Argues from physics-profession examples

q.t: should absolutely, definitely read Disciplined Minds[1] by Jeff Schmidt. What an important book.

s: Pulitzer-winning western about two retired Texas Rangers leading a cattle drive from Texas to Montana in the 1870s.
w: HN readers call it one of the best novels they have read, even those who normally avoid westerns. Commenters say it is long, funny and gets better with every page; some love the audiobook.
ab: For readers who want a long, character-rich epic
Over 800 pages; sequels and prequels follow
Westerns skeptics often end up loving it

q.t: Finally got around to reading Lonesome Dove and it is one of the best things I’ve ever read.

t: High-Speed Digital Design: A Handbook of Black Magic
s: A practical handbook on signal integrity, transmission lines, crosstalk, and grounding for engineers designing fast digital circuits and circuit boards.
w: Hardware engineers on HN name it as the classic on signal integrity, the one that explains why fast digital behaves like RF, and say they learned more from it than from undergrad.
ab: For EE students and hardware engineers working on fast digital boards
Practical transmission-line, impedance, and grounding insights
Assumes some EE background; the 1993 book is old but fundamentals hold

q.t: I learned more about signal integrity from reading it twice than I did during all of EE undergrad

t: The Mind's I: Fantasies and Reflections on Self and Soul
by: Douglas R. Hofstadter, Daniel C. Dennett
s: A collection of essays and stories on consciousness, selfhood and artificial intelligence, edited with commentary by Hofstadter and Dennett.
w: Recommended in threads about machine consciousness for its thought-provoking essays and stories. Commenters point to a story in it that tackles whether robots can suffer.
ab: For readers curious about consciousness and AI
Essays and fiction with commentary by the editors
Written in 1981; AI examples are dated

q.t: It has a lot of thought-provoking arguments.

s: A manga-format introduction to relational databases that follows a fictional kingdom's fruit shop through tables, SQL, and normalization.
w: HN recommends it as a surprisingly effective, light intro to databases, and the broader Manga Guide series gets praise for statistics, calculus, and electronics.
ab: For beginners who learn better from stories and pictures
Covers relational basics, SQL, and normalization at an introductory level
Basic content; manga style is not for everyone

q.t: I actually learned more from the manga database book than from many other serious database books.

t: Consciousness and the Brain: Deciphering How the Brain Codes Our Thoughts
s: A neuroscientist's account of experiments on conscious versus unconscious processing and his global workspace theory of consciousness.
w: HN recommends it as the rigorous, science-based overview of what is known about consciousness, as a contrast to philosophical speculation.
ab: For readers who want evidence-based neuroscience of consciousness
Describes experiments on masking, attention and brain imaging
Reflects one theory (global workspace); field debate continues

q.t: If you want to read a scientifically-based examination of our current understanding of conscious processes, I highly recommend

s: Christopher Alexander's multi-volume work on the principles of order in nature and buildings, a follow-up to A Pattern Language.
w: Mentioned as Alexander's most important later work, applied to everything from music to design. Commenters regret how expensive the volumes are.
ab: For readers of A Pattern Language wanting more depth
Multi-volume and expensive
Ambitious and philosophical

q.t: they deserve to be circulated more widely

t: I Am That: Talks with Sri Nisargadatta
s: Transcribed conversations between the Indian spiritual teacher Nisargadatta Maharaj and visitors about the nature of self, consciousness and non-duality.
w: HN readers recommend it in 'mind-blowing book' threads as a text that shifted their sense of self. One says it is logical but not intellectual, and another says it changed how he thinks about "I".
ab: For readers curious about non-dual philosophy and self-inquiry
Q&A talk transcripts, so easy to dip into
Pairs with Krishnamurti's Freedom from the Known in HN lists

q.t: It changed how I think about "I".

s: Leland Wilkinson's formal theory of statistical graphics, describing charts as combinations of data, geometry, scales, and statistics. It inspired ggplot2.
w: HN data-visualization people recommend it for serious attempts at expressing visualizations, and point out that it directly inspired ggplot2.
ab: For people building charting libraries or visualization tools
A formal framework behind ggplot2
Dense and theoretical, not a how-to

q.t: Yes, I would recommend "The Grammar of Graphics" for serious attempts to express visualizations

t: Switch: How to Change Things When Change Is Hard
s: A framework for making change stick by directing the rational mind, motivating the emotional mind and shaping the path.
w: Recommended to technical leaders who lean on logic to drive change. Commenters like it as a playbook for leading change.
ab: For leaders and managers driving change
Story-driven, easy read
Pop-psychology flavor

q.t: This book is an amazing read for people in your position

t: Creative Selection: Inside Apple's Design Process During the Golden Age of Steve Jobs
s: A memoir by an Apple software engineer on how demos and design were done under Steve Jobs.
w: Recommended as an inside look at Apple's creative process.
ab: For product and software designers
Insider anecdotes
One person's perspective

q.t: Also recommended: Creative Selection, by Apple engineer Ken Kocienda

t: Lords of Finance: The Bankers Who Broke the World
s: A narrative of the four central bankers whose decisions helped cause the Great Depression.
w: Recommended in threads on gold, deflation and central banking as a readable account of how interwar bankers mishandled the gold standard. One reader came to it through HN.
ab: For readers curious about the Great Depression and the gold standard
Narrative biography-style history
Won the Pulitzer Prize for history in 2010

q.t: A Keystone Cops level of professionalism displayed by the central bankers at the time.

t: Logitech MX Vertical Wireless Rechargeable Mouse
s: An ergonomic vertical mouse with a 57-degree angle, wireless connection and rechargeable battery.
w: Recommended to avoid RSI and to ease carpal tunnel; commenters call it the best mouse they have tried.
ab: For people with RSI or carpal tunnel
Wireless and rechargeable
Pricey; adjusting takes time

q.t: I personally love this vertical mouse for avoiding RSI

t: Skin in the Game: Hidden Asymmetries in Daily Life
s: Taleb's book arguing that people should bear the consequences of their decisions, and that those without exposure to risk give unreliable advice.
w: It turns up on HN desk and reading lists as part of Taleb's Incerto. One commenter recommends the central idea: weigh the opinions of people who have a stake in what they are saying.
ab: For readers of Taleb's Black Swan and Antifragile
Argumentative and opinionated rather than rigorous
Part of the five-book Incerto series

q.t: I have read quite a bit of his articles and watched his talks all of which I highly recommend.

s: Mill's 1859 essay defending individual freedom of thought and action against state and social pressure.
w: HN readers recommend it as a short, poignant classic of liberalism that appeals to the HN crowd and gives a foundation for political and ethical thinking.
ab: For readers of political philosophy
Short and readable
Free public-domain text

q.t: for political enlightenment and an impeccable defence of [classical!] liberalism

s: Kurt Vonnegut's 1973 satirical novel in which the author meets a car dealer and the sci-fi writer Kilgore Trout.
w: HN readers list it among favorite fiction: one calls it hilarious, another says it left them awestruck on the first Vonnegut read. A dependable pick in 'what are you reading' threads.
ab: For readers who like satire and short, odd novels
A quick read with the author's own drawings
Dark, absurdist humor is not for everyone

q.t: Breakfast of Champions, by Kurt Vonnegut. Hilarious stuff.

s: A near-future techno-thriller by Charles Stross in which police investigate a robbery inside an online game.
w: HN readers recommend it as a book for computer geeks and a cool cyberpunk-style cybercrime story. One notes that its near-future setting is now overrun by time.
ab: For programmers who like cyber-thrillers about games
Second-person style, geeky humor
Near-future tech is now dated

q.t: Halting State, by Charles Stross, great for computer geeks

s: A Dover paperback by Ian Stewart introducing topics in modern mathematics, including sets, groups, topology, and number theory.
w: Suggested to people who want mathematical intuition without a degree. Commenters say it needs only elementary algebra, with nice illustrations and humor.
ab: For curious readers wanting a tour of modern math
Needs only elementary algebra
Light on exercises and rigor

q.t: To get better intuition without a math degree I'd recommend: Concepts of Modern Mathematics which only requires elementary algebra

by: John F. Hughes, Andries van Dam, et al.
s: A comprehensive textbook on computer graphics theory covering modeling, rendering, and interaction, the long-running reference known as Foley and van Dam.
w: HN calls it a classic of computer graphics, like Knuth is for algorithms. A commenter adds it is not the book for practical graphics, which is why others suggest Abrash and Real-Time Rendering.
ab: For students of graphics theory
Broad coverage of the field's foundations
Not a practical programming guide

q.t: It's a classic in the computer graphics field, like Knuth is for algorithms.

t: Learn You a Haskell for Great Good!
s: Playful, illustrated beginner's guide to Haskell, covering functional programming, types, monads and more; free to read online.
w: HN's classic first Haskell tutorial: fun and accessible, a good companion to denser material. One reader adds that it is weaker on practical problems.
ab: For programmers new to Haskell
Free at learnyouahaskell.com
Light on practical projects; Real World Haskell fills that gap, but is dated

q.t: is a fun and accessible intro to Haskell that's a great complement to denser material

t: Mastery: The Keys to Success and Long-Term Fulfillment
s: An aikido master's short book on the learning curve, plateaus, and sticking with practice to reach mastery in any skill.
w: HN recommends it to people struggling to stay motivated or ready to quit a skill, as a short guide to plateaus and the value of practice.
ab: For learners hitting plateaus in programming, sports, or music
Short, readable, and focused on practice habits
Reflective rather than technical

q.t: very fascinating and useful read (also quite short)

t: Chip War: The Fight for the World's Most Critical Technology
s: A history of the semiconductor industry, how fabs moved to Asia, and the geopolitical contest over chips.
w: The default HN pick on semiconductors: recounts history, major players, why fabs ended up in Asia and China's catch-up attempts. Simply called a good read.
ab: For readers following semiconductors and geopolitics
Narrative history with business and military angles
Strong on US-China competition

q.t: Chip War by Chris Miller is a good read

t: American Kingpin: The Epic Hunt for the Criminal Mastermind Behind the Silk Road
s: A narrative account of Ross Ulbricht, the Silk Road dark-web marketplace, and the investigators who tracked him down.
w: HN readers recommend it as the go-to book on Silk Road, often alongside the Andy Greenberg-style coverage, and it works well as an audiobook.
ab: For fans of true crime and internet history
Fast-paced, reads like a thriller
Some dramatized scenes; one side of a contested case

q.t: highly recommend the book / audible — American Kingpin

t: Interconnections: Bridges, Routers, Switches, and Internetworking Protocols
s: A guide to how bridges, routers and switches work and why networking protocols were designed as they were, by the inventor of the spanning tree protocol.
w: HN network engineers repeatedly recommend it for explaining why networking works the way it does. One says every full-time network engineer they asked recommended it.
ab: For engineers who want to understand the reasoning behind networking
Funny, readable writing from Radia Perlman
1999 edition; material is dated, so pair it with modern references

q.t: has been recommended to me by every fulltime NetEng I've ever asked

s: T. H. White's retelling of the Arthurian legend, from The Sword in the Stone to Arthur's fall, mixing comedy, tragedy and political reflection.
w: HN readers call it a favorite fictional book and the best novelization of the problem of power, praising its modern retelling and Lancelot story. One came to it from the Disney film.
ab: For readers who like thoughtful retellings of Arthurian legend
Tone shifts from comic to tragic
Tells the story of Lancelot particularly well

q.t: best novelization of the problem of power

s: A textbook on programming language design and implementation covering syntax, semantics, types and compilation.
w: Recommended as a readable book on language design choices and implementation.
ab: For learning how languages work
Textbook, long
Implementation-focused

q.t: The explanations of many things I'd read in other sources are no less than fantastic

t: Creativity: Flow and the Psychology of Discovery and Invention
s: A study of creative people, drawn from interviews with scientists, artists and thinkers, by the psychologist who coined flow.
w: Recommended as the deeper follow-up to Flow, especially for entrepreneurs, with long interviews with accomplished creative minds.
ab: Interview-driven look at how creative people work
Good follow-up if you liked Flow
Academic in tone, with older interview subjects

q.t: His book Creativity is also excellent, particularly for entrepreneurs.

t: Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms
s: David MacKay's textbook linking information theory, Bayesian inference, coding and machine learning, with a free PDF available from the author's site.
w: HN regards it as a rare technical book that is also a pleasure to read. Commenters call it an eye-opener that ties together probability, coding and learning, and praise it for how well it's written.
ab: For ML and stats students who want a Bayesian, information-theoretic view
Broad coverage with exercises; free PDF from the author
Not a pure math text; some topics are dated by modern deep learning

q.t: Maybe start with MacKay's Information Theory, Inference, etc. (it is freely available online), very entertaining and accessible book

s: An ergonomic office chair from Herman Miller, designed with a flexible back that supports the spine, and often compared to the Aeron.
w: HN commenters call it supremely comfortable and an upgrade over the Aeron, helping people with back problems. They note it is costly, hard to clean and shows wear after years, and that Steelcase Gesture is a cheaper rival.
ab: For people sitting all day who want a premium ergonomic chair
Buying used can halve the price
Expensive; fabric is hard to clean

q.t: I ended up investing in a Herman Miller Embody, and have not been looking back since. Great chair!

s: Apple's 2020 13-inch fanless laptop with the first M1 chip, offering strong performance and long battery life in a thin body.
w: HN buyers call it dumb fast and dead silent, beating hot, fan-heavy older MacBook Pros and Thinkpads for daily work. One dev runs Chrome, simulators and Docker on the 8GB model.
ab: For developers and everyday users who want a silent, cool laptop
No fan, so heavy loads throttle eventually
Choose 16GB RAM if you run heavy dev workloads

q.t: MacBook Air M1: Dumb fast and dead silent. Everything I want from a computer.

s: Apple's line of smartwatches with activity rings, notifications and health sensors, including sleep tracking through third-party apps.
w: Commenters praise it for activity-ring motivation and for effortless sleep tracking with apps like AutoSleep. The main complaint is poor battery life.
ab: Works best with an iPhone
Fitness rings nudge people to move more
Battery life draws complaints; charge daily

q.t: Since I bought it the gamification of closing the rings and monthly challenges has definitely improved my physical health.

s: A collection of practical tips and habits for working programmers on craft, design, tooling and responsibility, updated for the 20th anniversary.
w: A top HN answer for career and craft. One commenter says it changed everything for them. Another calls it the best general-principles book they've read.
ab: For developers at any career stage who want good habits
Tips are general principles, not tied to one language
Updated 20th anniversary edition replaces the original

q.t: It's not overly specific to one single thing, it tries to teaches general principles and good practice.

t: Hands-on Rust: Effective Learning through 2D Game Development and Play
s: A Pragmatic Bookshelf project book that teaches Rust by building a roguelike dungeon-crawler game, covering map generation, ECS and event buses.
w: HN recommends it as a fun, project-based way into Rust and an excellent introduction to ECS, especially for those who want to make games. It uses the author's own engine, which hides some graphics detail.
ab: For Rust newcomers who learn best by building a game
Uses the Legion ECS, now discontinued
Priced around $30 for the ebook; also on O'Reilly

q.t: Highly recommend this book on rust if you want to make a roguelike.

s: A programmable electric multicooker that works as a pressure cooker, slow cooker, and rice cooker.
w: HN users call it one of the most useful kitchen purchases, saying it cuts takeout, makes bulk cooking and meal prep easy, and lives up to the hype.
ab: For home cooks who want fast, hands-off meals
Replaces slow cooker and rice cooker
Large sizes take counter space

q.t: I just got an InstantPot - so far it lives up to the hype.

s: A short book arguing that accelerating digital technology is displacing jobs faster than the economy adapts.
w: HN suggests it in threads on automation and unemployment. Commenters call it an excellent primer and pair it with The Great Stagnation for opposing views.
ab: For readers worried about automation
Short and accessible
Written in 2011; predictions need checking

q.t: the following books are excellent primers

s: John Doerr's guide to OKRs, the objective-and-key-results goal system used at Intel and Google.
w: HN readers use it as their reference for OKRs, calling it the best business book since The Lean Startup and a staple on technical leadership lists.
ab: For managers and founders setting team goals
Case studies from Google and others
Some commenters recall few details afterward

q.t: best business book since Lean Startup

t: Dark Pools: The Rise of the Machine Traders and the Rigging of the U.S. Stock Market
s: A narrative account of how electronic trading and high-frequency traders took over the U.S. stock market, with profiles of the hackers who built it.
w: HN recommends it as the readable history of high-frequency trading, and it features Josh Levine, the programmer behind Island ECN, whose story the community likes.
ab: For programmers curious about markets and high-frequency trading
Story-driven profiles of the people behind electronic exchanges
Journalistic and one-sided in places; HFT's value is debated

q.t: Great book about the evolution of HFT

s: A graduate-level textbook on compiler construction from the Rice University team, covering parsing, optimization, and code generation.
w: HN's modern alternative to the Dragon Book. Commenters call it readable, clear and up to date, and keep it on the desk as a reference.
ab: For anyone building or studying compilers
More current than the Dragon Book
Theory-heavy; pair with real compiler source

q.t: I found this book on compilers to be rather up-to-date, clear and useful when you start going into the topic:

t: Tools of Titans: The Tactics, Routines, and Habits of Billionaires, Icons, and World-Class Performers
s: A large compendium of tactics, routines and advice distilled from Tim Ferriss's podcast interviews with high performers.
w: HN readers list it among their favorite non-fiction, praising its concise body-and-mindset hacking from many experimenters. Some call it a must-read for wannabe achievers.
ab: For readers who like bite-size productivity and lifestyle ideas
Huge, skimmable collection; read it in pieces
Advice is anecdotal and varies in quality

q.t: A must-read piece for wannabe achievers like me

s: Parables set in ancient Babylon teaching basic personal finance: save a tenth of your income, avoid debt, invest wisely and make your money work.
w: HN's first-pick money book, valued for its simplicity: the habit of putting aside 10 percent is dead simple to implement. A recommended pairing with Think and Grow Rich.
ab: For beginners who want simple savings principles
Short parables, light on technical detail
Written in the 1920s, so no modern investment products

q.t: I like the simplicity of just putting aside 10 percent to start.

s: A book exploring geometry through turtle graphics programming in Logo, up to curved space and relativity.
w: Recommended as a Logo-for-grown-ups book with a DIY exploration spirit, for geometry through programming.
ab: For programmers who like geometry
Logo-based exercises
Math-heavy later chapters

q.t: It has a spirit of DIY exploration unlike any other math book I'd seen at the time.

t: Data Smart: Using Data Science to Transform Information into Insight
s: An introduction to data science techniques such as clustering, regression and Naive Bayes, taught using spreadsheets instead of code.
w: HN recommends it as the math-light way into data science. Commenters like that it implements real algorithms in Excel without notation overload or magic library calls.
ab: For beginners and spreadsheet users
Algorithms worked step by step in Excel
Not a path to production ML tooling

q.t: It's one of the few books on the subject that doesn't get bogged down with mathematical notation

s: The official guide to the Scala language, written by its creator and colleagues.
w: The pick for learning Scala, a best technical book of 2011 for one commenter. Called clear and well written and helped things click.
ab: For developers learning Scala
Written by the language's creator
Covers older Scala versions

q.t: Programing in Scala[1] helped make a lot of things click for me.

t: A Supposedly Fun Thing I'll Never Do Again: Essays and Arguments
s: A collection of essays by David Foster Wallace on cruise ships, tennis, television, state fairs and more, including the title piece.
w: HN calls it the friendlier way into David Foster Wallace than Infinite Jest: shorter, tighter essays, and the title essay is a terrific introduction to the author.
ab: For readers new to Wallace who find his novels intimidating
Essays on culture, sports and travel
Funny but long-winded footnote style

q.t: A much friendlier/more accessible place to start is A Supposedly Fun Thing I'll Never Do Again

t: Republic, Lost: How Money Corrupts Congress--and a Plan to Stop It
s: A law professor's account of how campaign finance and lobbying distort US politics, with proposals for reform.
w: A favorite of HN commenters in threads about lobbying and SOPA-style legislation. They call it well-considered and a good first step for anyone asking what to do about money in politics.
ab: For readers interested in campaign finance and US political reform
Short and quick to read
Written in 2011; US-focused and reform-oriented

q.t: If you want to know what to do, a nice first step would be to buy and read Republic, Lost.

t: Bad Pharma: How Drug Companies Mislead Doctors and Harm Patients
s: A physician's account of how clinical trials are rigged, hidden or misreported by drug companies, and how that harms patients.
w: Pointed to whenever medical research bias, unpublished trial data and industry influence come up. One reader calls it a good tome, albeit a bit dry.
ab: For readers interested in evidence-based medicine
Dense with detail; a bit dry in places
UK-centric examples in parts

q.t: this is a good tome on the subject (albeit a bit dry)

s: A large reference covering digital audio, synthesis, signal processing and computer-music composition techniques, published by MIT Press in 1996.
w: HN calls it an excellent, technical-yet-accessible overview of how digital audio and synthesis work, and a standard reference for synthesis algorithms, if an expensive one.
ab: For programmers getting into audio synthesis and DSP
Broad coverage, not tied to a single tool
Pricey and written in the 1990s

q.t: an excellent tour of the standard concepts and techniques of computer music

t: The Wisdom of Insecurity: A Message for an Age of Anxiety
s: Alan Watts's short 1951 book arguing that the search for psychological security is the source of anxiety and that we should live fully in the present.
w: HN readers call it tiny and among the best books they have read, gift it to friends, and say it helped center them. They like Watts's spirituality without supernatural belief.
ab: For anxious readers curious about Eastern-influenced philosophy
Very short and easy to finish in a sitting
Pairs with Watts's 'The Book: On the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are'

q.t: it's tiny, easily the best book I've ever read.

s: Thriller about a detective and a neuroscientist confronting a condition that rewrites memories and a technology that lets people relive their pasts.
w: HN readers call it one of Crouch's fast, fun and easy reads, often alongside Dark Matter and Upgrade, and highly recommend it as a page-turner.
ab: For readers who want a fast, twisty sci-fi thriller
Light on hard science; plot-driven
Best paired with Dark Matter by the same author

q.t: they were all really fun easy reads. Highly recommended.

s: A comic novel about an angel and a demon who try to stop the coming Apocalypse because they like life on Earth.
w: HN readers recommend it as a very funny gift book and a favorite re-read, and wish the two authors had written more together.
ab: For fans of Pratchett and Gaiman's humor
Light, funny take on the end of the world
Gaiman's novels can be long-winded to some

q.t: I wish Pratchett and Gaiman had written more books together.

t: RTL-SDR Blog V3 R820T2 USB Software Defined Radio
s: A USB software defined radio dongle with a TCXO and telescopic antennas for receiving signals from about 500 kHz to 1.7 GHz.
w: HN's first suggestion for exploring radio cheaply. Works with SDR# and GQRX for aircraft, weather satellites and ham bands.
ab: For hobbyists exploring radio, ADS-B and satellites
Receive only; no transmit
No license needed

q.t: Just buying an RDL-SDR [1] for $20-30 will open up an amazing world of possibilities

t: The Haskell Road to Logic, Maths and Programming
s: A textbook teaching discrete math, logic and proof writing through Haskell programs.
w: HN recommends this lesser-known book as a programmer's road to proofs. Commenters like that it covers math notation and discrete math while exploring Haskell.
ab: For programmers wanting to learn proofs and discrete math
Uses Haskell throughout
A 2nd edition fixes issues in the first

q.t: It's great to go over old and new math concepts and do so while exploring Haskell.

s: An undergraduate introduction to group theory built around pictures such as Cayley diagrams and visual examples.
w: Recommended as an approachable, conversational and picture-filled entry point to group theory, unlike most abstract textbooks.
ab: For beginners meeting group theory
Heavily illustrated, conversational tone
A separate problem book exists

q.t: an approachable introduction written in conversational style, full of great pictures

t: The Art of Insight in Science and Engineering
s: A guide to estimation, approximation, and problem-solving tools for science and engineering, free to download from MIT Press.
w: HN fans call it extremely useful for building intuition and Fermi-style estimation. It is often paired with the author's Street-Fighting Mathematics, and is open access.
ab: For students and engineers who want estimation skills
Free legal PDF from MIT Press
Harder and more comprehensive than Street-Fighting Mathematics

q.t: the most useful book I have read during my studies in physics and I highly recommend it to everybody with some technical interest

t: The Easy Way to Stop Smoking
s: A self-help book that argues smokers can quit by changing how they think about cigarettes rather than by willpower.
w: HN commenters repeatedly credit it with getting them to quit smoking, some giving it as a gift. They say its logical argument changed how they thought about willpower and cravings.
ab: For smokers who want to quit
Works by reframing thinking, not by scare tactics
Individual results vary

q.t: Read it, quit smoking two days later, and I have been enjoying fresh air, greater taste

s: A parallel novel to Ender's Game, retelling the Battle School story from the viewpoint of Bean, a street kid with a genius mind.
w: HN readers re-read it and often prefer it to Ender's Game, saying it resonates at different life stages. One recommends it with a caveat about the author's personal politics.
ab: For Ender's Game fans wanting Bean's side
Parallel story, not a sequel or prequel
Author's personal politics bother some readers

q.t: Every single time I've reread either I've found some part of the book that resonates precisely

s: A 2013-era 14-inch Lenovo business laptop with a socketed CPU, upgradeable RAM and storage, and a classic keyboard.
w: HN users buy it used as a cheap, repairable, Linux- and OpenBSD-friendly machine. They like the upgradeability and keyboard, though several upgrade the poor stock display and miss some keys.
ab: For tinkerers wanting a cheap used Linux laptop
Upgradeable RAM, SSDs, and CPU
Weak stock screen and aging hardware

q.t: Cheap, serviceable, extendable to 16gb RAM, with easily upgradable CPU... still one of the best in its category.

t: Can't Hurt Me: Master Your Mind and Defy the Odds
s: David Goggins's memoir and self-help book about overcoming abuse and poverty to become a Navy SEAL and ultra-endurance athlete.
w: HN readers name it as a book that changed their thinking about mental toughness, and one with ADHD credits it for breaking negative self-talk patterns.
ab: For readers looking for motivation and mental toughness
Intense, hard-driving tone
Not a substitute for therapy

q.t: Probably the biggest thing I've found helpful was David Goggins book

s: The collected comic strips about a boy and his stuffed tiger, in bound collections.
w: HN readers call it the perfect coffee table book, full of wisdom and creativity. It changed some people's views and a parent's son even built a clone machine.
ab: For fans of newspaper comics and gifts to kids
Full run of Watterson's strips
Large and expensive in complete box set

q.t: Bust it out at a random moment and receive the sum of all human wisdom in bite sized cartoon form.

s: A 17th-century treatise on strategy and swordsmanship by the Japanese swordsman Miyamoto Musashi, covering combat, timing, and the mindset of a master.
w: HN readers pair it with The Art of War as a classic on strategy and discipline, a quick read for managing yourself. One compares it to Sun Tzu for its strategic focus.
ab: For readers who like Sun Tzu and strategy classics
Short text with terse chapters
Translations vary a lot; the swordsmanship context needs some background

q.t: It's strategic more than tactical, and if you like Sun Tzu you might dig it.

t: An Introduction to Functional Programming Through Lambda Calculus
s: A Dover text teaching lambda calculus from basics through data types, recursion and lists.
w: Recommended as the gentlest path into lambda calculus, one even suggested for a curious 13-year-old.
ab: For beginners curious about functional programming
No math background needed
Cheap Dover paperback

q.t: This does not require any mathematical background, starting from simple substitution through list processing.

t: Proofs Without Words: Exercises in Visual Thinking
s: A collection of diagrams that demonstrate mathematical theorems and identities visually, with little or no text.
w: Suggested again and again as the next step for anyone who enjoys visual proofs, from the Pythagorean theorem to algebraic identities.
ab: For people who enjoy visual and geometric math
Short diagram-only proofs, easy to dip into
Not a systematic textbook

q.t: If you like this, you'll love the book Proofs without Words: Exercises in Visual Thinking

t: Against the Grain: A Deep History of the Earliest States
s: A history of early states and agriculture.
w: Recommended as an alternative view on early civilization.
ab: For history readers
Challenges progress myths
Dense

q.t: For evidence based narrative of the oldest known state like agricultural cultures I can't recommend enough James Scott's "Against the grain"

s: The story of the Kelly criterion, Claude Shannon and Edward Thorp, and how information theory was applied to betting and markets.
w: Recommended as an entertaining companion to Shannon's biography, covering Kelly betting and Thorp's blackjack and market ideas. Praised for its readability.
ab: For readers interested in Shannon, Thorp and the Kelly criterion.
Popular history that covers casinos and Wall Street.
Light on math; a story book.

q.t: Easy and entertaining to read, as are all William Poundstone books.

s: Nobel laureate Herbert Simon's essays on design, complexity, bounded rationality and artificial intelligence, arguing that engineering and design form a science of their own.
w: HN cites it as an inspiring read for young minds and as the lens that makes programming look like a science of the artificial, closer to design than natural science.
ab: For people interested in design, complexity and how we study man-made systems
Short essays that mix AI, economics and organization theory
Dense and abstract in places; first edition dates to 1969

q.t: See the Sciences of the Artificial by Herb Simon (a true legend)

t: Everything Is Obvious: Once You Know the Answer
s: A sociologist argues that common sense misleads us about society, business and prediction, and that hindsight makes outcomes seem obvious.
w: HN brings it up whenever someone appeals to common sense or after-the-fact explanations. Commenters describe it as a very good, interesting read from a researcher who tested these ideas.
ab: For people who work with predictions, forecasts or social data
Challenges narratives that only look obvious in hindsight
Argument can feel repetitive in places

q.t: Duncan Watts has a book titled Everything Is Obvious: Once You Know the Answer Very good and interesting read.

t: The Fish That Ate the Whale: The Life and Times of America's Banana King
s: A biography of Samuel Zemurray and the rise of United Fruit.
w: Recommended as a great read on the banana trade and United Fruit's influence in Latin America.
ab: For business-history readers
Narrative biography
Fruit company politics

q.t: An amazing story of the guy who took over the banana industry

t: I Contain Multitudes: The Microbes Within Us and a Grander View of Life
s: Ed Yong's popular science book on the microbes that live in and on our bodies and their role in health and evolution.
w: HN readers recommend it as an accessible, well-written look at the microbiome. Commenters say everyone should know more about bacteria.
ab: For curious readers wanting an accessible microbiome introduction
Readable popular science from a staff science writer
Written in 2016; the research has progressed

q.t: I highly recommend Ed Yong's book I Contain Multitudes

s: Greg Egan's collection of hard science fiction short stories exploring identity, mathematics and physics.
w: HN sci-fi readers recommend it as a good intro to Egan's hard sci-fi, with one saying it was the first time fiction clicked for them and another naming it the best they've read in recent years.
ab: For readers who like hard sci-fi and big ideas
Short stories on identity, math and physics
Characters can feel thin; the ideas are the point

q.t: I read a lot of books, the one I'd recommend the most is Greg Egan's

s: Keith Grant's Manning book that explains how CSS works, including layout, Flexbox, Grid and responsive design.
w: HN recommends it for developers who got by with Bootstrap and want to understand CSS. Readers say it explains the why behind CSS, filling gaps in modern CSS, including grid.
ab: For developers who want to properly learn CSS layout
Covers modern CSS including Flexbox and Grid
Focus is on concepts, not a quick reference

q.t: This book helped fill in the gaps for me when it comes to modern CSS.

s: Borges's 1944 short story collection with labyrinths, infinite libraries and invented books.
w: A repeated choice for HN's mind-bending fiction picks. Commenters call it a classic with each story intriguing and some built on incredibly creative ideas.
ab: For readers who like short, idea-driven fiction
Philosophical stories about infinity, memory and reality
Dense and allusive; translations differ

q.t: A real classic, each story is intriguing and some center on incredibly creative ideas.

s: Simon Singh's popular history of the 350-year problem and Andrew Wiles's proof of it.
w: Recommended on HN as a readable popular-math book. A math tutor says it inspired them by showing what mathematicians actually do, and commenters call it detailed but accessible.
ab: For curious readers and students without heavy math background
Narrative history of Fermat's problem and Wiles's journey
Not technical; no proofs to follow

q.t: Detailed yet extremely readable for a very wide audience.

s: Mario Puzo's 1969 crime novel about the Corleone mafia family, the basis for the film trilogy.
w: HN readers call it addictive and better than the film, and one calls it the best 'people management' book. The novel is a recurring answer in favorite-fiction threads.
ab: For fans of the films or crime sagas
Power, loyalty and family dynamics
Violent; includes dated attitudes

q.t: Such a brilliant and addictive book.

s: Erich Fromm's 1956 study arguing that love is a learned skill, covering romantic, brotherly and self love.
w: HN readers say it opened up psychology for them, and describe its idea that love must be practiced and takes constant work. It's recommended for relationship insight to younger people.
ab: For readers thinking about relationships and love as a skill
Short psychological and philosophical essay
1950s language and assumptions

q.t: To him love is a skill that has to be practiced and learned, love in a relationship is constant hard work

t: Labyrinths: Selected Stories and Other Writings
s: A collection of Borges's short stories, essays and parables on infinity, time, memory and books, including The Library of Babel.
w: HN readers love it for the way it bends math and infinity into fiction. One gifts it often, and others call it the best book they have read.
ab: For readers who like ideas, math, and metafiction in short form
Short pieces you can dip into
Dense and abstract; not a conventional story collection

q.t: I've gifted this many times

s: A 1956 sci-fi novel set in a world of teleportation, a revenge story modelled on The Count of Monte Cristo.
w: HN readers praise the Count of Monte Cristo-style plot with an antihero, and one says it was their standout for a surprising twist. Also published as Tiger! Tiger!
ab: For readers who like classic revenge plots in sci-fi
Also titled Tiger! Tiger!
Written in the 1950s

q.t: Really great Count of Monte Cristo type plot with teleportation and a great antihero.

t: Conquering Carpal Tunnel Syndrome and Other Repetitive Strain Injuries
s: A self-care program of stretches and technique changes for carpal tunnel and repetitive strain injuries.
w: Programmers with RSI recommend it for stretches that relieved pain, some saying better than physical therapy.
ab: For keyboard users with wrist pain
Simple daily stretches
Not medical advice; see a doctor

q.t: Changed my life -- no more typing pain.

s: A reference on collision detection algorithms and spatial partitioning for games.
w: Called one of the best technical books, with coverage of floating point and cache-friendly algorithms.
ab: For game and physics programmers
Dense reference
Strong on numerical issues

q.t: Each page is solid gold and very little space is wasted.

s: A book of short conceptual physics puzzles, each answered with a multiple-choice question and then explained in plain language.
w: HN readers recommend it for building physical intuition rather than formula-plugging. You try to answer each puzzle first, in the way Feynman-style thinking encourages.
ab: For curious people and students who want physical intuition
Hundreds of conceptual questions with explanations, almost no math
Rewards actually pausing to answer before reading on

q.t: teaches physics the way Feynman talks about, by trying to build intuition

t: Kelly: More Than My Share of It All
s: The memoir of Kelly Johnson, the Lockheed engineer who led the Skunk Works and designed aircraft including the U-2 and SR-71.
w: HN commenters recommend it for a first-hand look at how Skunk Works built advanced aircraft on time and under budget. It is the go-to pointer whenever Lockheed, the SR-71 or lean engineering teams come up.
ab: For engineers and aviation fans interested in how great teams work
First-person account, including Skunk Works management rules
Written in 1989; reads like an older memoir

q.t: it's a wonderful view into how they did things on time and below budget on projects like the SR71

t: Meditations on Violence: A Comparison of Martial Arts Training & Real World Violence
s: A corrections officer and martial arts instructor compares dojo training with how real violence actually unfolds.
w: Recommended for understanding how people react in violent situations and the dynamics of group violence, though one commenter calls it beautifully flawed.
ab: Realistic look at violence versus martial arts
Covers psychology and aftermath
Graphic subject matter; author's opinions are strong

q.t: Even if you've never been in a violent encounter, this book will help you understand how you will react.

s: A textbook on deriving programs together with their correctness proofs using predicate calculus and invariants.
w: Recommended as an accessible way to learn writing provably correct programs with pen and paper, no heavy theorem prover needed.
ab: For learning formal program derivation
Pen-and-paper reasoning, not tool-based
Dated notation and rigorous exercises

q.t: the basic methods of writing provably correct programs have been explained in plain English since at least the 70s

s: A short collection of Krishnamurti's talks on freeing the mind from conditioning, authority, and fear.
w: HN readers call it a mind-opening, restlessness-easing read, often paired with Nisargadatta's I Am That. One says you may disagree but it offers a new perspective.
ab: For readers questioning how they live and think
Short, about 128 pages
Spiritual and abstract; not everyone will agree

q.t: You may disagree with what they are saying, but these books will give you a new perspective.

s: Saša Jurić's Manning book on the Elixir language and the Erlang/OTP platform: processes, concurrency, supervision and building fault-tolerant systems.
w: The HN default for learning Elixir. Commenters call it a great introduction to the language and its ethos, with good explanations of OTP internals, and refer to it as the Elixir bible.
ab: For developers who want to learn Elixir and how OTP works
Third edition updated for modern Elixir
Assumes you can already program

q.t: it's a great introduction to the language and ethos of Elixir.

t: Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space
s: Carl Sagan's 1994 book on humanity's place in the cosmos and the case for exploring space, inspired by the Voyager photograph of Earth.
w: HN readers say it changed their worldview, with one praising its beautiful perspective on our place in the cosmos, and another loving the optimism of Sagan's writing.
ab: For readers who like Sagan and big-picture science
Essays on space exploration and the human future
Parts of the space-policy discussion date from the 1990s

q.t: Fundamentally altered my worldview and the way I perceive stuff.

s: Michael Ende's 1979 fantasy novel about a boy who reads himself into the magical land of Fantastica.
w: HN readers call it the most imaginative, wonder-filled fantasy, and say the film does not do the book justice. Others say they only fully appreciated its second half as adults.
ab: For readers of all ages who like imaginative fantasy
Far deeper than the film adaptation
Second half is darker and more philosophical

q.t: Best fantasy in terms of most imaginative and full of wonder: The Neverending Story by Michael Ende.

s: 1960 self-help classic by plastic surgeon Maxwell Maltz on self-image, goal-setting and visualization, using cybernetics as a model for the mind.
w: HN readers call it one of the most profound books they have read and a foundational work on self-image. Some say it contains most of what later self-help books repeat.
ab: For readers interested in self-image, goal-setting and mindset
A founding text of modern self-help
Dated language, and the evidence is anecdotal

q.t: was one of the most profound books I've ever read

t: Emotional Design: Why We Love (or Hate) Everyday Things
s: Don Norman's follow-up to The Design of Everyday Things, explaining how emotion and aesthetics shape how people use products.
w: HN designers recommend it as the next step after The Design of Everyday Things. Commenters point to it for the idea that attractive products work better.
ab: For designers and developers who read Design of Everyday Things
Visceral, behavioral, and reflective design levels
Earlier examples feel dated

q.t: Take a look at "Emotional Design" by Don Norman

t: BUGS in Writing: A Guide to Debugging Your Prose
s: A style guide for technical writing.
w: Recommended for technical writers, pressed into hands for years.
ab: Technical writing
Reference
Cutesy

q.t: which I've been pressing into people's hands for twenty years now

t: Sunburst and Luminary: An Apollo Memoir
s: A memoir by an MIT engineer who wrote lunar landing software for the Apollo guidance computer.
w: Recommended for space and Apollo enthusiasts as a first-person account of writing the guidance software.
ab: For fans of Apollo and early software history.
First-person account from a guidance software author.
Technical details appear throughout.

q.t: It recounts much of this history and is a worthwhile read for space and Apollo junkies.

t: The Body Electric: Electromagnetism and the Foundation of Life
s: A 1985 book by an orthopedic surgeon on bioelectricity, regeneration and the effects of electromagnetic fields on living things.
w: HN commenters call it fascinating and note that Michael Levin cites it as inspiration. Some of its claims, especially about wireless exposure, are fringe.
ab: For readers interested in bioelectricity and regeneration
Pioneering but dated in places
Fringe claims about EM fields; read critically

q.t: a fascinating book I read a few years ago about experiments using electricity to promote cellular healing

s: Peter Drucker's 1967 classic on managerial effectiveness, covering time, contribution, strengths, priorities and decisions.
w: HN readers recommend it as the first management book to read, one that changed how they track time, prioritize and focus. A new team lead said his company did not prepare him as well.
ab: For new managers and knowledge workers wanting a practical foundation
Short and principle-based
Written in 1967; examples are dated, ideas are not

q.t: I found it very interesting and it changed my outlook on the value of tracking time

t: The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America
s: A history showing how federal, state and local policy created residential segregation in the United States, including redlining.
w: HN commenters point to it in housing, inequality and redlining threads as the documented history of government-led segregation.
ab: For readers curious about U.S. housing policy and its legacy
Well-documented, quick read
Formatting is rough, per one reader

q.t: gives a really really good overview of the systematic, government led, programs designed and enforced explicitly against african americans

s: A short Pragmatic Bookshelf guide to the tmux terminal multiplexer, with a sample configuration for working without a mouse.
w: HN readers recommend it as a short, clear first book on tmux, and its included config makes a good starting point. Several say it is worth the ~$11 price over scattered blog posts.
ab: For developers starting out with tmux and terminal workflows
Short and concise; includes a starter tmux.conf
Written around tmux 1.x, so newer features are missing

q.t: I recently read the tmux book by the pragmatic programmers and highly recommend it

t: The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology
s: Ray Kurzweil's 2005 argument that exponential progress in computing, biotech and AI will lead to a merger of humans and machines.
w: HN readers say it taught them about accelerating progress and drew them into computing. Others call it speculative, and some put it down unfinished.
ab: For readers interested in AI futurism and exponential trends
Highly speculative; some consider it near-fiction
Predictions from 2005 are now checkable

q.t: that book really instilled in me that the pace of change could be really quite rapid through my career

s: A No Starch Press guide to GNU make, with advanced techniques, recipes and debugging tips from the author of the 'Ask Mr Make' column.
w: HN calls it the go-to GNU make reference: a fantastic general guide and a source of reusable recipes. One commenter calls it the most-referred book on their office shelf.
ab: For developers who maintain makefiles and want to go deep
Mix of explanation and ready-made recipes
Focuses on GNU make rather than other build systems

q.t: It is both a fantastic general guide and an amazing source of usable little recipes

t: All the Mathematics You Missed: But Need to Know for Graduate School
s: A concise survey of undergraduate mathematics, from linear algebra and analysis to topology and geometry, aimed at graduate-school preparation.
w: HN readers recommend it as a quick, compact introduction to undergrad math topics for filling gaps before more advanced study.
ab: For self-learners filling gaps in math background
Brief overview chapters with pointers to deeper texts
Survey, not a full course; go elsewhere for depth

q.t: which is a nice brief introduction to various undergrad maths topics

t: Clojure Programming: Practical Lisp for the Java World
by: Chas Emerick, Brian Carper, et al.
s: An O'Reilly guide to Clojure covering the language, concurrency, Java interop and practical applications.
w: Recommended as the best way to learn to think in Clojure, and as excellent for beginners and advanced users. Commenters contrast it favorably with the free documentation.
ab: For programmers learning Clojure
Practical examples and Java interop
Covers Clojure 1.3 and 1.4, so some APIs have changed

q.t: The Clojure Programming book, it's excellent both for beginners and advanced users

t: Tubes: A Journey to the Center of the Internet
s: A journalist's tour of the physical infrastructure of the internet, including data centers, exchanges and undersea cables.
w: Recommended as an accessible introduction to the physical side of the internet, including undersea cables, and described as a quick read. One reader wanted a more in-depth book on the topic.
ab: For non-specialists curious about cables, exchanges and data centers
Quick, narrative reporting rather than a technical text
One reviewer notes the dead squirrel anecdote is repeated

q.t: It's about the plumbing of the Internet that covers pretty much all the physical aspects of what make the Internet

t: Prisoner's Dilemma: John von Neumann, Game Theory, and the Puzzle of the Bomb
s: A biography of John von Neumann woven together with the history of game theory and the Cold War nuclear arms race.
w: Recommended as an engaging introduction to game theory in the context of von Neumann's life. One reader found it dragged in places.
ab: For readers interested in von Neumann and game theory
Mixes biography with Cold War history
Light on formal game theory; can drag

q.t: really quite fascinating, one of my favorite people to study.

s: A guide to rethinking your relationship with money, tracking your life energy spent earning, and reaching financial independence.
w: Praised as the best book on money, changing how readers think about spending and saving, and tied to the financial-independence crowd.
ab: For anyone rethinking money and work
Mindset first, with a step-by-step program
Frugality-oriented; some advice dated

q.t: Hands down the best book I have read on money is Your Money or Your Life

s: A 2010 Culture novel by Iain M. Banks about a virtual-hell war and a woman seeking revenge, mixing space opera with dark satire.
w: Banks fans on HN regularly name it among the best Culture novels, praising how he can make you laugh and cry within a few pages. One thread warns about a poor Kindle conversion.
ab: For space opera fans; can be read without prior Culture books
Big ideas, dark humor and an emotional core
Early Kindle edition was criticised for bad formatting

q.t: This man can make you laugh and cry within three pages, and it's damned good Sci-Fi, to boot.

s: A cheap resin digital watch with alarm, stopwatch, calendar and hourly chime.
w: HN's standard answer for a simple, durable watch costing under $20. Fans praise years of battery life.
ab: For people wanting a cheap, simple digital watch
Water resistant, long battery
No backlight modes or smart features

q.t: Durable, water resistant, stopwatch, alarm, calendar, timer

t: Alchemy: The Dark Art and Curious Science of Creating Magic in Brands, Business, and Life
s: An advertising executive argues that human decisions are driven by irrational psychology and that counterintuitive ideas often beat logic in marketing.
w: HN readers recommend it as a book of little gems about signaling and behavioral economics, written from inside the advertising business. One uses it to explain why marketing matters.
ab: For people building products who dismiss marketing
Anecdotal and witty rather than data-driven
Argues for non-logical solutions

q.t: Written by an advertising executive, it's filled with little gems, especially about signaling.

t: Market Wizards: Interviews with Top Traders
s: Interviews with successful traders across different markets and styles.
w: Suggested to software engineers learning finance as enjoyable interviews that give broad perspective from the best in the field.
ab: For aspiring traders and finance learners
Interview format, easy to read
Survivorship bias caveat

q.t: They're enjoyable reads, filled with insight, and give a good broad perspective

t: Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)
s: A Manning book that walks through implementing a GPT-style large language model in PyTorch, from tokenization and attention to pretraining and fine-tuning.
w: People looking to understand LLMs by building one point to it as exactly the right hands-on resource, and a few pre-ordered it. Raschka's writing is also admired on HN.
ab: For programmers who know Python and want to learn LLM internals
Hands-on code with PyTorch
Was still in early access in some threads

q.t: sounds like exactly what you're after

s: Urban fantasy series about Harry Dresden, a wizard private investigator in modern Chicago, beginning with Storm Front.
w: HN's comfort-read answer: fun, fast fantasy that gets better as the series goes. Commenters say the early books are weaker but the worldbuilding grows, and recommend the audiobooks for long drives.
ab: For readers who want a long, easy, plot-driven series
First few books are the weakest
Audiobook narration is divisive

q.t: this won't win any awards from literary critics, but is one of my favorite series that just keeps on getting better

s: Friedman's 1962 argument for free markets, limited government, school vouchers and monetary policy as the foundation of political freedom.
w: HN names it a readable, informative classic, often with Free to Choose, that explains economics without academic math. Readers pair it with a counterpoint such as Small Is Beautiful.
ab: For readers who want the free-market case from a Nobel economist
Persuasive, not neutral; one side of the debate
Written in 1962; some policy details are dated

q.t: Not so much academic discussions about partial derivatives applied to indifference curves, but very informative.

s: Gibson's 2003 thriller about a marketing consultant with an allergy to brands who hunts for the creator of mysterious internet film fragments.
w: HN readers recommend it as an entry point to modern Gibson in the present day, with internet culture, branding and ARG-like mystery. It grows on readers who stay with it.
ab: For readers who like Gibson and internet-era thrillers
Present-day setting, not far-future sci-fi
First of the Blue Ant trilogy

q.t: it became increasingly interesting and I finished it.

t: Joe Celko's Trees and Hierarchies in SQL for Smarties
s: A guide to storing and querying trees and hierarchies in relational databases, covering adjacency lists, nested sets and path enumeration.
w: The go-to reference HN keeps pointing at when someone needs threaded comments, nested categories, or ordered tree data in SQL.
ab: For developers modeling trees or threads in a relational DB
Covers nested sets and other classic approaches
Written before recursive CTEs were widespread

q.t: Highly recommended if you're modeling trees in your database.

t: Math from Three to Seven: The Story of a Mathematical Circle for Preschoolers
s: A Russian math educator's account of running a math circle for preschoolers, with games and experiments for teaching reasoning.
w: Recommended to parents and teachers as full of small experiments and games that show how kids' reasoning develops.
ab: For parents and educators of young children
Gives example activities and discussion
Soviet-era pedagogy context

q.t: There are a lot of little experiments and games that teach kids basic concepts and show how specific reasoning develops.

t: A Retargetable C Compiler: Design and Implementation
by: Christopher W. Fraser & David R. Hanson
s: A literate-programming walkthrough of the lcc C compiler's full source code.
w: Recommended as the compiler book where you read a real C compiler's code, front end through code generation.
ab: For readers wanting to see how a real C compiler works
Walks through lcc source line by line
Dated 1995 C

q.t: This is a good tour of front-end and back-end stuff, a decent intro to code gen

t: The Design and Evolution of C++
s: Stroustrup's account of how and why C++ was designed, with its compromises for C compatibility.
w: Recommended for understanding C++ warts and history from its creator.
ab: For C++ history buffs
Written 1994
Hit or miss by interest

q.t: They help understand all design compromises that were done to keep compatibility with C

t: Commodore: A Company on the Edge
s: A history of Commodore International covering Jack Tramiel, Chuck Peddle, the 6502, PET, VIC-20 and C64 through the 8-bit era.

ab: For retro computing fans and 6502 or C64 enthusiasts
