Heavy on interviews and corporate drama

q.t: If you want more context to the story I recommend the following, fascinating book.

t: Flying Blind: The 737 MAX Tragedy and the Fall of Boeing
s: A journalist's account of how Boeing's culture shifted from engineering to finance and led to the 737 MAX crashes.
w: Treated as essential reading on how financial priorities eroded engineering at Boeing, with comparisons to GE.
ab: For engineers and managers interested in corporate failure.
Traces Boeing's culture change after the McDonnell Douglas merger.
Journalistic narrative.

q.t: every person, and particularly every engineer, should read

s: A gentle introduction to programming using Ruby.
w: HN readers recommend it as a first programming book.
ab: For beginners
Gentle
Uses Ruby

q.t: Start with Learn To Program 2nd edition as it will get you familiar with programming concepts.

s: The first Earthsea novel: a young wizard's coming-of-age and the shadow he unleashes.
w: HN readers praise its wisdom and give it as a gift or recommend it for kids. One reader dropped it at 25% over the prose style.
ab: For fans of thoughtful, literary fantasy
Short, first of the Earthsea cycle
Spare prose that not everyone enjoys

q.t: A Wizard of Earthsea is still one of the wisest books I've ever read.

s: Dell's premium XPS laptop line, including Ubuntu Developer Editions.
w: Frequently suggested as the main non-Apple laptop for developers, light and well built for Linux. Several recent owners warn about falling quality and poor customer service.
ab: For developers wanting a compact Linux-friendly laptop
Recent models drew keyboard and quality complaints
Pricey for the performance, per some

q.t: Thinkpads or Dell XPS laptops are great for Linux development. Light, stylish, built well and reasonably-priced.

t: Probabilistic Graphical Models: Principles and Techniques
s: A graduate-level textbook on Bayesian networks, Markov networks, inference and learning.
w: Listed among canonical ML textbooks alongside Bishop and Russell and Norvig. People recommend it for fundamentals.
ab: For serious ML learners with math background
Huge, 1,200-page reference
Dense; not a quick intro

q.t: Koller's PGM book [3] for the fundamentals

t: Dataclysm: Love, Sex, Race, and Identity
s: An OkCupid co-founder's analysis of dating-site data about attraction, race and identity.
w: Recommended to people curious about the data behind online dating, with good graphs and analysis. One commenter says it matches their experience of online dating.
ab: For readers interested in dating data and statistics
Based on the OkCupid blog
Published 2014; apps have changed

q.t: I read it a couple years ago and I definitely recommend it if you’re interested in this kind of stuff.

s: Wittgenstein's later masterwork on language, meaning and rule-following, introducing the idea of language games.
w: HN readers call it eye-opening and say it changed how they interpret the world, even though it is dense and obscure. It is popular with programmers interested in meaning and language.
ab: For readers interested in philosophy of language and mind
Dense, aphoristic; pairing with a commentary helps
Written as numbered remarks, not a continuous argument

q.t: Just stunningly thoughtful and changed the way I interpret most things around me.

t: Coding the Matrix: Linear Algebra through Applications to Computer Science
s: A linear algebra textbook that teaches the subject by writing Python code for real applications such as image processing and search.
w: Programmers who find traditional linear algebra dry recommend it as the best way to learn the subject by coding, with the Brown lecture videos as companions.
ab: For programmers learning linear algebra for CS or machine learning
Python exercises tied to applications
Coursera course was removed; videos are on the Brown site

q.t: If you want to learn linear algebra by coding in python, this is hands down the best book out there.

s: A comprehensive textbook on relational database theory covering the relational model, algebra, normalization and SQL by C. J. Date.
w: HN's pick for foundational database theory. Commenters cite it for the relational model's grounding in set theory and logic, and as the source behind SQL-versus-relational-algebra debates.
ab: For those who want theory behind SQL
Dense, thorough and expensive
Date is opinionated about SQL's flaws

q.t: If you would like to learn database theory, then I recommend the following book:

t: Hard Drive: Bill Gates and the Making of the Microsoft Empire
s: A 1992 biography of Bill Gates and the early history of Microsoft, from BASIC through DOS and Windows.
w: Recommended as a balanced portrait of Gates and for its account of the 1980s: the PC, DOS, the clones, and Microsoft outmaneuvering IBM. It is also quoted for stories of intense work culture.
ab: For readers interested in Microsoft's early history
Focuses on the 1970s and 1980s
Written in 1992, so it stops before the Windows 95 era

q.t: It seemed to be a pretty balanced portrayal of Gates from those years.

s: A textbook on probabilistic methods for robot perception and navigation, including Kalman filters, particle filters and SLAM.
w: HN calls it the reference for robotics under uncertainty. Commenters recommend it for making robots that navigate uncertain environments.
ab: For robotics engineers and students
Covers localization, mapping and filtering
Math-heavy

q.t: generally considered the #1 reference on the subject

t: Running Lean: Iterate from Plan A to a Plan That Works
s: A practical process for testing a startup idea quickly with customer interviews and iterative experiments, built on Lean Startup ideas.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a hands-on lean-startup guide, and one reports that its interview scripts worked for finding product-market fit.
ab: For founders validating an idea
Includes a concrete process and interview scripts
Lean Startup material is now widely known

q.t: I used the scripts from the Running Lean book

t: Threaded Interpretive Languages: Their Design and Implementation
s: A 1981 book on how to build threaded-code interpreters such as Forth, including inner interpreters, dictionaries, and compilers.
w: HN Forth people name it as the definitive guide to building Forth-like systems, and one commenter says they used it to write Forth in assembler.
ab: For people who want to implement Forth or similar languages
Detailed internals of threaded code
Out of print and 1980s assembly; used copies and scans exist

q.t: was the definitive treatment of the topic, and what I mostly used back when I was writing Forth compilers.

t: On the Edge: The Spectacular Rise and Fall of Commodore
s: A detailed corporate history of Commodore, from the PET and C64 through the Amiga and the company's collapse.
w: Commenters call it an excellent book on Commodore, covering the C64, the 1541 drive and Amiga development. One reader says it changed their view of who made the personal computer popular.
ab: For retro-computing fans and tech history readers
Covers Commodore's engineers, deals and downfall
A later two-volume rewrite exists but stops at the 8-bit era

q.t: If you want an excellent book about Commodore:

s: A widely used introductory economics textbook covering microeconomics and macroeconomics.
w: Suggested on HN as the starting point for a newcomer to economics. The textbook's high price comes up repeatedly.
ab: For beginners to economics
Standard intro course textbook
Expensive new; older editions are cheaper

q.t: It is a solid book, and you cannot go wrong with it.

t: Losing My Virginity: How I've Survived, Had Fun, and Made a Fortune Doing Business My Way
s: Richard Branson's autobiography covering Virgin Records, Virgin Atlantic, and his unconventional approach to business.
w: HN readers describe it as honest and realistic, and say it humbled them about how hard Branson hustled. It appears on lists of inspiring biographies of entrepreneurs.
ab: For readers who like entrepreneur memoirs
Candid and fast-moving
Branson's own account; reflects his version of events

q.t: It made me realize I've never really hustled in my life. Reading it was a humbling experience.

s: A mathematician explains how opaque scoring algorithms in credit, hiring, policing and education can reinforce inequality.
w: Recommended as the readable critique of algorithmic harm whenever HN discusses ethics in machine learning or big data.
ab: For engineers and data people thinking about algorithmic fairness
Accessible, example-driven, little math
Argument is one-sided by design

q.t: Try Weapons of Math Destruction by Cathy O'Neill for a much more informed critique.

s: Edward Snowden's 2019 memoir about growing up with computers, working in US intelligence and why he leaked classified surveillance documents.
w: HN readers praise its clear, honest writing, the nostalgic account of growing up online, and its detail on government surveillance. Those with mixed views of Snowden say the book is compelling regardless.
ab: For readers interested in privacy, hacker culture and surveillance
Mix of personal story and policy argument
Reflects Snowden's own account; read alongside other sources

q.t: Edward Snowden's book is so good. It really described my life growing up with computers and the advent of the Internet.

t: Driven to Distraction: Recognizing and Coping with Attention Deficit Disorder
by: Edward M. Hallowell, John J. Ratey
s: A popular guide to ADHD in children and adults by two psychiatrists, with case stories, symptoms, and coping strategies.
w: HN readers who struggle with procrastination, focus, or wandering minds recommend it, even for those without a full ADHD diagnosis.
ab: For adults wondering whether ADHD explains chronic distraction
Case-based descriptions of ADHD symptoms and strategies
Not a diagnosis; see a clinician

q.t: you may resonate with some of these points (even if you don't experience a full-blown ADHD)

t: Fighting Traffic: The Dawn of the Motor Age in the American City
s: A history of how American city streets, once shared public spaces, were socially and legally reconstructed in the 1920s to give priority to cars.
w: HN cites it as the go-to history for how streets went from mixed-use to car-only, including the invention of jaywalking and the rise of the motor lobby. It comes up in threads about cars, self-driving and urban planning.
ab: For readers interested in urban planning and transport history
Academic MIT Press title; focused on 1900-1930
Useful context for modern street-safety debates

q.t: If you want to get up on the history you can grab a copy of "Fighting Traffic," by Peter Norton.

s: James Burke's companion book to his TV series tracing how unexpected chains of inventions and ideas produced modern technology.
w: HN readers like how it follows threads through history rather than one period at a time, showing how interconnected technological progress is. Many also recommend the documentary series.
ab: For readers curious about the history of technology
Chain-of-invention storytelling, many surprising links
Companion to the TV series; 1970s-80s era

q.t: He takes a step back to show how interconnected and interdependent technological progress is.

t: Are We Smart Enough to Know How Smart Animals Are?
s: A primatologist's look at animal cognition and how researchers test it.
w: Recommended as fascinating and as redefining ideas of intelligence.
ab: Animal cognition
Many examples
Includes a rant against skeptics

q.t: He does a great job of describing all kinds of surprisingly intelligent animal behaviors, and some very clever tests

s: Ray Bradbury's 1950 collection of linked stories about the colonization of Mars and what humans bring with them.
w: HN readers place it on their best and recommended sci-fi lists as worth reading, especially as an allegory.
ab: For fans of classic literary science fiction
Linked short stories rather than one plot
Mid-century attitudes and science

q.t: The Martian Chronicles is worth reading, especially as an allegory.

s: The second book in Adrian Tchaikovsky's Children of Time series, in which humanity meets intelligent octopus-like life on a terraformed world.
w: HN readers recommend it as a fun sequel to Children of Time, especially for readers interested in non-human intelligence like octopuses and squid.
ab: For readers who liked Children of Time
Explores alien intelligence and communication
Read the first book first

q.t: Lots of fun reading them, great author :)

s: The foundational scripture of the Latter Day Saint movement, presented as an account of ancient peoples in the Americas and the ministry of Jesus Christ.
w: Recommended in 'books that changed your life' threads by readers of faith, who find it comforting and hopeful. One commenter suggests it even to non-religious readers for its stories about getting along with others.
ab: For readers of faith or curious about Latter-day Saint belief
You get the full scripture text; many editions exist
Recommenders are overwhelmingly believers; religious in nature

q.t: it does not run out of ways to comfort, strengthen, give direction & confidence

t: Built to Last: Successful Habits of Visionary Companies
s: A study of long-lived, visionary companies and the principles that make them endure.
w: Cited by HN founders as the Collins book most useful for startups, and by Jeff Bezos as a favorite business book. Commenters like its principles for building enduring businesses.
ab: For founders and managers who care about durable culture
Principles drawn from comparing company pairs
Research method questioned by critics; 1990s examples

q.t: Great book that goes into the principles of how to build enduring businesses.

s: Pullman's fantasy trilogy beginning with The Golden Compass, about parallel worlds and a girl named Lyra.
w: HN readers say it had the greatest impact on them as youngsters and is one of the few series they reread. One listener recommends it to every parent, though ages 5-6 may be too young.
ab: For teens and adults who like thoughtful fantasy
Three-book trilogy with big ideas
Heavier themes; too intense for very young kids

q.t: had the greatest impact on me as a youngster

Covers rendering theory and practical techniques
Buy the newest edition; older ones miss modern GPU methods

q.t: My two biggest shelf pulls are Real-Time Rendering [0] by Akeine-Moller, Haines and Hoffman.

t: Art & Fear: Observations on the Perils (and Rewards) of Artmaking
s: A short book on the fears and obstacles artists face, famous for its story about quantity versus quality in pottery.

ab: For creators struggling with perfectionism
Short and aphoristic
Anecdotal rather than evidence-based

t: The Ascent of Money: A Financial History of the World

w: Recommended as a more engaging alternative to an econ textbook for understanding money and finance, and as a readable history of economics and technology.
ab: For readers wanting a narrative on how finance developed

Popular history, with Ferguson's own interpretations

q.t: It's much more engaging to read vs an econ textbook

t: Digital Minimalism: Choosing a Focused Life in a Noisy World
s: A guide to deciding which technologies serve your values.
w: Recommended as a practical framework for cutting distraction.
ab: For people overwhelmed by tech
Practical
Self-help

Rubber dome feel, not mechanical
Compact layout takes some adjusting

Slow-paced and melancholic
One reader struggled with it

Terse lecture-notes style

Insider access to Ellison
Pre-2003 and somewhat sympathetic

Academic but readable
Dark view of corporate life

t: Hello World! Computer Programming for Kids and Other Beginners

s: Kafka's unfinished 1925 novel about a man arrested and prosecuted by a mysterious, inaccessible court without being told his crime.

Humor depends on taste

Pre-1960 writing and characters

Dated computing details

t: The Lies of Locke Lamora (Gentleman Bastard, Book 1)

First in a series with long gaps between books
Violent in places; the sequel is less loved

s: An e-ink tablet with a stylus for handwritten notes, PDF reading and annotation, designed to feel like writing on paper.

Makes a one-sided case
Strong on play research

q.t: Or how and why parents and adults should really stop trying to control their children.

s: A comprehensive reference to Ruby on Rails, covering the framework's components in depth by a Hashrocket founder, in the Addison-Wesley Professional Ruby Series.
w: In the early Rails years, HN regularly named it the best Rails book and the one to keep on hand as a reference.
ab: For Rails developers who want a complete reference
In-depth coverage of Active Record, controllers, and routing
This 2008 edition covers Rails 2; later editions update it

q.t: It's definitely THE BEST book on Rails available today.

t: The Food Lab: Better Home Cooking Through Science
s: A large cookbook that tests techniques and explains the science behind recipes, from eggs and burgers to roasts and sauces.
w: HN cooks like its empirical, why-it-works approach and call it their first stop for an unfamiliar recipe. It is also recommended as a gift.
ab: For home cooks who want to understand why techniques work
Hefty hardcover with hundreds of tested recipes
Not every blog post is included

q.t: is still the first cookbook I turn to when investigating a recipe I haven't made before.

t: Real-World Functional Programming: With Examples in F# and C#
s: An introduction to functional programming concepts using parallel examples in F# and C# for .NET developers.
w: Recommended for C# developers who want to learn functional ideas, with commenters calling it excellent and the one really good book on the subject for .NET.
ab: For C# and .NET developers learning functional programming
Parallel F# and C# examples
Published in 2010; language versions are older

q.t: is an excellent resource for learning how and when to use composition over inheritance

by: Donella H. Meadows, Dennis Meadows et al.
s: A systems-dynamics study of how population, industry, food, and resource use interact, updating the 1972 World3 model and arguing the world is in overshoot.
w: Commenters point to it as the best systems-thinking treatment of population, environment, and the economy together, and cite it in debates about sustainability, overshoot, and whether technology alone can solve resource limits.
ab: For readers who want a systems view of growth, resources, and collapse
Scenario modeling from the original Limits to Growth team, updated to 2004
Contested conclusions; some HN readers dispute the pessimism

q.t: It takes a systems approach to these related issues, not looking at just one in isolation

t: Quantitative Trading: How to Build Your Own Algorithmic Trading Business
s: A practical introduction to designing, backtesting and running systematic trading strategies as an individual, with Matlab examples.
w: The default answer when HN asks where hackers should start with quant finance. Commenters like the mix of theory and practice, though one warns that making money is hard.
ab: For programmers curious about algorithmic trading on a small scale
Includes backtesting methods and code examples in Matlab
Strategies may have lost edge since 2009; profit is not guaranteed

q.t: It's a nice blend of theory and pragmatic practice.

by: T. Colin Campbell, Thomas M. Campbell
s: A nutritional biochemist presents the findings of a large China-Cornell-Oxford diet survey and argues for a whole-food, plant-based diet.
w: Vegan and vegetarian-curious HN commenters recommend it as a research-heavy case against animal protein. Others cite it while debating nutrition studies, so treat it as one argument rather than settled science.
ab: For readers exploring plant-based diets and nutrition research
Includes lots of epidemiological data and the author's personal research
Its conclusions are widely disputed by other nutrition researchers

q.t: is a really good book that contains a lot of research about the effect on chronic disease a vegan diet has

t: Project Oberon: The Design of an Operating System and Compiler
s: Wirth's complete description and source code for a small operating system, compiler and workstation.
w: Recommended for its clear explanations and for including the full source of the compiler and OS in a small amount of code.
ab: Full OS and compiler small enough to read
Written by Pascal and Oberon's creator
A different world from modern OS design

q.t: Not only it is well written with clear explanations, but it also includes the full source code for the compiler and operating system

t: The Image: A Guide to Pseudo-Events in America
s: A classic critique of manufactured media events and celebrity culture in America, first published in 1962.
w: Cited as a precursor to Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death, said to anticipate social media and PR culture.
ab: For readers interested in media, PR and manufactured events.
Pairs with Neil Postman's work.
Written in 1962, so examples are dated.

q.t: another good one is "The Image: A Guide to Pseudo-Events in America" by Daniel Boorstin

s: Illustrated reference covering TCP/IP and Internet protocols in depth.
w: Appears on HN reading lists for networking and devops, as a comprehensive protocol reference.
ab: For learning networking protocols
Very long and detailed
Published in 2005

s: A blend of fiction and history about Soviet planners and economists trying to run an economy with optimization.
w: Recommended for a vivid, fascinating look at Soviet central planning and why computing it was impossible.
ab: For fans of economics and Soviet history
Novelistic, historical vignettes
Part fiction, part history

q.t: There is a fascinating alternate-history book about this

s: Camus's essay on the absurd: whether life is worth living in a world without inherent meaning, using the myth of Sisyphus as its image.
w: HN picks it as the one philosophy book to start with. Commenters call it extremely readable, a classic of modern thought, and one that stuck in their heads for years.
ab: For first-time philosophy readers or fans of Camus's novels
Short, essay-length, and fairly approachable
Deals frankly with suicide and nihilism

q.t: A great philosophy book, not that hard to read, about the absurdity of life.

t: Good Strategy Bad Strategy: The Difference and Why It Matters
s: Richard Rumelt's guide to telling real strategy from vague goals and slogans, with examples from business and military history.
w: HN readers call it an awesome, plainly written book on how to build a strategy and spot a bad one. It shows up on lists for founders and engineering leaders.
ab: For managers, founders, and tech leads
Explains what a strategy actually is
Case studies including Nvidia

q.t: An awesome book on strategy, which explains very plainly how to construct a reasonable strategy, and see signs of bad strategy.

s: A novel about a small North Carolina town after an EMP attack knocks out the US electrical grid.
w: Recommended in EMP and grid-failure threads as a gripping look at the collapse of electronic infrastructure, written after the author briefed Congress.
ab: For readers curious about EMP and societal collapse scenarios
Gripping post-apocalyptic thriller
Grim and politically tinged

q.t: If you want a good read on the effect of a massive EMP attack, read "One Second After"

t: The Practice of System and Network Administration
s: A broad guide to sysadmin practice covering operations, networks, services and team workflow.
w: HN sysadmins call it the bible for the field and recommend it to developers who want sysadmin skills.
ab: For sysadmins and developers who run systems
Practices, not tool tutorials
2007 edition predates cloud

q.t: The closest I have found to a coherent set of ideas is

t: Poor Economics: A Radical Rethinking of the Way to Fight Global Poverty
s: Two Nobel-winning economists use randomized field studies to examine how poor people actually make decisions about saving, health, education and small business.
w: HN commenters recommend it for how it explains the choices of poor people, based on field studies. They cite its examples of saving behavior and why high interest rates and tiny markets make normal business advice fail.
ab: For readers interested in development economics and poverty
Based on randomized field experiments
Some conclusions have been debated since publication

q.t: is a good book about that topic, based on field studies of the authors

s: A business strategy book on creating uncontested market space rather than competing head-on with rivals.
w: Recommended for thinking about strategy and pricing beyond head-to-head competition, and the red versus blue ocean idea comes up often when discussing markets.
ab: For founders and strategists looking for a new market
Frameworks and case studies for finding uncontested space
Cases are from the 1990s-2000s and the framework is debated

q.t: The authors address how to move beyond mere competition, and pricing is one of those ways.

s: A guide to designing dashboards that communicate data clearly at a glance.
w: HN readers recommend it for internal reporting dashboards that please managers, alongside Tufte.
ab: For designers building dashboards
Specific to certain display types
Not meant for marketing or customer-facing visuals

q.t: Information Dashboard Design is pretty solid.

t: How to Invent Everything: A Survival Guide for the Stranded Time Traveler
s: A humorous guide to rebuilding civilization's technologies from scratch, from fire and writing to electricity and antibiotics.
w: Pitched when someone wants a stranded-in-the-past survival manual. People enjoy it as both funny and a tour of how key inventions work.
ab: For curious readers and gift buyers who like tech history
Funny tone with real science and history
Light reading rather than a real manual

q.t: From this fantastic book

s: An engineering treatment of how bicycles work, covering human power output, aerodynamics, gearing, braking and the history of the machine.
w: HN commenters recommend it for the physics and human-power material behind bicycles. It is the book people point to when a thread gets into cycling mechanics.
ab: For engineers and serious cyclists who want the physics
Covers power, aerodynamics, gearing, history
Technical; some sections are more reference than narrative

q.t: And there's always Bicycling Science for the serious nerds among us

t: Give and Take: Why Helping Others Drives Our Success
s: Adam Grant's book arguing that people who give generously, without being doormats, are often the most successful.
w: HN readers recommend it as one of their best reads of a year, and describe how givers show up at both the top and bottom of success. One notes it is popular and not niche.
ab: For managers and teams thinking about collaboration
Research-backed, story-driven
Popular business-book style

q.t: I enjoyed Give and Take by Adam Grant very much

s: Over-ear Bluetooth headphones with active noise cancellation, comfortable for long wear and popular for offices and travel.
w: HN praises the noise cancellation for open offices and flights, listing it with the Sony WH-1000XM3 and Bose 700 as the best choices; audio quality is called average.
ab: Top-tier noise cancelling for the era
Sound quality described as just average
Superseded by newer Bose and Sony models

q.t: Open office plans are terrible for my concentration and wearing noise canceling headphones makes a huge difference.

s: A 10.3-inch e-ink tablet for handwriting notes and reading PDFs and ebooks, with a paper-like screen, no apps or notifications, and cloud sync.
w: HN owners call it a daily-driver for notes, sketching and reading, and a rare gadget that changed how they work. It appears in many favorite-purchase threads, usually after months of regular use.
ab: For note-takers and PDF readers who want a distraction-free screen
Optional marker and folio sold separately; the cloud service has a subscription for extras
Limited apps; one person fears disappointing software and build quality

q.t: I've been using it almost daily for 4 months now, and I absolutely love it.

t: Capital: A Critique of Political Economy, Volume 1
s: Marx's foundational analysis of capitalism, covering commodities, labor, surplus value, and capital accumulation.
w: Cited as the primary text whenever HN debates how economists think or how politics and economic theory interlock. Respected as a source even by commenters who disagree with it.
ab: For readers who want the original rather than summaries
Dense and long; studying with a guide helps
Several editions exist; check which translation you get

q.t: Also look into Capital: A Critique of Political Economy

t: Effective C: An Introduction to Professional C Programming
s: A 2020 No Starch Press introduction to modern, professional C programming, written by a member of the C standards committee.
w: HN names it among the best modern C books alongside Modern C, for being current, compact (about 272 pages) and written by a standards-committee member who covers safe, professional practices. Its author also comments in one thread.
ab: For programmers who want an up-to-date, practical C introduction
Short at about 272 pages
Author is a CERT/NCC secure-coding expert

q.t: a very good modern C book that's only 272 pages

t: It's Not Carpal Tunnel Syndrome! RSI Theory & Therapy for Computer Professionals
s: A guide to repetitive strain injury for computer users, covering causes, trigger-point therapy, stretching, and ergonomics.
w: Programmers with RSI repeatedly name it as the book that finally explained their pain and led them to trigger-point massage and other fixes that worked.
ab: For programmers and heavy computer users with wrist or arm pain
Practical self-treatment, trigger points, and workplace changes
Not a substitute for a doctor; some advice is anecdotal

q.t: this book is very good and covers a wide variety of bases to help you understand your problem

by: Samuel P. Harbison, Guy L. Steele Jr.
s: A detailed reference to the C language and standard library, written by Harbison and Steele, covering C99 and implementation details.
w: HN C programmers recommend it over K&R for precision and up-to-date coverage. Commenters call it what many people actually want.
ab: For C programmers who need a precise reference
Covers standard C, with many small examples
A reference, not a gentle tutorial

q.t: For learning C I strongly recommend C: A Reference Manual (Harbison and Steele), not K&R.

t: Cryptography Engineering: Design Principles and Practical Applications
by: Niels Ferguson, Bruce Schneier et al.
s: A guide to designing and implementing cryptographic systems, focused on protocols, key management and avoiding implementation mistakes.
w: HN's go-to suggestion for implementers and system designers who want crypto done right, favored over Applied Cryptography. Tptacek notes it is dated and a little wrong in places.
ab: For engineers who use or implement crypto in real systems
Readable, with practical advice on pitfalls and best practices
Published in 2010; newer books cover modern practice

q.t: It's amazingly readable, covers the basics, the theory necessary to understand how things works

t: This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends: The Cyberweapons Arms Race
s: A New York Times reporter's account of the zero-day exploit market and the cyberweapons race among governments.
w: HN security readers recommend it as a detailed account of how the zero-day market evolved and why nations keep buying exploits. It is somewhat repetitive and loose on technical details.
ab: For readers wanting the story of nation-state hacking and zero-days
Reporter's narrative rather than a technical manual
Technical descriptions sometimes shaky; a bit repetitive

q.t: which is a great book about the zero-day market and how it evolved over the years.

t: The Man Who Loved Only Numbers
s: A biography of the wandering, prolific mathematician Paul Erdos and his search for the proofs in God's Book.
w: Described as a poignant and excellent biography of Erdos, recommended as the grown-up book about him. Commenters also use it to explain his idea of The Book of perfect proofs.
ab: For readers of math history and biography
Accessible portrait of Erdos with no heavy math
Written in 1998, before later Erdos scholarship

q.t: There is also an excellent book about Erdos for adults

t: The Art of Software Security Assessment: Identifying and Preventing Software Vulnerabilities
by: Mark Dowd, John McDonald et al.
s: A detailed reference on finding vulnerabilities by auditing source code, covering memory corruption, race conditions, and application-level flaws.
w: Called the best book on the topic by commenters who know the authors, and recommended to developers moving into security. Seen as essential reading for code auditing.
ab: For security researchers and code auditors
Deep dive on vulnerability classes and auditing methods
Large and dense; older examples

q.t: without a doubt, the best book on the topic is

s: A deep technical dive into how id Software built Wolfenstein 3D, with the history of early PC game development.
w: HN loves it as a nostalgia trip and for the history of low-level game programming on early PCs, and Fabien's DOOM book is praised the same way.
ab: For retro game dev and graphics fans
Details of early PC hardware limits
Historical rather than current practice

q.t: Fabien's books are also phenomenal

t: Engineering a Safer World: Systems Thinking Applied to Safety
s: An MIT Press text on accident causation and system safety that replaces chain-of-events thinking with the STAMP systems-theory model; freely available as open access.
w: Recommended to anyone who cares about postmortems and why complex systems fail. Commenters value Leveson's decades of experience and appreciate that the full PDF is free.
ab: For engineers, SREs and anyone writing incident postmortems
Academic and dense, but free to read online
Challenges the 'operator error' view of accidents

q.t: if you're interested in this stuff, I can't recommend enough

s: A 2012 15.6-inch mobile workstation laptop with a quad-core Core i7, up to 32GB RAM, Nvidia Quadro graphics and a replaceable backlit keyboard.
w: HN developers call it a beast that runs Linux well and takes up to 32GB RAM, with multi-monitor docking. One user laments Lenovo dropped the W line, and another struggles with Optimus GPU switching.
ab: For tinkerers wanting a powerful, repairable used laptop
Optimus graphics switching and external ports are fiddly on Linux
Old hardware; buy used and check the battery

q.t: I'm on a W530. It's a beast and everything works.

s: Tim Harford's popular introduction to economics through everyday situations like coffee shops, used cars, and pricing.
w: HN readers recommend it as a fun, accessible entry to economics for non-specialists, and cite its examples of pricing and self-selection when designing prices.
ab: For beginners wanting everyday economic intuition
Fun, accessible, and example-driven
Pop economics; read more advanced texts afterward

q.t: The Undercover Economist is quite a fun read and very accessible to the layperson

s: A small HDMI streaming dongle that plays video and audio from a phone, tablet, or Chrome browser on a TV.
w: HN users call it a cheap, convenient way to stream to a TV with a phone as the remote. Others regret it for same-network limits and lack of user control over the device.
ab: For streaming from phones to a TV cheaply
Phone acts as remote
Limited formats; no VPN use; locked-down software

q.t: Chromecast, its just awesome and you get quite a bit of change.

s: Hermann Hesse's 1930 novel following two friends in medieval Germany, a disciplined monk and a wandering artist, and the contrast between intellect and sensual life.
w: A frequent pick from HN readers who loved Siddhartha and want more Hesse. Commenters say it makes you feel you have lived the characters' struggles, and cite the free spirit versus disciplined mind theme.
ab: For readers of Hesse, philosophical fiction and coming-of-age stories
A contemplative novel about art, faith and desire
Slow and reflective; translations vary

q.t: What I love about HH's books is that I feel as if I've lived the lives of his characters vicariously

s: A guide to tuning PostgreSQL performance, covering hardware, benchmarking, configuration and query plans.
w: Recommended for sysadmins running PostgreSQL. A reader said it was their first introduction to Postgres.
ab: For DBAs and engineers tuning Postgres
Version 9.0 era
Hardware advice is dated

q.t: which I agree is a great book if you're a sysadmin supporting PostgreSQL.

s: The second book of Dan Simmons's Hyperion Cantos, continuing the Canterbury-style space pilgrimage and the war with the Ousters.
w: HN readers call Hyperion and its sequel two of the best novels they have read, and say they have held up well against newer science fiction. It is meant to be read after Hyperion.
ab: For readers who finished Hyperion
Literary space opera with big ideas
Not standalone; start with Hyperion

q.t: Dan Simmons Hyperion and The Fall of Hyperion are two of the best novels I've read.

by: Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau, Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau
s: A free-to-read operating systems textbook organized around virtualization, concurrency and persistence, with approachable prose and hands-on homework.
w: HN's default recommendation for learning how operating systems work. People read it cover to cover and say it covers the interesting parts clearly, including a good section on persistence.
ab: For students and working engineers learning OS fundamentals
Three clear sections: virtualization, concurrency, persistence; free online
Light on specific modern kernels; more concepts than code walkthroughs

q.t: another +1 to Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces [2], which was mentioned in this thread. I read this one cover to cover.

t: Apollo: The Race to the Moon
s: An engineering-focused history of the Apollo program, told through the people at NASA and its contractors rather than the astronauts.
w: HN readers call it the best place to start on Apollo and a favorite book about hard engineering projects, praising how it shows what a big-budget engineering effort can do.
ab: For readers who like engineering history and project management
Focuses on engineers and managers, not astronauts
Long and detailed

q.t: The best place to start is Apollo by Murray/Cox

t: Measuring and Managing Performance in Organizations
s: An analysis of why performance metrics tied to rewards distort behavior, using principal-agent theory and examples from software work.
w: Recommended when anyone proposes metrics or OKRs. One reader says it was the only book worth reading when researching team metrics.
ab: For managers designing metrics or incentives
Academic in tone
Core lesson: be careful using metrics to motivate

q.t: This was the only book worth reading when I was researching metrics for our team at work.

t: IBM and the Holocaust: The Strategic Alliance Between Nazi Germany and America's Most Powerful Corporation
s: A history of how IBM's Hollerith punch-card technology and its German subsidiary were used to identify and track victims of the Nazi regime.
w: HN brings it up in every thread on data registries and ethical tech work, as the cautionary history of data collection for persecution.
ab: For readers interested in tech ethics and the Holocaust
Documents punch-card census and tracking systems
Historians dispute some of its claims about IBM's culpability

q.t: if you haven't you really should read IBM And The Holocaust

s: A book arguing for becoming indispensable at work through creative, emotional labor.
w: Appears on HN reading lists about finishing projects and doing meaningful work.
ab: For people thinking about career differentiation.
Short, motivational chapters.
Typical Godin style.

t: Incognito: The Secret Lives of the Brain
s: A neuroscientist's popular account of how much of the mind operates below conscious awareness.
w: Enjoyed for its look at the unconscious, recommended alongside Society of Mind, and quoted in debates on choice and responsibility.
ab: For general readers curious about the brain
Accessible neuroscience
Popular science, some simplifications

q.t: I enjoyed Incognito, which explores similar ideas

s: Ta-Nehisi Coates's letter to his teenage son about race, the Black body, and growing up in America.
w: HN readers cite it as a book that gave them insight into institutional racism and fear, and one recommends it as more nuanced than Hacker News comments could be.
ab: For readers wanting a personal view of race in America
Short, essay-style and lyrical
Personal and political; not a neutral survey

q.t: I adored Between the World and Me by Ta-Nahisi Coates

t: Material World: The Six Raw Materials That Shape Modern Civilization
s: Ed Conway's tour of sand, salt, iron, copper, oil, and lithium and the global supply chains that turn them into modern products.
w: HN readers called it fantastic and informative, with a look at how ore becomes the materials behind chips and everything else, and pair it with Chip War.
ab: For readers curious about supply chains and materials
Mix of travel reporting and science
Optimistic tone about human ingenuity

q.t: I guessed about four but i was completely blown away by some

s: The Pragmatic Programmers guide to building web applications with Elixir and the Phoenix framework, written by its creators with Bruce Tate.
w: HN Elixir users call it the go-to Phoenix book, a good way into the language and framework, with a structure reminiscent of the first Rails book. It is still a recommended read.
ab: For developers new to Phoenix and Elixir
Written by the framework's creators
Phoenix has changed since early editions

q.t: It's a good way to get into the language/framework.

s: Niklaus Wirth's classic 1976 text on program construction, teaching data structures and algorithms together through Pascal examples, including a small compiler.
w: A recurring pick for the 'books that shaped me' threads. Commenters call it practical grounding in software engineering and credit its Tiny Pascal compiler as a blueprint for later tools, if you can tolerate Pascal.
ab: For readers who like short, foundational classics from a language designer
You get structured-programming ideas plus a compact working compiler
All examples are in Pascal; the style is dated

q.t: worth its weight in gold if you can get past the Pascal syntax

s: John Fowles' 1965 psychological novel about a young Englishman teaching on a Greek island who becomes the subject of an elaborate, bewildering game.
w: Several HN readers say it was a formative novel, one that changed how they saw themselves or opened up fiction for them in their teens. A recommendation that shows up in many 'favorite books' threads.
ab: For readers who like mind-bending, atmospheric literary fiction
A long, twisting plot that plays with illusion and identity
Dense and slow at times; some find the ending divisive

q.t: its twisting plot and content really opened up the world of fiction and writing for me

s: Leo Brodie's 1984 book on software design philosophy and style, using the Forth language to illustrate decomposition, factoring and simplicity.
w: HN programmers recommend it even if they will never use Forth, for its ideas on keeping software small and well factored. The author's PDF is available free.
ab: For programmers interested in minimalism and design, not Forth itself
Practical lessons on decomposition and factoring
Examples are in Forth; the style is dated

q.t: Even knowing that you will never touch Forth in your life is really worth it.

t: The Open Society and Its Enemies
s: Popper's 1945 defense of liberal democracy and critique of Plato, Hegel and Marx as sources of totalitarian thinking.
w: HN readers call it a book that changes how you see politics and one of the great works of liberal thought. Recommended on every 'best philosophical books' list.
ab: For readers of political philosophy and liberal democracy
Attacks Plato, Hegel and Marx directly
Long and dense, 1940s context

q.t: No doubt the number 1 book I recommend anybody to read.

s: A 1970s conspiracy-comedy sci-fi trilogy by Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson.
w: HN readers list it among mind-bending, favorite and life-changing books, often paired with Gödel, Escher, Bach. One calls it slightly dated.
ab: For readers who like psychedelic conspiracy satire
Three-volume cult classic
Dated 1970s counterculture style

q.t: Probably reading GEB and The Illuminatus! trilogy at the same time

s: A short marketing classic setting out 22 rules on positioning, branding and focus, each explained in a brief chapter with examples.
w: HN founders and engineers recommend it as a short, practical introduction to marketing that does not read like a textbook. It is on many lists of must-read books for startup founders.
ab: For engineers and founders who find marketing unfamiliar
Short chapters, each one rule with examples
Examples date from before the internet era

q.t: this old little gem is full of practical mental models and use cases

t: Logitech MX Ergo Wireless Trackball Mouse
s: A wireless trackball mouse with an adjustable hinge angle, designed to keep the hand and wrist still.
w: Recommended by people with wrist pain as a trackball that works well for long computer sessions.
ab: For people with wrist or hand pain
Adjustable angle and wireless
Trackballs take time to adapt to

q.t: I found a great mouse solution, a Logitech trackball mouse that sits in my RH sling

s: A tutorial on Common Lisp that moves from the language basics to practical projects such as a spam filter, an MP3 database and a web server.
w: HN readers recommend it as the best first book on Common Lisp, and one commenter was moved to start learning Lisp after reading it. It is long but has good case studies.
ab: For programmers learning Common Lisp from scratch
Project-based chapters with real case studies
Long, and written in 2005

q.t: a really nice albeit long tutorial with interesting case studies.

t: Facts and Fallacies of Software Engineering
s: Robert Glass's short collection of 55 facts about software projects, backed by research.
w: HN recommends it as a concise, evidence-based reality check on software engineering. One commenter says it may be getting dated but is still valuable.
ab: For developers and managers
Short, 224 pages
Some research references are old

q.t: It's quite concise (224 pages), but it's chock full of quite excellent

s: Tolkien's posthumously published mythology of Middle-earth, from the creation of the world through the First Age and the fall of Numenor.
w: HN Tolkien fans call it the only successful epic mythology of modern times, and recommend it after The Lord of the Rings. Some say the Martin Shaw audiobook is excellent.
ab: For readers who finished The Lord of the Rings and want the lore
Reads like scripture or history, not a novel
Audiobook version praised by one commenter

q.t: The Silmarillion is perhaps the only successful epic mythology written in modern times

s: Jesse Eisinger's investigation of why the Justice Department rarely prosecutes corporate executives.
w: HN cites it in threads on corporate crime and the financial crisis. Commenters call it worthwhile for understanding why cases end unsatisfactorily.
ab: For readers on white-collar crime
Investigative journalism
US-focused

q.t: This is a worthwhile book that might help clear up some of your bewilderment

t: The Paradox of Choice: Why More Is Less
s: A psychologist argues that an abundance of options makes people less satisfied, and distinguishes maximizers from satisficers.
w: HN cites it in threads on product lines, interface design, and chasing deals, recommending it for its research showing that maximizing leaves people less happy than settling for good enough.
ab: For designers, product people, and chronic over-researchers
Research on maximizers, satisficers, and regret
Some findings, like the jam study, have mixed replication

q.t: I highly recommend The Paradox of Choice

t: Where Are the Customers' Yachts? Or a Good Hard Look at Wall Street
s: A witty 1940 account of Wall Street's brokers, advisers, and their blunders, built on the question of why the customers never own the yachts.
w: HN brings it up whenever financial advisers, robo-advisers, or crypto come up, as an entertaining, slightly sad reminder of who profits from Wall Street.
ab: For anyone who invests or pays financial advisers
Funny, cynical tour of Wall Street's habits
Written in 1940; the institutions changed, the behavior hasn't

q.t: very entertaining and funny, in a kind of sad way

s: Edward Tufte's illustrated book on presenting multidimensional information using space, color, layering and small multiples.
w: Recommended as a starting point for design and data visualization, alongside The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. Commenters call it beautiful and a favorite.
ab: For designers and data visualization practitioners
Large, richly illustrated, in print-quality color
Tufte's taste is opinionated and print-oriented

q.t: I would highly recommend Edward Tufte's beautiful tome Envisioning Information

s: Popular book on the search for a single universal learning algorithm.
w: Recommended as an enjoyable overview of machine learning approaches.
ab: For general readers interested in ML
Accessible overview
Opinionated

q.t: You may enjoy The Master Algorithm

t: Gang Leader for a Day: A Rogue Sociologist Takes to the Streets
s: A sociologist recounts the years he spent inside a Chicago housing-project crack gang, showing its hierarchy, economics and role in the community.
w: Readers say it gives real insight into the roles gangs play in communities, and note the author's data fed the drug-dealer economics chapter of Freakonomics.
ab: For readers curious about urban poverty and informal economies
First-person field account that reads like a narrative
Methods and some details have been questioned by critics

q.t: Gang Leader for a Day gives great insight into the many role gangs play in their communities

t: Manufacturing Consent: The Political Economy of the Mass Media
s: Herman and Chomsky's 1988 study arguing that economic and political forces shape mass media coverage through a propaganda model.
w: HN readers credit it with changing how they see the media, and one calls it prime reading for anyone in the US because it is about media manipulation. It appears on many lists of formative books.
ab: For readers interested in media criticism and propaganda
Presents the propaganda model with case studies
Dense and one-sided; examples are from the Cold War era

q.t: Manufacturing Consent, which is prime reading right now for anybody in the US because it's about media manipulation in free society.

t: Luxe Bidet Neo 120 Non-Electric Bidet Attachment
s: A non-electric bidet attachment that connects to a toilet's water supply, with a self-cleaning nozzle.
w: HN commenters call it a cheap, five-minute install they would not give up. It is the bidet people recommend first.
ab: For anyone wanting to cut down on toilet paper
Installs in minutes with included tools
Uses cold water only; fit varies by toilet

q.t: It's terrific, can't go back to TP ever.

t: Ordinary Men: Reserve Police Battalion 101 and the Final Solution in Poland
s: A historical study of a German reserve police unit whose middle-aged members became mass killers of Jews in Poland.
w: HN commenters recommend it when conformity, obedience and complicity come up. They say it shows who follows appalling orders and why, and how ordinary people commit atrocities.
ab: For readers interested in the Holocaust and group psychology
Draws on trial testimony of the perpetrators
Disturbing content throughout

q.t: the book is about who follows appalling orders, why they do, and what does (and doesn't) happen to them if they don't.

t: The Two-Income Trap: Why Middle-Class Parents Are Going Broke
s: An argument that two-earner households became financially fragile because families bid up housing and school costs, raising bankruptcy risk.
w: HN commenters cite it on housing, childcare costs, homeschooling and stagnating wages. They credit it for showing how a second income got absorbed into housing and school competition.
ab: For readers following housing and family-cost debates
Written 2003-2004; the data is dated
Policy-oriented, with a political author

q.t: To go into more detail check out Elizabeth Warren's book: The Two-Income Trap: Why Middle-Class Parents are Going Broke

s: A book that builds geometry and measurement from first principles, by the author of A Mathematician's Lament.
w: Recommended as the follow-up to Lockhart's Lament for readers who want to do math.
ab: For adults who want to do math rather than memorize it.
Conversational, exploratory style.
Requires effort.

q.t: looks like the best starting point since this resonated with you

t: Liftoff: Elon Musk and the Desperate Early Days That Launched SpaceX
s: A journalist's account of SpaceX's early years and the Falcon 1 development, told largely through the early employees.
w: Called the best SpaceX book by one commenter, praised for accuracy from many interviews and for focusing on the engineers, not Musk.
ab: For space fans wanting the early SpaceX story
Based on interviews with early employees
Covers Falcon 1 era only

q.t: It's the best SpaceX book there is and is very accurate

s: A comic-format introduction to probability and statistics covering distributions, inference and hypothesis testing.
w: HN calls it the clearest, most intuitive statistics intro, and one teacher uses it for a class despite the cartoons.
ab: For programmers and beginners wanting stats intuition
Includes the equations, explained visually
Basic level only

q.t: It's no joke. Rather, perhaps the book that explains statistics in the clearest way.

t: Soft Skills: The Software Developer's Life Manual
s: A broad guide for working developers covering career, learning, productivity, finances and fitness, in short chapters.
w: Offered to developers asking how to grow into senior roles or improve non-technical skills; one reader says even high-level engineers should read it.
ab: For developers building a career beyond coding
Short chapters on careers, money, health and mentoring
Broad rather than deep; light on technical content

q.t: the rest of the book is a must have if you’re a software engineer

s: A comprehensive Unix and Linux sysadmin guide.
w: Cited as a general sysadmin reference.
ab: Sysadmin
Reference
Dated

s: Beginner-friendly book that teaches neural networks by building them from scratch in Python with NumPy, with minimal math prerequisites.
w: HN learners praise it as a gentle, from-scratch intro to deep learning that needs only Python and high-school math. Commenters liked it more than other tutorials and followed it as it was written.
ab: For beginners who want to understand neural nets by coding them
Light on math and modern libraries; predates transformers
Builds a small network, not production systems

q.t: This is a fantastic book that assumes no prerequisites other than knowing python

s: A Manning book applying cognitive science (memory, reading, learning) to how programmers read, understand, and write code.
w: HN keeps pointing to it for cognitive load and code reading. Commenters say the author did her homework on what science knows about learning and memory.
ab: For developers who want to read code faster
Grounded in cognitive-science research on memory and learning
Practical exercises rather than theory alone

q.t: Any discussion of cognitive load in programming needs to include awareness of this book

s: Nabokov's novel narrated by Humbert Humbert, a manipulative, self-justifying abuser, famed for its prose.
w: HN readers praise it as an incredible example of writing, with Nabokov writing in his second language. It is a disturbing subject, and the book is admired for its style.
ab: For readers who value ornate, ambitious prose
Disturbing subject matter and an unreliable narrator
Admired for language rather than plot

q.t: Incredible writing, maybe the best ever.

s: A 2012 techno-thriller by Daniel Suarez about autonomous armed drones and the people trying to stop them.
w: Suarez fans on HN recommend it alongside Daemon and Freedom (TM), and several note it has only grown more relevant as AI-enabled drones become real.
ab: For technothriller fans who liked Daemon or Freedom (TM)
Fast-paced plot about autonomous weapons
Less meaty than some sci-fi; read it for the ideas and pace

q.t: His most recent book, Kill Decision, is along similar lines and also great.

s: Eric Raymond's collection of essays contrasting centrally planned software development with open, bazaar-style open source collaboration.
w: A staple of HN reading lists on open source culture. Readers say it is inspiring about collaboration and useful for managing projects, and some are surprised when a thread leaves it out.
ab: For anyone interested in open source history and project dynamics
Short essays; readable in a weekend
Written in the late 1990s, and some claims are debated

q.t: It's inspiring for embrace Open Source collaboration and also very useful for manage projects.

s: Arthur Conan Doyle's detective stories and novels about Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson.
w: Named in HN favorite-book threads as a delight to reread, and as a source of focused awareness and logic. Free on Project Gutenberg.
ab: For fans of classic detective fiction
Complete stories and novels, public domain
Victorian language and attitudes

q.t: I re-read some Sherlock Holmes, which was delightful.

s: A stock-picking classic in which a famed fund manager argues that ordinary investors can find winners by paying attention to businesses they know.
w: Often paired with The Intelligent Investor on HN's reading lists for beginners. Commenters like its plain, easy approach, though some say it worked better before the internet.
ab: For beginners learning fundamentals-based stock picking
Easy to read, with everyday examples
Written before the internet age; some advice shows its age

q.t: it's still a very solid and easy to read book

s: The first novel in the Southern Reach trilogy, about an expedition into a mysterious, quarantined coastal region called Area X.
w: Picked on HN as a creepy, atmospheric, well-written weird fiction novel, with the rest of the trilogy recommended too, though one reader found the sequels weaker.
ab: For readers who like weird, eerie fiction
Atmospheric and slow-burning, part of a trilogy
Sequels are divisive

q.t: Effectively creepy and well written

s: A 1920s Russian dystopian novel about a mathematically ordered One State, widely seen as a forerunner of 1984 and Brave New World.
w: HN readers call it a highly overlooked dystopia that predates Orwell and Huxley, and are struck that it was written in 1920.
ab: For readers who liked 1984 or Brave New World and want the original.
Short, strange early-20th-century dystopian classic.
Several translations exist, so quality varies.

q.t: Insane to think this book has been written in 1920.

s: A short catalog of the surprising ways C code goes wrong, from lexical quirks and pointer semantics to preprocessor and library traps.
w: Recommended as the companion to K&R that explains the unintuitive corners of C. Commenters list it alongside Expert C Programming and secure-coding references.
ab: For programmers who know basic C and want to avoid classic mistakes
Compact, example-driven chapters on one pitfall category each
Written in 1989, so predates modern C standards

q.t: both help with all of the less intuitive parts of the language that you don't really get out of K&R

t: Rocket Surgery Made Easy: The Do-It-Yourself Guide to Finding and Fixing Usability Problems
s: A short how-to guide to running quick, cheap usability tests on your own website or product.
w: Recommended as the best book for learning usability testing and a quick read that prevents beginner mistakes. Commenters suggest it to anyone starting to test with real users.
ab: For founders and designers who want to start usability testing
Short, practical, readable in about an hour
Companion to Krug's Don't Make Me Think

q.t: It will probably take you less than an hour to read and will stop you making the basic mistakes

t: Overthrow: America's Century of Regime Change from Hawaii to Iraq
s: A history of US-backed overthrows of foreign governments from the 1893 Hawaii coup to the Iraq war.
w: Recommended as a survey of US regime-change operations, covering many incidents. Commenters point to it when threads discuss American foreign interventions.
ab: For readers curious about US foreign-policy history
Covers a century of interventions
Takes a critical view; ends with the 2003 Iraq invasion

q.t: It covers not just this incident, but many others throughout history when the US has overthrown foreign governments.

t: Love and Math: The Heart of Hidden Reality
s: A mathematician's memoir that introduces the Langlands program and ideas from group theory, number theory and physics.
w: Recommended as a fun introduction to modern math and a memoir by a Langlands researcher. A reader says the last chapters get hairy but the story is gripping.
ab: For math lovers wanting a story of modern research
Introduces the Langlands program for general readers
Later chapters become harder

q.t: Such a great book for people who love math.

t: The Score Takes Care of Itself: My Philosophy of Leadership
s: The 49ers coach's leadership philosophy, from building a team culture to running standards of performance.
w: Jack Dorsey recommended it at Startup School, and it appears on YC's reading list and in lists of books for managers.
ab: For managers and founders wanting a coaching perspective
Sports stories, not tech
Culture and standards over results

q.t: Jack Dorsey recommended this title at Startup School 2013 and I got around to reading it in 2014.

t: Framework Design Guidelines: Conventions, Idioms, and Patterns for Reusable .NET Libraries
s: Design rules for building reusable libraries and APIs, drawn from the development of the .NET Framework, covering naming, exceptions and extensibility.
w: The recommendation when someone asks for books on API design. Commenters call it a thoughtful treatise on usable APIs, though C#-oriented and somewhat dated.
ab: For library and API designers, especially on .NET
Naming, exceptions, extensibility and common patterns
C#-centric and written for an older .NET

q.t: the really, really fantastic Framework Design Guidelines by Brad Abrams and Krzysztof Cwalina is a thoughtful treatise on designing usable APIs

s: Dawkins walks backward through evolutionary history, meeting the common ancestors of humans and other life along the way.
w: Suggested as a broad, enjoyable overview of evolution, and a good source on origin-of-life ideas; it is long but readers say worth it.
ab: For readers wanting a big-picture tour of evolution
About 700 pages; a long read
Told backward in time, a distinctive structure

q.t: It's a 700 page book, but so worth the read.

t: Thanks for the Feedback: The Science and Art of Receiving Feedback Well
s: From the Harvard Negotiation Project, a guide to receiving feedback, covering types of feedback, triggers that make it hard to hear, and how to use it.
w: HN engineers recommend it for handling code review and annual review criticism, and for learning to give feedback as well.
ab: For people who bristle at criticism or review comments
Separates praise, coaching and evaluation
Self-help tone; more theory than checklists

q.t: Highly recommended if you're interested both in the mechanisms and improving how you receive/give feedback.

t: Getting Past No: Negotiating Your Way from Confrontation to Cooperation
s: A negotiation guide on dealing with difficult or hostile counterparts and turning confrontation into problem solving.
w: Recommended alongside Getting to Yes for negotiating with difficult people, separating the problem from the person, and focusing on interests rather than positions.
ab: For anyone negotiating with difficult counterparts
Companion to Getting to Yes
Some advice is common sense for experienced negotiators

q.t: helpful when negotiating with difficult people

t: Bird by Bird: Some Instructions on Writing and Life
s: Anne Lamott's funny, encouraging guide to writing.
w: HN readers recommend it for motivation to write.
ab: For writers
Funny
Not technical

q.t: Bird by Bird, by Anne Lamott is an amazing book about writing.

s: Wired closed-back studio monitor headphones with a coiled cable and folding design, widely used in recording and broadcast work.
w: HN buyers recommend them as an accurate, rugged and cheap pair of working headphones that survive years of being shoved in bags, a good answer to the best headphones for about $100 question.
ab: For people who want flat, accurate sound and durability
Wired only, with a coiled cable
Clinical sound and clamp-heavy fit; not for bass lovers

q.t: they've lasted for 2 years of being shoved in a bag or pocket many times a day

t: The Gift of Fear: Survival Signals That Protect Us from Violence
s: A security expert explains how to recognize the warning signs of violence and trust intuition in dangerous situations.
w: HN readers pass it on as excellent information to keep in mind, from a security professional's recommendation to a summary that it is all about listening to your gut.
ab: For anyone who wants to spot danger and stalking early
Case-driven, accessible writing
Some advice dates from the 1990s

q.t: as a source of excellent information to always have in mind.

s: A collection of memory, learning and mental-tool techniques from the O'Reilly Hacks series.
w: Recommended on HN in threads about spaced repetition and getting more out of your brain. It is a handy list of mental tricks.
ab: For tinkerers who like memory and learning techniques
Short, self-contained hacks
Dated; many ideas are better covered elsewhere

q.t: A good book on brain hacks like the aforementioned spaced repetition is

t: Eat That Frog!: 21 Great Ways to Stop Procrastinating and Get More Done in Less Time
s: A short self-help book of 21 time-management tips built around doing your hardest task first each day.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a quick, practical book for people who procrastinate.
ab: For chronic procrastinators wanting simple rules
Short, tip-by-tip format
Typical self-help style with little research

q.t: Brian Tracy's book "Eat that Frog!" which is a great book on stopping procrastination.

t: The Pattern on the Stone: The Simple Ideas That Make Computers Work
s: A short, nontechnical introduction to how computers work, from Boolean logic to universal computation and parallelism.
w: Recommended as a tiny, approachable book for total newcomers. One reader says the idea of a universal computer shocked them.
ab: For beginners wanting the big ideas without code
Short and readable
Older examples; fundamentals still hold

q.t: This book shocked me with the idea of a universal computer

t: Who We Are and How We Got Here
s: Geneticist David Reich's account of how ancient DNA is rewriting the history of human migration and mixing.
w: HN readers point to it as the book on ancient DNA and human history, with one calling it a delight because it settles many open questions. It's also recommended in DNA-sequencing threads.
ab: For readers interested in genetics, archaeology and human history
A very up-to-date synthesis from a leading researcher
Some sections are technical; findings keep updating

q.t: was just a delight, to have so many open questions be slammed shut.

t: Unbroken: A World War II Story of Survival, Resilience, and Redemption
s: Laura Hillenbrand's biography of Louis Zamperini, Olympic runner turned WWII airman who survived a crash, a raft at sea and a Japanese prison camp.
w: HN readers describe it as an astonishing true story of grit and survival and tell you not to judge it by the movie. It is a repeat pick from the best-books lists.
ab: For readers who like gripping true survival stories
Biography of Louis Zamperini
Graphic scenes of war and captivity

q.t: Story of human grit and survival in the Pacific WWII theater that I hadn't heard of before.

s: Kafka's 1915 novella about Gregor Samsa, who wakes up transformed into a giant insect, and how his family reacts.
w: HN readers name it a favorite and a must-read short work, one of the most brilliant books they have read, often with Kafka's other works. It's short enough to read in a sitting.
ab: For first-time Kafka readers, a short and accessible start
Absurdist, existential themes about alienation and family
Very short; editions vary a lot in page count

q.t: Never had a chance to read it and now I think it's one of the most brilliant book I ever red.

t: Designed for Use: Create Usable Interfaces for Applications and the Web
s: Lukas Mathis's practical guide to designing usable software interfaces, covering the UI/UX process, user research and testing.
w: Recommended to developers who ask how to improve usability, as a readable introduction to the design process. A commenter says the print edition is badly laid out and to get the ebook.
ab: For developers and PMs who want to design more usable interfaces
Covers UI/UX process, research and empirical testing
Print layout criticised; get the epub

q.t: It has great chapters on the UI/Ux process.

t: Programming Ruby 3.3 (5th Edition): The Pragmatic Programmers' Guide
s: The updated Pickaxe, the Pragmatic Programmers' long-running guide and reference to the Ruby language, covering recent features such as Ractors and static typing.
w: Nicknamed the Pickaxe, it's the book HN suggests as the closest thing to the official Ruby documentation. Veterans who learned from early editions still recommend the latest.
ab: For Ruby learners and users wanting a complete guide and reference
Updated for modern Ruby versions; newer editions exist
Bigger and more reference-like than quick tutorials

q.t: The PickAxe is still amazing.

s: Alan Moore and David Lloyd's dystopian graphic novel about an anarchist in a fascist future Britain.
w: Often paired with Watchmen when HN recommends graphic novels, praised as well-written storytelling that raises philosophical questions in an accessible form. Some commenters say it changed how they saw the world.
ab: For readers new to graphic novels or who like political dystopia
Collected single volume; dark and adult themes
Moore's politics are prominent, so expect a strong ideological point of view

q.t: Alan Moore tackles important philosophical questions in a really accessible medium.

s: Patrick Rothfuss's fantasy series, beginning with The Name of the Wind, in which the innkeeper Kvothe recounts his life as a legendary magician.
w: HN fantasy fans praise the depth of the magic system and the writing, and one says it redefined what fantasy fiction can do. The big caveat is that the trilogy is still unfinished.
ab: For fantasy readers who like detail and a literary style
A magic system that feels plausible, and rewards rereading
Third book never released; flaws noted

q.t: Patrick Rothfuss' Kingkiller Chronicle books have redefined what is possible with fantasy fiction, with incredible depth and subtlety and literary flourishes.

s: A true story of amateur deep-sea divers who discover a sunken German U-boat off New Jersey and spend years identifying it.
w: HN readers call it intense and amazing, a page-turner for anyone into deep-sea adventure or U-boats. One reader finds it as ambitious as a startup story.
ab: For fans of true adventure like Into Thin Air
Deep wreck diving, WWII U-boat mystery
Risky, intense subject

q.t: If you like deep sea adventure or anything U-boat, it's a worthy read.

s: A children's fantasy about a bored boy who drives through a magic tollbooth into a land of words and numbers.
w: HN readers reread it every year as kids and call it the most mind-expanding book. They suggest reading it before age 10, and some read it to their children.
ab: For kids and adult fans of wordplay and puzzles
Fantasy full of puns that reward curiosity
Best read young, per commenters

q.t: The Phantom Tollbooth. Hands down.

s: A split, fully programmable mechanical keyboard with modules and layers, aimed at developers.
w: HN users say it relieves wrist pain and is the most solid, customizable keyboard they have owned, with a travel case. One notes V1 had issues and V2 is better.
ab: For developers with wrist strain who want a split keyboard
Every key customizable via a configuration app
First version had issues; pricey

q.t: It's helped me get over a lot of wrist pain, and I love how customizable it is

s: A Discworld comic fantasy novel in which a conman is forced to revive Ankh-Morpork's failing post office.
w: HN readers suggest it as the best first Discworld book for tech and business people. It is funny, has a plot about finance and communication networks, and can be read without the earlier books.
ab: For readers new to Discworld who like clever, satirical fantasy
Standalone story that works without earlier books
Humor is British and satirical, with some darker moments

q.t: For the HN crowd "going postal" is probably a good first read.

t: How to Stop Worrying and Start Living
s: A self-help classic from the author of How to Win Friends and Influence People, offering practical rules for handling worry and stress.
w: HN readers who struggled with stress or anxiety recommend it for its practical advice, and say it helped them when they were down.
ab: For anyone looking for practical anxiety and stress advice
Short rules and stories
Written in the 1940s; dated examples

q.t: It's really good if you are stressed with your lifestyle

s: A mesh-back ergonomic office chair from Steelcase with an automatic weight-sensing reclining mechanism.
w: A simpler, lighter alternative to the Leap that HN owners keep for a decade or more and call comfortable and good value over time.
ab: For long desk hours on a budget
Lighter and simpler than the Leap
Buy used or refurbished to save money

q.t: for about 12 years and have found it to be superlative

s: A 1972 Hugo-winning novel about an exchange between our universe and a parallel one that threatens the Sun.
w: HN readers call it one of Asimov's best and a truly mind-blowing easy read, even if his characters are a bit wooden.
ab: For fans of idea-driven classic science fiction
Three-part structure with alien chapters
Characters are thin, per commenters

q.t: is a easy to read but truly mind blowing book

s: A 1937 novel in which a narrator's mind travels across the cosmos, witnessing countless civilizations and the creation of universes.
w: Repeatedly named as a mind-blowing classic, one of the most epic science fiction scopes ever attempted. Several commenters call it a favorite of all time, though a hard read.
ab: For readers who like cosmic, big-idea science fiction
Dense, philosophical prose; not plot-driven
Pairs with Stapledon's Last and First Men

q.t: Olaf Stapledon's "Star Maker" Is one of my favorite books of all time.

s: Huxley's short essay describing his 1953 experience taking mescaline and reflecting on perception and consciousness.
w: A short, much-listed title in HN threads on life-changing and formative books; commenters mention it for its account of a mescaline experience and how it pushed them to explore the mind.
ab: For readers curious about consciousness and psychedelics
Short essay, quick to read
Mid-century perspective; more reflective than scientific

q.t: The book covers Aldous' thought about his experience while under the influence of mescaline.

s: A far-future space opera about humanity's wormhole-linked worlds and an alien threat, first of the Commonwealth Saga.
w: HN sci-fi fans rank it among the best science fiction they've read and a favorite of epic space opera.
ab: For readers who like big, ambitious space opera
Long book; the story continues in Judas Unchained
Slow to build

q.t: A old book, yes, but a part of some of the best science fiction

s: H. G. Wells's 1895 novella about a traveler who journeys to the far future and finds humanity split into two species.
w: HN readers say it still holds up and credit it with starting a lifelong love of speculative fiction. It is free on Project Gutenberg.
ab: Short classic that founded time-travel fiction.
Public domain and free to read.
Victorian prose, but brief.

q.t: still holds up very well, and seems strangely eerie and prescient in places

t: The Definitive Book of Body Language
s: A popular guide to reading and using non-verbal communication, with diagrams of common gestures and postures.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a short, light book that helped them notice body language in sales, meetings and social situations. One says there may be better ones.
ab: For beginners curious about non-verbal cues
Short, with plenty of diagrams
Pop psychology; some claims are not well supported by research

q.t: It is short, to the point and has nice diagrams.

s: High-attenuation over-the-head hearing protection earmuffs from 3M Peltor.
w: Recommended as a cheap fix for noisy offices and neighbors: commenters call them remarkably effective, comfortable for hours, and good with earplugs. They are bulky.
ab: For open offices, construction noise and loud neighbors
Very effective for about $30
Large, look funny, and may not fit with earbuds

q.t: They are remarkably effective and proved to be a terrific investment.

t: Assembly Language Step-by-Step: Programming with Linux
s: A beginner-oriented introduction to x86 assembly on Linux, starting with how the machine works.
w: Recommended as the friendly entry to assembly. Commenters like its conversational style and its approach of explaining the machine before the instructions.
ab: For beginners wanting a gentle path into assembly
Conversational style; teaches machine concepts first
32-bit x86 focus; not modern ARM or x86-64

q.t: I can heartily recommend this book for beginners

s: A history of how mathematics lost its claim to absolute truth, from Greek geometry through non-Euclidean geometry and modern foundations.
w: Recommended to non-mathematicians for a readable account of how rigor and truth in math have evolved. Cited in foundations-of-math threads.
ab: For readers curious about the philosophy and history of math
Semi-popular and readable
Written in 1980, so no modern developments

q.t: very insightful in regards to the development and current state of mathematics

t: Procrastination: Why You Do It, What to Do About It Now
by: Jane B. Burka, Lenora M. Yuen
s: Two psychologists explain the emotional roots of procrastination, such as perfectionism and fear, and give strategies for change.
w: Recommended for people who want to understand why they procrastinate rather than get a quick fix. Commenters call it helpful and an amazing read on the psychology.
ab: For chronic procrastinators who want the emotional causes
Draws on workshops and counseling experience
Not a quick-fix productivity system

q.t: It's not a 'quick fix' type book, but I found it helpful.

s: A richly illustrated guide to how everyday machines and technology work, from levers to computers, narrated through woolly mammoth cartoons.
w: Suggested as a book for curious kids and an adult favorite, one commenter remembers poring over it unlike any book since. Recommended for explaining mechanisms visually.
ab: For curious kids and adults who like mechanisms
Illustrated explanations of machines and electronics
