1998 edition; recent technology is not covered

q.t: Haven't opened it in 20 years, but I don't think I've poured over a book the same way since.

t: Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much
s: Behavioral-science book on how scarcity of money or time narrows focus and impairs decision-making.
w: Cited as evidence that poverty and time pressure shape behavior beyond willpower, including procrastination.
ab: For readers interested in behavioral economics
Applies to money and time
Research-based

q.t: it is a really interesting book which explores maladaptive frugality.

s: Antony Beevor's narrative history of the 1942-43 battle of Stalingrad, drawing on newly opened Soviet archives and soldiers' letters.
w: HN's go-to military history recommendation on the Eastern Front. Commenters say it tells the story of the siege well, with one noting Beevor's books can get bogged down in troop movements.
ab: For readers interested in World War II's Eastern Front
Vivid mix of strategy and individual soldiers' experience
Long stretches of detailed unit movements

q.t: I can recommend Antony Beevor.

t: The Fourth Turning: An American Prophecy
s: Strauss and Howe's theory that American history moves in repeating generational cycles, with a crisis era due around the 2020s.
w: HN commenters recommend it on cycles of crisis and corruption. Fans find it hard to put down, while skeptics dispute its predictions.
ab: For readers interested in generational theory
Offers a sweeping model of US history
Considered pseudo-scientific by critics

q.t: The 4th Turning is a good read on the subject

t: Getting More: How You Can Negotiate to Succeed in Work and Life
s: A negotiation guide from a Wharton professor emphasizing emotions, perception and trading what the other side values.
w: Recommended for soft skills, with commenters noting Google has brought in the author and one saying the workshop paid off.
ab: For engineers building negotiation skills
Practical, example-heavy
Academic origins, workshop-style

q.t: the book and workshop helped me understand how to use negotiation to get what I want

t: The Essays of Warren Buffett: Lessons for Corporate America
s: Buffett's Berkshire shareholder letters reorganized by topic, covering investing, corporate governance, accounting and finance.
w: Recommended as the easy-to-read bound version of the letters, with nuggets of wisdom throughout; one commenter calls it probably the best single place to start.
ab: For investors and business readers
Letters organized by theme, not year
About a decade old now; newer letters are online

q.t: a classic and probably the best single place to get started

t: Albion's Seed: Four British Folkways in America
s: A history of four British migrations that shaped American regional cultures.
w: Called the usual book on American regional folkways.
ab: For US cultural history
Scholarly
Long and dense

q.t: The usual book on this subject is Albion's Seed.

t: Kettlebell Simple & Sinister: Revised and Updated
s: A minimalist kettlebell program built around swings and Turkish get-ups, with technique instruction.
w: HN lifters recommend it as a minimal-effort, maximum-effect routine: a couple of kettlebells and a few sessions a week.
ab: For busy people wanting a simple strength routine
Needs only one or two kettlebells
Technique matters; get form coaching if possible

q.t: It's very much a minimal effort, maximum effect program.

t: Inadequate Equilibria: Where and How Civilizations Get Stuck
s: An essay-length book on why societies and institutions get stuck in bad equilibria and when individuals can expect to outperform them.
w: HN readers use it to explain why large organizations get stuck in bad incentive structures, praising the analysis even though there is no direct fix. One calls it horribly written but salient.
ab: For readers interested in incentives and institutional failure
Analysis of causes, not a how-to for fixing them
Writing style divides readers

q.t: an excellent assessment of where things go wrong and why they are hard to fix

t: The First Fifteen Lives of Harry August
s: A novel about a man who is reborn into the same life every time he dies, and what happens when the world's end speeds up.
w: HN readers call it clever and thought-provoking, including one who found it the most impactful book of his recent reading. One warns it may not be for everyone.
ab: For readers who like time-loop and reincarnation puzzles
Literary pacing rather than action
Some readers find it not their cup of tea

q.t: The most impactful book I've read recently has been The First Fifteen Lives of Harry August by Claire North

by: Richard S. Sutton, Andrew G. Barto
s: The standard textbook on reinforcement learning, covering core ideas such as Markov decision processes, temporal-difference learning and policy gradients.
w: HN names Sutton and Barto as the book to learn reinforcement learning, and people note the second edition is free online. Readers mark it up and recommend it as a core ML text.
ab: For students and engineers who want a rigorous RL foundation
Second edition adds modern topics; free online
Needs some math background

q.t: Sutton & Barto's Reinforcement Learning book is pretty good

t: A Man for All Markets: From Las Vegas to Wall Street, How I Beat the Dealer and the Market
s: Memoir of mathematician Edward Thorp, who beat blackjack with card counting and then built one of the first quantitative hedge funds.
w: HN readers keep naming it among their best nonfiction of the year: a math-minded autobiography that moves from counting cards in Vegas to quant investing, readable even without a finance background.
ab: For readers who like math, gambling history, or the origins of quant finance
You get a first-person story, from Depression-era childhood to hedge fund
Memoir, not a how-to manual for investing or card counting

q.t: Loved his stories about counting cards and then moving onto hedge funds etc.

s: A long popular-psychology book on human behavior, with chapters on traits like narcissism and group dynamics, illustrated with historical figures and stories.
w: Fans on HN call it spectacular and recommend it to people who need to read office politics and other people. They like the historical stories, and note the length.
ab: For readers who want to understand motives and social dynamics
Big book packed with historical anecdotes
Pop psychology, not academic research

q.t: not a word seems to be wasted!

s: Surreal comic novel by Irish writer Flann O'Brien, narrated by a murderer who ends up in a bizarre police world governed by its own absurd physics.
w: Commenters recommend it as a favorite fiction find: short, surreal, and funny. It turns up in answers about best unknown books and books worth giving as gifts.
ab: For readers who like absurdist, darkly comic fiction
Short novel, quick to read but strange
An acquired taste; it is deliberately bizarre

q.t: an author who died in the 60s but who had been completely unknown to me until this year.

t: Ecology of the Planted Aquarium: A Practical Manual and Scientific Treatise for the Home Aquarist
s: Science-based manual on how plants, microbes, and soil work together in freshwater aquariums, written for hobbyists who want to understand why planted tanks stay healthy.
w: Aquarium hobbyists on HN call it the book that explains why planted tanks work, with the biology rather than just recipes. It comes up repeatedly in best-book and eye-opening-text threads.
ab: For aquarium keepers who want the science behind planted tanks
Explains plants, soil, microbes, and water chemistry in depth
More of a scientific treatise than a quick beginner's guide

q.t: It's extremely obvious that it works, and why it works

s: David Hume's 1748 philosophy classic on empiricism, causation, induction, and the limits of human knowledge.
w: HN readers credit it with teaching them to think about causality and induction, and for showing that philosophy can be clear and readable. It is a staple on lists of books that changed minds.
ab: For readers wanting an entry point to empiricism and skepticism
Short and unusually clear for an eighteenth-century work
Edition matters; pick a modern annotated one

q.t: It showed me that intellectual curiosity doesn't need to be coupled with abstruse language

t: Capitalist Realism: Is There No Alternative?
s: Short critical-theory book arguing that capitalism has become the only imaginable system, and linking culture, mental health, and bureaucracy to that sense of inevitability.
w: HN readers recommend it as a short, compelling critique of how everything gets seen through an economic lens. It's on many life-changing-books lists.
ab: For readers interested in culture, politics and mental health
Short and accessible critical theory
Left critique; some HN readers will disagree

q.t: It links together Postmodernism in the cultural, social and economic domains

s: Tom Wolfe's 1968 account of Ken Kesey, the Merry Pranksters and their psychedelic bus trip across the US.
w: Named as a favorite and as a vivid portrait of the 1960s counterculture and early LSD experiments. Readers say it's an experience to read.
ab: For readers curious about 1960s counterculture and psychedelics
New Journalism style
Narrative nonfiction, not a clinical history of LSD

q.t: Reading this book has been an experience, although I'm not sure what exactly.

s: A short, poetic exploration of what physics says about time, by a theoretical physicist.
w: Frequently mentioned as the book to read on whether time exists, and loved by readers who found it settling.
ab: For curious readers with no physics background
Short and lyrical
More philosophical than technical

q.t: Carlo Rovelli’s The Order of Time restored my sense of mental sanity.

s: The first novel in the YA dystopian trilogy about a teenager forced to fight in a televised death match.
w: Readers say it's a fast read that makes you think, and some finished the whole trilogy in days.
ab: For readers who like fast YA dystopias
First of a trilogy
Reads quickly

q.t: Young adult fiction that reads fast but makes you think.

s: A collection of David Foster Wallace essays on topics such as lobster boiling, a porn awards show and political talk radio.
w: Repeatedly named as essays worth reading, with readers saying everything in the collection is good.
ab: For readers of literary essays
Wide range of topics
Wallace's long footnoted style

q.t: Basically everything in that collection and Consider the Lobster is worth reading.

s: A time-travel novel in which a teacher goes back in time to try to prevent the Kennedy assassination.
w: A recurring pick in HN reading threads, praised as a gripping time-travel story with King's usual momentum and a good way into his work for people who haven't read him.
ab: For readers who like time travel and historical detail
Long, immersive novel that is hard to put down
Recommended even for people new to Stephen King

q.t: An interesting twist on time travel with the usual King propulsiveness.

s: An advanced Common Lisp book about macros, closures and writing code that writes code.
w: Readers call it fun and one of the few programming books they read cover to cover. One suggests reading a few careful pages a day.
ab: For programmers who know some Lisp
Dense, opinionated macro techniques
Read slowly

q.t: One of the few programming books I've read cover to cover.

s: Erich Fromm's 1976 essay contrasting a life focused on owning things with one focused on being and experience.
w: One reader says it greatly affected their life and thinking by putting a discomfort with consumer society into words. Another summarises Fromm's argument that society and language are built around having.
ab: For readers questioning consumerism
Short, essay-like
Dated social analysis

q.t: it had an quite an impact on my life and thinking.

s: A visual, puzzle-filled introduction to Java and object-oriented programming from the Head First series.
w: Pointed out as a good introductory Java text for beginners; one commenter says to buy it to support the author, not pirate it.
ab: For beginners to Java and OOP
Quirky, graphic teaching style
2nd edition covers Java 5; newer editions exist

q.t: Another good introductory text is Head First Java

s: A far-future space opera about clone dynasties who travel the galaxy over millions of years.
w: HN sci-fi readers call it a standout standalone with incredible world building, comparing Reynolds to Iain M. Banks.
ab: Standalone space opera, no series commitment.
Big-scale galactic civilizations.
Readers wish it were a series.

q.t: The world building in this one book is amazing, wish he'd made a series out of it.

s: Gelfand's algebra textbook for high school students.
w: HN recommends Gelfand's books as excellent basic math texts. Commenters note they were used for distance learning in Russia.
ab: For self-learners and parents
Part of a series
Unconventional style

q.t: has books aimed at high school students that served as education materials for distance learning in russia

s: A budget adjustable high-back office chair with a mesh-style back and adjustable arms, similar in look to the Herman Miller Aeron.
w: HN commenters recommend it as an inexpensive Aeron alternative. They say it is adjustable, sturdy and comfortable enough that whole teams have bought it.
ab: For programmers wanting an ergonomic chair at a fraction of Aeron prices
Many adjustments including removable arms
Model has changed over the years; reviews of older versions may not apply

q.t: It's the Hyundai of chairs: 90% of what an Aeron is design-wise, but also more comfortable.

t: The Strategy and Tactics of Pricing: A Guide to Growing More Profitably
s: A textbook on value-based pricing covering how to set prices, segment customers and avoid price wars.
w: HN commenters name it as the best book on pricing, saying it is worth the price and warning that it lays out how deep the topic is. It comes up whenever someone asks how to price a product.
ab: For founders and product managers setting or changing prices
Value-based pricing frameworks and case examples
Pricey textbook; dense and written for larger firms

q.t: It's pretty expensive as far as books go, but very much worth it.

t: How We Got to Now: Six Innovations That Made the Modern World
s: Steven Johnson traces how six inventions, such as cold and glass, shaped modern life.
w: Recommended as an interesting quick read on how innovations enabled each other.
ab: Quick narrative history
Adjacent possible theme
Pop-history depth

q.t: Really interesting book on how development in certain fields enabled other innovations

t: Small Giants: Companies That Choose to Be Great Instead of Big
s: Profiles of companies that deliberately stay small and focus on being excellent.
w: Recommended for people who want sustainable companies instead of growth.
ab: Anti-growth case studies
Profiles of companies
Selective examples

q.t: This entire book is literally about companies that focus on deliberately growing but still staying excellent.

t: Mindfulness: A Practical Guide to Finding Peace in a Frantic World
s: An eight-week mindfulness program with guided audio.
w: Recommended for people struggling with regret and stress.
ab: Eight-week program
Includes audio
Self-paced

q.t: Just self-paced, listen to a 5-min mp3 once or twice a day.

t: Mastering the Core Teachings of the Buddha
s: A frank, technical guide to meditation stages and maps of progress, written by a physician-practitioner.
w: Recommended by meditators who want maps of progress and a non-mystical, geeky treatment, including when practice goes badly.
ab: For serious meditators who like models and maps
Blunt, technical, and very detailed
Controversial claims; some find it too hardcore

q.t: The author is super-geeky about this stuff.

s: Manning book on domain modeling with functional programming in Scala, covering algebraic data types, event sourcing, CQRS and reactive design.
w: HN readers recommend it as one of few books on building real-world software with functional programming. It is cited for domain-driven design and CQRS in a functional style.
ab: For Scala and FP developers doing domain-driven design
Covers event sourcing and CQRS
Scala-centered; check how current the examples are

q.t: I can't recommend this enough

t: Awareness: The Perils and Opportunities of Reality
s: Talks by Jesuit priest and psychotherapist Anthony de Mello on spiritual awareness, attachments, and waking up to how one actually perceives reality.
w: HN readers cite it as a mind-expanding and life-changing read, including people who say it helped through hard times. It's often listed next to other contemplative and Eastern-leaning books.
ab: For readers interested in mindfulness and spiritual self-inquiry
Collected talks with a conversational tone
Spiritual, not scientific; the Vatican once questioned de Mello's writings

q.t: I highly recommend two books

t: Inventing Accuracy: A Historical Sociology of Nuclear Missile Guidance
s: A history of how nuclear missile guidance accuracy was developed, and how technology and strategic need shaped each other.
w: HN threads on nuclear weapons and missile guidance recommend it as a fascinating look at inertial guidance and how technology drove policy and strategy.
ab: For readers interested in Cold War technology and policy
Mixes technical history with sociology
Academic in tone

q.t: "Inventing Accuracy" is a fascinating history of ICBM inertial guidance.

s: Russell's short 1912 introduction to philosophy, covering knowledge, reality, and the value of philosophical questions.
w: HN commenters recommend it as an accessible, thought-provoking short intro to philosophy, and a few have reread it many times, though it is a bit dated.
ab: For beginners wanting a short intro to philosophy
Readable and compact
Written in 1912, so some arguments are dated

q.t: It's one of the most accessible and thought provoking books on philosophy I've read.

t: Havit HV-KB390L Mechanical Keyboard with Low-Profile Kailh Switches
s: A wired tenkeyless mechanical keyboard using thin, low-profile Kailh switches in an extra-slim aluminum case.
w: HN commenters point to it as an affordable low-profile mechanical keyboard, praised as the one board that stayed after trying around ten. It is suggested as a wired alternative for Apple keyboard users.
ab: For people who want a thin, cheap mechanical keyboard
Tenkeyless layout with low-profile switches
Budget build; the original model is now old

q.t: i found a low-profile kalih switch keyboard and it's the first of around 10 mechanical keyboards that im not returning.

t: Wrong: Why Experts Keep Failing Us and How to Know When Not to Trust Them
s: A journalist examines why expert advice in science, medicine and business is so often wrong, and offers guidance on whom to trust.
w: HN commenters recommend it for its detailed accounts of failures in the research system, including invalid results and gaming. One had to put it down repeatedly in dismay.
ab: For readers skeptical of expert and media claims
Many case studies from medicine, finance and consulting
Provocative thesis; some say it overstates

q.t: which talks about a number of failings in our current research system, why invalid results persist, and how people game the system

s: A 13-inch ASUS ultrabook from around 2014, popular with developers who ran Linux on it.

ab: For people wanting an inexpensive older Linux-friendly ultrabook
Works well with Linux; RAM upgradeable
Old hardware, mostly available used

q.t: got one (UX32LN) and worked flawlessly for many years (on linux)

s: A mid-range Herman Miller ergonomic office chair with a flexible back and mesh seat, priced below the Aeron.
w: HN owners say its back support is better than the Aeron's, with some preferring it for reclined work, and recommend buying used from office liquidators. One warns the newest models are built cheaper.
ab: For people wanting a comfortable chair cheaper than an Aeron
Good back support; stiffer feel; recline friendly
Older Mirra v1 reportedly better built than the latest

q.t: Compared to the Aeron, it is stiffer and has better back support for sitting upright.

s: A study of how tech firms profit from collecting and predicting human behavior.
w: HN cites it in privacy threads. One reader says it puts developments in context and argues for banning the business model.
ab: For readers worried about tech privacy
Long and dense
Strongly polemical

q.t: A lot of people have an intuitive feeling of how things have gotten out of control but she places the developments in context

t: The Coddling of the American Mind: How Good Intentions and Bad Ideas Are Setting Up a Generation for Failure
s: An argument that overprotective parenting and campus culture teach young people to avoid discomfort and disagreement, with proposed remedies.
w: HN commenters bring it up in debates about free speech, safetyism and parenting. Fans say it outlines what changed over thirty years and the resulting generational gap.
ab: For readers following campus and speech debates
Grounded in cognitive behavioral therapy ideas
Contested on causes and scope

q.t: does a great job of outlining what has changed in the last 30 years and why there is very much a generational gap

s: A line of premium mechanical keyboards from Das Keyboard, offered with Cherry MX switches in clicky and brown variants.

ab: For typists who want a sturdy full-size mechanical keyboard
Choose clicky or brown switches depending on noise tolerance
Full-size layout; some later preferred compact boards

q.t: I liked my Das Keyboard because it felt like I was interacting with a premium device

t: Where Good Ideas Come From: The Natural History of Innovation
s: A popular-science book arguing that innovation comes from connected networks, hunches and open environments rather than lone flashes of genius.
w: HN commenters recommend it for understanding creativity and the role of in-person serendipity. One called it the best book they had read in five years, with lessons easy to apply.
ab: For readers curious about creativity and innovation
Readable popular-science style
Broad thesis; light on actionable rules

q.t: It's easy to apply the lessons to your typical working day. Best book I've read in probably 5 years.

s: A guide to projects that are doomed by unrealistic schedules, staffing and expectations, and how to survive them.

Covers negotiation, triage and survival strategies
Published 1997 and revised in 2004; examples are dated

Third edition covers kernel 2.6; recent kernels differ

t: The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect

Popular-science writing with limited math and many examples
Reflects Pearl's school of thought, not every view of causality

s: A Harvard geneticist's argument that aging is a treatable condition, summarizing research on longevity genes, NAD and lifestyle.

Mixes science with the author's personal habits
Optimistic and promotional in places; verify claims independently

s: A contoured ergonomic mechanical keyboard with concave key wells, thumb clusters, and Cherry MX switches.

ab: For people with wrist strain or heavy typists
Takes a few weeks to adjust
Expensive; unusual layout

q.t: Love the ergonomic hand positioning/dished layout, the switch feel

s: Near-future novel about a billionaire who unilaterally launches stratospheric sulfur to cool the climate, and the geopolitical fallout across the world.

Not as strong as his earlier books, per HN
Plot-light in places; geoengineering theme

s: Google's high-end 2013-2015 Chromebook with a high-resolution touchscreen and Intel processor, popular for running Linux.

Excellent hi-res display for its time
Discontinued; hardware now very old

t: Dark Sun: The Making of the Hydrogen Bomb
s: Richard Rhodes's history of the US and Soviet hydrogen bomb programs, including Teller, espionage and the early Cold War.
w: Recommended as the follow-up to The Making of the Atomic Bomb, with the Soviet program and espionage woven in. Commenters call it fantastic and great reading.
ab: For readers who liked The Making of the Atomic Bomb
Covers the US H-bomb and Soviet bomb projects together
Narrative is more fractured and factual than its predecessor

q.t: which is a fantastic follow on read to The Making of the Atomic Bomb.

s: David Ogilvy's practical, opinionated guide to how advertising works, drawn from decades running one of the world's biggest agencies.

ab: For founders and marketers who want fundamentals of persuasion and copy
Concrete rules, case studies and Ogilvy's strong opinions
Written in 1985, so media examples feel dated

s: First novel of The Expanse: a detective and a ship's officer uncover a conspiracy that could start a war across the solar system.

ab: For fans of realistic space opera and political intrigue
Nine-book series plus novellas
TV show is based on it but loosely

q.t: I enjoyed this whole series.

s: Ishiguro's quiet, haunting novel following three friends raised at an English boarding school who slowly learn what they were created for.

Plain prose, slow-building dread
Avoid spoilers; hard to categorize

s: Teaches Elixir and the Erlang VM, including processes, OTP, fault tolerance and building concurrent, distributed systems.

Check for the newer edition

s: Joseph Conrad's 1899 novella about a steamboat journey up the Congo, a critique of European colonialism and the darkness within people.
w: HN readers call it an amazing, short classic that influenced 20th-century literature and exposed colonial exploitation and racism ahead of its time.
ab: For readers of classic literature
Short, but dense and bleak
Contains period language; read as a critique of colonialism

q.t: A book that should be on everyone's list!

t: Making Things Happen: Mastering Project Management
s: A practical guide to managing software and creative projects, covering vision, specs, schedules, politics and shipping.
w: HN managers and engineers recommend it for project management and technical leadership, with one wishing they had read it before moving into management.
ab: For new project leads and engineering managers
Covers office politics and decision making
Software-era examples can feel dated

q.t: definitely something to read if you ever get into management

t: Kicking Away the Ladder: Development Strategy in Historical Perspective
s: An economist argues that rich countries industrialized through protectionism and state support, then pushed free-market rules on developing nations.
w: HN commenters cite it in debates over free trade, protectionism, and industrial policy as evidence that developed countries did not follow the policies they now prescribe.
ab: For readers debating trade policy and economic development
Historical evidence on how rich countries industrialized
Argumentative and contested by free-trade economists

t: The Apollo Guidance Computer: Architecture and Operation
s: A detailed technical description of the Apollo Guidance Computer's hardware, software and operation.

Covers AGC architecture, instruction set and operation
Technical and niche; much of it is previewable on Amazon

t: Zero: The Biography of a Dangerous Idea
s: A popular-history book tracing the number zero from Babylon and Greece through India and the Church to modern physics.

Short, story-driven history rather than a textbook
Covers Babylon, Greece, India, medieval Europe and physics

s: Larry Niven and Jerry Pournelle's 1974 first-contact novel about humanity's first meeting with an alien species near a red star.

Strong aliens and political intrigue
1970s cultural assumptions show; slow in places

t: Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In
s: The Harvard Negotiation Project's method of principled negotiation focused on interests rather than positions.

Short and practical
Not for hardball tactics

t: The Emperor's Handbook: A New Translation of The Meditations
s: A modern English translation of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, rendered in a looser, more readable style than literal versions.

Looser, more modern than literal translations
Purists may prefer a more literal version

s: Plain-language guide to reading financial statements and understanding the numbers behind a small business.

ab: For founders and non-finance people
Explains financial statements in plain language
Introductory; not a deep accounting text

t: The Art of Deception: Controlling the Human Element of Security

Story-driven, with composite scenarios and countermeasures
Not a technical hacking book

Covers modernization strategy, not just code
Aimed at organizational as well as technical problems

Narrative style mixing history and personal story
Published in 2000, so newer research is missing

s: A budget ergonomic office chair with a high mesh-and-fabric back, lumbar support and a long warranty.

Some prefer IKEA Malkolm or other chairs

s: A seven-book fantasy series about children who travel to the magical land of Narnia.

Seven linked books, usually sold as a boxed set
Christian allegory, which some readers may not want

One-sided by design; written in 2017

s: A narrative history of the 1990s competition between Sega and Nintendo in the US video game market.
w: Recommended as an insider-style account of the Sega versus Nintendo fight, including tensions between the Japanese and American arms. Fans call it a great audiobook.
ab: For readers curious about video game business history
Mostly follows Sega's American side
Dramatized; scenes are reconstructed

q.t: It provides an insider's perspective of the Sega v. Nintendo battle during the 80s and 90s.

by: David S. Dummit, Richard M. Foote
s: A standard undergraduate and graduate textbook on groups, rings, fields and Galois theory, with many exercises.
w: The textbook HN people name for abstract algebra self-study, for its many examples and exercises. Commenters note the exercises are challenging and the book is expensive.
ab: For math students and self-learners studying abstract algebra
Example-heavy with a very large problem set
Expensive and demanding; review linear algebra first

q.t: Most people like the Dummit & Foote book; it tends to be loaded with examples rather than a lot of dense symbolic arguments

t: Legacy of Ashes: The History of the CIA
s: A National Book Award-winning history of the CIA from 1947 onward, built on declassified records and interviews, focused on its failures.
w: Recommended when threads turn to intelligence agencies. One reader expected a spy thriller and found a documented chronicle of blunder after blunder.
ab: Readers wanting a sober, documented view of CIA history
Long and relentlessly critical in tone
Covers Cold War through the early 2000s

q.t: turned out to be a chronicle of blunder after blunder by the CIA. Fascinating stuff.

s: The CEO of Semco describes running a company with self-managed teams, open books and no fixed rules on hours or titles.
w: Recommended among the best business and management books, and as the original example of a democratic company. Commenters cite Semco whenever flat organizations come up.
ab: For founders and managers curious about flat organizations
Case studies from Semco, a Brazilian manufacturer
Extreme autonomy may not translate to every company

q.t: The best business book I've ever read is The Seven Day Weekend by Ricardo Semler.

t: Bloodlands: Europe Between Hitler and Stalin
s: History of the mass killings in Eastern Europe between 1933 and 1945 under both the Nazi and Soviet regimes.
w: Recommended to anyone wanting to understand how Eastern Europe suffered in the 20th century and how the Holocaust fits into that picture.
ab: For readers of serious modern European history
Grim subject matter
Covers Nazi and Soviet violence together

q.t: If you want to educate yourself on how Eastern Europe suffered in the 20th century, then I recommend this book

s: Asimov's classic collection of linked short stories about robots, the Three Laws of Robotics, and the puzzles that arise when they are applied.
w: HN readers name it as the first science fiction they read and a good start on Asimov's robot series. Others still find its ideas relevant when set against modern AI.
ab: For newcomers to classic science fiction and robot stories
Short, idea-driven stories rather than action novels
Written in the 1940s and 50s, so the tech is dated

q.t: The ideas Isaac Asimov put forward in I, Robot (written in the 1940/50s!) juxtaposed with a factual description of the current use of AI

s: A short book of 22 marketing rules centered on positioning, focus and owning a category in customers' minds.
w: Recommended as a quick read on positioning for developers, true as ever for finding a niche.
ab: For developers new to marketing
Short, punchy chapters
Dated corporate examples

q.t: It's a quick read, well-written, and the points it makes are as true now as ever

s: A cheap dual-band VHF/UHF handheld two-way radio covering the 2 m and 70 cm amateur bands.
w: Cited as the cheapest way into ham radio, around $25. Hobbyists say you may outgrow it.
ab: For beginners entering ham radio
License needed to transmit
Mediocre quality; many upgrade

q.t: you can get a Baofeng UV-5R handheld radio which works on the 2m and 70cm bands for $25.

t: JavaScript Patterns: Build Better Applications with Coding and Design Patterns
s: A guide to JavaScript idioms and design patterns covering functions, objects, code reuse, namespaces and common anti-patterns.
w: HN developers called it a favorite and a book you will refer to often after learning the basics of JavaScript.
ab: For developers past the basics who want to write idiomatic JavaScript
Pattern-by-pattern reference you can dip into
Published 2010, so it predates ES6 and modern syntax

q.t: One book that I found to be really good was 'JavaScript Patterns' by Stoyan Stefanov.

t: The Happiness Trap: How to Stop Struggling and Start Living
s: An introduction to Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) for handling difficult thoughts and feelings and acting on personal values.
w: HN commenters suggest it to people struggling with low mood, anxiety or poor sleep, and give it as a gift. They value its idea of accepting ups and downs.
ab: For anyone stuck in worry, rumination or low motivation
Teaches ACT exercises you can practice on your own
Popular self-help format; seek a clinician for serious depression

q.t: I found the following useful

t: Basic Category Theory for Computer Scientists
s: A short introduction to category theory aimed at computer scientists, with examples from type theory and programming languages.
w: HN readers name it as their favourite entry point to category theory: concise, clear, and framed for programmers. One reader found it brutally difficult past the first few pages.
ab: For programmers curious about categories and type theory
Compact, with examples from computer science
Math notation ramps up quickly

q.t: Concise and clear, with examples that should speak to computer scientists.

s: Hilary Mantel's Booker Prize-winning historical novel about Thomas Cromwell's rise in the court of Henry VIII.
w: HN readers list it among their favorite novels and the kind of book worth rereading, praising the portrait of Cromwell. One commenter struggled to get through it.
ab: For readers of dense, literary historical fiction
First of a trilogy; continue with Bring Up the Bodies
Present-tense style and pronouns can be hard going

q.t: Finishing up Wolf Hall right now. I quite enjoy it.

s: A 15.6-inch 2012 Lenovo business laptop with a classic ThinkPad keyboard, replaceable parts and optional discrete GPU.
w: HN owners call it an extremely capable, easy-to-repair daily driver that runs Linux well, and a classic of the last ThinkPad generation with good keyboards and upgradable RAM, SSD and screen.
ab: For tinkerers wanting a cheap, repairable used ThinkPad
Upgradable RAM, SSD and screen; a good keyboard
Old and thick; used units only

q.t: With new RAM, an SSD, and Linux, it's an extremely capable machine.

s: Apple's pressure-sensitive stylus for the iPad, used for handwriting, drawing and annotation with apps like GoodNotes.
w: HN note-takers pair it with an iPad and GoodNotes to replace paper for notes, diagrams and PDF markup, and some use it as a whiteboard substitute in video calls. A few still prefer plain paper.
ab: For people who want handwritten, searchable-ish notes on an iPad
Requires a compatible iPad; sold separately
Handwritten notes are hard to search

q.t: iPad and Apple Pencil. I missed whiteboards badly, this is the next best thing.

t: Open Sources: Voices from the Open Source Revolution
by: Chris DiBona, Sam Ockman, et al.
s: An O'Reilly collection of 1999 essays by open source pioneers, including Linus Torvalds and Eric Raymond, with the Tanenbaum-Torvalds debate as an appendix.
w: HN mostly cites it as the home of the famous Tanenbaum-Torvalds microkernel debate and the Torvalds, Perens and McKusick chapters, and recommends reading Linus's chapter.
ab: For readers interested in open source and Linux history
Chapters were freely posted online by O'Reilly
Written in 1999, so strictly a historical snapshot

q.t: The chapter by Torvalds in the same book is also worth reading

t: Disrupted: My Misadventure in the Start-Up Bubble
s: Dan Lyons's humorous memoir of working at the startup HubSpot after being laid off from journalism, satirizing startup culture.
w: HN readers list it in best-of-the-year reading lists as a funny, interesting inside view of startup culture. One calls it love-it-or-hate-it, and another notes unpleasant news about the author.
ab: For tech workers amused by startup culture
Funny take on HubSpot's culture from an older employee
Polarizing, with a subjective perspective

q.t: You will like or hate this book a lot, but it's surely an interesting read and perspective.

t: Tao Te Ching: A New English Version
s: Stephen Mitchell's poetic English rendering of the Tao Te Ching, the foundational text of Taoism.
w: HN commenters list it among favorite and gift-worthy books, and one calls the Mitchell version beautiful. Others advise Red Pine for a more faithful translation.
ab: For a first, readable encounter with Taoist verse
Mitchell's version is poetic and loose
Scholars prefer Red Pine for fidelity

q.t: The Stephen Mitchell translation of the Tao Te Ching

s: Rutger Bregman's argument that people are mostly decent, using history, anthropology, and psychology to challenge cynical views of human nature.
w: HN readers say it improved their trust in people and offers an optimistic, fact-based view, including a contrast between Hobbes and Rousseau. One bought copies for MPs.
ab: For readers who want a hopeful view of human nature
Mixes history, psychology, and anecdotes
Some of its claims are debated

q.t: had a profound influence on my trust in people, and expecting good intentions by default

t: The Almanack of Naval Ravikant: A Guide to Wealth and Happiness
s: A compilation of Naval Ravikant's tweets, essays, and podcast remarks on building wealth, judgment, and happiness.
w: HN readers praise it as a condensed summary of practical philosophy with a good reading list, and list it among founder books. One felt the first half on wealth was great but lost interest in the later meditation parts.
ab: For founders and aspiring entrepreneurs
Quotable and easy to dip into
Later sections on meditation and diet lost one reader

q.t: It has a good condensed summary of practical philosophy as well as a great list of books to check out for further ideas.

s: A 14-inch convertible business laptop with a pen, a 360-degree hinge, optional OLED screen and the ThinkPad keyboard.
w: HN Linux users like it for working out of the box on Linux and folding into a tablet for pen use, and older generations are cheap secondhand. A few mention Bluetooth or ports issues.
ab: For ThinkPad fans wanting a 2-in-1 with a pen
Older generations are cheap used
Some prefer the X1 Carbon for weight and ports

q.t: The whole device is a no-brainer and just works.

t: This Is How You Lose the Time War
s: A short epistolary novel in which two agents from rival futures exchange letters across time and fall in love.
w: HN readers call it unique, poetic, and fantastic, with one naming it an all-time favorite regardless of genre. It is a light read rather than hard science fiction.
ab: For readers who like poetic, romantic science fiction
Short and quick to read
Not hard SF; more about language and feeling

q.t: This is How You Lose the Time War is fantastic.

t: Intellectual Property and Open Source: A Practical Guide to Protecting Code
s: A practical guide to copyright, patent, trademark, and licensing issues for open source projects and the businesses that use them.
w: HN open-source developers recommend it as the best single work on software IP. Commenters call it a must-read for starting a business or an open source project.
ab: For open source maintainers and startup founders
Plain-English coverage of copyright, patents, and licenses
US-centric legal framework; not legal advice

q.t: The best single work I've read on the subject is Van Lindberg's _Intellectual Property and Open Source_

s: A deep look at the .NET Common Language Runtime and C# by Jeffrey Richter.
w: Recommended as essential reading for .NET developers, particularly for chapters on concurrency and I/O.
ab: For .NET developers wanting runtime internals.
Covers the CLR in depth.
Check the edition.

q.t: An absolutely necessary read for anyone using .NET

t: Red Notice: A True Story of High Finance, Murder, and One Man's Fight for Justice
s: A memoir of a Western investor in Russia and his fight over the death of his lawyer Sergei Magnitsky.
w: HN recommends it as a window into Russian oligarchs and politics, though one reader warns of the author's self-aggrandizing tone.
ab: For readers of finance and politics
Thriller pacing
Author's own account; self-flattering in places

q.t: it's a really interesting perspective on business dealings amongst the elites in Russia

t: Food of the Gods: The Search for the Original Tree of Knowledge
s: A speculative history of plants, drugs and human evolution, including the stoned ape hypothesis.
w: Recommended in psychedelics threads as an interesting read on mushrooms and evolution and on drug laws. Commenters treat its theories as entertaining speculation.
ab: For psychedelic and ethnobotany readers
Speculative; scientifically contested
Written in 1992; dated

q.t: theres a great book by Terrence McKenna on this subject called Food of the Gods

t: Functional Web Development with Elixir, OTP, and Phoenix
s: A Pragmatic Programmers book that builds a game as a functional core in plain Elixir and OTP before adding Phoenix as the web interface.
w: HN readers value its approach of building the functional core first and wrapping Phoenix around it, and say it improved their grasp of GenServer and OTP.
ab: For Elixir developers learning OTP and Phoenix design
Teaches separating core logic from the web layer
Written for Phoenix 1.3; some details have changed

q.t: It gave me a better understanding of GenServer/OTP

s: Robert Greene's guide to applying military and historical strategy to business, politics and everyday conflict.
w: HN readers enjoy the historical examples and sidebars, and one says it benefitted them most directly of any book. A frequent follow-on to The 48 Laws of Power.
ab: For readers who like strategy told through history
Lots of historical anecdotes per chapter
Pop-history style; the cynical advice isn't for everyone

q.t: If I were to choose one that benefitted me the most, directly, I would pick

s: The ancient Greek account of the Persian Wars and the peoples of the known world, often called the first work of history.
w: HN readers describe it as an amazing, life-changing read and good context for Thucydides. Several warn that translation matters, and that the free online versions are not the best ones.
ab: For readers of ancient history and the classics
Choose a modern translation such as the Landmark edition
Long, digressive, not always accurate

q.t: Best i read was the histories by Herodotus - the first history book in the western tradition.

s: Ishiguro's Booker-winning novel about an English butler reflecting on duty, service and missed chances.
w: HN readers name it a favorite and one of the books that changed them, a short novel on the work/life split, loyalty and regret.
ab: For readers of quiet, character-driven literary fiction
Short Nobel winner's novel
Slow and restrained

q.t: Amazing short fictional novel by a Nobel Prize winning author.

s: Dumas's classic 1844 adventure novel of d'Artagnan and the king's musketeers in 17th-century France.
w: HN readers list it among favorites and books that stand up well, funny and a good picture of 17th-century France. A commenter calls it a lesson in friendship and bravery.
ab: For fans of swashbuckling classics
Funny, fast, historical flavor
Long 19th-century novel; some outdated attitudes

q.t: In fiction Sherlock Holmes and the Three Musketeers is some of my favorites.

s: Richard Dawkins's case that natural selection can produce complex design without a designer.
w: HN readers say it deepened their understanding of evolution and impacted how they think about religion and the origin of complexity, often paired with The Selfish Gene.
ab: For curious readers who want to understand evolution
Written to convince skeptics
Tied to Dawkins's atheism, which some readers dislike

q.t: Evolution is the reason we exist!

s: The central religious text of Islam, read in many English translations.
w: HN commenters name it as part of the canon you need for understanding Western literature and history, and a few say it reshaped how they think about religion.
ab: For readers curious about Islam or the cultural canon
Many translations exist; the comments don't name one
Cited mostly in broad 'books everyone should read' lists

q.t: but it's a part of the canon, must be read

s: Paul Graham's tutorial and reference to Common Lisp, covering the language and example programs.
w: HN programmers say it has a high signal-to-noise ratio and rewards a second read, and it is a favorite for learning Lisp for fun.
ab: For programmers who want to learn Common Lisp.
Concise, little filler.
First read can be confusing; second clarifies.

q.t: His book "ANSI Common Lisp" is definitely on the top of my reading list, I've already started and it is great.

t: The Scout Mindset: Why Some People See Things Clearly and Others Don't
s: Julia Galef's book on motivated reasoning, contrasting the defensive soldier mindset with the truth-seeking scout mindset, with practical habits for judging more accurately.
w: HN readers recommend it widely as a light, practical book on making better decisions and holding calibrated opinions. People who already know the rationality community may find less that is new.
ab: For anyone who wants to reason and decide more clearly
Light read with practical habits and examples
Less new if you already know LessWrong-style rationality

q.t: It is a light read so I recommend it widely.

s: A 1990s guide to writing a 32-bit x86 operating system, with the MMURTL source.
w: HN readers who wrote their own OS say they learned from it. Commenters call it writing an operating system from scratch for dummies.
ab: For hobbyists writing an x86 OS
Includes MMURTL source
1990s x86 content

q.t: Writing an Operating System from Scratch for Dummies

s: An introduction to reverse engineering software, covering assembly, disassemblers, decompilation, binary patching, copy protection and malware analysis.
w: HN commenters have recommended it since 2009 as the book for learning reversing and binary patching. One notes it is probably a bit out of date.
ab: For beginners to reverse engineering and low-level security
Covers tools, assembly and real examples
Published in 2005; tools and platforms have changed

q.t: I can't recommend this book enough

t: Parasite Rex: Inside the Bizarre World of Nature's Most Dangerous Creatures
s: A popular science account of parasites and how they manipulate their hosts and shape evolution.
w: HN readers describe it as gross and fascinating, recommend it whenever parasite-controlled hosts come up, and credit it with inspiring researchers. One notes some science is outdated.
ab: For anyone who likes biology, evolution and nature weirdness
Readable stories of parasite life cycles and host control
Published in 2000; some details outdated

q.t: The book manages to be gross and fascinating and occasionally beautiful.

t: 3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development
s: A textbook on the vectors, matrices, transforms and geometry needed for 3D graphics and game programming.
w: HN commenters call it the book to start with for graphics math, and one of their biggest shelf pulls. It is the usual first recommendation to people self-learning graphics programming.
ab: For programmers learning the math behind 3D graphics and games
Covers vectors, matrices, rotations and transforms
Needs a separate book for rendering techniques

q.t: 3D Math Primer is the book I always recommend starting with

t: The Mystery of Capital: Why Capitalism Triumphs in the West and Fails Everywhere Else
s: De Soto argues poor countries stay poor partly because their property systems exclude most people from formal ownership.
w: Cited as an explanation for why property rights and legal institutions matter for development.
ab: Explains informal property and capital
Relevant to development economics
Contested by some economists

q.t: which espouses the theory that the root of a lot of problems is that countries set up formal property systems that exclude most

s: Tim Berners-Lee's account of inventing the World Wide Web and his hopes for its future.
w: Recommended as a non-technical, inspiring read on the web's inception and as a starting point for a curious teenager's computer history.
ab: For anyone curious how the web began
Non-technical memoir
Written in 1999, so ends optimistic

q.t: If you're interested in the history of the Web and its inception, I highly recommend you this (non-technical) reading

s: Sony's over-ear Bluetooth headphones with active noise cancellation, long battery life, and quick charging.
w: HN users call its noise cancelling the best they've tried, comparing it favorably to Bose QC35 and 700. Complaints are minor, like clunky switching between devices.
ab: For commuters, flyers, and open offices
Strong ANC with comfortable fit and long battery life
Switching between devices is clunky

q.t: I've used several ANC headphones before. None of those come close to this.

t: Effective Modern C++: 42 Specific Ways to Improve Your Use of C++11 and C++14
s: A guide to using C++11 and C++14 features well, covering type deduction, move semantics, lambdas and smart pointers.
w: HN's pick for learning modern C++. Commenters praise the clear writing and the explanation of pros, cons and design reasoning behind each feature.
ab: For C++ programmers moving past C++98
Covers C++11/14 only; newer standards not included
Collects caveats and edge cases

q.t: It cover very smoothly most of the main C++11/14 features, while explaining the pros and cons and the inner choices

t: Chaos Monkeys: Obscene Fortune and Random Failure in Silicon Valley
s: A memoir by a former Facebook product manager and founder of a YC startup, about the ad industry and Silicon Valley.
w: Recommended for its prose and its inside view of startups, YC and Facebook, and cited as a data point on early-stage startups.
ab: For readers who like Silicon Valley insider stories
Opinionated and often irreverent
Insight into YC and ad tech

q.t: enjoying the author's excellent prose, while walking through the sausage factory of startups

t: The Hardware Hacker: Adventures in Making and Breaking Hardware
s: Bunnie Huang's essays on hardware manufacturing, reverse engineering and the maker world.
w: Shared with enthusiasm when it was published.
ab: For hardware makers and tinkerers
Mix of essays on manufacturing and hacking
Some blog content

t: Software Design for Flexibility: How to Avoid Programming Yourself into a Corner
s: Hanson and Sussman on techniques for building flexible, evolvable programs, using generic procedures, pattern matching and propagators, with Scheme code.
w: HN SICP fans awaited it eagerly as the follow-up on handling complexity. Commenters note it came from Sussman's Robust Systems course and focuses on avoiding painting yourself into a corner.
ab: For experienced programmers interested in extensible system design
Examples in Scheme; code is free under GPL
Advanced and unusual; not a beginner book

q.t: This is a book that focuses on managing software complexity

t: How Big Things Get Done: The Surprising Factors That Determine the Fate of Every Project
s: An Oxford professor of megaprojects analyzes why most large projects run over budget and shows how planning, modularity and reference-class forecasting improve odds of success.
w: HN commenters recommend it for project estimation and planning, backed by real examples and case studies. It comes up in threads on failed software projects, with advice to start small, modularize and scale.
ab: For project managers, engineers and founders planning big efforts
Case studies from construction, IT and film
Core message is simple; some find it repetitive

q.t: Really good read if you want to look into project estimations and planning

t: Only the Paranoid Survive: How to Exploit the Crisis Points That Challenge Every Company
s: Andy Grove's account of strategic inflection points and how Intel navigated the shift away from memory chips.
w: Cited when Intel's fortunes come up. One commenter calls it a loved book from the man who made Moore's law happen.
ab: For founders and executives facing industry shifts
Intel-centric case studies
Short, readable

q.t: Gordon Moore created Moore's law and Andy Grove made it happen.

t: Mastering Bitcoin: Programming the Open Blockchain
s: A technical guide to how Bitcoin works, covering keys, transactions, the network and mining for developers.
w: HN's default technical book on Bitcoin. Commenters call it fairly technical but a good explanation of how everything works.
ab: For developers wanting to understand Bitcoin internals
Technical rather than investment oriented
Later editions cover updated protocol features

q.t: It's fairly technical, but gives good explanation of how everything works.

s: A short book by the 37signals founders arguing for remote work and explaining how to run distributed teams.
w: Pointed to when people ask how to keep a job while moving or how to manage remote teams. HN likes that it comes from people who actually ran a remote company.
ab: For managers and employees making the case for remote work
Short, opinionated, easy read
Written pre-2020, so some arguments now feel familiar

s: A Manning book on separating code from data and modeling information with generic immutable structures, in the style of Clojure and similar languages.
w: Mentioned when people look for ways to escape heavy object-oriented design; one says it helped them stop thinking in objects. Note it differs from data-oriented design in game development.
ab: Not the same as data-oriented design
Aimed at application developers fighting complexity
Mostly recommended through links in threads

q.t: This book and some articles and videos made by others on Data Oriented Programming can be huge helpers and big time savers for me.

t: Modern C++ Design: Generic Programming and Design Patterns Applied
s: A book on advanced C++ template techniques, policy-based design and generic programming.
w: Called wonderful and a good primer for C++ template metaprogramming, though commenters note C++11 simplified much of it. One reader says it blew them away.
ab: For C++ programmers curious about template metaprogramming
Introduces policy-based design
Predates C++11; some techniques are now simpler

q.t: Modern C++ Design (Andrei Alexandrescu)[1] is wonderful, but C++11 has "simplified" much of what he covers.

s: A guide to designing, building and operating systems composed of small, independently deployable services.
w: The usual first recommendation for learning microservices, and for learning when they are not the right call. Commenters like its balanced view of the tradeoffs.
ab: For engineers deciding whether to adopt microservices
Covers design, deployment, testing and monitoring
Newman cautions against rushing in; a second edition exists

q.t: Very good read that gives a pretty high level description of services

t: Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics
s: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics taught by writing Scheme programs, in the spirit of SICP; also free online.
w: HN SICP fans recommend it for mathematics and mechanics taught through code, calling it a good read for programmers and an example of Lisp as a language for developing math. Many have not read it cover to cover.
ab: For programmers who want classical mechanics through code
Requires physics and calculus background
Free online from MIT Press

q.t: The struct and interpretation of classical mechanics is a good one.

t: All Quiet on the Western Front
s: Remarque's 1929 novel of a young German soldier's experience in the trenches of World War I.
w: HN readers cite it as a book that showed the suffering of war and shattered a naive view of right and wrong. Some read it in school, others on a classic book club.
ab: For readers wanting an unvarnished WWI soldier's view
Short, heavy and sad
Several translations; the 1929 English translation is classic

q.t: All Quiet really shows the suffering of war.

s: Ryan Holiday draws on history and philosophy to show how ego at each stage of success or failure undermines work and relationships.
w: HN readers recommend it as a growth-spurring book on how ego gets in the way, including as advice for coping with resentment. One quit after 10 percent.
ab: For people dealing with ambition, setbacks or office politics
Stoic-leaning, built on anecdotes
Some find it repetitive, per HN

q.t: I really enjoyed this one and I will read it again.

t: Lions' Commentary on UNIX 6th Edition, with Source Code
s: A line-by-line commentary on the Sixth Edition Unix kernel, bundled with its source code.
w: Commenters call it still the best resource for understanding the basic concepts behind UNIX. It is the companion people suggest alongside xv6 for studying a small, readable kernel.
ab: For readers who want to study a real, small kernel line by line
Includes the V6 source code alongside the commentary
Covers PDP-11 era Unix, far from modern Linux

q.t: Lions' Commentary on UNIX is still the best resource out there

t: Ruby Under a Microscope: An Illustrated Guide to Ruby Internals
s: An illustrated tour of how Ruby's MRI interpreter works inside, covering parsing, compilation to bytecode, objects, garbage collection and more.
w: Suggested to anyone wanting to understand how Ruby works. Commenters like that it is approachable and points to the relevant MRI source code.
ab: For Rubyists curious about interpreter internals
Written for older Ruby versions; details have changed
Accessible even without a CS background

q.t: It gives a nice overview of the internals of MRI.

s: University textbook covering processes, scheduling, concurrency, memory management, file systems and protection in modern operating systems.
w: Recommended as a more thorough alternative to Tanenbaum, especially for concurrency, and listed among core texts for kernel work.
ab: For students learning how operating systems work
Strong on concurrency and core OS theory
Textbook style; best paired with hands-on kernel code

q.t: I personally recommend the book by Silberschatz

t: Designing Your Life: How to Build a Well-Lived, Joyful Life
s: Stanford design professors apply design thinking to career and life decisions, with exercises such as prototyping new paths.
w: Recommended to people considering a career change; commenters like its approach of small explorations and talking to people in other roles.
ab: For people weighing a career change
Includes practical exercises
Self-help format

q.t: It's based on a Stanford course of a similar name, and is an excellent read.

t: The Machine That Changed the World: The Story of Lean Production
by: James P. Womack, Daniel T. Jones
s: The MIT study that introduced lean production, documenting how Toyota's methods outperformed Western car makers.
w: HN commenters recommend it as the introduction to lean manufacturing and how it developed at Toyota, ahead of more hands-on books.
ab: For readers who want to understand lean origins
Based on a large auto-industry study
Research is from the 1990s

q.t: The first in the list below is a wonderful introduction to how lean manufacturing principles evolved at Toyota over decades.

s: A popular explanation of superstring theory and the search for a unified theory of physics.
w: A string-theory introduction for general readers; HN readers name it in physics recommendation lists, though one says extra dimensions are hard to visualize.
ab: For curious readers new to string theory
Analogies and no heavy math
String theory is debated; some claims dated

t: Thinking in Bets: Making Smarter Decisions When You Don't Have All the Facts
s: Former poker player Annie Duke applies the logic of betting to decisions under uncertainty, separating decision quality from outcomes.
w: HN readers recommend it for thinking about decisions like a gambler. A commenter says it changed how they judge bad outcomes from good decisions.
ab: For people making decisions with incomplete information
Poker-derived framework for thinking about odds and results
Anecdotal in places; business readers may want more depth

q.t: Approaching situations from the perspective of a gambler and how to choose what to do when you don't know all the facts.

s: Damian Conway's guide to writing readable, maintainable Perl, with 256 coding guidelines on layout, naming, documentation and testing.
w: Perl programmers on HN cite it as the source of the community's style rules, which tools like Perl::Critic and Perl::Tidy are based on. One veteran calls it the best general programming book they've read.
ab: For Perl developers who want a consistent coding style
Guidelines on layout, documentation, regexes and testing; relevant to other languages too
Published in 2005; some advice predates modern Perl

q.t: is the best general programming book I have ever read.

s: Octavia Butler's 1993 dystopian novel following a young woman in a collapsing near-future California who founds a new belief system.
w: HN readers put it on lists of books to go into blind and say it shaped their values. Often paired with its sequel, Parable of the Talents.
ab: For readers of dystopian and near-future science fiction
First of the Parable series
Bleak and violent themes

q.t: it helped change and focus my values around extending the story of life on earth

s: Salinger's 1961 book of two linked stories about Franny and her brother Zooey, members of the Glass family, and their search for spiritual meaning.
w: HN readers re-read it for the long conversations and the characters' attitudes, and one credits it with introducing them to the Stoics and Zen. It has little plot, so it's about the talk.
ab: For readers who like dialogue-driven literary fiction
Little plot; the conversations carry it
Part of Salinger's Glass family stories

q.t: I love the conversations and the attitude of the characters.

s: Schrödinger's 1944 lectures asking how physics can explain the living cell, anticipating the genetic code before DNA's structure was known.
w: Commenters call it a mind-changing read: reasoning from first principles, Schrödinger predicted properties of the genetic material and inspired a generation of physicists to move into biology.
ab: For physics-minded readers curious about biology
Short classic, often bundled with Mind and Matter
Some details are outdated after DNA discovery

q.t: Just using pure reason and inference he not only made accurate predictions about DNA

s: A rigorous treatment of generic programming that builds algorithms from mathematical foundations, using a small subset of C++.
w: HN readers praise it as a mathematically grounded foundation for software engineering, mapping abstract algebra onto C++ code, from the designer of the STL.
ab: For experienced programmers who like math and precise reasoning
Derives algorithms from algebraic concepts in a small C++ subset
Dense and terse; expect to work through it slowly

q.t: It's the first and only rigorous foundation of software engineering that I've seen.

s: An intuition-first DSP textbook covering filters, FFTs and sampling with minimal math.
w: Called an even better introduction than online tutorials and one reader's all-time favorite DSP book.
ab: For engineers and hobbyists new to DSP
Intuitive rather than proof-heavy
Includes practical tricks

q.t: my all-time favorite book about DSP

s: Textbook on the TCP/IP protocol suite and how Internet protocols work and are implemented.
w: Recommended for anyone writing a TCP/IP stack, praised as more readable and coherent than Stevens.
ab: For learning TCP/IP in depth
Useful for building a stack
Textbook style

q.t: always found Comer's books more readable and more coherent than Stevens

t: Data Mining: Practical Machine Learning Tools and Techniques
s: A practical textbook on machine learning and data mining techniques, built around the Weka toolkit.
w: Recommended as a hands-on first book for data mining and machine learning, pairing with the free Weka tool. A later commenter calls it a popular way to learn ML with Weka.
ab: For beginners who want hands-on ML using Weka
Covers classic data mining algorithms and evaluation
This 2005 edition is old; later editions exist

q.t: I recommend starting with weka and this great book:

s: William Gibson's 1988 cyberpunk novel, the third in the Sprawl trilogy, weaving together several characters around an AI-driven plot.
w: HN readers mention it as the end of Gibson's Sprawl trilogy, calling the trilogy taut, awesome writing and perfection. It is nearly always recommended alongside Neuromancer and Count Zero.
ab: For readers who have read Neuromancer and Count Zero
Cyberpunk with several interleaved storylines
Best read in order; the first book is the easier entry

q.t: The trilogy of Neuromancer, Burning Chrome, and Mona Lisa Overdrive is still my favorite work of fiction

t: A Little History of the World
s: A short, readable world history written for young readers by the author of The Story of Art.
w: HN readers say they could not put it down and recommend it as a gift for kids and a good family audiobook. One calls it the best history book that also covers religion.
ab: For kids, families and adults wanting an easy world history
Short chapters in a storytelling voice
Eurocentric 1930s framing; newer edition available

q.t: I've never been too enthusiastic about History in general, but I couldn't put this book down until finished.

t: This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate
s: Investigative-journalist argument that climate change cannot be solved within the current market-driven economic system and requires a political and economic overhaul.
w: Commenters bring it up whenever climate and capitalism collide, praising it as well written and as an alternative view of how the world is run. Even skeptics treat it as the standard statement of that thesis.
ab: For readers wanting the left-leaning case on climate policy failure
Reported, narrative style rather than technical or scientific
HN calls it liberal and one-sided; some agree only in principle

q.t: It's a very well-written, liberal book on climate policy failures written by an investigative journalist.

t: Made in Japan: Akio Morita and Sony
s: Memoir by Sony co-founder Akio Morita about building the company from a postwar Tokyo workshop into a global electronics brand.
w: HN readers list it among their favorite business autobiographies and as a motivating story of people doing hard things. They like the engineer-founder perspective on postwar Japan and Sony's rise.
ab: For readers interested in hardware companies, founders, and Japanese business history
First-person story of Sony from its postwar beginnings
Written in the 1980s, so no modern Sony chapters

q.t: Made in Japan had a profound impact on me

t: Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge, and the Teachings of Plants
s: Essays by botanist and Potawatomi writer Robin Wall Kimmerer that combine plant science with Indigenous teachings on reciprocity and our relationship to the natural world.
w: HN readers name it as a best book of the year, saying it introduced them to ideas like reciprocity and the Three Sisters. Recommended to gardeners, parents, and people curious about Native American perspectives.
ab: For gardeners, nature lovers, and readers curious about Indigenous thought
Reflective essays that mix botany with personal stories
More lyrical and spiritual than a typical science book

q.t: If you have kids, an interest in gardening, or a curiosity about Native American culture

t: Master of the Senate: The Years of Lyndon Johnson
s: Third volume of Caro's Lyndon Johnson biography, covering his Senate years from 1949 to 1960 and how the Senate worked.
w: HN readers call it among the best books they have read, praising Caro's detail on Johnson, the Senate, and American politics. One commenter finished it and wanted to read it again right away.
ab: For readers who like political history and long biography
Third in the LBJ series, but readable on its own
Very long; plan for weeks of reading

q.t: It was so good I'm already ready to read it again.

s: Lem's 1964 nonfiction book of essays that speculate on technology and the future of civilization, from artificial intelligence and virtual reality to evolution.
w: HN readers call it among the most important books they read, a prescient work on technology despite its age. It is often recommended together with Lem's fiction.
ab: For readers interested in futurism, technology, and philosophy
Essayistic and dense, not a novel
Some of its science is dated, and it can be hard going

q.t: Among the most important books for me was Summa technologiae by Stanislaw Lem

s: Kazantzakis's 1946 novel about a scholarly narrator who meets the exuberant Alexis Zorba in Crete, and what Zorba teaches him about living fully.
w: HN readers recommend it as a book that makes you think about how to spend your days and appreciate what you have. It looks light but carries real wisdom.
ab: For readers of philosophical literary fiction
Appears light but takes on big questions
Translated; wording varies by edition

q.t: an enjoyable, seemingly light read but a beautiful contrast of intellectual understanding

t: Darwin's Dangerous Idea: Evolution and the Meanings of Life
s: Dennett's argument that Darwinian natural selection is a universal algorithm that explains design, minds, and morality without any need for a designer.
w: HN readers call it life-changing, explaining how complex design and the mind can come from simple rules without a designer. One calls it one of the two most important books they have read.
ab: For readers interested in evolution, consciousness, and naturalist philosophy
Argues a strong atheist-leaning naturalist position
Long and dense in places

q.t: one of the two most important (IMHO, of course) books I've read

s: An 1889 comic novel about three friends and a dog on a boating holiday up the Thames.
w: HN readers hold it up as an uplifting, laugh-out-loud classic that turns ordinary vexations into comedy, and one worth rereading.
ab: For readers who like Victorian British humor
Free on Project Gutenberg
Some period references will be lost on modern readers

q.t: How he squeezed out stomack-aching laughter out of real events

s: Mitchel Resnick shows how decentralized systems and emergent behavior can be explored with StarLogo, a parallel version of Logo.
w: HN readers love it for building intuition about decentralized systems and emergence. It's recommended on emergent AI and Logo programming threads.
ab: For readers interested in emergence, simulations and education
Uses StarLogo, a Logo dialect
Mid-1990s book, but ideas still hold

q.t: uses a parallelized version of logo to explore ideas about decentralized systems and is really excellent

s: A 1971 science fiction novel in which a man's dreams can rewrite reality, and his psychiatrist tries to exploit that.
w: Recommended in several Ask HN fiction and sci-fi threads, usually alongside Le Guin's other novels. One commenter says it showed there are more ways of knowing than a scientific mind assumes.
ab: For readers who like idea-driven, philosophical sci-fi
Short novel from a widely admired author
Often paired with The Left Hand of Darkness and The Dispossessed

q.t: Both taught me there are more ways of knowing (and being) than my scientific brain had realized.

s: A near-future biopunk novel set in a Thailand reshaped by energy scarcity and genetic engineering corporations.
w: HN sci-fi fans call it a harsh, plausible near-future with compassion and redemption. It shows up in several favorite-sci-fi lists.
ab: For readers who like grim, realistic near-future sci-fi.
Won Hugo and Nebula awards.
Dark, cruel tone.

q.t: Harsh, hot, cruel, realistic and futuristic. I'm enjoying it a lot.

t: How the Internet Happened: From Netscape to the iPhone
s: A narrative history of the consumer internet from the Netscape IPO through the dot-com era to the smartphone.
w: Readers enjoyed it and use it to frame the open web versus centralized online services. It is a go-to history for the internet's commercial era.
ab: For readers who want the business story of the web
Anecdote-driven and easy to read
Covers mainly 1990s to 2010s US internet scene

q.t: Really enjoyed this read!

s: Self-teaching mathematics textbook for engineering students that covers algebra to calculus through frames of worked examples and exercises.
w: HN readers call it the best math book for self-study and for engineers, praising how many worked examples and exercises it has. Several used it from first year to a master's degree.
ab: For self-learners and engineering students needing practical maths
Hundreds of worked examples and exercises
Older style; coverage is applied, not theoretical

q.t: The best book, because it is full of worked examples and exercises, is K.A Stroud Engineering Mathematics

s: Ellison's 1952 novel about an unnamed Black narrator's search for identity in the United States, from the South to Harlem.
w: HN readers include it in favorite-fiction lists and credit it as a book that changed them, praising the prose and its sharply observed scenes.
ab: For readers of classic American literature
Rich prose and vivid scenes
Heavy themes of race and identity; dense in places

q.t: I really enjoyed the writing, among other things

t: Debugging Teams: Better Productivity through Collaboration
s: Book from two Google engineers on working in and leading software teams, including the Humility-Respect-Trust principles.
w: HN readers recommend it as a favorite book for team success and for understanding how to work as part of a software team. The HRT idea comes up in code-review tone threads.
ab: For engineers, tech leads and new managers
Covers team culture and collaboration
Reads like Google-engineer advice

q.t: For general success of teams, this is my favorite book

t: The Years of Rice and Salt
s: An alternate-history novel in which the Black Death kills most Europeans and other civilizations shape the world.
w: HN readers recommend it as a great alternate history that shows how arbitrary the world as we know it is.
ab: For alternate history fans.
Spans centuries of invented history.
Slow, sweeping structure.

q.t: Robinson's "The Years of Rice and Salt" is great

s: First book of the LitRPG series in which a man and his ex-girlfriend's cat are dropped into a deadly dungeon game show after Earth is destroyed.
w: A big recent HN favorite: funny, addictive, and especially good as an audiobook. One reader got bored in the denser third book.
ab: Dark comedy LitRPG series
Audiobook narration widely praised
Gets denser; one reader stalled mid-series

q.t: Carl was hilarious, can’t wait for the final books

s: George Eliot's 1871 novel of provincial English life, following the marriages, ambitions and failures of several interlinked residents of a fictional town.
w: HN readers call it their favorite classic and the best book they have read, and read it aloud with partners. One says it has everything; another does not find it life-changing but still recommends it.
ab: For readers up for a long, dense Victorian classic
Slow, character-driven; rewards patience
Public-domain editions are cheap and plentiful

q.t: Middlemarch is my favorite classic.

s: A 14-inch business laptop from 2011 with a classic ThinkPad keyboard, widely available used.
w: Cheap on the used market, tough, easy to upgrade and well supported by Linux. HN buyers on a budget treat it as the sensible hacker laptop, with the usual ThinkPad keyboard.
ab: For budget buyers wanting a repairable used Linux laptop
Classic keyboard, swappable battery, mSATA and RAM upgrades
Old hardware: i5 model has weak battery life, no IPS

q.t: the T420s/X220s are pretty cheap ($250-400USD depending on configuration) and still very good machines

t: Wherever You Go, There You Are
s: A guide to mindfulness meditation in everyday life.
w: Recommended as secular mindfulness.
ab: Secular
Short
Gentle

q.t: He is my favorite author when it comes to meditation because he focus on mindfulness and not Buddhism

t: Immune: A Journey into the Mysterious System That Keeps You Alive
s: An illustrated popular science explanation of how the immune system works, by the founder of the Kurzgesagt channel.
w: HN readers call it the best pop-sci book they read in a given year. It makes a complicated biological system understandable, even for people who never clicked with biology.
ab: For lay readers curious about immunology
Clear explanations in a friendly, visual style
Popular science level, not a textbook

q.t: Best pop-sci book I've read in a while.

s: A 13-inch privacy-focused Linux laptop with hardware kill switches for camera, microphone and wireless, built around libre-friendly firmware and drivers.
w: HN privacy and open-source folks point to it as the laptop that actually puts freedom first, with kill switches and Qubes-friendly hardware. Owners say it works well, but it's pricey for the specs.
ab: For privacy-minded Linux users who want hardware kill switches
Open firmware and libre drivers where feasible; Qubes-oriented design
Expensive for the internals; you're paying to support the mission

q.t: Purism's laptop seems to get good battery life at a light weight, comparable to MBP in build quality

s: Ellul's critique of technique as an autonomous force shaping modern society.
w: HN cites it as the foundational critique of technology and globalization; the recommender warns it's not an easy read.
ab: For readers interested in philosophy of technology
Dense and demanding
1964 text; framework still discussed

q.t: It's not an easy read, the sort of book where you take lots of notes and then learn from the notes

s: A strength-training book arguing for brief, high-intensity workouts, about 12 minutes a week, based on exercise research.
w: HN fitness skeptics recommend it as research-based alternative to long gym routines. One commenter calls it the most interesting and useful fitness resource found.
