ab: For people wanting minimal time-efficient strength training
Explains physiology behind high-intensity training
Contrarian claims; not everyone agrees

q.t: This is, by far, the most interesting and useful resource I have found when it comes to fitness:

t: Blondie24: Playing at the Edge of AI
s: The story of how Fogel and a graduate student evolved a neural-network checkers program that learned by playing online under the name Blondie24.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a fun, quick read about neuroevolution before deep learning. They enjoy the story of the Blondie24 persona and note the idea is older than people think.
ab: For readers curious about early evolutionary AI and game-playing
Popular-science style; no AI background needed
Dated technically, but the story holds up

q.t: It's a really fast read even if you have no experience in AI.

s: A C++ guide to game AI techniques including state machines, steering behaviors, pathfinding, fuzzy logic and goal-driven agents, with working example code.
w: HN commenters name it the go-to starting point for game AI. They like the concrete examples, such as the soccer simulation, and call it a great introduction to the main techniques.
ab: For game programmers new to AI techniques
Practical C++ examples, state machines and goal-driven behavior
Pre-dates behavior trees; some content is dated

q.t: If you are developing AI for games, then Programming Game AI By Example by Mat Buckland

t: Programming Ruby: The Pragmatic Programmer's Guide (the Pickaxe book)
s: The standard reference and tutorial for the Ruby language, known as the Pickaxe book, with a tutorial section and a language reference.
w: HN's default answer for learning Ruby, often named alongside Rails guides and tutorials. One commenter says its spiral approach to teaching stayed with them.
ab: For programmers learning Ruby, or wanting a reference
Tutorial plus complete library reference
Check the edition against your Ruby version

q.t: Try 'Programming Ruby' (aka 'the Pickaxe book')

t: Unit Testing: Principles, Practices, and Patterns
s: Manning book on writing good unit tests, covering the goals of testing, test quality, mocks, and when and how much to test.
w: HN commenters call it the best book on unit testing, backed by evidence. It is recommended by experienced developers, including in TDD debates.
ab: For developers who want a principled view of testing
Covers mocks, test design and code types
Opinionated about mocks and TDD

q.t: it's the best book on the subject and is presenting the matter with good evidence.

s: A concise overview of modern C++ by its creator, covering the language and standard library in a few hundred pages.
w: Recommended as the short route to modern C++ for people who already program. One commenter used it after years of writing C-with-classes.
ab: For programmers who know another language and want modern C++
Short tour of language and standard library
Fast-paced and not a beginner tutorial

q.t: Just get the "Tour of C++" from Bjarne.

s: The third and final novel of Cixin Liu's Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy, following The Three-Body Problem and The Dark Forest.
w: HN readers recommend the whole trilogy as big-idea space opera that explores human nature and time on a cosmic scale. Read it after the first two books.
ab: For finishing the Three-Body trilogy
Huge scale, hard science, and bleak ideas
Not standalone; start with The Three-Body Problem

q.t: Expanded my perception of life, death, love, time and our potential purpose, via some very well written fiction

t: Super Thinking: The Big Book of Mental Models
s: A catalog of mental models across fields.
w: Recommended as a cheaper, shorter alternative to Farnam Street's series.
ab: For beginners to mental models
Short entries
Broad

q.t: Written by the duckduckgo folks

t: UNIX Network Programming, Volume 1: The Sockets Networking API
by: W. Richard Stevens, Bill Fenner, et al.
s: The standard reference on writing networked programs with the sockets API on Unix systems, in C.
w: Repeatedly named as the book to read for network programming, often alongside Advanced Programming in the Unix Environment. People pair it with the HTTP spec and Wireshark experiments.
ab: For C programmers writing servers and network clients
Covers sockets, I/O models and protocol details in depth
Large and dense; the 3rd edition dates from 2003

q.t: As others have suggested, read W. Richard Steven's book

s: A readable history of the great economic thinkers, from Adam Smith to Keynes, with their biographies and core ideas.
w: Repeatedly named as the friendly way into economics: it tells the story of the field through its personalities and schools of thought rather than equations.
ab: For readers new to economics who want ideas through stories
Biographical sketches plus summaries of each school of thought
A history of ideas, not a modern textbook

q.t: describes the high points of their theories along with some biographical detail, in a very engaging style.

s: A collectible trading card game where players build decks of spells and creatures and duel one another.
w: HN players call it strategic, like poker meets chess, and some say it teaches programming ideas like state, conditionals, and stacks. The barrier to entry and ongoing spending can be high.
ab: For strategy-minded players, including programmers
Deep rules; high barrier to entry
Collectible format means ongoing cost

q.t: I have strong personal belief that the trading card game Magic: The Gathering is a perfect introduction to programming

t: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
s: The first novel of the Millennium trilogy: a journalist and a hacker investigate a decades-old disappearance in a wealthy Swedish family.
w: HN readers list it among favorite re-reads and page-turners, with one commenter saying the trilogy pulled them toward computing. It is seen as great entertainment rather than deep literature.
ab: Fast-paced Swedish crime thriller with a hacker heroine.
First of three Millennium books, easy to burn through.
One commenter notes it is entertaining but not profound.

q.t: It was good entertainment that challenged some of my notions about human nature.

s: Albert Camus's 1947 novel about an Algerian city quarantined during an outbreak of plague, and how its residents respond.
w: HN readers revisit it in times of crisis and call it a series of character studies in how people respond to the same pressure. For some it was a first look at existentialism.
ab: For readers of existentialist and philosophical fiction
A quarantined city in a plague, told through several characters
Slow and allegorical; one reader did not enjoy it but valued it

q.t: I've found all three very enjoyable and unexpectedly applicable to real life for being philosophical texts.

s: A light 14-inch ThinkPad from 2014 with an optional 1080p IPS screen and a swappable external battery.
w: HN Linux users praise its light weight, 1080p panel and very long battery life with the 6-cell. The most-cited flaw is the clickpad trackpad.
ab: For used-laptop buyers wanting a light Linux ThinkPad
Optional 1080p IPS, internal plus external battery
Trackpad is poor; aging hardware

q.t: I love my t440s. With 6-cell battery I can survive for almost 20 hours of continuous work on single charge

s: The central religious text of Christianity, in many translations and editions.
w: HN commenters name it as the book that most influenced them, valued for its insight into human nature and as the foundation of Western culture, even setting aside faith.
ab: Pick a translation; the ESV is one popular edition.
Praised for cultural and literary weight regardless of belief.
Several readers cite it as life-changing.

q.t: Even without the religious aspects, it's an incredible document.

t: Stiff: The Curious Lives of Human Cadavers
s: A humorous popular science book about what happens to human bodies after death, from dissection to crash tests.
w: Cited across threads for its entertaining, informative chapters, including on incapacitation after gunshots and cadaver use in medical practice.
ab: For readers who like quirky popular science
Funny and informative
Graphic subject matter

q.t: Stiff (an amazing book, by the way)

s: A line of very light Windows laptops with large screens and big batteries, in 14 to 17-inch sizes.
w: HN buyers praise its feather weight, big screen and long battery life, with some running Fedora on it. Often named as the lightweight non-Mac competitor.
ab: For developers wanting a light laptop with a big screen
Long battery life, numpad on larger models
Lightweight build; check Linux compatibility

q.t: That's why the LG Gram 17inch 2020 is the best laptop I've owned.

t: About Face: The Essentials of Interaction Design
by: Alan Cooper, Robert Reimann et al.
s: A long-running reference on interaction design that covers goal-directed design, personas and interface patterns.
w: Recommended in threads on UI design; one commenter cites its advice to avoid modal questions and let users undo later.
ab: For developers and designers working on software interfaces
Broad and reference-like
Parts feel dated

q.t: I have yet to read it, but I've seen good opinions on 'About face' in some threads on the topic

s: A lighthearted comedy about a programmer who discovers reality is code and uses it to travel to medieval England as a wizard.
w: HN readers recommend it as a fun, lighthearted read, especially for programmers since magic is just programming. It is the first of the Magic 2.0 series.
ab: For programmers who like funny sci-fi
First of the Magic 2.0 series
Light and silly rather than deep

q.t: I highly recommend Off to be the Wizard

t: Hydrofarm Autopilot Desktop CO2 Monitor and Logger
s: A desktop carbon dioxide monitor with a display and data logging, originally made for greenhouse growers.
w: HN's go-to affordable CO2 meter for tracking indoor air and ventilation. Commenters say it works well, is happy with it in homes, and shows readings change clearly as ventilation changes.
ab: For tracking indoor CO2 at home or the office
Logs readings over time
Greenhouse-oriented; accuracy may trail pricier meters

q.t: I got this model several months back and have been really happy with it

t: The Happiness Hypothesis: Finding Modern Truth in Ancient Wisdom
s: Jonathan Haidt tests ancient ideas about happiness and virtue against modern psychology, including his elephant-and-rider metaphor.
w: Recommended for combining philosophy and psychology, and for the rider-and-elephant picture of conscious and subconscious minds.
ab: For readers interested in happiness and moral psychology
Elephant and rider metaphor is widely cited
Some research has since been challenged

q.t: It intertwines philosophy and psychology while providing a lot of insight on how a life is well lived.

s: A collection of especially elegant proofs across number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics and graph theory, inspired by Paul Erdos.
w: Recommended as a collection of beautiful short proofs whose sections start accessibly and finish in deeper math.
ab: For math lovers who enjoy elegant proofs
Short self-contained chapters
Some chapters need real mathematical background

q.t: Stuffed with beautiful short proofs. Each section starts at a fairly basic level, but finishes with some fairly deep maths.

s: A guide to transitioning into new leadership roles.
w: Called the gold standard for job transitions.
ab: For new managers.
Frameworks.
Corporate.

q.t: I re-read it every time I change roles.

s: James Altucher's self-help and career book arguing that people should stop waiting for institutions to pick them and build their own paths.
w: HN commenters name it a life-changing book of their year, though one accuses a thread poster of using it for affiliate spam.
ab: For readers wanting an entrepreneurial self-help push
Altucher's personal and confessional style
Some HN readers dislike the self-promotion

t: The Wager: A Tale of Shipwreck, Mutiny and Murder
s: A narrative history of HMS Wager's 18th-century shipwreck off Patagonia and the mutiny and conflicting accounts that followed.
w: HN readers list it as a favorite of their year for the gripping story and strong research. A reader who liked Killers of the Flower Moon found it good, though slightly less so.
ab: For fans of narrative nonfiction and exploration history
Built from conflicting survivor accounts
Brutal subject matter

q.t: It's very well researched and pieced together from conflicting accounts.

s: Atwood's dystopian novel of a theocratic regime that forces fertile women into reproductive servitude.
w: A recurring entry in HN reading lists, called a classic, and also picked when people deliberately read more female authors. One reader noted it is spare and unsettling.
ab: For readers of dystopian fiction
Lean prose, dark and unsettling subject matter
Also a long-running TV series

q.t: The Handmaid's Tale by Margaret Atwood - A classic, glad to finally read it.

t: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time
s: A mystery novel narrated by a teenage boy with autism who investigates a neighbor's dead dog.
w: A frequent favorite in HN reading threads, where people call it creative and engaging. It is often listed among best novels read in a year.
ab: For readers who like voice-driven literary mysteries
Short, quick read with a distinctive narrator
Over 20 years old; its portrayal of autism is debated

q.t: I also enjoyed The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time. It was very creative.

t: Fluent Python: Clear, Concise, and Effective Programming
s: An O'Reilly book for experienced programmers that explains Python's idioms and advanced features, such as data model, decorators and concurrency.
w: HN's go-to suggestion for programmers who know Python and want to understand it deeply, mentioned beside Effective Java as the kind of language book worth reading cover to cover.
ab: For intermediate programmers moving to idiomatic Python
Covers the data model, generators, concurrency and more
This is the first edition; a newer edition covers newer Python

s: A guide to multithreaded programming in modern C++, covering the C++11 and later memory model, threads, atomics and lock-free design.
w: C++ programmers recommend it as the book for understanding the standard memory model and practical multithreading, and list it in the best C++ book recommendations.
ab: For C++ developers writing concurrent code
Written by a Boost.Thread maintainer
Dense; assumes solid C++ knowledge

q.t: found it very helpful in understanding these concepts

t: The Man in the High Castle
s: Philip K. Dick's alternate-history novel set in a United States ruled by the victorious Axis powers after World War II.
w: HN readers regularly name it in sci-fi favorites and re-read lists next to Ubik and Scanner Darkly. One reader found it well written but wanted a bigger payoff.
ab: Classic alternate-history sci-fi from a major author.
Often paired with Dick's Ubik in recommendations.
Ending may feel unresolved.

q.t: The man in the high castle and Ubik by Philip K. Dick. They're next on my wishlist

s: A cognitive scientist explains how the mind learns and what it means for teaching, in nine principles.
w: Recommended by readers for explaining how learning and memory work and why background knowledge matters. Commenters call it a good, careful popular science book on education.
ab: For teachers, parents and self-learners
Nine cognitive principles for how learning works
Written for a general audience, not a research text

q.t: it's very much worth a read if you're at all interested in the topic

s: A book on compiling functional languages using continuation-passing style, based on the Standard ML of New Jersey compiler.
w: Recommended to people building compilers for functional languages, and listed among favorite compiler books alongside Engineering a Compiler and Appel's Modern Compiler Implementation in ML.
ab: For compiler writers targeting functional languages
Based on the SML/NJ compiler
1992 text; newer techniques have emerged

q.t: Compiling with Continuations is a fantastic book

t: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
s: A short case for low-cost index fund investing, written by the founder of Vanguard.
w: The go-to recommendation when HN argues index funds beat active management. Cited next to Buffett's famous hedge fund bet as the book for ordinary investors.
ab: For beginners wanting a simple long-term investing approach
Argues for low-cost, diversified index funds
US-centric; this is general reading, not financial advice

q.t: I'd also recommend The Little Book of Common Sense Investing

t: Secrets of Mental Math: The Mathemagician's Guide to Lightning Calculation and Amazing Math Tricks
s: A guide to mental arithmetic tricks, from squaring numbers to fast multiplication, by a mathematician and magician.
w: The standard HN answer when a thread turns to squaring numbers or casting out nines. Commenters recommend it as fun and wish schools taught this material.
ab: For anyone who wants faster mental arithmetic
Teaches methods with practice problems
Mostly tricks and techniques, not deep math

q.t: there are a couple of fun mental math books I can recommend

t: The Artist's Way: A Spiritual Path to Higher Creativity
s: A twelve-week program of exercises, including morning pages, to unblock creativity.
w: Suggested to people stuck in a rut as a way to get creative again.
ab: For creative blocks
Weekly exercises
Spiritual language puts some off

t: Working Backwards: Insights, Stories, and Secrets from Inside Amazon
s: Two former Amazon executives describe the company's practices, including written narratives, the PR/FAQ and single-threaded leadership.
w: Cited as the book behind Amazon's 'working backwards' method, such as writing a fake press release first to clarify what matters.
ab: For product leaders curious about Amazon's internal process
Covers PR/FAQ, narratives and bar raisers
Written by insiders, so it is flattering

q.t: Gives overview of Amazon’s core practices that made them successful.

s: James Joyce's 1914 collection of fifteen short stories about ordinary life in Dublin.
w: HN readers name it among books that changed their thinking, and the most approachable Joyce, with each story built around a moment of epiphany.
ab: For readers new to Joyce
Short stories, readable in pieces
Early 1900s Irish setting

q.t: Another from this year was The Dubliners, collection of short stories from James Joyce.

t: Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow
s: A practical introduction to machine learning and deep learning using Scikit-Learn, Keras and TensorFlow, with code examples throughout.
w: HN readers recommend it as the standard starter book for machine learning, and note the second edition was rewritten for TensorFlow 2. Cited when beginners ask how to get started.
ab: For programmers who want a code-first path into ML and deep learning
Covers classical ML and neural networks
TensorFlow-centric; frameworks evolve quickly

q.t: One good starter book is Hands-On ML by Aurelien Geron

t: The Art of the Start: The Time-Tested, Battle-Hardened Guide for Anyone Starting Anything
s: Guy Kawasaki's practical guide to launching a startup, covering mantras, pitching, fundraising, hiring and marketing.
w: HN commenters list it among the best startup books for hackers. One says it motivated them to put it down and get back to work.
ab: For first-time founders who want a short, practical playbook
Covers pitching, bootstrapping and recruiting
Written in 2004; some advice predates modern startup tooling

q.t: because every time I picked it up, it motivated me to put it down and get back to work

t: Where Mathematics Comes From: How the Embodied Mind Brings Mathematics into Being
s: Cognitive scientists argue that mathematical ideas arise from embodied human experience and conceptual metaphor, and analyze concepts like infinity and sets.
w: HN commenters recommend it before diving into math textbooks and call it absolutely fascinating, citing a Bret Victor recommendation. It is also cited in discussions of embodied cognition, though some mathematicians reject the thesis.
ab: For readers curious about the cognitive roots of mathematics
Covers infinity, sets, limits and calculus through metaphor
Controversial among mathematicians; not a math textbook

q.t: Before digging into the various books others have suggested, you would do well to read

s: Investigation into tax havens, offshore banking and how they distort the global economy.
w: Recommended to learn how corporations use tax havens and what damage they do; one reader found it hard to put down.
ab: For readers interested in tax havens
Journalistic; critical tone
Somewhat bleak

q.t: I can thoroughly recommend Nicholas Shaxon's book, Treasure Islands

t: The Horse, the Wheel, and Language
s: An archaeological account of the Proto-Indo-European steppe origins of Indo-European languages and Bronze Age riders.
w: Named as the best accessible archaeology reference on the subject, with the caveat that genetics has since moved on.
ab: For readers into archaeology and linguistics
Accessible but detailed
Some findings superseded by genetics

q.t: The best accessible archaeology reference I can recommend

t: Lying for Money: How Legendary Frauds Reveal the Workings of the World
s: A tour of famous frauds, grouped by type, showing how fraud works and what it reveals about trust in finance and business.
w: HN readers recommend it for anyone interested in fraud and finance. Commenters tie crypto collapses to patterns it describes going back centuries, and it inspired a popular essay on the optimal amount of fraud.
ab: For readers curious about fraud, finance and trust
Case studies from long firm frauds to rogue traders
Anecdotal; not a how-to

q.t: If you’re interested in fraud and finance, I highly recommend this book

t: Never Lost Again: The Google Mapping Revolution That Sparked New Industries and Augmented Our Reality
s: A first-hand account of Keyhole, Google Earth and Google Maps by one of the Keyhole founders.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a good account of the Keyhole to Google Earth to Google Maps story, calling it a fantastic read about the pre-Maps era.
ab: For readers interested in Google Maps, mapping tech and startup history
Written by one of Keyhole's founders
Insider perspective; may lean favorable to its own story

q.t: which is a fantastic read if you want to learn more about the pre-google-maps and google earth days

s: A negotiation book from Jim Camp's training firm that teaches counterintuitive tactics, starting with letting the other side say no.
w: Recommended for its actionable advice that contradicts conventional negotiation wisdom. Commenters like the focus on questions and not making assumptions.
ab: For people who negotiate with customers, vendors or employers
Actionable advice built on questions and not making assumptions
Counterintuitive; may feel unnatural at first

q.t: Very actionable advice about using interrogative led questions and avoiding the pitfalls of making assumptions during negotiations.

t: Manias, Panics, and Crashes: A History of Financial Crises
s: A history of bubbles and financial crises over several centuries, showing a recurring pattern of speculation and collapse.
w: Cited in bubble and crash threads as authoritative on how leverage turns downturns into crashes. Commenters say bubbles are common and well documented.
ab: For readers who want historical context on financial crises
Covers recurring boom-bust patterns
Academic-leaning and dense

q.t: if you believe Kindleberger (and you should)

s: O'Reilly guide to computer vision with the OpenCV library by its creator.
w: HN readers recommend it as a well-written, wide-ranging intro to computer vision with OpenCV.
ab: For programmers starting with computer vision
Covers a wide range of topics
Older OpenCV APIs

q.t: O'Reilly "Learning OpenCV" is very well written and covers a wide range of topics.

s: Drucker's classic HBR essay on knowing your strengths, values and how you work.
w: HN readers recommend it for deciding how to handle a job.
ab: For career thinkers
Short
Classic

q.t: Have a look at Peter Drucker's classic "Managing Oneself"

s: A biography of General Douglas MacArthur covering his career from World War I through Korea and the occupation of Japan.
w: Highly recommended as the story of a fascinating, brilliant man who is too little remembered today, with sharp coverage of postwar Japan.
ab: For readers of military and political history
Detailed and long
Manchester's admiration is evident

q.t: a great biography of Douglas MacArthur. I highly recommend it as the story of a fascinating and brilliant man

t: Grokking Simplicity: Taming Complex Software with Functional Thinking
s: A Manning book that teaches pragmatic functional thinking by separating code into data, calculations and actions to tame side effects.
w: Recommended for learning functional-core, imperative-shell style design without dogma; readers like the practical framing of data, computation and side effects.
ab: For working programmers new to functional ideas
Language-agnostic, uses JavaScript examples
Not dogmatic about purity

q.t: I can recommend Grokking Simplicity by Eric Normand.

t: Learning the vi and Vim Editors
s: O'Reilly's guide to the vi and Vim text editors, covering editing, ex commands, regular expressions and customization.
w: HN readers recommend it as the way to learn vi properly and credit it with teaching the depth of ex and vi commands. One says practice plus this book works.
ab: For beginners and intermediate users who want to learn vi and Vim systematically
Teaches classic vi/ex commands as well as Vim features
Reference-style; practice matters as much as reading

q.t: Practice, practice, practice. The ORA book will help.

s: A premium adjustable ergonomic office chair from Steelcase with a flexing back and seat, in V1 and V2 models.
w: HN chair-nerds often rank it above the Aeron for comfort, saying it ended their back pain. Many buy used or refurbished for a few hundred dollars; one owner had trouble getting warranty service.
ab: For people who sit all day and want back support
Highly adjustable; some prefer it to an Aeron
New is pricey; most HN owners bought used

q.t: An ergonomic chair (namely, the Steelcase Leap). I haven't had back pain since.

s: First novel of George R. R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire, a political fantasy about rival noble houses in the land of Westeros.
w: HN readers praise the grounded, low-magic world and call Martin a genius at worldbuilding. Commenters say the books are huge, and one gave up half-way through the first one.
ab: For readers who like political, gritty epic fantasy
Very long; the series remains unfinished
Mild, grounded fantasy with little magic

q.t: GRRM manages to create an alternate world that feels

t: Seiki SE39UY04 39-Inch 4K Ultra HD LED TV
s: A 39-inch 3840x2160 LED television from 2013 that was popular as a very cheap 4K computer monitor, limited to 30Hz over HDMI 1.4.
w: In 2013 it was the cheap way to get a huge 4K desktop at a fraction of the price of real 4K monitors, and a few developers used it daily despite the 30Hz limit.
ab: For budget 4K desktop experimenters, from the 2013 era
Large 39-inch panel with a low price for its time
Only 30Hz at 4K because of HDMI 1.4; early 4K tradeoffs

q.t: 4K is a substantial step forward from 3 or 4 1080p screens

s: Apple's slim Bluetooth aluminum keyboard, sold in numpad and compact versions over several generations.
w: HN users praise its form, key feel and tidy desk look, especially if you already live in the Apple ecosystem. A few note odd key placement but easily adjusted.
ab: For Mac users wanting a slim, tidy Bluetooth keyboard
Low-profile scissor keys, compact layout
Odd key placement for some; not mechanical

q.t: Apple wireless keyboard is great. Really good form and function.

s: Valve's handheld gaming PC running Linux-based SteamOS, able to play most of a Steam library on the go.
w: HN buyers love it for working through game backlogs while traveling and for being an open, tinkerable Linux machine rather than a locked console. It shows up in many favorite-purchase lists.
ab: For gamers who want portable PC games without a locked ecosystem
Runs Linux, modifiable hardware, big Steam library
Not every game runs; battery life varies by title

q.t: Fantastic for catching up on your gaming backlog when traveling.

s: A 12.5-inch 2015 ThinkPad ultraportable with a swappable battery system, good keyboard, and strong Linux compatibility.
w: HN users like it as a light, cheap, refurbished Linux development laptop with long battery life. One reports an aging unit with a worn battery and flaky touchpad.
ab: For developers wanting a light, used Linux laptop
Hot-swappable batteries give long runtime
Aging hardware; batteries wear out

q.t: I adore this laptop, it runs like a constant stream of freshly melted butter.

s: A 14-inch 2016 ThinkPad with quad-core processors, up to 32GB RAM, and extended batteries, often bought used.
w: HN users call it a fast, solid workhorse for software engineering and Linux, with decent battery life with the extended pack. A few miss the older X230's feel, and the fingerprint reader doesn't work on Linux.
ab: For developers wanting a used quad-core Linux laptop
Upgradeable RAM and SSD
Fingerprint reader unsupported on Linux; screen could be brighter

q.t: Could use a slightly brighter display but overall this machine is great!

s: A Dover textbook introducing groups, rings and fields with a gentle approach and many exercises.
w: Praised as accessible for self-study, with one reader calling it the best math book ever.
ab: For self-learners starting abstract algebra
Many exercises
One reader found it too wordy

q.t: This the best math book ever( I dislike math)

s: A textbook that teaches programming language concepts by building interpreters in Scheme for a series of small languages.
w: HN commenters cite it as the standard course text for understanding interpreters and language semantics. It is mentioned alongside The Little Schemer as a rigorous but rewarding route into how languages work.
ab: For readers who want to build interpreters and understand language design
Uses Scheme throughout; hands-on exercises
Dense and academic; not a casual read

q.t: They follow a lot of conventions that I find really useful for software development

t: Genius: The Life and Science of Richard Feynman
s: James Gleick's biography of physicist Richard Feynman, covering his work on quantum electrodynamics, the Manhattan Project and his personality.
w: The biography HN points to when Feynman comes up, called very interesting and cited as a source on his life and work.
ab: For fans of Feynman and the history of physics
Thorough biography with real physics content
Long and detailed

q.t: Gleick is also the author of a very interesting biography of Richard Feynman, the book Genius.

t: The Ego Tunnel: The Science of the Mind and the Myth of the Self
s: A philosopher uses neuroscience to argue the self is a model the brain builds rather than a thing.
w: Brought up in consciousness threads as an interesting blend of philosophy and 2010-era neuroscience on the feeling of self.
ab: For readers curious about consciousness
Philosophy with neuroscience
Speculative and dense

q.t: A related book that I found interesting is "The Ego Tunnel" by Thomas Metzinger

s: A series of novels by Charles Stross about a bureaucratic British secret agency defending against occult horrors unlocked by mathematics.
w: A go-to pick for tech and sysadmin readers: spy-thriller Lovecraftian horror with office-bureaucracy humor, recommended in several HN fiction threads.
ab: For readers who like Lovecraft with spies and bureaucratic jokes
Long running series; start at book one
Tone shifts darker in later books

q.t: Sort of Lovecraft meets James Bond meets Dilbert

t: Div, Grad, Curl, and All That: An Informal Text on Vector Calculus
s: A short, informal introduction to vector calculus built around electromagnetism examples.
w: Recommended to physics and EE students as the go-to book for understanding electromagnetism's math.
ab: For physics and EE students
Informal and intuition-first
Not rigorous enough for pure math readers

q.t: check out the book. it's great

t: A Thousand Brains: A New Theory of Intelligence
s: A theory of how the neocortex works.
w: Cited on reference frames.
ab: For AI and neuroscience fans
Speculative
Readable

q.t: An interesting theory as to why spatiality helps so much is outlined in Jeff Hawkins' "1000 brain theory"

s: A textbook on concurrent programming covering locks, wait-free and lock-free data structures, and correctness theory.
w: Recommended as the deep book on lock-free data structures, teaching you to think about concurrency in a structured way.
ab: For programmers going deep on concurrency
Theory with code
Java-based; dense

q.t: you owe it to yourself to get Herlihy and Shavit's

s: A puzzle book that introduces combinatory logic through riddles about talking birds, leading up to the lambda calculus.
w: HN commenters call it the best introduction to combinatory logic and a favorite book. The puzzles are fun, and the bird names are the source of combinator names such as the Thrush and the Kestrel.
ab: For programmers curious about combinators and lambda calculus
Playful puzzles that build up to real logic
Puzzles can be tough; you may not finish them all

q.t: It presents itself as a puzzle book that teaches combinatory logic along the way.

s: A hand-lettered, illustrated beginner's introduction to electronic components and building simple circuits.
w: HN's go-to first book for hobby electronics, recalled fondly from the Radio Shack era and recommended as the 'basic' starting point for newcomers.
ab: For total beginners who want to build circuits
Hand-drawn diagrams and simple breadboard-style projects
Decades old in spirit, but the fundamentals still hold

q.t: Back in the 80s, Forrest Mims was 'the guy' for hobby electronics books.

s: A math book for programmers covering proofs, polynomials, calculus, linear algebra and more, with code examples.
w: Suggested in math self-study threads, though one commenter warns that Amazon reviews were not particularly kind.
ab: For programmers wanting math maturity
Programmer-friendly examples
Mixed reviews on exposition

q.t: Also, take a look at A Programmer's Introduction to Mathematics by Jeremy Kun

s: A line of slim aluminum gaming laptops from Razer with high-end graphics.
w: HN developers cite the MacBook-like build quality and gaming-class specs, and some run it as a Linux dev laptop for CUDA. It tends to be the pick when gaming matters.
ab: For developers who also want serious gaming/GPU power
Aluminum unibody, high-end GPU
Gaming branding and price; ports and heat vary by year

q.t: Excellent build quality, aluminum unibody

s: A surreal Murakami novel following an advertising man's hunt for a mysterious sheep across Japan.
w: HN readers list it among their favorite fiction, with one saying it is hilarious and hard to summarize but a great read by their favorite author.
ab: For fans of surreal contemporary Japanese fiction
Funny, strange and plot-light
Mysterious ending; plot is hard to summarize

q.t: I really cannot summarize the plot, but it is such a good read. My favorite author.

s: Ken Kesey's 1964 epic novel of a stubborn logging family in Oregon during a strike.
w: Appears on HN lists of best and life-changing books, described as a rich, human story about what drives people, with a river as an unrelenting foe. Several are rereading it.
ab: For readers of long American literary novels
Rich, demanding story of a logging family
Long and dense; experimental narration

q.t: A very rich, very human story generally about what drives people, with a river as an unrelenting foe.

t: The Way of the Superior Man: A Spiritual Guide to Mastering the Challenges of Women, Work, and Sexual Desire
s: A self-help book on masculine purpose, relationships and sexuality, urging men to commit to a life mission and to be present in intimate relationships.
w: Several HN commenters credit it as a rare self-help book worth reading, one that pushes men to find a purpose and accept themselves. It is often named on relationship and masculinity threads.
ab: For men thinking about purpose, relationships, and masculinity
Takes a traditional masculine and feminine polarity view
Spiritual and sometimes dated on gender roles; polarizing

q.t: The only "self help" book I give any credit.

t: Outlive: The Science and Art of Longevity
s: A physician's guide to extending healthy lifespan through exercise, nutrition, sleep and managing chronic disease risk.
w: Often named in HN's yearly reading lists for reframing fitness as long-term health, though not everyone agrees: one reader called it a waste of attention and another said not to take everything as gospel.
ab: For readers interested in longevity and preventive health
Strong focus on exercise and metabolic health
Divisive; some find it overlong or overconfident

q.t: liked it for how it made me think about fitness as part of life into old age

s: Vonnegut's first novel, about a society run by machines in which engineers rule and ordinary workers are made redundant.
w: People point to it as a prescient look at automation and the gap between engineers and everyone else. It's the Vonnegut they pick for technology and society themes.
ab: For readers who like dystopian sci-fi about automation
Early Vonnegut, less famous than Slaughterhouse-Five
Computers are vacuum-tube based, which adds period charm

q.t: Essential reading for anyone who forgets how powerful and often out of touch engineers are as a class of professionals.

s: The classic property-trading board game for two to eight players.
w: HN commenters call it a beloved classic, with some playing house rules to shorten it. One dissenter says it is not worth the paper money.
ab: Familiar family game of trading and bargaining.
Plays best if the group likes negotiation.
House rules can cut the length to about an hour.

q.t: I still love Monopoly. One of the classics, it will always be great fun.

t: Science, Strategy and War: The Strategic Theory of John Boyd
s: An academic study of John Boyd's strategic theory, including the OODA loop.
w: HN readers point to it as the in-depth treatment of Boyd's ideas.
ab: For strategy and military history readers
Academic, dense
Focused on Boyd's theory

q.t: Frans Osinga's book would be more insightful for anyone who was interested in this article.

t: Voltaire's Bastards: The Dictatorship of Reason in the West
s: A critique of Western rationalism and technocracy arguing that reason has hardened into an unthinking structure of power.
w: HN readers list it among books that changed their perspective; it is described as an in-depth criticism of the overly rational, though a reader needs some historical and philosophical background.
ab: For readers interested in critiques of technocracy and rationalism
Assumes some historical and philosophical background
Dense and polemical

q.t: It is an in depth criticism of the overly rational.

t: DOM Scripting: Web Design with JavaScript and the Document Object Model
s: A book on unobtrusive JavaScript and the DOM.
w: Recommended for unobtrusive JavaScript.
ab: For web developers
Older
Fundamentals

q.t: If you don't know how to do unobtrusive JS, I would recommend DOM Scripting by Jeremy Keith:

t: Idea Man: A Memoir by the Cofounder of Microsoft
s: Paul Allen's memoir of cofounding Microsoft and his later life.
w: Recommended as a first-hand account of early Microsoft and its history with Bill Gates.
ab: For readers interested in early PC history.
First-person from a cofounder.
One-sided.

q.t: The first half of the book is full of anecdotes of those early days, the relationship with Bill Gates, and the beginnings of Microsoft.

t: Metaprogramming Ruby: Program Like the Ruby Pros
s: A guide to Ruby's object model and metaprogramming: define_method, method_missing, eval, blocks, procs and scopes.
w: HN names it as the book that takes you from Ruby basics to understanding Rails internals and Ruby's scoping. One commenter calls it a short, succinct and excellent read.
ab: For Ruby developers past the basics
Short and playful, with a clear mental model of scopes
Covers Ruby 1.9 era; newer features missing

q.t: the rather short and succinct Metaprogramming Ruby is an excellent read

t: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems
s: A collection of essays by Google engineers on running large-scale production systems reliably.
w: The standard recommendation for how Google runs infrastructure, with insight into both technical systems and business practice.
ab: For SREs and operations engineers.
Essays by many Google engineers.
Written for Google scale.

q.t: I highly recommend reading the SRE book Google has released. It's got a ton of insight into both their business practices and technical infrastructure.

s: HP's line of business laptops, with lightweight builds, enterprise support plans and broad Linux compatibility across models.
w: HN developers use EliteBooks for years and report they work well with Ubuntu and are lightweight and fairly reliable. Complaints include some cosmetic build issues and awkward RAM upgrades; a couple of people disliked them.
ab: For developers who want a business laptop that runs Linux
Models vary by generation; check specs before buying
RAM upgrades can be a hassle

q.t: I've used HP EliteBook series since G1 (current is G5) all worked great with Ubuntu.

s: Rakuten Kobo's line of e-ink readers, which support open EPUB files and easy transfer from a computer.
w: HN's main alternative to the Kindle: open formats, easy loading of your own books and PDFs, and a device that gets years of updates. Commenters flag the store's DRM and some format quirks.
ab: For readers who want an alternative to Amazon's ecosystem
Reads EPUB and PDF; drag and drop transfer
Kobo store has DRM; some DRM-removal hassles

q.t: Transferring books or PDFs is as easy as plugging the device into my computer.

t: Quantum Computation and Quantum Information, 10th Anniversary Edition
by: Michael A. Nielsen, Isaac L. Chuang
s: The standard graduate textbook on quantum computing and quantum information, covering qubits, algorithms, error correction, and information theory.
w: HN calls it the standard reference for quantum computing, well written for readers who have linear algebra and probability, and repeatedly names it as the place to start.
ab: For readers with linear algebra and probability who want a real quantum computing text
Comprehensive coverage from basics to error correction
Demanding; requires solid math background

q.t: It is well written and light if you have the math background

s: Dijkstra's text on deriving programs from specifications using predicate transformers and weakest preconditions.
w: Recommended for the math-minded as the foundation of provably correct programming, described as advanced but readable.
ab: For programmers who like proofs and formal methods
Uses Dijkstra's own notation
Dense and demanding

q.t: Also advanced, but quite readable

t: Programming Interviews Exposed: Secrets to Landing Your Next Job
s: A guide to technical programming interviews covering the process, common coding questions, data structures and behavioral questions.
w: Recommended as a useful book for preparing for algorithm exercises in interviews, though others point to Cracking the Coding Interview as the better-known option.
ab: For job seekers preparing for coding interviews
Sample questions with worked solutions
Interview norms have changed since publication

q.t: This book was very useful to me

s: A thorough guide to Ruby 1.8 and 1.9 from the author of JavaScript: The Definitive Guide and Ruby's creator.
w: Recommended over the Pickaxe for learning Ruby. HN readers like that it explains why features work the way they do.
ab: For programmers learning Ruby seriously
Co-written by Ruby's creator
Covers old Ruby versions

q.t: gives a very good overview on why features are how they are and even gives some advice from the creator of the language himself

t: The Logic of Failure: Recognizing and Avoiding Error in Complex Situations
s: A psychologist's study of why people fail when managing complex systems, using simulation experiments and cases like Chernobyl.
w: Recommended as a fantastic book about failure, with famous examples like Chernobyl. It comes up in threads about how large systems fail through chains of causes.
ab: For anyone who manages complex projects or systems
Combines experiments with real disaster case studies
Written in the 1980s; the examples show their age

q.t: The Logic of Failure is a fantastic book about failures, including some famous examples of failure (e.g. Chernobyl).

s: An O'Reilly book from 2007 that teaches resource-oriented design and REST principles for web APIs.
w: HN developers point to it as the book that explains HTTP and resource-oriented architecture properly, and link it as the reference for REST questions. It also comes up in debates about what counts as truly RESTful.
ab: For API designers who want the REST model explained at length
Published in 2007, before JSON APIs dominated
Useful for HTTP fundamentals; the HATEOAS purism is debated

q.t: has a really good overview of HTTP in general and some hints on resource oriented architectures

t: The End of Error: Unum Computing
s: A book proposing the unum number format as a replacement for IEEE floating point.
w: Cited by numerics fans interested in alternatives to floating point.
ab: For numerics and HPC readers
Radical proposal
Unum later revised to posits

q.t: The original unum proposal is in [1] which was very interesting read.

t: The Coming Plague: Newly Emerging Diseases in a World Out of Balance
s: A journalistic history of emerging infectious diseases such as Ebola, Marburg and AIDS, and the public health failures behind them.
w: HN commenters cite it as a 1995 warning about pandemics, especially in Ebola and COVID threads. They say it details disease origins and shows epidemics reflect political will and economics.
ab: For readers interested in epidemics and public health
Detailed case histories of outbreaks
Dated in places but still relevant

q.t: The Coming Plague[2] by Laurie Garrett, ISBN 0140250913, is a good read.

s: Henry Petroski's study of how design failures, from bridges to buildings, drive engineering progress.
w: Recommended in threads about bridge and structural failures as a readable look at how failures teach engineers. Commenters link it to the Hyatt Regency collapse.
ab: For engineers and curious readers interested in failure analysis
Case studies including bridges and the Hyatt walkway
Somewhat dry in places

q.t: The whole book is great.

t: The Undoing Project: A Friendship That Changed Our Minds
s: A narrative of the partnership between psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky and their research on judgment.
w: HN recommends it as a story-driven look at the pair behind Thinking, Fast and Slow, blending biography with their research.
ab: For readers of behavioral economics
Narrative biography, light on technical detail
Companion to Kahneman's own books

q.t: In my opinion a very good combination of telling the story of the main characters and also giving interesting points from their research.

s: A high-end adjustable ergonomic office chair from Steelcase, often found refurbished or used.
w: A staple of HN chair threads, praised as the most comfortable chair people have owned. Regulars say to buy it used, often for $150-300, and some prefer it over the Aeron for long sessions.
ab: For long desk hours and back comfort
Cheap used or refurbished; headrest versions are harder to find
Buy used unless you want to pay full price

q.t: Best chair I've ever had at home or at work.

t: Algorithmic Trading & DMA: An Introduction to Direct Market Access Trading Strategies
s: A practitioner's textbook on algorithmic execution strategies and direct market access, written by a former Morgan Stanley algo-trading team member.
w: Called the best book on order execution and the one to read first for electronic trading. It is described as dry but thorough and clear, reading like a university textbook.
ab: For engineers entering electronic trading or execution systems
Thorough on order types, market microstructure and execution algorithms
Dry and getting old, written around 2010

q.t: The best book that I've read on order execution was "Algorithmic Trading and DMA".

s: A collection of practical recipes for designing RESTful HTTP services, covering scalability, versioning and caching.
w: Recommended as a concise, practical complement to the longer REST texts, explaining real REST cases and when not to use REST.
ab: For developers designing HTTP APIs
Terse cookbook style with real-world cases
Language-neutral; no deep theory

q.t: It's not just a recipies list, it explains a lot of very important REST cases

s: The definitive biography of Alan Turing.
w: Recommended as the definitive and detailed biography.
ab: Definitive
Math detail
Long

q.t: if you haven't read Andrew Hodges' excellent biography of Alan Turing, you should put it on your holiday reading list

t: The Innovator's Solution: Creating and Sustaining Successful Growth
s: The follow-up to The Innovator's Dilemma, on how established companies can build disruptive growth businesses.
w: Brought up in disruption threads and compared to jobs-to-be-done thinking. One commenter calls rewriting code the Innovator's Solution to the Innovator's Dilemma.
ab: For managers and founders thinking about disruption
Follow-up to The Innovator's Dilemma
Corporate focus; mentions here are brief

s: A textbook on concurrent programming, covering locks, wait-free and lock-free data structures and memory models, with Java examples.

Hands-on
Fastai specific

q.t: As a sysadmin, I recommend Tom Limoncelli's "Practice" books

t: Stay Awhile and Listen: How Two Blizzards Unleashed Diablo and Forged a Video-Game Empire
s: A history of Blizzard's early days and the development of Diablo and Warcraft.
w: Recommended to anyone interested in how Diablo and Warcraft came to be, covering their development from humble beginnings.
ab: For game developers and fans of Blizzard games
Focuses on early Blizzard and Diablo
Part of a series on Blizzard history

q.t: Really interesting read, covers Diablo/Warcraft development from its humble beginnings.

t: How to Talk to Anyone: 92 Little Tricks for Big Success in Relationships
s: A collection of 92 practical techniques for conversation, rapport and networking.
w: Recommended to socially awkward readers as a source of basic tricks, with one reader noticing they had absorbed many of its techniques.
ab: Short, specific conversation techniques
Aimed at beginners in social skills
Some tips feel gimmicky

q.t: I was shocked how many techniques I had internalized to the point that I thought they were my own ideas

t: Sustainable Energy - Without the Hot Air
s: A numbers-driven look at what it would take for the UK to run on sustainable energy, comparing consumption and supply honestly.
w: Recommended repeatedly as the data-heavy guide to what actually makes a difference in energy and climate. Free online, and noted as UK-centric.
ab: For readers who want real numbers about energy and climate
Back-of-the-envelope calculations on consumption and supply
UK focus; figures date from 2008

q.t: To get a better sense what you can do to actually make a difference, I highly recommend

s: Beginner-friendly book on the Linux shell, basic commands and shell scripting.
w: Recommended as a very readable starting point for command-line skills.
ab: For beginners learning the shell
Free PDF available
Readable and thorough

q.t: I picked up a lot of command-line fu from this book.

t: The Path Between the Seas: The Creation of the Panama Canal, 1870-1914
s: David McCullough's history of the building of the Panama Canal, covering engineering, disease and politics.
w: Recommended in canal threads as a fascinating history of engineering, geography and nineteenth-century politics, even covering Nicaragua canal plans.
ab: For readers who like engineering history
Narrative history covering French and American efforts
Long

q.t: it's one of the most fascinating books I've ever read.

s: Herb Cohen's popular guide to negotiating in business and life.
w: HN readers call it a classic and an inexpensive investment for salary and deal negotiations.
ab: For anyone negotiating jobs or deals
Classic
1980 vintage

q.t: You Can Negotiate Anything is a classic, and very inexpensive investment considering the upside.

t: Beautiful Architecture: Leading Thinkers Reveal the Hidden Beauty in Software Design
s: An O'Reilly essay collection in which the designers of real systems such as Facebook's data architecture and the Xen hypervisor explain their design choices.
w: Suggested as vacation reading and as a software-architecture pick. Commenters liken it to Beautiful Code: independent chapters, each covering a different real-world system.
ab: For developers who want architecture lessons from real systems
Independent chapters, easy to read out of order
2009 edition; some systems covered are dated

q.t: I suggest Beautiful Architecture from O'Reilly.

s: A textbook introducing geometric algebra and its applications in physics, from rotations and relativity to electromagnetism.
w: Offered as the friendly way into geometric algebra for people who like quaternions or tensors. One commenter calls it very clear and gently paced.
ab: For physics or graphics people curious about geometric algebra
Clear, gradual treatment of bivectors and rotors
Physics-oriented; some prior math is assumed

q.t: Geometric Algebra for Physicists is very clear and gently paced.

s: A neuroscience-based guide to focus, distraction and decision-making at work, told through two fictional days in the lives of workers.
w: Recommended on HN to explain what happens in your head when you work, make decisions or feel overloaded. Commenters like its story format and explanations.
ab: For knowledge workers fighting distraction
Uses story to explain how the brain reacts at work
Neuroscience claims are simplified

q.t: He does a great job at explaining what goes on in your head on a given day, for a given decision.

s: A book showing how to evolve existing code toward design patterns through small, test-backed refactorings.
w: Recommended after the Gang of Four book and Refactoring as the way to learn when patterns are worth using. Commenters apply its test-first, evolve-the-design method.
ab: For developers who know basic refactoring and patterns
Applies patterns incrementally rather than up front
Java-based examples

q.t: There's a great book called Refactoring to Patterns which I would suggest after GoF

s: Colin Wilson's 1956 study of alienated creative figures in literature and philosophy, from Camus to Nietzsche, asking why outsiders see more clearly.
w: HN commenters recommend it to people interested in artists, alienation and the creative temperament and often list it among formative books.
ab: For readers drawn to existential and creative-type thinkers
Mixes literary criticism and philosophy
Written in the 1950s

t: Do the Work: Overcome Resistance and Get Out of Your Own Way
s: A short motivational book on defeating procrastination and resistance to finish creative projects.
w: Handed out as the blunt answer to perfectionism and procrastination, usually paired with The War of Art.
ab: For procrastinators and perfectionists
Very short and punchy
Light on research, heavy on exhortation

q.t: Obligatory, but important:

t: The Backroom Boys: The Secret Return of the British Boffin
s: Stories of British engineers behind projects like Elite, the Black Arrow rocket and GSM.
w: Recommended as a good, enjoyable book on the British tech scene, including how Elite was made.
ab: For fans of British tech history
Engaging narrative
Less famous than Red Plenty

q.t: is very enjoyable, too, even if Red Plenty is really in a league of its own

t: Five Proofs of the Existence of God
s: A philosopher's modern defense of five classical arguments for God's existence.
w: Offered by commenters as rigorous logical arguments for theism.
ab: For philosophy of religion readers
Rigorous Thomist arguments
Contested conclusions

q.t: here is a book that goes through some logical arguments for God's existence

t: Way of the Peaceful Warrior: A Book That Changes Lives
s: Semi-autobiographical novel in which a college gymnast meets a mentor at a gas station and learns a path of mindfulness and living in the present.
w: HN readers list it as a book that pushed them toward philosophy and a life-changing read. It's usually mentioned in lists rather than argued for in detail.
ab: For readers looking for a story-style self-help book
Fictionalized spiritual and mindfulness teaching
Mentioned in lists; few details from HN

s: The first volume of The Lord of the Rings, following Frodo as he sets out to destroy the One Ring.
w: HN readers name it as a lifelong favorite and the book that introduced them to fantasy. Some reread it aloud to their kids or relisten to the audiobook on drives.
ab: For anyone who has only seen the films
Slow, descriptive pacing; works well read aloud
Great as an audiobook for long drives

q.t: reading these stories that I think I know so well to my children

s: A popular-science tour of cognitive biases and self-deceptions, each chapter backed by psychology studies.
w: Commenters say it made them distrust their own brain and started a habit of self-reflection. Recommended as an accessible intro to cognitive biases.
ab: For readers new to cognitive biases
Short chapters with references to studies
Some research cited may not have replicated

q.t: I will never trust my brain again.

s: A collection of Liu Cixin short stories, including the title story and 'The Wages of Humanity'.
w: Mentioned in sci-fi lists as big-history storytelling by the author of the Three-Body Problem. Easy to finish quickly.
ab: For fans of hard sci-fi and the Three-Body Problem
Short stories, quick reads
Collection contents vary by edition

q.t: Short enough to read in a night.

s: Investigative account of Jho Low and the 1MDB scandal, in which billions were siphoned from a Malaysian state fund.
w: Recommended as a gripping look at how dirty money moves through banks and law firms, and how many institutions were complicit.
ab: For readers interested in finance, fraud and money laundering
Reads like a thriller
Journalistic account centered on the 1MDB case

q.t: A fascinating read of fraud at the highest level.

s: A hard sci-fi novel about intelligent creatures living on a neutron star whose lives run a million times faster than ours.
w: Called the best hard sci-fi book by one reader and recommended for its idea that fast aliens evolve technology in days. It's also written by a physicist.
ab: For fans of hard science fiction
Written by a physicist
Concept-driven; characters are secondary

q.t: Humans are the slow ones and the Aliens are creatures living on the surface of a neutron star.

s: Histories of disasters from the Halifax explosion to Katrina, arguing that communities usually respond with cooperation instead of panic.
w: Recommended as evidence that people tend to pull together in disasters. Readers say it changed their view of human nature and how societies can be organized.
ab: For readers interested in disasters and social behavior
Case studies from several real events
Optimistic view of human nature

q.t: people generally pull together in disasters rather than society falling apart.

t: The Smartest Guys in the Room
s: The story of Enron's rise and collapse, covering the executives, accounting tricks and culture behind one of the largest corporate frauds.
w: Recommended as a gripping account of Enron and corporate fraud, and as a deep read beyond the documentary and Wikipedia summary.
ab: For readers interested in business fraud and corporate culture
Also made into a documentary
Reads best as a case study in hubris

q.t: Not directly related to computer tech but definitely tech and people.

s: A long novel following four friends over decades in New York, centering on one man's trauma.
w: Readers say it grips them and leaves a lasting impression, calling it emotionally intense and beautifully written. They warn it's long and its subject matter is difficult.
ab: For readers who want an emotional, long novel
Heavy subject matter including abuse
Long and demanding

q.t: I haven't been this gripped by a book in a while.

s: A post-apocalyptic novel narrated in a phonetic, invented dialect of English.
w: HN readers list it among best fiction and books worth rereading; it's not unknown but not widely read. The made-up language makes it distinctive.
ab: For readers who like experimental language
Post-apocalyptic Britain
Dialect takes time to get used to

q.t: Post apocalyptic novel written in a made up language (think Clockwork Orange).

s: Dennett's 1991 account of the mind, arguing against a central 'Cartesian theater' and offering the multiple drafts model of consciousness.
w: Readers say it changed how they think about the mind, showing intuitions about consciousness are often wrong. One says the field has not caught up.
ab: For readers interested in philosophy of mind and AI
Dense but rewarding
Controversial; some argue it explains away consciousness

q.t: It's like finally seeing the image in the Great Stereogram of life.

s: A cooking guide built on four elements of good food, teaching how to season, balance and cook without strict recipes.
w: Recommended to people who want to cook more confidently. Readers say it taught them to understand cooking rather than follow recipes, and it makes other cookbooks easier to use.
ab: For beginners who want to cook without delivery apps
Teaches principles over recipes
Illustrated; reads well even before bed

q.t: It's made me a lot more competent at cooking than I was

s: The true story of Oleg Gordievsky, a KGB officer who spied for British intelligence during the Cold War.
w: Readers call it an amazing, well-written story that reads like a thriller, and it turns up in recommendations for both Cold War history and spy stories.
ab: For fans of Cold War espionage
Narrative nonfiction
Focuses on one defector

q.t: It's about the KGB spy-turned-MI6 agent Oleg Gordievsky and reads like a thriller.

s: A friendly, cartoon-illustrated introduction to the Forth programming language and its stack-based style.
w: Commenters say it is the book that teaches Forth, written in a casual, funny way that even experienced programmers enjoy. Some learned from it decades ago.
ab: For anyone curious about Forth
Casual style with illustrations
Older book; Forth tools have changed

q.t: Written in a casual, funny, beginner friendly way, and even though I'm not a beginner I still enjoyed it immensely.

t: Your Code as a Crime Scene
s: Uses forensic-style analysis of version control history to find hotspots, hidden coupling and risk in a codebase.
w: Recommended to people trying to understand large or inherited codebases, and for the techniques and tools it offers.
ab: For developers and teams inheriting big codebases
Uses git history data
Companion tools exist

q.t: has a number of interesting techniques and tools for this

t: Web Development with Clojure, Third Edition
s: The updated Pragmatic Programmers guide to building web applications in Clojure with Kit and modern libraries.
w: Recommended as the book-format guide to wiring Clojure libraries into a web app, from the author of Luminus. Commenters like the first chapters.
ab: For Clojure developers building web apps
Updated edition for newer tools
Not a first Clojure book

q.t: I haven't yet read it all, but I really liked the first few chapters.

s: A Manning book teaching functional techniques such as higher-order functions, immutability and monads in C#.
w: Recommended to .NET developers who want to learn functional programming without leaving C#. One reader notes monads can be hard if you haven't already tried inventing them.
ab: For C# developers curious about functional style
Covers LINQ-style techniques and monads
Some parts assume prior experience

q.t: If you come from a C# background, this book is excellent:

s: A translation of the Hindu scripture with Prabhupada's commentary from the Hare Krishna tradition.
w: HN readers say it changed how they see the world and gives principles for starting something new. One suggests skipping the religious commentary and reading the verses.
ab: For readers curious about Hindu philosophy
Translation includes devotional commentary
Commentary reflects the Hare Krishna tradition

q.t: Made me see the world, my life, my code and my desires, everything in a total different way.

s: A humorous military sci-fi series about a US soldier and a snarky alien AI, starting with Columbus Day.
w: Recommended as funny light sci-fi, especially the R. C. Bray audiobooks, which make some listeners laugh out loud.
ab: For fans of comic military sci-fi
Audiobooks are popular
Long series

q.t: Has become my favourite light sci-fi.

t: When We Cease to Understand the World
s: A hybrid of fiction and history following scientists like Haber, Schwarzschild and Heisenberg as their discoveries unsettle their minds.
w: Called fascinating, well-written historical fiction about scientists consumed by their work, and a favorite read for the year.
ab: For readers of science history and literary fiction
Real scientists in fictionalized accounts
Short and unsettling

q.t: was fascinating historical fiction, which felt more like fiction because the stories were so out there and well-written.

s: A graduate-level textbook on measure theory, integration, Fourier analysis and complex analysis, known as 'Papa Rudin'.
w: Mathematicians keep it within arm's reach and recommend it as the standard text. It is considered rigorous and demanding.
ab: For serious math students
Terse and demanding
Graduate-level analysis

q.t: Maths: Rudin's Real and Complex analysis.

s: A cooperative card game in which players see everyone's hand but their own and must give each other clues to build fireworks.
w: HN gamers recommend it for logic, deduction and cooperation, with surprisingly deep play from simple rules. It's quick and good for small groups.
ab: For fans of co-op and deduction games
Simple rules, short games
Needs 2-5 players

q.t: Hanabi is absolutely fantastic, with surprisingly deep gameplay given how simple the rules are.

s: A short novel of imagined dreams in which Einstein envisions worlds where time behaves in different ways.
w: A favorite in HN threads about books that alter your view of reality: a quick read that explores many different perceptions of time.
ab: For readers who like physics-flavored literary fiction
Very quick read, made of short vignettes
Poetic and thought-provoking rather than plot-driven

q.t: This book is a quick read, but shows a bunch of different perceptions of time.

s: The second novel in Gibson's Sprawl trilogy, a cyberpunk story of a hacker, an art dealer and a mercenary entangled with AIs.
w: Mentioned by HN readers as part of the Sprawl trilogy they love; one commenter calls the three books perfection and another says it hooked them as a teenager.
ab: For cyberpunk fans, best read after Neuromancer
Second in the Sprawl trilogy
Dense, atmospheric prose

q.t: Neuromancer, Mona Lisa Overdrive, Count Zero (Sprawl Trilogy) – perfection

s: A children's science-fantasy novel in which a girl travels through space and time with the help of three strange guides to rescue her father.
w: HN commenters give it as a gift to kids and credit it with teaching them early about physics, time, creativity and nonconformity; one calls it a profound children's book with lifelong impact.
ab: For kids and for adults revisiting a childhood favorite
First of the Time Quartet
Mix of science and Christian-tinged themes

q.t: Taught me very early on about physics, time, creativity, nonconformity, love

t: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto
s: Rothbard's 1973 case for anarcho-capitalism, arguing for a society without a state and applying libertarian principles to law, police, courts and roads.
w: Libertarian-leaning HN readers list it as a life-changing book that lays out a clear vision of a stateless society, often recommended to fans of Ayn Rand.
ab: For readers exploring libertarian and anarcho-capitalist thought
Systematic, polemical argument for a stateless society
Strongly ideological; many will disagree

q.t: It presents a clear vision of a society without government

s: A compact 75% wireless mechanical keyboard with Bluetooth and USB-C wired mode, Mac and Windows layouts and a choice of switches.
w: HN users recommend it as an accessible, do-everything mechanical keyboard that works wirelessly at home and wired at work, and a common entry point into the hobby.
ab: For people wanting a compact wireless mechanical keyboard
Bluetooth or USB-C wired, Mac and Windows support
Gateway into a costly custom keyboard hobby

q.t: It's the closest to a 'do everything well' keyboard I could get.

t: Vector Calculus, Linear Algebra, and Differential Forms: A Unified Approach
by: John H. Hubbard, Barbara Burke Hubbard
s: An undergraduate textbook that teaches multivariable calculus, linear algebra and differential forms together in a unified approach.
w: HN math readers call it a favorite and a beautiful introduction to multi-dimensional math, one of few books that takes you from basics to a serious level without a teacher.
ab: For strong students or self-learners studying multivariable calculus
Teaches linear algebra intuitively alongside calculus
Demanding; one commenter notes it is a lot of book

q.t: This is my all time favourite math book.

s: A dark, inventive weird-fantasy novel set in the sprawling city of New Crobuzon, the first of Miéville's Bas-Lag books.
w: HN readers call it fantastic and intense, with one saying it may be the best fiction they've read; it's often offered to people who want more adventurous fantasy.
ab: For readers who like dark, inventive worldbuilding
First of the Bas-Lag books
Dark and intense in tone

q.t: Perdido Street Station might be the best fiction I have ever read.

s: A textbook explaining how a computer works layer by layer, from digital logic and microarchitecture to the instruction set and operating system.
w: HN recommends Tanenbaum's computer-architecture textbook as the way to see the computer as a system of abstractions, and one reader enjoyed it cover to cover like a novel.
ab: For programmers who want to understand how hardware works
Clear and readable for a textbook
Large; some hardware examples are dated

q.t: I read it cover to cover like a novel.

s: A 1994 novella about an AI that gains control of reality, exploring the singularity, power and human choice.
w: HN calls it a lesser-known great sci-fi book and a mind-shifting read for technologists. Recommended on George Hotz's word, and available free online.
ab: For readers interested in AI and the singularity
Short and available free online
Contains graphic and disturbing content

q.t: A few lesser known but great sci-if books

s: Hard science fiction novel about a mining crew whose ship is commandeered to chase a Saturn moon that turns out to be an alien artifact.
w: Listed in HN favorite-fiction threads and brought up when discussions touch on spacecraft with indefinite thrust or mysterious moons. Fans rank it among Reynolds' best.
ab: For hard sci-fi fans who like big ideas and relativistic travel
Standalone novel, so no series commitment
Fairly dark and slow in places

q.t: followed closely by Pushing Ice by the same author

s: A light 12.5-inch Lenovo ThinkPad ultraportable from 2018 with a quad-core option, TrackPoint and a serviceable design.
w: Commenters like its balance of low weight and real performance, its Linux compatibility and the vendor-published service manual. The TrackPoint gets praise from programmers who live on the keyboard.
ab: For people who want a small, light Linux-friendly ThinkPad
Easy to repair, with an official hardware manual
Discontinued; buy used or clearance and check the battery

q.t: I think it's fantastic and really hits the sweet spot between weight and performance

s: A mid-priced System76 laptop that ships with Ubuntu or Pop!_OS.
w: HN Linux users say it just works, with good sleep, upgradeability and value, and one finds it better than a MacBook Pro for development. The trackpad draws complaints.
ab: Budget Linux laptop that works out of the box.
Easily upgradable.
Trackpad is weak.

q.t: In my opinion, the System76 is superior as a development machine.

s: A 14-inch 2017 ThinkPad known for durability, a good keyboard and long battery life with a swappable battery.
w: HN commenters say it runs Linux flawlessly, is durable and ergonomic, and is cheap used. One post shows very low power draw.
ab: For programmers who want a durable Linux laptop used.
Great keyboard and battery life.
Not for graphics work.

q.t: The Thinkpad t4xx line are one of the most durable and ergonomic laptops out there.

s: John Wyndham's 1951 post-apocalyptic novel in which most of humanity goes blind and carnivorous plants attack.
w: HN readers list it among favorite sci-fi and as their gateway to post-apocalyptic fiction, praising its themes of morality and society.
ab: Classic British post-apocalyptic sci-fi.
Influenced later zombie stories, per one reader.
Dated 1950s sensibilities.

q.t: one of the first science fiction books I ever read, and the one that introduced me to post apocalyptic fiction.

s: A 15.6-inch 2013 ThinkPad with a TrackPoint, optional high-resolution screen and removable battery.
w: HN users say Linux works perfectly on it and call it solid, often found cheap used or on discount.
ab: Solid used ThinkPad.
Linux compatible out of the box.
Big and old.

q.t: Nothing fancy, but it's really solid.

t: Beginning Ruby: From Novice to Professional
s: An introductory Ruby programming book that moves from basics to object-oriented and practical Ruby use.
w: Suggested to newcomers learning Ruby, often before Rails. Commenters liked it as a friendly first book on the language itself.
ab: Good for beginners learning Ruby before Rails
Covers the language, not just web development
Published 2007, so it predates modern Ruby versions

q.t: I highly recommend Peter Cooper's Book: Beginning Ruby

t: Heuristics and Biases: The Psychology of Intuitive Judgment
s: An academic collection of research papers on judgment errors and mental shortcuts, edited around Kahneman and Tversky's work.
w: Recommended as the more detailed source behind pop books like Predictably Irrational and Thinking, Fast and Slow.
ab: Primary research rather than a pop summary
Good for going deeper than bestsellers
Academic and dense; some findings have since been challenged

q.t: Heuristics & Biases is a great book with more detail

t: Service-Oriented Design with Ruby and Rails
s: A guide to splitting Rails applications into services, with API design and Sinatra examples.
w: Recommended whenever someone asked about building APIs or services in Ruby, with step-by-step instructions.
ab: For Rubyists designing service-based architectures
Practical API and Sinatra walkthroughs
From 2010, so tools and gems are dated

q.t: I highly recommend the book written by Paul Dix if that's what you are using.

t: Boo Hoo: A Dot-Com Story from Concept to Catastrophe
s: The co-founder's account of how Boo.com burned through about $135 million in 18 months.
w: Recommended as a hilarious and scary cautionary tale about dot-com excess, told unapologetically by one of the founders.
ab: Cautionary startup failure story
First-person account of the dot-com bubble
Founder's view may be self-serving

q.t: makes for both hilarious and scary reading

t: Rails AntiPatterns: Best Practice Ruby on Rails Refactoring
s: A catalog of common Rails mistakes and the refactorings that fix them.
w: Recommended whenever someone asked about Rails mistakes or architecture, especially for keeping controllers thin.
ab: For Rails developers cleaning up code
Concrete refactoring advice
Written for Rails 2/3; much is dated

q.t: Easiest mistake in large rails apps is to let your controllers get too thick

t: Self-Discipline in 10 Days: How to Go from Thinking to Doing
s: A short self-help book on building self-discipline and acting instead of procrastinating.
w: Called a life-changer by one HN reader who found most other books useless, though hard to get hold of for years.
ab: For chronic procrastinators
Short and action-focused
Was long out of print and hard to find

q.t: This book is a massive PITA to get your hands on (in some countries, perhaps it's back in print?), but a life-changer

t: Scratch Beginnings: Me, $25, and the Search for the American Dream
s: A recent graduate's experiment of starting a new city with $25 and trying to build a stable life in a year.
w: Offered as a counter-narrative to books about poverty, showing someone working his way to savings, an apartment and a truck.
ab: Real-life experiment narrative
Contrasts with Nickel and Dimed
Critics note he had advantages such as a college degree

q.t: See also the book "Scratch Beginnings", about how a guy started with only $25 and got himself into a stable financial situation

t: Drugs Without the Hot Air: Minimising the Harms of Legal and Illegal Drugs
s: A former UK drugs adviser's evidence-based comparison of harms from legal and illegal drugs.
w: Recommended as a well-argued, credible look at the data, though one commenter notes it leans UK-centric.
ab: Compares drug harms by evidence
Written by a neuropsychopharmacologist
Focuses on UK policy

q.t: It's perhaps a little UK-centric, but I found it well argued and the author is eminently credible.

t: An Epidemic of Absence: A New Way of Understanding Allergies and Autoimmune Diseases
s: A science journalist's survey of the hygiene hypothesis and research on gut microbes, parasites and allergies.
w: Recommended on microbes, allergies and gut bacteria, though noted that the research is young.
ab: Readable overview of immune research
Covers hygiene hypothesis
Field has moved since 2012

q.t: There's a great book written about exactly this that I highly recommend

t: Smartphones and Beyond: Lessons from the Remarkable Rise and Fall of Symbian
s: An insider's detailed account of Symbian, the early smartphone OS, and why it declined.
w: Recommended as an accurate, insanely detailed insider story of Symbian and Nokia's fall.
ab: Insider history of Symbian
Highly detailed with internal memos
Niche subject

q.t: a great (and insanely detailed) book on the rise and fall of Symbian by a guy who was there

s: A Cisco Press guide to BGP and internet routing design.
w: Known as the BGP book and recommended for learning the basics, though not the most up-to-date.
ab: BGP and AS basics
Cisco-focused
Dated

q.t: If you really want to understand BGP, read

t: Logitech K400 Plus Wireless Touch Keyboard
s: A compact wireless keyboard with a built-in touchpad for PCs and TVs.
w: Recommended for living-room and media PC use with an integrated mouse, though not great for typing.
ab: Cheap living room keyboard
Integrated touchpad
Typing feel is basic

q.t: In my experience its far nicer then most "Smart TV" or media devices in a similar price range.
