s: A short intro to what mathematics is about, by a Fields medalist.
w: Recommended as a quick and easy introduction to math.
ab: Short
Easy
Conceptual

q.t: It's a quick read, and the way Gowers writes about important Mathematical topics is interesting and, for the most part, easy to understand.

t: Bill & Dave: How Hewlett and Packard Built the World's Greatest Company
s: A history of Hewlett-Packard and its founders, and how the HP Way shaped Silicon Valley.
w: Recommended to understand how HP went from admired to diminished, and as the story behind much of Silicon Valley's culture. One commenter calls the author a fan.
ab: For readers interested in HP and Silicon Valley history
Covers founders' management style and the HP Way
Author is openly admiring

q.t: Everything good about Silicon Valley is owed to that company, and to its founders.

t: An Economist Gets Lunch: New Rules for Everyday Foodies
s: Tyler Cowen's guide to finding good food, covering restaurants, ethnic cuisine and why American food is the way it is.
w: Recommended for people who like eating out, with a tip to order what other patrons of ethnic restaurants are eating. Cited for why Americans do not demand high-quality food.
ab: For food lovers and restaurant explorers
Mixes economics and practical dining advice
US-centric examples

q.t: This is a great book if you like eating out.

t: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
s: A 1956 sociology classic that analyzes social interaction as theatrical performance, with roles, stages and impression management.
w: Cited on HN as a foundational classic of social psychology and a book that changed how people see everyday behavior, especially in the age of online personas.
ab: For readers curious about social behavior and online personas
Uses a theater metaphor throughout
Academic and mid-century in tone

q.t: uses the metaphor of theater to explain how we perform roles

s: A near-future novel about a world where a cure for aging arrives and society must cope with people who no longer die of old age.
w: HN commenters bring it up in threads about reversing aging as a good read and a solid thought experiment on overpopulation, though not a masterpiece.
ab: For readers interested in life extension and its consequences
Dystopian near-future thought experiment
One commenter calls it good but not a masterpiece

q.t: Ready Player One and The Postmortal were really rad.

t: The End of Alchemy: Money, Banking, and the Future of the Global Economy
s: Former Bank of England governor Mervyn King on how banking and monetary systems work and why they are fragile.
w: HN commenters recommend it for understanding monetary policy and banking from the ground up; one says it gave an economics graduate eye-opening mental models.
ab: For readers wanting to understand banks and central banking
Written by a former central bank governor
Argues for reform of the financial system

q.t: is a great book that explains fiscal/monetary policy and the modern banking system from the ground up.

s: A beginner's book on digital design and FPGA development, using Verilog and VHDL with hands-on projects on a starter board.
w: HN commenters getting into FPGAs recommend it as a practical starting point, paired with a cheap starter board and free open-source tools.
ab: For programmers new to hardware design
Pairs with a low-cost starter FPGA board
Introductory; you will outgrow it

q.t: I would also recommend this book:

t: Stand Out of Our Light: Freedom and Resistance in the Attention Economy
s: A former Google strategist argues that attention-harvesting technology undermines human freedom and calls for a defense of attention.
w: HN commenters in Big Tech and smartphone-quitting threads recommend it as a short, engaging book on the attention economy, and it is free to read as an open-access Cambridge title.
ab: For readers worried about tech, attention and distraction
Short, open-access book
More philosophical than a how-to guide

q.t: Freedom and Resistance in the Attention Economy that I highly recommend.

s: A book on simulating natural systems with code, covering physics, particle systems, autonomous agents, fractals, evolution and neural networks.
w: HN commenters put it alongside SICP as a favorite programming text, and recommend it for creative coding, including for teaching kids with Processing and p5.js.
ab: For creative coders and learners who like visual results
Uses Processing and p5.js
Available free online

q.t: simulating nature through code -- also is really interesting

s: Gogol's 1842 satirical novel about a swindler who travels Russia buying the names of dead serfs.
w: HN readers list it as a favorite classic, a book worth giving as a gift, and one commenter read it to understand how Russia sees itself.
ab: For readers of classic Russian satire
Free editions exist at Standard Ebooks
Translation choice affects readability

q.t: It is an amazing book

s: Fermor's memoir of walking across Europe from Holland toward Constantinople in 1933 and 1934, the first of a trilogy.
w: HN readers love it as a comfort book and a travel memoir; commenters describe dense, rich prose and urge people interested in Europe to read it.
ab: For readers who like travel writing and European history
Dense, ornate prose
First of a trilogy

q.t: Just finished Patrick Leigh Fermor's "A time of gifts" and I can't recommend it enough!

s: Robert Anton Wilson's exploration of how perception and belief shape reality, drawing on quantum physics and psychology.
w: HN readers list it as a mind-blowing, life-changing pick in threads asking for little-known books, and recommend Wilson's other works alongside it.
ab: For readers curious about belief, perception and mind
Playful, counterculture and unconventional
Science content is loose, not rigorous

q.t: I can recommend all books written by Robert Anton Wilson, especially the Cosmic Trigger series, Quantum Psychology and The New Prometheus.

s: James Dyson's memoir of inventing the bagless vacuum cleaner and building a company through years of failure and rejection.
w: HN commenters recommend it as an inspiring story of perseverance and a look at the business skills an inventor must teach himself. One calls it hugely underrated.
ab: For inventors and founders facing long odds.
Shows sales, funding and legal learning curve behind an invention.
First-person memoir, so Dyson's own telling.

q.t: It is an excellent book about original thinking and it is hugly underrated.

t: The Boy Who Loved Math: The Improbable Life of Paul Erdos
s: An illustrated children's biography of the wandering, eccentric mathematician Paul Erdos, illustrated by LeUyen Pham.
w: Parents and math fans on HN read it to their kids and recommend it for showing that strange, passionate people belong in math.
ab: For young children and parents who like math
Picture book with witty, detailed illustrations
Short read; a gentle introduction rather than real mathematics

q.t: There is an IMO outstandingly illustrated children's book about Erdős

by: Israel M. Gelfand, E. G. Glagoleva et al.
s: A Dover edition of a short Gelfand text that builds intuition for functions and their graphs, drawn from the Soviet correspondence school for high schoolers.
w: HN commenters recommend the Gelfand series for relearning school math with real intuition and rigor. It appears in lists for adults refreshing basics before more advanced math.
ab: For self-learners refreshing algebra and functions
Short, problem-driven and intuitive
Part of a series; others cover trigonometry and algebra

q.t: israel gelfand, a top russian mathematician, has books aimed at high school students that served as education materials for distance learning in russia

s: A popular-science overview of fusion research written by two fusion physicists.
w: Recommended on a commenter's strong word as a good, honest summary of where the field stands, written by working researchers.
ab: For readers who want a credible overview of fusion.
Written by two active fusion researchers.
Published in 2018, so recent firms are missing.

q.t: as a good summary of the current state of the field. It's written by two fusion researchers and is legit

s: A No Starch Press book walking through real software vulnerabilities the author found, how he found them, and how they were reported.
w: Recommended to people asking how security researchers find bugs: a practical, case-by-case walkthrough with helpful appendices for those without the background techniques.
ab: For aspiring vulnerability researchers
Real case studies of bugs in real software
Published 2011; targets and tooling are older

q.t: a practical walk-trough in finding these kinds of security bugs

s: A Steelcase ergonomic office chair designed around modern device use, with highly adjustable arms and a flexible back.
w: HN lists it among the four kings of office chairs alongside the Aeron, Embody and Leap. Owners call it very adaptable and the best chair they have had; one prefers mesh chairs.
ab: For people who want a highly adaptable premium chair
Arms that follow different postures and device use
Expensive new; try before buying if you can

q.t: Steelcase Gesture.  Big fan, very adaptable.

t: Elements of Programming Interviews: The Insiders' Guide
s: A collection of coding interview problems with detailed solutions covering data structures, algorithms and system-level topics.
w: Commenters pair it with Cracking the Coding Interview as the serious interview-prep books. It is seen as harder and more thorough, good for a few months of weekend practice.
ab: For engineers preparing for technical interviews
Hundreds of worked problems with solutions
Language-specific editions exist; choose yours

q.t: You can see the proof for yourself when you burn through the following two books within the three months.

s: A 14-inch Lenovo ThinkPad from 2010 known for sturdy build, good keyboard and trouble-free Linux support.
w: In 2010-2012 threads it was a default answer for a developer Linux laptop: drivers worked out of the box and the keyboard and build held up for years.
ab: For fans of old ThinkPads running Linux
Sturdy chassis, great keyboard, easy to service
Slow and heavy by today's standards

q.t: everything worked out of the box with absolutely no configuration or fuss, and on that basis I would recommend it

s: Nozick's 1974 Rawls-era response in political philosophy, arguing for a minimal state and introducing the entitlement theory of justice and the utility monster.
w: Offered as the standard libertarian counterpart to Rawls's A Theory of Justice; commenters point people to it when debates turn to the proper role of the state.
ab: For readers who want the main libertarian case in political philosophy
Pairs naturally with Rawls's A Theory of Justice
Dense academic prose; not a casual read

q.t: After reading Rawls, I'd suggest maybe reading Robert Nozick's libertarian leaning Anarchy, State, and Utopia

s: The official Rust book in print, a complete guide to the language from ownership and borrowing to concurrency.
w: HN lists it as the default way to learn Rust. It is free online, though people also buy the print copy; one finds the big book awkward to carry.
ab: For anyone learning Rust from scratch
Free online version matches the print book
Large and heavy as a physical book

q.t: I want to build simple CLIs in Rust as my gateway into the language - will use what I lean here to do it.

s: Edward Bernays's 1928 book by the founder of modern public relations on how elites shape public opinion.
w: HN readers cite it as the classic of public relations, from the person who invented it. Some comments mix it up with Jacques Ellul's book of the same title.
ab: For readers interested in PR, advertising and persuasion
A short, candid 1920s manual by a PR pioneer
Not to be confused with Ellul's Propaganda

q.t: Propaganda by Eduard Bernays would be the second.

s: A thin Linux laptop from System76 shipping with Ubuntu or Pop!_OS.
w: HN Linux users like the hardware, high-dpi screen and System76 support, though one owner warns about small battery life and suspend drain.
ab: Linux-first ultrabook with vendor support.
Light and small; reasonably priced when well specced.
Battery life drew a complaint.

q.t: I have a Galago Pro from system76 and love both the hardware and System76 tech support for Ubuntu

t: Modern Vim: Craft Your Development Environment with Vim 8 and Neovim
s: Drew Neil's follow-up to Practical Vim, covering advanced editing workflows, plugins and tooling in Vim 8 and Neovim.
w: HN recommends Drew Neil's books as stellar Vim guides, with Modern Vim as the up-to-date, more advanced companion to Practical Vim, covering modern plugin and language server setups.
ab: For Vim users who want to modernize their setup
Covers Vim 8 and Neovim
Best after Practical Vim; the Vim ecosystem moves quickly

q.t: For a more up to date approach I'd suggest Drew Neil's Modern Vim book (still in beta)

s: A book series that digs into the core mechanisms of JavaScript such as scope, closures, this, and types.
w: The go-to pick for learning how JavaScript really works under the hood. HN suggests it after a beginner book like Eloquent JavaScript, and it's free to read online first.
ab: For people who already write some JavaScript
Deep dives on scope, closures and types
Free on GitHub to preview; first edition predates newer JS features

q.t: reading You Don't Know JS: Scope & Closures was really great

t: An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Volume 1
s: A classic probability textbook.
w: Recommended for its exposition of combinatorics.
ab: For math students
Classic
Dense

q.t: his exposition of combinatorics at the beginning of the first volume is a great introduction to that subject!

by: Chris McCord, Bruce Tate, et al.
s: The official Pragmatic Bookshelf guide to building web applications with the Elixir Phoenix framework, written by its creator and collaborators.
w: HN points Elixir newcomers to it as the official Phoenix book, read after Programming Elixir, and recommends buying it DRM-free from Pragmatic. One reader found it a joy while leaving full-stack JS fatigue.
ab: For web developers learning Elixir and Phoenix
Written for Phoenix 1.4; newer versions have changed
Best paired with Programming Elixir by Dave Thomas

q.t: I second Elixir, but I'd add Phoenix to the pile, especially if you do any web programming.

s: Barbara Tuchman's Pulitzer-winning narrative history of the first month of World War I and the decisions that set it in motion.
w: A go-to history recommendation on HN, praised for gripping prose and for lessons that feel current. One dissenter prefers The Sleepwalkers for covering Austria-Hungary better.
ab: For readers wanting a narrative account of how WWI began
Vivid, character-driven storytelling; an audiobook is available
Focuses on Western Front powers; little on Austria-Hungary

q.t: The audio book is also great. The writing style is gripping

s: True story of Max Butler, a hacker who took over the credit-card fraud underground.
w: Recommended as a good read that feels like a technology novel and explains how cybercrime rings really worked.
ab: For readers of true-crime and hacking stories
Reads like a thriller
Journalistic, not technical

q.t: I've read it and can confirm its a good read.

by: Dimitri P. Bertsekas, John N. Tsitsiklis
s: The MIT textbook on probability, with many worked problems, used in the 6.041 course.
w: Recommended as a well-written beginner text that mirrors the free MIT OCW video lectures. Commenters list it first when asked how to build a probability foundation.
ab: For self-learners starting probability
Companion MIT OCW lectures and problem sets
Textbook length and needs some calculus

q.t: It is textbook for EECS Probability course at MIT and very well written for beginners.

s: MIT Press book on procedural audio: building sound effects from scratch with synthesis in Pure Data, including physical models of engines, footsteps and weather.
w: HN readers treat it as the classic on procedural audio and sound synthesis, useful for game audio and physical modeling. One commenter recommends it to beginners alongside Pure Data.
ab: For sound designers, game audio programmers, and synthesis hobbyists
Uses Pure Data to build effects like engines and wind
Large book; beginners should expect a learning curve

q.t: There is one absolute classic work in that field that I know of.

t: Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order: Why Nations Succeed and Fail
s: Ray Dalio's account of the rise and fall of empires over history, using data to describe a recurring big debt cycle.
w: Recommended as a look at the historical ups and downs of world empires, comparing the US with the Dutch and British. Cited in debates on dollar and debt.
ab: For readers interested in macro and geopolitics
Data-heavy, sweeping thesis
Pattern-matching across eras is debated

q.t: Takes a look at historical ups and downs and gives hard data without too much colour being added

t: 23 Things They Don't Tell You About Capitalism
s: An economist challenges free-market orthodoxy in 23 short essays on topics such as trade, inequality, and the role of the state.
w: HN commenters recommend it as an approachable introduction to critical views of capitalism, and cite it in debates about protectionism and development.
ab: For general readers new to economics
Short chapters, accessible style
Strongly opinionated; critics call it one-sided

q.t: Ha-Joon Chang has very approachable books about capitalism and economics.

t: Cynical Theories: How Activist Scholarship Made Everything about Race, Gender, and Identity
s: A critical account of the intellectual roots of critical race and gender theories and how they spread in universities.
w: Recommended by commenters trying to understand where these ideas came from. One calls it very well researched. The book is highly contested.
ab: For readers curious about the critique of critical theory
Strongly critical viewpoint
Authors known for Sokal-style hoaxes

q.t: is a very well researched guide to CRT and it's affects on society

t: The Mother Tongue: English and How It Got That Way
s: A humorous popular history of the English language, its quirks, borrowings and spelling oddities.
w: Recommended in threads about English accents, spelling and language history as an entertaining, easy read. One commenter was assigned it in high school.
ab: For curious readers interested in the English language
Funny and accessible, with plenty of trivia
Popular treatment, not a linguistics text

q.t: A good book which also covers this (and is quite entertaining) is Mother Tongue by Bill Bryson.

t: Stop Stealing Sheep & Find Out How Type Works
s: An approachable introduction to how type works and how to choose and use typefaces, by designer Erik Spiekermann.
w: Offered as the accessible starting point for typography. Commenters recommend it alongside The Elements of Typographic Style for design newcomers.
ab: For beginners wanting an accessible typography intro
Explains type anatomy, choice and layout
Light compared to a full reference

q.t: A fantastic and accessible starting point

t: The Pixar Touch: The Making of a Company
s: A history of Pixar from computer graphics research to a movie studio.
w: HN readers recommend it for the early business and technical history of Pixar.
ab: For animation and tech history fans
Covers business and technology
2008 vintage

q.t: The Pixar Touch by David Price is a pretty fantastic look at the early history

t: Disciplined Entrepreneurship: 24 Steps to a Successful Startup
s: A step-by-step framework for building a startup, from picking a market to pricing and scaling.
w: Recommended to people validating ideas or quitting jobs to launch startups, as a step-by-step guide.
ab: For first-time founders
24 clear, ordered steps
Framework-heavy; better for B2B than hobby projects

q.t: Literally a step by step to get a successful company off the ground.

t: Exploding the Phone: The Untold Story of the Teenagers and Outlaws Who Hacked Ma Bell
s: A history of phone phreaking: the hackers, blue boxes and outlaws who explored and exploited the Bell telephone network.
w: Recommended by several HN commenters as the definitive account of phreaking history. The author himself chimes in once, but others recommend it independently.
ab: For hackers interested in the roots of hacker culture
Thoroughly researched with personal stories
Author is an active HN participant

q.t: you'll like Exploding the Phone[1] which details the history of phone phreaking

t: The Art of Electronics: The Student Manual
s: The lab companion to The Art of Electronics, with exercises, experiments and worked problems for learning circuit design by building.
w: HN commenters tell people learning electronics to buy it alongside The Art of Electronics, noting that many do not know it exists. They like the intuition-first, hands-on approach.
ab: For hobbyists and students working through The Art of Electronics
Hands-on labs and exercises covering analog and digital basics
Meant as a companion, not a standalone textbook

q.t: I highly recommend the Student Guide to the Art of Electronics

t: The New Market Wizards: Conversations with America's Top Traders
s: Interviews with successful traders across futures, stocks and currencies about their methods, psychology and mistakes.
w: Recommended with the rest of the Market Wizards series for profiling different trader mindsets. Commenters say it is a bit dated but still good.
ab: For people curious how professional traders think
Interview format; easy to read in chunks
Older market examples

q.t: The Market Wizards books are a bit dated, but still do a good job of profiling various trader mindsets

s: A startup guide to validating customer problems and building a repeatable process for developing a business before scaling.
w: Recommended as a more thorough alternative to The Lean Startup, with a practical product development process centered on customer research.
ab: For founders validating ideas and product development
Practical process with customer research front and center
Overlaps in spirit with Lean Startup

q.t: I highly recommend the book Nail it Then scale it.

t: Recoding America: Why Government Is Failing in the Digital Age
s: A former US deputy CTO describes why government technology projects fail and how to fix them.
w: Recommended for its stories of digitizing public services, including SNAP sign-up and IRS and VA systems.
ab: For people building or working with government tech.
Stories from healthcare.gov and California benefits.
US-focused.

q.t: The book this was adapted from is absolutely fantastic.

t: Essentials of Compilation: An Incremental Approach in Racket
s: An MIT Press compiler-construction book that builds a compiler for a Lisp-like language step by step in Racket, with a Python edition and free PDFs.
w: HN names it a real gem because it skips the usual heavy focus on parsing and instead builds the middle and back end of a compiler incrementally. Draft PDFs for the Racket and Python versions are freely available.
ab: For programmers wanting a hands-on, language-focused compiler course
Free PDF drafts for both Racket and Python editions
Less coverage of parsing than traditional compiler books

q.t: A big portion of most compiler books focus on parsing. This book instead focuses on implementing a lisp

t: The Myth of the Paperless Office
by: Abigail J. Sellen, Richard H. R. Harper
s: MIT Press study of why paper persists in offices, using the concept of affordances to explain what paper does that screens do not.
w: HN readers send people to it whenever paper, note-taking and the failure of the paperless office come up. One calls it a wonderful read, another the authoritative book.
ab: For readers interested in human factors, note-taking and office technology
Research-based and clearly argued
Written in 2002; the digital examples are old

q.t: The Myth of the Paperless Office is a wonderful read.

t: Pain Free: A Revolutionary Method for Stopping Chronic Pain
s: A posture-therapy book offering targeted exercises and stretches to correct muscular imbalances that the author says cause chronic pain.
w: HN commenters recommend it as the book that finally fixed their wrist, back or posture problems from desk work. They credit its simple exercises and the supine groin stretch.
ab: For people with desk-related aches or poor posture
Self-diagnosis chart with targeted exercises
Anecdotal evidence; not a substitute for medical advice

q.t: This book completely changed my life. The exercise can seem a bit odd, but they worked amazingly well for me.

s: A networking and relationship-building guide built around generosity, follow-up and making connections one person at a time.
w: HN folks grudgingly rate the advice highly even when they dislike the author's style. The tips on building a network are called practical and actionable.
ab: For people who dread networking and want a concrete method
Practical tactics for building lasting professional relationships
Author's self-promotional tone annoys some readers

q.t: every bit of advice he offers is pure gold and extremely practical.

t: Masterminds of Programming: Conversations with the Creators of Major Programming Languages
s: A collection of interviews with the designers of languages including C++, Python, Haskell, Lua and others, about why they made the choices they did.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a way to learn language history from the designers themselves. They point to it for the thinking behind language choices and a chapter with Anders Hejlsberg.
ab: For programmers curious about why languages are designed as they are
Interview format; read chapters in any order
Published in 2008, so newer languages are missing

q.t: is a pretty great read. You can get a ton of historical context from reading what the language designers were thinking

t: Surfing Uncertainty: Prediction, Action, and the Embodied Mind
s: A cognitive science book on the brain as a prediction machine.
w: Cited in threads on predictive processing and the Bayesian brain.
ab: For readers interested in how the brain works
Academic
Dense

q.t: which convincingly details many brain subsystems as approximating Bayesian updates.

s: A novel, a companion to The Phoenix Project, following a developer fighting a broken organization to modernize how software gets built.
w: HN managers and engineers recommend it with The Phoenix Project as a story about how teams and organizations should work, popular as an audiobook, though some rate it below the first book.
ab: For engineers and tech managers interested in DevOps culture
Novel format; companion to The Phoenix Project
Rated below The Phoenix Project by some

q.t: I would recommend "The Phoenix Project" and "The Unicorn Project" and "The Goal" to all tech managers.

s: A tile-placement board game where players build a medieval landscape and place followers to score points from cities, roads and fields.
w: HN players list it among favorite simple board games; with the Traders and Builders and Inns and Cathedrals expansions it deepens, and it works for kids with simplified scoring.
ab: For families and casual board gamers
Simple rules; adjust scoring for young kids
Base game is limited without expansions

q.t: I would really recommend Carcassonne with these two expansions

s: A short illustrated essay collection based on a 1972 BBC series about how we look at art and images.
w: Described as a life-changing book that changes how you look at the world; the video series is recommended for the images.
ab: For anyone curious about art and images
Short, richly illustrated
Marxist critique; the TV series shows images better

q.t: a life-changing political book on art history that changes the way you look at the world.

s: A study of self-managing, purpose-driven organizations and how they work.
w: Cited as an influential book on agile, self-management and what factors really matter in organizations.
ab: For managers interested in flat orgs
Case studies of real companies
Idealistic; hard to apply in traditional firms

q.t: For me it is the most influential book on how I think about

t: The Shock Doctrine: The Rise of Disaster Capitalism
s: An argument that free-market reforms are pushed through crises.
w: Recommended and cited in political threads; some call it insightful.
ab: For readers of political economy
Strong left-leaning argument
Contested thesis

q.t: is another insightful book of hers, I highly recommend it, it was written in 2008 as the financial crisis happened

s: Ridley's argument that trade and exchange of ideas have driven human prosperity and will continue to.
w: HN readers say it changed their sense that the world is only getting worse. Others call its argument debatable but a refreshing, compelling case for optimism.
ab: For readers wanting an optimistic economic history
Argues for trade and innovation as drivers of progress
Debatable claims; one-sided in places

q.t: Presents a compelling case for being optimistic that economic growth really will keep making the world continually better

s: Lenovo's 14-inch business ThinkPad line with AMD or Intel options, positioned as the mainstream Linux-friendly workhorse.
w: HN Linux users say it just works under Ubuntu and Debian, and one prefers a T14 with Linux to both a MacBook Air and Pro. The AMD Ryzen versions get the best reviews.
ab: For developers wanting a Linux-friendly business laptop
Upgradeable RAM, classic ThinkPad keyboard, AMD or Intel
Pick the generation carefully; early ones had soldered RAM

q.t: I prefer T14+Linux to both of them.

s: A compact 12.1-inch ThinkPad from 2010, popular for Linux and BSD use.
w: HN users love its small size, durability, battery life and trouble-free Linux, CentOS and FreeBSD support, and bought it cheap used. It sits in the 'last classic keyboard' ThinkPad line.
ab: For fans of small, used Linux/BSD ThinkPads
Compact, durable, decent battery with extended cell
Very old; 12-inch screen and limited power

q.t: It's cheap, good battery life, durable, does everything I need from a laptop.

s: A slim 14-inch ThinkPad from 2012, one of the last with the classic keyboard layout, popular with Linux users.
w: HN users say it is solid and the best balance of size and power, running Ubuntu and Arch for years. The trackpad is missed by a former user who moved to a Retina MacBook.
ab: For used-laptop buyers wanting a slim, solid ThinkPad
Great balance of size and power, Linux-friendly
Old hardware; battery and display are dated

q.t: I find it to be the best balance of physical size and computing power there is to find.

s: Sony's wireless over-ear headphones with strong active noise cancellation and long battery life.
w: HN buyers recommend it for long coding sessions, Zoom calls and travel. Users praise its noise cancelling and Bluetooth, though one prefers AirPods Max for physical buttons and charging while in use.
ab: For people wanting top noise-cancelling for work or travel
Bluetooth, ANC, long battery life
Touch controls; ear cups can get sweaty

q.t: Works great for cancelling out the dog yipping during multi-hour zoom meetings.

s: A satirical Christian epistolary novel of letters from a senior demon advising his nephew on tempting a human.
w: HN readers call it life changing, with one letter in particular, and value how it plays with logic in fiction. Several reread it, noting it is written from a Christian point of view.
ab: For readers who like satire and moral reflection
Short epistolary format
Written from a Christian viewpoint

q.t: I love the way the book plays with logic in a fictional style.

s: Bertrand Meyer's large treatise on object-oriented design, design by contract and the Eiffel language, in its second edition.
w: HN programmers call it a classic, well-written and engaging, even if they don't agree with all of it, and suggest it as an alternative deep read to SICP.
ab: For programmers who want a rigorous take on OO design
Introduces design by contract, with Eiffel
Very long; second edition is far bigger than the first

q.t: A classic, written in an engaging style that makes the book very readable and conveys important ideas about programming and software engineering

s: A sweeping history of how states, the rule of law and accountable government emerged, from prehuman times to the French Revolution.
w: HN readers call it the best history of political institutions, something that made political history fall into place, with the sequel Political Order and Political Decay also mentioned.
ab: For readers wanting to understand how states and institutions form
Broad history from early humans to 1789
Long and academic in style

q.t: Still, it explains so much about institutions, governing, and generally how societies work.

t: Metamagical Themas: Questing for the Essence of Mind and Pattern
s: A collection of Douglas Hofstadter's Scientific American columns on cognition, creativity, self-reference, Lisp, game theory and the nature of mind.
w: Readers describe it as mind-expanding and a real game changer for how they think, and recommend it beyond Hofstadter's more famous Godel, Escher, Bach.
ab: For readers who loved Godel, Escher, Bach
Essays on AI, creativity, cooperation and Lisp
1980s columns; some topics are dated

q.t: this book was a game changer for me

t: Ending Aging: The Rejuvenation Breakthroughs That Could Reverse Human Aging in Our Lifetime
s: Biogerontologist Aubrey de Grey lays out the SENS research agenda, which treats aging as a set of repairable cellular damage.
w: HN longevity fans point to it as the thorough, optimistic overview of the science of aging and the case for funding repair-based research like SENS.
ab: For readers curious about longevity research and rejuvenation
Explains seven categories of age-related damage and proposed therapies
Controversial; de Grey's claims and record draw skepticism on HN

q.t: It's interesting, thorough, and optimistic.

t: Teach Your Child to Read in 100 Easy Lessons
s: A scripted phonics program with 100 short daily lessons for teaching a young child to read English.
w: HN parents say it works with about 15 minutes a day and needs no special training. Several used it to teach children before kindergarten.
ab: For parents of children about 3 to 5 not yet reading
Scripted lessons that build step by step
Uses a modified alphabet early on; English only

q.t: It is so intelligently organized, each day building on the last.

s: A rigorous, proof-based treatment of high-school mathematics covering arithmetic, algebra, geometry and trigonometry, by the Yale mathematician Serge Lang.
w: HN commenters recommend it for adults who want to rebuild a solid math foundation before calculus. It is described as streamlined and rigorous, though somewhat dry.
ab: For adults refreshing math before calculus or proofs
Proof-based approach rather than mechanical drills
Dry in places; needs real effort

q.t: for a rigorous proof-based approach to high school math, you may enjoy

t: Developer Hegemony: The Future of Labor
s: A book on how corporations treat software developers and the labor economics behind it, with advice on becoming an independent, strategic-minded professional.
w: HN readers point to it when someone is stuck in a bad job or asking about leverage. They like the practical advice on dealing with corporate politics and on engineers having a say in strategy.
ab: For developers frustrated with corporate career structures
Mix of labor-history argument and practical career alternatives
Pointed, opinionated, and not for everyone

q.t: makes the case for engineers being involved in planning and strategy

t: The Last Lion: Winston Spencer Churchill
s: Multi-volume biography of Winston Churchill, begun by William Manchester and completed by Paul Reid, tracing his life from childhood through the Second World War.
w: HN readers name it as the best biography or best read of a year, giving a close view of Churchill and how close Europe came to falling. It is enormous, and one commenter hedges on recommending it.
ab: For history readers who want a deep biography of Churchill
Three volumes, thousands of pages
Takes a major time commitment

q.t: The best thing I read this year was "The Last Lion", a three-volume biography of Winston Churchill.

t: Stalin: The Court of the Red Tsar
s: Biography of Joseph Stalin that focuses on his inner circle, rivalries and daily life at the Soviet court.
w: HN readers recommend it as a gripping, almost unbelievable account of Stalin's rule, often along with Montefiore's other books. One says the stories read like fiction.
ab: For readers interested in Soviet history and Stalin's inner circle
Narrative, anecdote-heavy style
Dark subject matter; long

q.t: It's honestly hard to tell if the narratives outlined in the book are real; it reads like fiction

t: Artificial Life: A Report from the Frontier Where Computers Meet Biology
s: A journalist's account of the early artificial life field, from von Neumann and Turing to the researchers simulating evolution and life in computers.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a fascinating, accessible history of early computing pioneers and artificial life research, with the caveat that it is dated.
ab: For readers curious about alife, cellular automata and early computing
Narrative journalism rather than technical
Written in 1993, so recent work is missing

q.t: It's slightly dated, but I thought it was a really good introduction.

t: Your Memory: How It Works and How to Improve It
s: A practical guide to how memory works and a range of techniques for improving it.
w: Recommended as a more instructional alternative to Moonwalking with Einstein, and by one reader as one of the books that influenced their life.
ab: For readers who want practical memory training
Explains both the science and the techniques
Not a narrative like Moonwalking with Einstein

q.t: But what may have influenced my life the most is this book:

s: A standalone wireless virtual reality headset that can also connect to a PC for desktop VR.
w: Showed up again and again in best-purchase threads: people credit it with making VR cheap and portable, and with getting them to exercise and stay sane through lockdowns.
ab: For gaming, fitness and casual VR
Standalone or tethered to a PC
Facebook account requirement annoyed some; superseded by newer Quest models

q.t: incredible multipurpose entertainment and excercise device

t: Working in Public: The Making and Maintenance of Open Source Software
s: A study of how open source communities and maintainers work today, including a taxonomy of project types and the role of attention.
w: HN brings it up in threads on maintainers, bounties and burnout. Commenters call it super relevant research into open source projects and communities.
ab: For maintainers, contributors and OSS funders
Defines project types like federations and stadiums
Focus on GitHub-era dynamics

q.t: I will take this opportunity to mention Nadia Eghbal's book covering her work researching open source projects & communities.

s: A marketing framework for clarifying your message by telling a customer-centered story.
w: Recommended for focusing a startup's message.
ab: For founders and marketers
Framework
Popular

q.t: I found this book very helpful in getting my startup to focus:

s: A guide to building an outbound sales process with specialized roles, cold email and repeatable pipeline.
w: Recommended to technical founders who struggle with sales and cold outreach, because it makes sales a process.
ab: For B2B founders building outbound sales
Process-focused
Written for SaaS of 2011

q.t: I was spinning my wheels as a technical guy for many years, and that book really clicked for me

t: AntiPatterns: Refactoring Software, Architectures, and Projects in Crisis
by: William J. Brown, Raphael C. Malveau et al.
s: A catalog of recurring bad practices in software development, architecture and project management, each with its causes and a refactored solution.
w: HN commenters recommend it for brownfield work, where recognizing common failure patterns and their fixes is most useful. One calls it an all-time favorite.
ab: For developers and leads working in messy existing codebases
Covers code, architecture and management antipatterns
From 1998; the examples lean on CORBA-era enterprise software

q.t: one of my all-time favorite books

t: Methods of Mathematics Applied to Calculus, Probability, and Statistics
s: A Dover text by Richard Hamming that teaches calculus, probability and statistics with an emphasis on applying mathematics to real problems.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a rigorous but approachable way to relearn the math they forgot from college. It comes up in threads on learning math from first principles.
ab: For programmers and engineers rebuilding their math foundations
Covers calculus, probability and statistics in one volume
Rigorous and dense; exercises matter

q.t: is an excellent and rigorous introduction text

t: The Model Thinker: What You Need to Know to Make Data Work for You
s: A tour of many mathematical models for thinking.
w: Recommended for mental models.
ab: For analytical thinkers
Reference-like
Some math

q.t: That said this book has helped enormously

s: The 1934 foundational text of value investing, teaching how to analyze stocks and bonds from financial statements.
w: HN readers cite it as the book that gets to the heart of what stocks and bonds are; commenters note the authors write clearly, though the data is old.
ab: For serious investors studying value investing
Dense and long; The Intelligent Investor is the easier start
Examples are from the 1930s

q.t: It's ancient, but it really gets to the heart of what bonds and stocks actually are

s: A small 12-inch IBM/Lenovo ThinkPad from 2006, now popular with free-software users because it can run Libreboot.
w: HN commenters loved its build quality, keyboard and battery life when new, and today recommend it for fully libre, blob-free setups.
ab: Old but rugged; best for libre-software enthusiasts.
Used units only; slow by modern standards.
Great keyboard and build quality per owners.

q.t: As far as hardware is concerned, it's the Lexus of laptops.

s: A skeptic's examination of pseudoscience, superstition and why smart people believe strange things.
w: HN uses it when explaining brainwashing, cults and denial.
ab: For skeptics
Covers Holocaust denial and cults
Early 2000s examples

q.t: does a good job of reviewing historical evidence for the Holocaust, and responding to claims of deniers

t: Tricks of the 3D Game Programming Gurus
s: A tutorial on building a software 3D rasterizer from scratch, covering the math, lighting, shading and textures.
w: Recommended for learning how 3D graphics actually work without relying on a graphics API. Commenters call it timeless despite its late-90s C and DirectX code.
ab: For learners who want to build a 3D renderer from scratch
Covers rasterization, lighting, textures and the math
C and DirectX code is old

q.t: An absolutely phenomenal book I'd recommend on writing your own computer graphics from scratch

s: An illustrated encyclopedia of 125 design principles, each explained on a two-page spread with examples from many fields.
w: Recommended to developers who want design vocabulary without a heavy textbook. Handed to new hires as a design primer, and cited when explaining why things like helmets behave counterintuitively.
ab: For developers and non-designers building design intuition
Short, visual entries you can dip into in any order
Broad survey; shallow on any single principle

q.t: Developers looking to increase their design vocabulary and skillset outside of top five lists may find this introductory book beneficial

s: Clausewitz's 19th-century treatise on the nature of war, strategy and politics.
w: HN cites it as the foundational work on military strategy and a surprising source of ideas for business leaders and strategists, though translation choice matters.
ab: For readers interested in strategy, politics and leadership
Dense 19th-century prose
Many translations; pick carefully

q.t: An important essay about strategy and war, politics and management

s: A Manning book that teaches Elixir and the OTP framework by building small, practical, fault-tolerant concurrent applications.
w: HN's frequent pick for experienced coders learning Elixir and OTP. Readers say it's short and helps you understand how Erlang/Elixir projects are structured.
ab: For experienced programmers new to Elixir and OTP
Project-based and fairly short
Covers older Elixir versions; check what is current

q.t: it helped me wrap my head around OTP and how erland/elixir projects are structured

s: A 14-inch ThinkPad business laptop from 2016 with a classic keyboard, replaceable batteries and good Linux support.
w: HN users liked it as a cheap, durable used laptop with a great keyboard, long battery life and Linux that works out of the box.
ab: For developers who want a cheap used ThinkPad
Great keyboard and battery life
Old hardware by now

q.t: Great keyboard, great battery life, great linux support out of the box

t: Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation
by: John E. Hopcroft, Rajeev Motwani et al.
s: The standard textbook on finite automata, formal languages, context-free grammars, Turing machines and computability.
w: Often listed among the CS theory books worth owning in print, because the content doesn't expire. One commenter calls it approachable and complete.
ab: For self-taught programmers ready for formal theory
Covers automata, grammars, decidability and complexity
Nicknamed the 'Cinderella book' after its cover

q.t: It is very approachable and presents some very interesting topics

t: How to Build a Car: The Autobiography of the World's Greatest Formula 1 Designer
s: The memoir of Formula 1 designer Adrian Newey, covering his career, car design process and the engineering behind championship-winning cars.
w: Engineering and F1 fans find it an enjoyable look at a designer's technical thinking and the process behind winning cars, and it keeps turning up in year-end reading lists.
ab: For F1 fans and engineers who like design stories
Mix of memoir and technical process
Racing-heavy; non-fans may find parts niche

q.t: that famous F1 car designer... Great read.

s: A 1909 short story about humanity living underground, wholly dependent on a vast machine that mediates all communication and needs.
w: HN readers keep pointing to it as eerily prescient about internet-mediated life, and a short enough read to recommend to anyone.
ab: For anyone wanting a classic of early sci-fi
Very short, about 35 pages
Edwardian prose can feel dated

q.t: Extremely prescient and a fun, short book.

t: The Blade Itself (The First Law Trilogy)
s: Joe Abercrombie's dark fantasy trilogy beginning with The Blade Itself, known for gritty characters and violence.
w: HN readers love the grim tone and character development and praise the audiobook narration by Steven Pacey. One finds the early books too violent.
ab: Dark, violent grimdark fantasy.
Audiobooks narrated by Steven Pacey are well loved.
Early books are very violent.

q.t: Grim and gritty, with phenomenal character development that hones in on the fallibility of people.

by: Eric R. Kandel, James H. Schwartz et al.
s: The standard graduate-level neuroscience textbook covering cells, circuits, perception, movement, cognition, and disease.
w: Whenever HN argues about brains, consciousness, or neural nets, someone points to Kandel as the real neuroscience reference, the book to read before holding strong opinions.
ab: For readers who want actual neuroscience, not pop-science summaries
Encyclopedic, over 1,700 pages, and heavy to carry and read
Newer editions exist; the fundamentals still hold up

q.t: Neuroscience has discovered a lot about consciousness. I recommend Principles of Neural Science if you're interested

s: Mojang's open-ended sandbox building and survival game, available on PC, consoles and mobile, with strong modding support.
w: HN parents mention it as a screen-time-friendly game their kids play, and a suggested route to modding and Java for a tech-curious child. Commenters contrast it with endless YouTube.
ab: For kids and families who like building and creating
Modding offers a route into programming
Multiplayer needs supervision; time limits are common

q.t: Setup Minecraft which I would assume she already plays if she likes tech.

s: A Humanscale ergonomic chair with no manual adjustments that uses counterbalanced recline, available with an articulating headrest.
w: HN owners like that it lets gravity do the work, with a headrest that follows you and no knobs to fiddle with. One buyer found it painful after a week, so try before buying.
ab: For people who want a self-adjusting, knob-free chair
Optional articulating headrest; sturdy and heavy
Fit is personal; one commenter got sore

q.t: I now swear by the Humanscale Freedom w/ Headrest. Extremely comfortable

s: A classic Swiss-style text on using grids to organize layouts.
w: HN recommends it as the best resource on why and how to use grids. Programmers learning design say it informed layouts and frameworks like Bootstrap.
ab: For developers learning layout
Swiss design classic
Print-focused examples

q.t: The best resource on why and how to use grids is

s: A mid-priced adjustable ergonomic office chair from Herman Miller with a flexing back and customizable colors.
w: HN users say it cured back pain from a cheap chair and don't regret the price. Many compare it with the Aeron and advise trying chairs in person since fit is personal.
ab: For long desk days at home or work
Pricey, though cheaper than the Aeron
Fit is personal; try in a showroom if possible

q.t: I ended up going with the Mirra 2 and fell in love with it. It completely solved my back pain within two months.

s: The foundational text on causal inference, introducing causal graphs, do-calculus and counterfactuals.
w: HN points people here as the source of causal inference, from the Turing Award winner who pioneered the field.
ab: For stats and ML readers wanting causal methods
Technical and dense
Pearl's Book of Why is a gentler start

q.t: see the work by Judea Pearl, he pretty much singlehandedly pioneered the field.

s: A guide to writing idiomatic Ruby, teaching the language's conventions and style through short chapters.
w: Recommended as a good book for learning idiomatic Ruby, including for beginners. One commenter warned against it for Rails newcomers, citing RSpec and outdated idioms.
ab: For people learning Ruby who want idiomatic style
Short chapters on conventions
One HN reader found it dated for Rails beginners

q.t: Eloquent Ruby is an excellent book for beginners.

t: Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action
s: Nobel laureate Elinor Ostrom's empirical study of how communities manage shared resources without either privatization or central control.
w: HN uses it as the counterweight to the tragedy of the commons, from Tesla debates to open source sustainability. Commenters stress it is built on real case studies.
ab: For readers interested in institutions, economics and open source
Case studies of communities managing shared resources
Academic in tone

q.t: There is a body of literature on the subject how self governing groups escape the tragedy of the commons.

s: The standard university textbook on derivatives pricing, covering options, futures, swaps and risk management.
w: The go-to reference for derivatives; a trader says he survives on it. Older editions are cheap used.
ab: For finance students and quants
Heavy, textbook-style; not a casual read
Older editions work fine and cost less

q.t: The standard text on the topic is the Hull book.

s: Teaches Rust through systems-programming projects such as a key/value store, a CPU emulator and a network client, aimed at developers who already know the basics.
w: HN commenters recommend it for learning Rust through systems programming, with worked projects rather than abstract exercises. One notes it covers networking too.
ab: For programmers who want to learn Rust through real projects
Assumes some programming background
Based on the Rust of its release year; check for updates

q.t: Rust in Action teaches Rust through systems programming

s: Heidegger's 1927 foundational work of existential phenomenology on the meaning of being and human existence.
w: Cited by HN readers as a landmark of philosophy, with one finding its idea of readiness-to-hand useful for thinking about usability. Everyone warns it is very hard to read unprepared.
ab: For serious readers of continental philosophy
Dense, difficult prose; consider a companion guide
Author's Nazi ties noted by commenters

q.t: Heidegger's explanation of readiness-to-hand in Being and Time has done more for my usability and process inefficiency evaluating skills

s: A low-profile wireless keyboard that connects to up to three devices by Bluetooth or USB receiver.
w: HN typists who find mechanical boards fatiguing like its low profile and easy switching between devices. It pairs with the MX Master mouse for multi-computer desks. Some people simply dislike low-profile keys.
ab: For people who want a comfortable low-profile keyboard
Multi-device pairing, wireless, backlit keys
Not mechanical; low-profile feel is a taste

q.t: IF you're not gaming, I really like the Logitech MX keys. Its super low profile, you can attach 3 devices to it

t: The Great Leveler: Violence and the History of Inequality from the Stone Age to the Twenty-First Century
s: A history of economic inequality arguing that only mass violence and catastrophe have ever substantially reduced it.
w: Comes up on HN whenever inequality is debated. Readers cite it as the key book for the thesis that wars, revolutions and plagues are the great levelers.
ab: For readers interested in the long history of inequality
Covers thousands of years of evidence
Bleak, contested conclusion

q.t: I recommend Walter Scheidel's "The Great Leveler".

t: An Astronaut's Guide to Life on Earth
s: Former ISS commander Chris Hadfield's memoir and life lessons from astronaut training and spaceflight.
w: HN readers call it an inspirational tale with lots of general advice, showing how seemingly insurmountable preparation can be accomplished by determined people.
ab: For readers who like memoir with practical lessons
Behind-the-scenes look at astronaut training
Self-help flavor; light on space science

q.t: really shows how seemingly insurmountable tasks can be accomplished by determined individuals

s: 12.5-inch Lenovo ThinkPad ultraportable from 2015 with a TrackPoint, an internal battery plus a hot-swappable external one, and standard ports.
w: HN developers run Linux on it, praising the keyboard and TrackPoint, six or more hours of battery with heavy use, and expandable battery life. A few say ThinkPads have slipped on quality control.
ab: For developers who want a small ThinkPad for Linux
Great keyboard and TrackPoint, expandable battery
Old hardware now; HN says ThinkPad QA is a lottery

q.t: Thinkpad x260 is pretty good

s: A short nonfiction book arguing that modern society lacks the close communal bonds that people feel in times of hardship and war.
w: Showed up on many HN favorite nonfiction and mind-expanding book lists. Readers say it showed them the importance of community and why people feel close in crisis, though one reader rated it only 6/10.
ab: For readers interested in community, war and belonging
Short and readable
Uneven, per one reader

q.t: taught me how important it is to be part of a close community

t: Information Rules: A Strategic Guide to the Network Economy
s: A strategy book explaining how pricing, lock-in, standards, and network effects work in information markets with near-zero marginal cost.
w: Called an excellent guide to the economics of information goods by HN commenters, and cited for its treatment of vendor lock-in and platform competition.
ab: For founders and product people in software and media
Covers pricing, versioning, lock-in, and network effects
Written in 1998; examples are dated

q.t: Information Rules is an excellent book going into details of how markets work in information economies

t: The $12 Million Stuffed Shark: The Curious Economics of Contemporary Art
s: An economist's look at how contemporary art is priced and sold, covering auction houses, galleries, branding, and why some works fetch millions.
w: HN turns to it to explain art markets and status goods, from why a tax bill can run into millions to why an NFT of a tweet behaves like contemporary art.
ab: For readers curious about how the art market works
Case studies of dealers, auctions, and artists
Focuses on the high end of the market, circa 2010

q.t: Once you are branded, you can pretty much sell anything as expensive art.

s: A short parable-style management book teaching three techniques: one-minute goals, one-minute praisings, and one-minute reprimands.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a quick, simple starting point for new managers and tech leads. It is short and built on just three ideas that can be used straight away.
ab: For first-time managers and technical leads
A very quick read in story form
Simple and basic; experienced managers may find it thin

q.t: It's simple but effective and malleable once you've had some experience.

t: An Introduction to Information Theory: Symbols, Signals and Noise
s: A readable, non-technical introduction to Shannon's information theory, covering entropy, coding and noise.
w: Recommended as an easy-to-approach introduction to information theory and a cheap, surprisingly good text. Commenters cite its chapter on randomness and entropy.
ab: For curious readers new to information theory
Low-math exposition; cheap Dover paperback
First published 1961, so later developments are absent

q.t: I was introduced to Shannon's theory through Pierce's text, which is also surprisingly good and cheap

t: Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions
s: Gary Klein's study of how experts such as firefighters and pilots make fast decisions under pressure using intuition and pattern recognition.
w: Recommended in threads on intuition, mental models and decision-making. Commenters say it shows how experience feeds good intuition, especially under pressure.
ab: For leaders and engineers making decisions under pressure
Field research on firefighters, pilots and other experts
Describes naturalistic decision-making, not a how-to

q.t: It talks about how experienced people can make higher quality decisions by taking into account their intuition vs just trying to decide using logic.

s: A collection of essays by Ayn Rand and others making the moral and economic case for laissez-faire capitalism.
w: Cited in political debates as a core laissez-faire text, including by commenters who answer 'what is capitalism?' with it. Appears in a reading list.
ab: For readers exploring Objectivist and libertarian ideas
Essays by Rand, Greenspan and others
Polemical; one side of the debate

s: Pulitzer-winning collection of John McPhee's five books on the geology of North America, told through road trips with working geologists.
w: Commenters point non-geologists to it as a gripping, beautifully written tour of North American geology and the people who study it.
ab: For curious readers with no geology background
Five books in one big volume
Heavy on portraits of geologists

q.t: I have no geology background but found it utterly riveting

t: Ratio: The Simple Codes Behind the Craft of Everyday Cooking
s: Cookbook built around basic ingredient ratios rather than fixed recipes.
w: Recommended for explaining the why of recipes so cooks can improvise, with one complaint that it uses volume instead of weight.
ab: For cooks wanting technique over recipes
Ratio-based approach
Mixes weights and volumes

q.t: Ratio by Michael Ruhlman does a great job of breaking down the whys of recipes

s: A short primer on how central banks and the Fed operate, written by a former Fed trader, covering reserves, QE and fractional reserve banking.
w: Recommended repeatedly as the gentle, current introduction to how central banking really works. Commenters like that it is written post-Covid and by someone who worked on the Fed's trading desk.
ab: For readers new to central banking, monetary plumbing and QE
Short, plain-language primer with a post-2020 viewpoint
Introductory, so experts will find it light

q.t: Fantastic overview of how the current central banking system works

by: John H. Conway and Richard K. Guy
s: A popular tour of number facts and mathematics.
w: HN readers praise it as full of little gems.
ab: For math lovers
Browsable
Illustrated

q.t: It describes everything I loved in math that I wasn't able to pinpoint.

t: Higher-Order Perl: Transforming Programs with Programs
s: A book on functional programming techniques in Perl: closures, iterators, parsers and higher-order functions.
w: Called an unusually good book whose longevity comes partly from being a free download; recommended for learning to think differently with a language.
ab: For Perl programmers wanting functional techniques
Free PDF from the author
Perl 5 era examples

q.t: Part of this is that it's an unusually good book.

s: The 1986 foundational volume of the connectionist PDP research program that revived neural networks.
w: HN commenters cite it as the founding text of 1980s neural-network research, recommended as classical pioneering work and read by people reviewing early AI history.
ab: For readers of the history of neural networks and cognition
Foundational connectionist papers from 1986
Technical and dated; not a modern deep learning guide

t: The Charisma Machine: The Life, Death, and Legacy of One Laptop per Child
s: An academic case study of the One Laptop per Child project and why its technology-first vision failed.
w: HN readers point to it whenever OLPC or edtech comes up, praising its detailed fieldwork in Paraguay and its account of what went wrong.
ab: For readers of tech history and edtech critique
Based on on-the-ground research in Paraguay
Academic, critical of techno-utopianism

q.t: excellent 2019 book on the OLPC project, "The Charisma Machine" [1], does a really good job looking at all the things that went wrong

s: The O'Reilly guide to the sed stream editor and the awk text-processing language.
w: HN commenters call it fun and a quick read, around two hours, for learning two Unix tools that work together as a team.
ab: For anyone learning Unix text processing
Covers sed and awk together
Written in the 1990s

q.t: The O'Reilly Sed & Awk book is a lot of fun, too.

s: A clinical psychologist's argument that your twenties matter for career, relationships and identity, with advice on using them.
w: HN readers recommend it as a gift for anyone in their twenties and say it motivated their move into a fulfilling tech career. It is often read while still young.
ab: For people in their twenties or early thirties
Case-based advice on work, love and planning
Pop psychology; written for a US audience

q.t: "The Defining Decade" by Meg Jay to anyone in their twenties.

t: Barbarians at the Gate: The Fall of RJR Nabisco
s: Narrative account of the 1988 leveraged buyout battle for RJR Nabisco, the biggest takeover of its time, told through the executives and bankers involved.
w: HN readers call it a classic of business writing, with a gripping inside view of Wall Street and deal-making. It is regularly named among the best business books.
ab: For readers who like Wall Street stories, finance, and corporate drama
Real-life deal told as a page-turner
About the late 1980s; not tech-related

q.t: not tech-related but one of the best business books of all time

s: 14-inch Lenovo ThinkPad business laptop, a lighter T-series model sold with AMD Ryzen or Intel processors.
w: HN developers like it for good Ryzen performance, a sturdy chassis and the classic ThinkPad keyboard, and several switched to it from MacBooks or X1 Carbons. Linux mostly runs on it.
ab: For developers who want a portable ThinkPad that runs Linux
Ryzen option has good performance for the weight
Linux may need some tweaking; check the generation

q.t: Good ryzen performance, nice keyboard (it's a thinkpad) and lightweight

s: A Discworld novel in which con man Moist von Lipwig is made master of the Ankh-Morpork Royal Bank and Mint.
w: Suggested alongside Going Postal as funny Discworld fantasy about finance and currency, and as a fun story with full characters.
ab: For Discworld fans and readers who like humor
Best after Going Postal
One commenter meant Desan's non-fiction book of the same title

q.t: I'd also strongly recommend Terry P's Going Postal and Making Money.

s: Mitch Albom's memoir of weekly conversations with his former professor Morrie Schwartz as he dies of ALS.
w: HN readers recommend it as a moving short book about life and death, and one found it through a suggestion on the site.
ab: Short, gentle memoir about life lessons near the end of life.
A common gift book.
Emotional subject matter.

q.t: really great book about life and everything brilliant about it.

s: A high-performance System76 Linux laptop with an NVIDIA GPU that ships with Pop!_OS or Ubuntu.
w: HN developers praise it as a fast development machine with open-source-friendly vendor support, though one owner who switched to Razer wasn't impressed with hardware.
ab: Powerful Linux laptop with discrete GPU.
Choice of Pop!_OS or Ubuntu.
Heavy desktop-replacement size; hardware quality criticized by one owner.

q.t: as a developer it’s the best laptop I’ve owned

s: A steampunk alternate-history novel in which Babbage's computer arrives in Victorian Britain.
w: HN readers recommend it as a cornerstone of steampunk and a computing-history-flavored novel by Gibson and Sterling.
ab: For fans of alternate history and computing lore.
Co-written with Bruce Sterling.
Dense Victorian setting.

q.t: the first and, so far, best steampunk novel

s: The second Dune novel, set twelve years after Paul Atreides takes the throne.
w: HN readers recommend it as a worthwhile Dune sequel, with one saying it made them critical of organized religion. One didn't enjoy the sequels.
ab: Read after the original Dune.
Darker and more political than the first book.
Slower paced; opinions split on sequels.

q.t: Dune, Dune Messiah and Children of Dune by Frank Herbert are my favorites.

s: A wired vertical ergonomic mouse that holds the hand in a handshake position to reduce wrist strain, made for right-handed users.
w: Commenters with RSI or tendonitis say it fixed their hand pain, and it is the mouse Acme editor users tend to mention.
ab: For people with wrist, hand or tendon pain from regular mice
Handshake grip keeps the forearm from twisting
Takes a few days to get used to; right-handed model only

q.t: It has been fantastic (though I have the 3rd gen model).

t: Work Rules! Insights from Inside Google That Will Transform How You Live and Lead
s: Google's former HR head describes the company's approaches to hiring, culture and talent management.
w: Recommended for hiring ideas like hiring people better than you and hiring by committee. One reader called it a bit effusive but broadly applicable.
ab: For managers and HR-minded founders
Google-scale; may not translate to small teams
Reads somewhat like corporate PR

q.t: highlights many things that have been tried and implemented at Google to improve recruiting and retention

s: Short book arguing that prisons are an outdated institution and exploring abolitionist alternatives.
w: Recommended as a starting point for people wanting to understand prisons and mass incarceration from an abolitionist perspective.
ab: For readers new to prison abolition arguments
Short and polemical
Strongly one-sided viewpoint

q.t: I urge everyone looking for starting knowledge to start with Angela Davi's Are Prisons Obsolete?

t: A Theory of Fun for Game Design
s: Illustrated book arguing that fun in games comes from learning, drawing on game design and psychology.
w: Recommended even to non-game-makers as an accessible but deep look at motivation, learning and fun.
ab: For game designers and curious readers
Accessible and illustrated
Short and quick to read

q.t: It's a great read that's accessible but also deep and thorough.

t: Black Holes and Time Warps: Einstein's Outrageous Legacy
s: A popular-science history of black holes, relativity and gravitational waves, written by a Nobel-winning physicist who helped found LIGO.
w: Recommended as the best lay introduction to black holes and gravitational waves, straight from the physicist behind LIGO. Repeatedly offered whenever LIGO or black hole news comes up.
ab: For curious readers with no physics degree
Covers relativity, black holes and the road to LIGO
Published in 1994, so newer discoveries are missing

q.t: I would recommend (as I've done before) Kip Thorn's book _Black Holes and Time Warps_

t: Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models
s: A graduate-level text on regression and multilevel modeling with R and BUGS code, covering both frequentist and Bayesian approaches.
w: HN's practical pick for applied statistics. Commenters call it among the most readable books on data analysis, with plenty of code, and mention its causal inference techniques.
ab: For analysts and researchers modeling real data
Plenty of R and BUGS example code
Code is dated; Stan has since taken over from BUGS

q.t: It's one of the most readable books on data analysis I've come across

t: Notes on the Synthesis of Form
s: Alexander's early book on design as fitting form to context, a precursor to his pattern language work.
w: Praised as dense and meaning-rich, and cited as a classic critique of designed environments. Influential among software designers.
ab: For designers and architects of software or buildings
Short but extremely dense
Abstract and academic

q.t: is the most meaning-dense book

t: How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking
s: A popular math book showing how mathematical reasoning applies to everyday decisions and problems.
w: HN's pick when someone asks how to apply mathematics in life; it also gets cited for examples like flawed lottery design.
ab: For general readers who like math
Story-driven and accessible
Light on formal technique

q.t: There are quite a few popular books on this topic, e.g. How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking

s: Comic fantasy and sci-fi novel by Scott Alexander, first published as a web serial, about a Kabbalistic sweatshop in Silicon Valley and an alternate history where magic works.
w: HN readers describe it as a delightful, funny yarn with echoes of Douglas Adams. It's a favorite from Slate Star Codex readers, and one rated it only 7 of 10.
ab: For readers of absurdist fiction and Slate Star Codex
Heavy with puns, Kabbalah and theodicy
Long and quirky; may not appeal to everyone

q.t: The funnest and funniest sci-fi yarn since Douglas Adams

s: Ortega y Gasset's 1930 essay on the rise of mass society and what the dominance of the 'average man' means for civilization.
w: Appears on HN lists of eye-opening books and old books that remain relevant. A commenter links it while saying its warnings still feel timely.
ab: For readers interested in political and social philosophy
Short and written in 1930
Cited more often than discussed in detail

s: A 1957 exposé of how advertisers use psychological research to manipulate consumer behavior.
w: People say it changed how they see advertising and sales gimmicks. Even though it's old and perhaps exaggerated in places, they say its tricks are still everywhere.
ab: For anyone interested in advertising and persuasion
1950s examples, some exaggerated
Good primer on motivational research

q.t: I read this book as a kid, it changed how I view the world and I've never forgotten it's lessons.

t: Masters of Deception: The Gang That Ruled Cyberspace
s: A true-crime account of the New York hacker gangs MOD and the Legion of Doom and their conflict in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
w: Recommended on lists of true hacker stories and cyber history, and one commenter says it captures the spirit of the era.
ab: For readers who like hacker history and true crime
Covers the late 80s and early 90s hacker scene
Dated technology, but a good period piece

q.t: is a true crime story covering the late 80s/early 90s era of hacking in the US

t: The Little Learner: A Straight Line to Deep Learning
s: A Scheme-based, dialogue-style introduction to deep learning that builds gradient descent and neural networks from basic functions.
w: Recommended as a fun route into machine learning and Lisp together, with no frameworks. One reader calls it fundamental.
ab: For programmers who want ML basics from first principles
Uses Scheme and the Malt toolkit
Question-and-answer format

q.t: was just released and is a very fun treatment of both lisp and machine learning.

s: Dante's 14th-century epic poem describing a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise.
w: Cited as a foundational work and sometimes called the greatest work of literature, with a huge influence on culture and many later references.
ab: For readers of classic literature
Many translations exist
Dense with medieval references

q.t: It is hard to underestimate how much it has influenced our culture.

s: A widely used undergraduate textbook on classical electromagnetism, covering electrostatics, magnetostatics, Maxwell's equations and radiation.
w: HN physics people name it as the standard intermediate E&M text, and commenters praise Griffiths for writing that is a pleasure to read.
ab: For physics undergraduates and self-learners with calculus background
Clear, conversational style compared with other physics texts
Pairs well with Griffiths' Quantum Mechanics

q.t: David Griffiths Electrodynamics and Quantum Mechanics are such a pleasure to read for their style of writing.

t: Journey to the End of the Night
s: Céline's 1932 novel following a misanthropic French soldier and doctor from the trenches of WWI to colonial Africa, America and Paris.
w: Recommended by HN readers as a harsh, hopeless but compelling classic that changed their life; one calls it their favorite book in the world.
ab: For readers who like bleak, misanthropic literary fiction
Simple style but not an easy read emotionally
Author's later politics are controversial

q.t: my favorite book in the world. Very misanthropic, set in WWI.

s: An eleven-volume narrative history of Western civilization from ancient times to the Napoleonic era, by Will and Ariel Durant.
w: HN readers describe it as a deeply rewarding, humanist long-form history and one of the most satisfying learning experiences of their lives.
ab: For patient readers wanting a sweeping narrative history
Eleven volumes; a big time commitment
Written in the mid 20th century, scholarship is dated

q.t: 11 volumes of pure joy. Will and Ariel Durant will make you fall in love with mankind.

t: The WEIRDest People in the World
s: Argues that Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic societies are psychological outliers, shaped by medieval Church kinship policies, and explains their rise.
w: HN readers recommend it as a new framework for why societies evolved differently and why the modern West arose. Commenters say its ideas stick with you long after reading.
ab: For readers interested in cultural psychology and the origins of modernity
Long and sweeping, with academic detail
The central thesis is debated by historians

q.t: the ideas in there have really stuck in my head

s: William Burroughs' 1959 fragmentary, hallucinatory novel about addiction and control, a landmark of the Beat movement and of transgressive fiction.
w: Shows up in favourite-fiction lists from HN readers who like the strange and extreme. One calls it smutty and insane and compares it to Deleuze and Guattari's A Thousand Plateaus.
ab: For readers who want experimental, non-linear fiction
Graphic content about drugs and sex
Not a conventional narrative

q.t: It's smutty and insane. Oddly reminds me of 1000 Plateaus by Gilles Deleuze and Felix Guattari

s: Hemingway's 1926 novel about expatriates in 1920s Paris and Spain.
w: HN readers describe it as a great book and one of Hemingway's finest, with refreshing language that moves even readers who expected less.
ab: Short classic of the Lost Generation.
Spare, direct prose.
Slow and plotless to some.

q.t: The Sun Also Rises - Hemingway (recommended, refreshing language)

s: Douglas Coupland's satirical novel about game developers in a Vancouver tech company.
w: HN readers like it as a funny tech-industry novel, with one saying it helped them see that corporatism, not themselves, was broken. Several rank it with Microserfs.
ab: Satire of 2000s software and game development.
Companion in spirit to Microserfs.
Dated tech references.

q.t: helped me realize that it was corporatism, not me, that was broken.

s: Buckminster Fuller's 1969 short book on treating Earth as a system with finite resources, and on comprehensive thinking.
w: HN readers say it changed how they think about the world and its history, and that it shows Fuller was much more than the inventor of Bucky Balls.
ab: For systems thinkers.
Short and visionary.
Written in the 1960s.

q.t: It turns out Bucky was a lot more than the man who invented Bucky Balls

t: Walkable City: How Downtown Can Save America, One Step at a Time
s: An urban planner's case for walkable downtowns, with ten steps to make American cities more pedestrian-friendly.
w: HN commenters recommend it as an accessible, compelling guide to fixing car-dominated cities, and pair it with the parking book by Donald Shoup.
ab: For people interested in cities, transit and housing policy
Ten practical steps with real-world examples
US-focused; assumes some familiarity with American planning

q.t: I have nothing to do with city planning, but I found it super-interesting.

t: The Great Game: The Struggle for Empire in Central Asia
s: A narrative history of the nineteenth-century rivalry between Britain and Russia for control of Central Asia and the approaches to India.
w: HN readers recommend it as the best way to understand Afghanistan and Central Asia's long role as a geopolitical football, and say it reads like an adventure novel.
ab: For readers of history and geopolitics
Narrative style, full of spies and explorers
Covers the 1800s up to World War I

q.t: It reads like a Game of Thrones novel.

t: Class: A Guide Through the American Status System
s: A witty 1983 anatomy of American social class, covering speech, taste, homes, and clothing across status levels.
w: HN readers cite it for how class shows in behavior, from profanity to taste. One calls it dated but holding up, funny, sad, and brutal in its characterizations.
ab: For readers curious about status and social class in the US
Satirical, opinionated tour of class markers
Dated 1980s references and a snobbish tone

q.t: I highly recommend this book, which is dated but holds up pretty well.

s: Short parable about coping with change in work and life.
w: Some HN readers have given away copies as a gift for its short lesson on handling change.
ab: Very short read
Simple parable format
Some find it simplistic

q.t: It is a great little book, which deals with how we handle change in our lives

t: Tribes: We Need You to Lead Us
s: A short book on leadership and building communities of people around a shared idea.
