Heavy, comprehensive and theory-focused
Written in 1990; modern GPU techniques are not covered

q.t: And then personally I've found this to be the clearest theory:

t: Delivered from Distraction: Getting the Most out of Life with Attention Deficit Disorder
by: Edward M. Hallowell, John J. Ratey
s: A guide to adult ADHD by two psychiatrists, covering what the condition is, how it feels, and strategies for coping and treatment.
w: The book HN pulls out when ADHD, procrastination or heavy caffeine use comes up. Commenters say it explains the condition well and is also useful for family members.
ab: For adults who suspect or live with ADHD, and their families
Mixes explanation, case stories and practical coping tips
Older book; treatment advice predates newer research

q.t: It's a fantastic book that explains the condition extremely well

t: Simple Heuristics That Make Us Smart
s: A collection of research on fast and frugal heuristics, showing how simple decision rules can perform as well as complex ones.
w: HN points to it for when simple rules beat elaborate models, including programmers working under limited time or compute.
ab: For readers interested in decision research and algorithms
Shows simple rules rivaling complex models
Academic; edited research collection

q.t: It explains how to get programs to give good answers when time and processing power are limited

s: A bodyweight strength training program built around six progressive movements, each with ten variations.
w: HN's pick for training strength without a gym. Commenters say all you need is floor space and a pull-up bar.
ab: For people who want to train without gym equipment
Progressions for pushups, squats, pull-ups and more
Marketing tone is overblown

q.t: you can do a lot with just a little space on the floor and a pull up bar in the door frame.

t: Web Operations: Keeping the Data On Time
s: An O'Reilly collection of essays by practitioners on running and scaling large web applications.
w: HN's go-to answer on how to run a web app at scale. Commenters recommend it for technical co-founders and for learning scalability.
ab: For developers and ops people running web services
Essays from experienced practitioners
Written around 2010; tooling has changed

q.t: It deals with all the components of building and operating a large web application.

t: Zhuangzi Speaks: The Music of Nature
s: A comic-book version of the Daoist classic Zhuangzi, drawn by Tsai Chih Chung and translated by Brian Bruya.
w: HN readers recommend the comic for getting into the Zhuangzi when the original is impenetrable. One calls it the best English version they know.
ab: For readers new to Daoist philosophy
Illustrated, easy to read
Simplified interpretation of the text

q.t: the best version in English I know is the comic book drawn by Tsai Chih-chung

t: Presentation Zen: Simple Ideas on Presentation Design and Delivery
s: A guide to designing and delivering clean, story-driven presentations with minimal text and strong visuals.
w: HN commenters repeatedly name it the best book on giving presentations, usually as the antidote to bullet-point-heavy slide decks.
ab: For engineers and founders who give talks
Teaches visual simplicity and storytelling
Slide-tool examples are somewhat dated

q.t: By far the best book I've read on this stuff is Presentation Zen

s: The journals the creator of Prince of Persia kept while making his first game, Karateka, as a college student.
w: HN commenters recommend the journals as inspirational reading for game developers and suggest reading them in order alongside the Prince of Persia volume.
ab: For game developers and retro computing fans
Primary-source diaries of an early indie game
Best read together with the Prince of Persia journals

q.t: I found them to be very inspirational.

t: Death by Meeting: A Leadership Fable
s: A business fable about a leader who fixes bad meetings by changing their structure and purpose.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a quick, story-style fix for running better meetings and list it among leadership books.
ab: For managers who run frequent meetings
Told as an easy-to-read fable
Business-book style with simple prescriptions

q.t: terrible at conducting meetings until the main character comes and helps address the issues

s: The autobiography of Walmart's founder, covering how he built the retail giant from a small-town store.
w: HN commenters call it a primary source on Walmart and one of the best business books, citing its retail strategy lessons.
ab: For readers interested in retail and entrepreneurship
Written in the founder's own voice
Some tales are self-congratulatory

q.t: Sam Walton's biography is one of the best business books I've ever read

t: Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life
s: A self-help workbook introducing acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT).
w: Several commenters recommend it as a self-study book for ACT, a blend of CBT and Buddhist meditation concepts.
ab: For self-study of ACT
Exercises throughout
Not a replacement for professional help

q.t: Here's the self-study book I used:

t: Statistics Done Wrong: The Woefully Complete Guide
s: A short guide to common statistical mistakes in research, with concrete examples of how analysis gets abused.
w: Recommended to anyone who consumes studies; even talented engineers often draw wrong conclusions from statistics.
ab: For readers of research and data analysts
Short and example-driven
No heavy math required

q.t: It is a short read but is filled with all the most common ways in which statistical analysis is abused with concrete examples.

t: The New Confessions of an Economic Hit Man
s: John Perkins' memoir of working as a consultant who allegedly helped the US push developing countries into debt.
w: Recommended in threads on the dollar and Chinese lending, though one commenter calls it embellished.
ab: For readers of geopolitics
Memoir; claims disputed
Some details may be embellished

q.t: highly recommended book on the topic of how this works

s: A 1999 popular science book on the enteric nervous system, the gut's network of neurons.
w: Recommended in gut-brain threads as an approachable, still-relevant explanation of the gut's nervous system.
ab: For readers curious about the gut-brain axis
Approachable tone
Published in 1999, so parts are dated

q.t: There is a really good book written in 1999

t: Self-Directed Behavior: Self-Modification for Personal Adjustment
s: A psychology textbook on analyzing and changing your own behavior using behavior-modification methods.
w: HN readers pick it for building and breaking habits, since it is grounded in research and teaches you to find the antecedents of your behavior.
ab: For people who want to change habits systematically
Research-based but readable textbook
Expensive and textbook-formatted

q.t: It's based on scientific research, but the ideas are presented clearly and in a practically useful way.

t: Small Unit Leadership: A Commonsense Approach
s: A short military leadership book on leading small groups, based on the author's Army experience.
w: Recommended by managers for new managers; a commenter likes its lessons on turning around underperformers when you can't fire them.
ab: For new managers and team leads
Short and practical
Military context; some examples dated (1983)

q.t: as having some good lessons for business leaders as well.

t: Work Clean: The Life-Changing Power of Mise-en-Place to Organize Your Life, Work, and Mind
s: Applies the kitchen discipline of mise-en-place to organizing work and daily tasks.
w: Recommended when threads discuss mise en place and productivity systems; readers took away practical organization habits.
ab: For anyone building work routines
Kitchen-derived system
Somewhat repetitive

q.t: does a great job of explaining the system of mise en place beyond just setup and precutting vegetables

t: Eyes in the Sky: The Secret Rise of Gorgon Stare and How It Will Watch Us All
s: A book on wide-area aerial surveillance, from the military's Gorgon Stare camera system to its use over American cities.
w: Offered as the deeper read on persistent aerial surveillance. One reader found it informative and eye-opening, though disconcerting.
ab: For readers interested in surveillance technology and privacy
Goes well beyond a single podcast episode on the topic
Sobering subject matter

q.t: I found it to be an informative, and eye-opening (albeit disconcerting) read.

s: A guide to using writing as a tool for thinking, arguing that generating ideas and expressing them are not separate steps.
w: Recommended for people who use writing to think clearly, and for the idea that writing to understand differs from writing to communicate.
ab: For writers and engineers who think by writing
Separates writing for understanding from writing for readers
Older book; examples show its age

q.t: Writing is used for understanding and for communication. These are two different activities.

s: Fukuoka's account of his no-till, no-fertilizer natural farming method and the philosophy of living simply that goes with it.
w: HN readers cite it in farming and soil threads as a compelling alternative view, one that argues for diversity and soil health instead of heavy inputs, and as a life-changing book.
ab: For gardeners and farmers curious about natural farming
Part memoir, part philosophy of simple living
Anecdotal rather than rigorous agronomy

q.t: It's an autobiography that uses permaculture to inspire a simple life.

s: A 1955 Isaac Asimov time-travel novel about an organization that manipulates history across the centuries.
w: Asimov readers pick it as a standout among his non-Foundation novels, and one commenter cites its twist ending when discussing timelines.
ab: For fans of classic time-travel science fiction
Standalone novel
Mid-century style; strong twist

q.t: Oh, and The End of Eternity!

t: Brain Rules for Baby: How to Raise a Smart and Happy Child from Zero to Five
s: A developmental biologist's research-based guide to early childhood brain development, with advice on sleep, screens, play and bonding.
w: Parents on HN say it made them better fathers and a staple for expecting parents; one points to its advice against TV for infants.
ab: For expecting parents and parents of young kids
Science-based but accessible
Some advice may have been refined since 2010

q.t: Brain Rules for Baby by John Medina, because it made me a better father

t: Empires of Light: Edison, Tesla, Westinghouse, and the Race to Electrify the World
s: A narrative history of the rivalry between Thomas Edison, Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse in the war of the currents that electrified America.
w: HN names it as a highly engaging and detailed true story of electrification, recommended as a favorite non-fiction book, in true tech story lists and in audiobook form.
ab: For readers of technology and business history
Also works as an audiobook
Long and detailed

q.t: An extremely detailed and engaging book on how electricity was

s: A science fiction detective story set after a technological singularity, where survivors who missed it investigate what happened.
w: HN readers recommend it as a little-known gem among Vinge's work, with a mind-expanding vision of accelerating AI, and a good detective story.
ab: For Vinge fans and singularity readers
Second book in the Across Realtime series but works alone
Technology details are 1980s

q.t: contains a mind-expanding vision of exponentially accelerating AI

s: A collection of Isaac Asimov's robot short stories, gathering the I, Robot tales and later robot fiction.
w: HN readers name it a comfort book and a reminder that we are living in the future, enjoyed again and again since their teens.
ab: For fans of classic robot science fiction
Short story collection
1940s-1980s stories; some dated

q.t: pretty cool to read some things in this collection of short stories

s: How cultural learning and accumulated group knowledge, more than individual intelligence, drove human evolution and made our species successful.
w: HN readers use it to explain why traditions and practices that look arbitrary often encode hard-won knowledge. It comes up in threads on engineering, culture and trial-and-error learning.
ab: For readers curious about cultural evolution and why traditions persist
Packed with anthropological case studies, from food processing to survival skills
Argument is broad; some readers find it repetitive in places

q.t: Societies are full of random stuff we learned just by trial and error and we don't even know why we do it.

t: Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents
s: A psychotherapist's guide to recognizing how emotionally immature parenting shapes adults, with exercises for setting boundaries and healing.
w: Commenters point to it as an accessible way to understand emotional neglect and why boundary-setting feels hard. It is recommended alongside other mental-health books, usually as a second read.
ab: For adults who feel emotionally neglected or struggle with boundaries
Gives names and frameworks for patterns you may already feel
One HN reader suggested starting with 'How We Change' first

q.t: Emotional neglect has real and serious consequences.

t: Life 3.0: Being Human in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
s: Physicist Max Tegmark surveys how advanced AI could reshape work, society and the future of life, opening with a fictional scenario of a runaway AI.
w: HN readers recommend it as an approachable overview of long-term AI possibilities and risks. It is often cited as a good starting point rather than a technical text.
ab: For general readers wanting a broad tour of AI futures
Mixes speculative scenarios with physics and ethics
Not technical; some scenarios are highly speculative

q.t: great glimpse into the current and potential future of AI

s: A short biography of Isaac Newton by the author of Chaos and Genius, covering his science, secrecy, alchemy and religious obsessions.
w: HN readers like that Gleick does not airbrush Newton's religious and occult interests, and they pair it with his Feynman biography as some of the best science biographies.
ab: For readers who like well-written science biography
Short and readable compared with doorstopper Newton biographies
Treats Newton's mysticism as integral rather than an embarrassment

q.t: Gleick's Isaac Newton is also fantastic.

t: Happy: Why More or Less Everything Is Absolutely Fine
s: Magician and mentalist Derren Brown's guide to living well, built around Stoic and Epicurean philosophy and a modern take on happiness and death.
w: HN readers describe it as an approachable gateway to Stoicism that summarizes many classic works. It shows up in favorite non-fiction and life-changing book threads.
ab: For beginners wanting an entertaining introduction to Stoic philosophy
Explicitly not a typical self-help book
Draws on classical sources, so it works as a reading map

q.t: a stoic interpretation for the modern world (how to live, and die, happy)

s: Peter Singer's foundational argument for the ethical treatment of animals, introducing the term speciesism and criticizing factory farming and animal testing.
w: HN commenters credit it with changing their diet and convictions, and recommend it to people sceptical about animal ethics. It is called the bible of the animal rights movement.
ab: For readers open to examining the ethics of eating and using animals
Utilitarian philosophy argument with disturbing factual sections
Original dates to 1975; newer editions update the facts

q.t: I read it over 20 years ago. I've been a vegetarian/vegan ever since.

t: Why Fish Don't Exist: A Story of Loss, Love, and the Hidden Order of Life
s: Part biography, part memoir: Invisibilia host Lulu Miller follows taxonomist David Starr Jordan and finds lessons about chaos, order and resilience.
w: HN readers recommend it as a surprising, emotional read that starts as a science story and turns personal. It pops up whenever fish taxonomy comes up.
ab: For readers who enjoy narrative science writing with a personal twist
Quick read; one commenter binged it in two nights
More memoir and philosophy than biology

q.t: a deeply personal and poignant exploration of the chaos that rules are lives

s: A short book by economist Thomas Sowell examining why outcome gaps between groups arise and whether discrimination alone explains them.
w: Commenters recommend it as a concise, data-driven argument about disparities, and cite it in debates over affirmative action. Fans call it an eye opener.
ab: For readers wanting a short economist's take on group disparities
Argument is contested and politically charged
Brief and accessible, building on his earlier essays

q.t: Disparities and Discrimination by Thomas Sowell was a real eye opener for me.

t: SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome
s: Classicist Mary Beard's single-volume history of ancient Rome from its legendary founding to the early third century AD.
w: HN readers call it an engaging overview and the best starting point for Roman history, ahead of heavier works. It also shows up on lists of what to read instead of canon wars.
ab: For readers who want an engaging one-volume introduction to Rome
Focuses on Republic and early Empire, not the late empire
Written with scholarly humility about uncertain evidence

q.t: SPQR is likely a better start with a more complete timeline.

s: Ron Chernow's biography of Alexander Hamilton, the immigrant founder who built the US financial system, and the basis for the musical.
w: HN readers recommend it as a great read on the birth of the United States and an easy way into American history. Some quip about Hamilton as America's greatest loser.
ab: For readers wanting a narrative biography of the American founding
Very long, around 800 pages
The source material for Lin-Manuel Miranda's musical

q.t: An excellent introduction to the birth of US.

s: Scott Young's playbook for mastering hard skills quickly through intense self-directed projects, with case studies of rapid learners.
w: Frequently listed on HN among the best books on learning faster, next to Mindset and Deep Work. Readers like the practical principles behind aggressive self-study.
ab: For self-directed learners who want a concrete learning method
Mixes research with stories of dramatic learning feats
Method demands heavy time commitment

q.t: Ultralearning (Young) - how to learn anything faster

t: The Culture Map: Breaking Through the Invisible Boundaries of Global Business
s: A framework for understanding how national cultures differ in communication, feedback, decision-making and trust, to help managers work across borders.
w: HN readers recommend it for managers of international or remote teams who need a map of cultural differences. One calls it a framework to think within, though not perfectly correct.
ab: For managers and remote workers collaborating across countries
Gives scales for comparing cultures on trust, disagreement and scheduling
Generalizes by country; one HN reader was not fully sold on its accuracy

q.t: I've found Erin Meyer's Culture Map[1] a good guide to navigating different cultures.

s: Dave Ramsey's step-by-step plan for getting out of debt, building an emergency fund and saving for retirement, built around the debt snowball method.
w: A few HN commenters say it changed their lives, arguing that being debt-free gives you the freedom to take career risks. It appears in life-changing book threads, though not as an intellectual pick.
ab: For people in debt who want a simple behavior-based payoff plan
Prescriptive and motivational rather than mathematically optimal
Advice is US-specific and strongly opinionated

q.t: has definitely changed my life for the better. I wish I had read it years ago.

s: A novel about a woman who, between life and death, visits a library of alternate lives she could have lived had she made different choices.
w: HN readers recommend it as a gentle reflection on regret and the paths not taken. Commenters say it helped them reframe their own life choices.
ab: For readers who want a hopeful novel about regret and second chances
Fast, accessible read
Premise is familiar to fans of alternate-life fiction

q.t: It helped me process my regrets.

s: A guide to designing reputation and rating systems for web communities, drawing on Yahoo's experience with ratings, reviews and karma.
w: HN readers send people to it whenever threads discuss rating systems or reputation, calling it the book on the subject. It covers considerations commenters say designers often miss.
ab: For product designers and developers building ratings, reviews or karma
Covers pitfalls in ratings and incentive design
Published 2010; examples predate current social platforms

q.t: for anyone looking at web reputation systems, read the book on the subject

s: A detailed tutorial on Kubernetes that explains core concepts like pods, services and deployments with hands-on examples.
w: HN readers say it is the Kubernetes book they actually recommend: well written, beginner friendly and easy to follow. One reader keeps it on their desk.
ab: For developers and ops engineers learning Kubernetes from scratch
Builds up concepts clearly with examples
Kubernetes changes quickly; check the edition

q.t: wonderfully written, easy to follow and for me, was a page turner.

t: Apprenticeship Patterns: Guidance for the Aspiring Software Craftsman
s: A collection of patterns for growing as a software developer, with advice on learning, seeking mentors and staying challenged.
w: HN readers recommend it to people starting out and as a compact career book under 200 pages. It supports the idea of working among stronger developers.
ab: For early-career developers wanting guidance on growth
Short pattern format, free online
Some patterns are dated

q.t: Read the book Apprenticeship Patterns

t: Rust for Rustaceans: Idiomatic Programming for Experienced Developers
s: An intermediate-to-advanced Rust book covering ownership, traits, concurrency, unsafe code and testing for programmers past the basics.
w: HN readers call it the best next step after 'the book', recommending it to those comfortable in Rust who want deeper understanding. It comes up in many learn-Rust threads.
ab: For developers who already know Rust basics
Covers advanced topics like unsafe, traits and async
Not a beginner introduction

q.t: might be the best intermediate to advanced rust book

s: A Pragmatic Programmers book that teaches genetic algorithms by implementing them in Elixir, from selection and crossover to practical problem solving.
w: HN readers call it excellent and say it exceeded their expectations. It is recommended to Elixir developers wanting focused, advanced material.
ab: For Elixir programmers interested in optimization and evolutionary algorithms
Hands-on, project-style teaching
Niche topic and Elixir-specific

q.t: what I did read definitely exceeded my expectations

s: A humorous book that solves the same small JavaScript problems in the styles of 25 famous authors, with commentary on their prose.
w: HN readers recommend it as a fun, engaging read for programmers, a good companion to quirky code curiosities. Not a professional reference.
ab: For JavaScript developers who enjoy literature and wordplay
Funny rather than instructional
Light, entertaining code reading

q.t: Another book of note that is funny and engaging

s: A guide to what happens inside a Linux system, covering booting, kernel, devices, networking, storage, and in the latest edition virtualization and containers.
w: HN readers call it a great Linux reference and recommend it for understanding how computers boot and how Linux fits together. It is a regular pick in sysadmin and learn-Linux threads.
ab: For developers and admins who want to understand Linux internals
Practical command-line coverage
Assumes basic command-line comfort

q.t: How Linux Works book is another great Linux reference.

t: Type Theory and Formal Proof: An Introduction
s: A textbook introducing type theory, from untyped lambda calculus to a dependently typed proof calculus, used for formal proofs.
w: HN readers call it one of the better books on type theory and say it is excellent for those interested in the topic. It's recommended in threads on dependent types and proof assistants.
ab: For readers wanting rigorous grounding in lambda calculus and dependent types
Works up gradually from the basics
Mathematically demanding

q.t: The book[0] mentioned is excellent if you are interested in this kind of thing.

t: The Lucifer Principle: A Scientific Expedition into the Forces of History
s: Howard Bloom argues that evolution, group behavior and memes drive aggression and the rise and fall of civilizations.
w: HN readers list it among their best reads and say it introduced them to evolutionary psychology. It is suggested to fans of Harari and Jared Diamond.
ab: For readers who like sweeping big-picture theories of human behavior
Early evo-psych perspective, now contested
Written in the 1990s

q.t: introduced me to evolution and evo-psych thinking

t: The Kingdom of God Is Within You
s: Tolstoy's treatise on Christian nonviolence and anarchism, which influenced Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.
w: HN readers call it life-changing, crediting its thinking about sin and nonviolence, and note its influence on Gandhi and MLK. It appears often in books-that-changed-you threads.
ab: For readers interested in nonviolent resistance and Christian anarchism
Long and sometimes polemical
Nineteenth-century religious framing

q.t: was the most life changing book I read this year.

s: Alain de Botton explores why we worry about our standing in society and how philosophy, art and religion have tried to ease that anxiety.
w: HN readers find it insightful on how modern meritocracy ties self-worth to status, and call it a pretty good pop psychology book. It is among Botton's titles readers often cite.
ab: For readers who worry about career comparison and success
Accessible, essay-style philosophy
Pop-psychology style, not rigorous science

q.t: how we have come to live in a meritocracy, where your status depends on what you have achieved

s: Aristotle's collected works on logic, including the Categories, Prior Analytics and Sophistical Refutations, which founded formal reasoning in the West.
w: HN readers call it the basis of Western logical thought, recommend learning about fallacies from it, and some say it helps them design and model systems.
ab: For readers wanting the origins of formal logic
Ancient text; translation and commentary matter
Dense and demanding

q.t: the more I think in Aristotelian terms, the easier it is to design and model my systems

s: A 15-inch Dell mobile workstation laptop from 2018, sold with Ubuntu preinstalled in a developer edition.
w: Linux users report that the hardware just works out of the box on Ubuntu, with Dell shipping drivers and firmware updates. A commenter also praises the build quality of the Precision 5000 line and buys refurbished ones.
ab: For developers wanting a well-supported Linux laptop
Cheap refurbished units turn up years later
It is an older model; check battery health when buying used

q.t: I use a Dell Precision 5530 daily with Ubuntu 20.04, works great with no problems.

s: Willa Cather's 1918 novel about an immigrant girl growing up on the Nebraska prairie, as told by a family friend.
w: Recommended in Ask HN reading threads as a classic worth making time for. One commenter put it among their year's favourites for its wonderful characters.
ab: For readers wanting a quiet American classic
Strong characters and a prairie setting
Slow, reflective pace

q.t: My Antonia, wonderful characters

t: Journey Through Genius: The Great Theorems of Mathematics
s: A popular history presenting twelve landmark theorems and their original proofs, from Hippocrates to Cantor.
w: HN readers call it one of the best popular maths books because it keeps real mathematical detail. It turns up in lists of introductory math reading with Stillwell's history.
ab: For curious readers with high-school-level maths
Walks through actual proofs, not just stories
Companion to Dunham's Euler book

q.t: For a "popular" treatment of mathematics that does go into some mathematical detail

s: A collection of Borges' short stories, including the title story about a point in space containing all other points.
w: Named in favourite-fiction lists, with commenters noting that Borges anticipated ideas like recursion and infinity that programmers like.
ab: For fans of short, idea-dense fiction
Stories about infinity, libraries and labyrinths
Pairs with Ficciones

q.t: Borges' Aleph, and his essays (for example Other Inquisitions). He was fascinated about concepts programming is famous for now

t: Through the Ages: A New Story of Civilization
s: A heavy civilization-building card board game for two to four players, with a digital version also available.
w: Appears repeatedly in HN favourite board game lists. A commenter who knew it from the digital version says to retract the pick if the bookkeeping is a chore in the physical game.
ab: For experienced gamers who like deep strategy
Long playtime and a lot of bookkeeping
Digital version removes the upkeep

q.t: Through the Ages: A New Story of Civilization - I've played it before a couple times, but really only got into it more this year.

t: Team of Teams: New Rules of Engagement for a Complex World
s: General Stanley McChrystal explains how the US military in Iraq replaced a rigid hierarchy with a network of small, connected teams.
w: Recommended as required reading on how groups of humans work together, and summed up as agile, adaptable, transparent and decentralised. One reader found the first third a slog but the rest full of insights.
ab: For managers of growing, complex organisations
Military case study applied to business
First third is slow

q.t: Fundamentally about being agile, adaptable, transparent, collaborative and decentralised.

s: Jack London's 1909 semi-autobiographical novel about a poor sailor who educates himself and becomes a famous writer.
w: Recommended as a tragic coming-of-age story, especially for readers in their early twenties. One commenter says it shows why education matters.
ab: For readers who like self-improvement stories with a dark turn
Late 19th-century setting
Tragic ending

q.t: Some of the best books you'll ever read about character development.

s: Hardy's short 1940 essay defending pure mathematics as an art, written in his later years.
w: Readers say they expected a maths book and got a book about life. It is often read after Kanigel's biography The Man Who Knew Infinity.
ab: Short and readable, no maths required
Reflective essay on creativity and ageing
Hardy's views on usefulness are dated

q.t: Went into it thinking I was reading a book on math and ended up reading a book about life.

s: A 1981 fantasy novel following several generations of a family linked to a hidden world of magic.
w: HN readers call it a fantasy classic, noting it was reportedly critic Harold Bloom's favourite novel. One commenter says it changed their reading habits.
ab: For readers who like literary, atmospheric fantasy
Multi-generational story
Unlike typical epic fantasy

q.t: For a fantasy classic, you could try John Crowley's Little, Big, which was reputedly the late lit critic Harold Bloom's favorite novel.

s: Thomas Hardy's 1895 novel about a working-class man whose dream of education and a happy marriage is defeated by social convention.
w: Called brilliant by HN readers, who praise the crafted narration and the literary references. Gutenberg links make it easy to read free.
ab: For readers of Victorian classics
Bleak and shocking ending
Public domain, free online

q.t: The way Hardy 'smuggles' Jude's viewpoint into the narrative is so ridiculously well crafted, a pleasure to read.

s: Physicist Lawrence Krauss's popular-science argument for how a universe could arise from nothing according to quantum physics and cosmology.
w: Appears in recommendation lists from HN readers who found it amazing. It is usually one entry among several science picks.
ab: For lay readers curious about cosmology
Some critics dispute its philosophical claims
Published 2012

q.t: "A universe from nothing" was also amazing!

t: Mini Habits: Smaller Habits, Bigger Results
s: A short book arguing that building habits from tiny daily goals, like one push-up, is more reliable than relying on willpower.
w: HN readers say it is the only routine-building method that worked for them. It is a short book with a simple method that people keep using.
ab: For people who fail at big habit goals
Short read with one core idea
Limited depth beyond the method

q.t: Mini Habits - the only routine building method that worked for me.

s: A free algorithms textbook by a University of Illinois professor, covering design, analysis and models of computation.
w: Recommended as a great free resource, and HN readers like that the full book is available online. Commenters say it's good value.
ab: For students and self-learners of algorithms
Free to download
Proof-oriented

q.t: Jeff Erickson's Algorithms text is a great resource

s: Tracy Kidder's account of physician and anthropologist Paul Farmer and his work treating disease in Haiti and elsewhere.
w: Recommended in lists of engineering team reading and general biographies. Commenters describe a man who gave up everything to solve easily preventable disease.
ab: For readers interested in public health and humanitarian work
Biography written as narrative nonfiction
Published 2003

q.t: A biography of Dr Paul Farmer and how he dedicated his life and sacrificed everything

t: Patterns in Network Architecture: A Return to Fundamentals
s: John Day's 2007 book arguing for a unified model of network protocols, drawing on his experience with early Internet and OSI work.
w: Described as highly opinionated and by an insider; recommended to learn why networks work the way they do. One reader sums it up as a grand unification of network protocols.
ab: For networking specialists wanting a fresh theory
Opinionated take on OSI and the Internet
Niche and not beginner-friendly

q.t: a pretty good too if you want to learn the why of how networks are the way they are today.

t: Wanting: The Power of Mimetic Desire in Everyday Life
s: Luke Burgis applies René Girard's mimetic theory to explain how people copy the desires of others, with examples from business and daily life.
w: HN readers recommend it as an accessible introduction to Girard's ideas. One says it made them aware how much of our nature is simply copying others.
ab: For readers curious about Girard without the dense theory
Applied to startups and life
Popular treatment

q.t: It makes the works of Rene Girard accessible.

s: Edward de Bono's method of looking at a decision from six defined perspectives, each represented by a coloured hat.
w: Readers say the concept is simple but a useful tool, helping them structure their thoughts and see problems from different viewpoints.
ab: For anyone running discussions or making decisions
Simple framework
Some find it basic

q.t: The concept is very simple, but this idea of looking at something from different defined perspectives is a useful tool

s: Richard Dawkins' 1982 follow-up to The Selfish Gene arguing that genes' effects extend beyond the body of the organism.
w: Listed alongside The Selfish Gene by HN readers. One describes it as the more technical, expert-level follow-up and notes Dawkins calls it his favourite of his own books.
ab: For readers who finished The Selfish Gene
More technical than Dawkins' popular books
Published 1982

q.t: Some while ago I reread Richard Dawkins's The Extended Phenotype, which he has referred to as his favorite work.

t: How to Get Filthy Rich in Rising Asia
s: A novel by Mohsin Hamid told in second person, parodying a self-help book to follow a boy from a village to wealth.
w: HN readers rate it highly and some read it in a single day. They like the second-person style and how fresh the writing is.
ab: For readers who like short, inventive novels
Satire of self-help books
Quick read

q.t: This is my book of choice for the year: I read it cover-to-cover in a single day.

t: The Thrilling Adventures of Lovelace and Babbage
s: Sydney Padua's steampunk graphic novel about Ada Lovelace and Charles Babbage with annotated footnotes on the real history.
w: HN readers gave it as a gift and call it geeky fun. One says the comic is zany fiction but the author's notes teach the real proto-history of the computer.
ab: For people interested in early computing
Comic with long annotations
Mostly fictional story

q.t: If you want to learn about the proto-history of the computer, a graphic novel called "The Thrilling Adventures Of Lovelace And Babbage" is well worth your time.

s: John Irving's 1989 novel about a small, odd boy who believes he is an instrument of God, narrated by his best friend.
w: Repeatedly named in favourite-fiction lists. One commenter first met it while struggling with their religious views.
ab: For readers who like big character-driven novels
Themes of faith and fate
Long

q.t: A couple immediately come to mind: “A Prayer for Owen Meany” by John Irving and “The Awakening” by Kate Chopin.

s: Jack London's 1903 adventure novel about a domestic dog stolen and sold into the Yukon gold rush.
w: Recommended as a classic and a children's introduction to literature. One commenter says it shows how to adapt to change, using Buck's life.
ab: Short and readable classic
Good for young readers
Some violence

q.t: it shows how possible it is to adapt in order to benefit maximally from change -- using a dog's (Buck) life.

s: A hands-on book that builds an interpreter for the Monkey language from scratch in Go, with tests along the way.
w: HN readers call it an elegant book for learning interpreters, worth every cent, and often pair it with its sequel on compilers and Crafting Interpreters.
ab: For programmers new to language implementation
Hands-on and test-driven
Sequel covers compilers

q.t: Writing an Interpreter in Go is a very elegant book for learning how to write an interpreter from scratch using Go.

s: A 1959 children's novel about a boy who runs away to live alone in the Catskill woods.
w: HN readers remember it fondly from childhood, one saying it was basically their ideal personality, independent and self sufficient.
ab: For kids who love nature adventure
Classic children's novel
Nostalgic pick

q.t: this was basically my ideal personality as a kid - independent and self sufficient

s: Agatha Christie's 1926 Hercule Poirot mystery famous for its surprising ending.
w: HN readers call it a masterpiece with a very surprising plot, and warn not to look it up in advance. It tops lists of Christie recommendations.
ab: For mystery fans
Avoid spoilers
Poirot novel

q.t: the first is a masterpiece

s: Arthur Koestler's 1940 novel about an old Bolshevik imprisoned and interrogated during Stalin's purges.
w: Called the best political critique ever by one reader, and listed in favourite-books posts as recently as 2025.
ab: For readers interested in totalitarianism
Political novel of the 1930s
Bleak

q.t: Darkness at Noon may have been the best political critique ever.

s: William Goldman's 1973 comic fantasy adventure, framed as an abridgement of a classic by S. Morgenstern.
w: HN readers say it's even better than the movie, with better action sequences. One has given it away seven times and bought it eight.
ab: For fans of the film
Funny, with a meta frame
Differs from the movie

q.t: it was a revelation that even the action sequences are better in the book.

s: A Discworld novel in which City Watch commander Sam Vimes is thrown back in time to his own youth during a street revolution.
w: HN readers call it one of their favourites to give, and some say it is a high point of the Discworld series. It is easier to start with than most.
ab: For readers of Pratchett's Discworld
Works as a standalone
Time-travel story

q.t: they're really fantastic. The pinnacle of the series?

s: A standalone epic fantasy novel by Brandon Sanderson set in the Cosmere, in which magic runs on colour and breath.
w: HN readers recommend it as a starting point for Sanderson's Cosmere, and one calls it his best.
ab: For epic fantasy fans
Standalone and available free
Part of the Cosmere

q.t: Pick 1 - Start with Warbreaker or Mistborn.

s: David Mitchell's 2014 novel spanning decades of one woman's life, with a hidden war of immortals.
w: HN readers praise the time-hopping, detailed characters and ambitious scope. One says you should not google it because of spoilers.
ab: For fans of Cloud Atlas
Mixes literary and fantasy
Avoid spoilers

q.t: The best mix of beautifully detailed characters and ambitious scope that I've read.

s: Robin Sloan's 2012 novel about a bookstore clerk using programming and Google to decode a mysterious book society.
w: HN readers enjoy it as a casual read with tech themes, calling it a mix of history, mystery, humour and technology.
ab: For tech readers wanting a light novel
Programming and books
Easy to read

q.t: a brilliant mix of history, mystery, humour and technology

s: A split ergonomic keyboard whose two halves are joined by a cable, with optional tenting accessories.
w: HN users have used it for years at work and ask employers to buy one. They like its soft key feel and the easy adjustment compared with fully programmable boards.
ab: For people wanting a split keyboard with little retraining
Adjustable split and tenting
Not programmable

q.t: For me, the angle matters, but also the softness of the touch.

s: An introduction to game theory for business and everyday decisions, with many practical examples.
w: HN readers call it a great primer on game theory, one saying everything changed colour for them after reading it. It also appears in negotiation reading lists.
ab: For readers new to game theory
Practical, non-technical
Written in 1991

q.t: A great primer on game theory. Everything changed colors for me after I read this.

s: Dickens' 1850 novel following a boy's life from a miserable childhood to becoming a writer.
w: Called very long novel that gets better with every page, and beautifully written, by HN readers choosing big books.
ab: For readers wanting a long Victorian novel
Long
Classic

q.t: Both are very long novels that get better and better with every page.

s: Milan Kundera's 1990 novel weaving several characters around themes of identity, fame and love.
w: HN readers list it as a lifetime favourite. One says it made them think about mortality, love and sexuality in new ways.
ab: For readers of philosophical fiction
Interwoven plots
Translated

q.t: It made me think about mortality, love and sexuality in ways I'd never thought of before

s: A dark fantasy novel about adopted children raised by an all-powerful father to master different branches of knowledge.
w: Recommended across several yearly book threads as a strange, gripping read that is unlike anything else, good for readers of Stephen King and Clive Barker.
ab: For readers who like weird, dark fantasy
Violent and disturbing in places
Plot twists reward patient readers

q.t: a new great magical realism book, great if you like Stephen King / Clive Barker / Robert McCammon

s: A compact, slim Bluetooth keyboard that pairs with up to three devices.
w: HN users like it as a portable keyboard with a crisp, comfortable typing feel and very long battery life.
ab: Small and travel-friendly.
Pairs with three devices.
Low-profile keys, not mechanical.

q.t: I love it so much that I bought it twice.

s: Roger Penrose's argument that human consciousness involves non-computable processes, ranging across math, physics and mind.
w: HN readers call it a brilliant, eye-opening book and a fantastic rebuttal to Hofstadter's Godel, Escher, Bach, a must read regardless of views on AI.
ab: For readers who want a skeptical take on strong AI.
Mixes physics, math and philosophy.
Written in 1989; thesis is controversial.

q.t: Both are must reads regardless of one's views on AI (or approaches to AI).

s: Lewis Mumford's 1934 history of how machines and technology shaped Western civilization.
w: HN readers recommend it, with Mumford's other books, for a humanist, anthropological view of technology and society written from a 1930s perspective.
ab: For readers interested in philosophy of technology.
Historical perspective from the 1930s.
Dense, academic style.

q.t: Lewis Mumford talks about technology, but from an anthropological pint of view.

t: Lost Connections: Uncovering the Real Causes of Depression
s: Johann Hari's popular-science argument that depression and anxiety stem largely from social and environmental causes, not just brain chemistry.
w: HN readers found it an interesting, study-backed look at the sources of depression, though one notes controversy over the author.
ab: For readers curious about causes of depression.
Cites many studies.
The author has credibility controversies.

q.t: Interesting book backed with a lot of studies.

s: Plato's dialogue in which guests at a banquet give speeches on the nature of love.
w: HN readers recommend it among Plato's dialogues for philosophy beginners and re-read it often, but warn the dialogues are dense.
ab: Short Platonic dialogue on love.
Many translations exist.
Pair with Phaedrus and the Republic.

q.t: I'd recommend a couple of his dialogues: Phaedrus, Symposium, and the Republic

t: How to Live, or A Life of Montaigne
s: Sarah Bakewell's biography of Montaigne framed around the question of how to live.
w: HN readers call it a fantastic, refreshing take on Montaigne's essays and say it started their journey into philosophy.
ab: Accessible introduction to Montaigne.
Gateway to philosophy.
Biography organized around life lessons.

q.t: a fantastic take on Montaigne's essays by a contemporary scholar with a refreshing take on everything

s: A comic fantasy mystery set in an ancient China that never was, following Master Li and Number Ten Ox.
w: HN readers rave about the storytelling and humor and give it as a gift, one calling it far better than The Princess Bride.
ab: Funny adventure-mystery in mythical China.
Often called a hidden gem.
Part of a three-book series.

q.t: Easily some of the best storytelling I've ever read.

s: Mary Doria Russell's novel about a Jesuit-led first-contact mission to another planet and its tragic aftermath.
w: HN readers list it among favorite sci-fi, praising its treatment of religion and faith, though one almost didn't finish.
ab: Thoughtful first-contact novel.
Emotionally heavy.
Sequel is Children of God.

s: Paul Lockhart's critique of school mathematics teaching and a plea to treat math as an art.
w: HN readers recommend it, particularly parents, for insight into how math is taught and for its author's passion for mathematics.
ab: For parents and teachers worried about math education.
Short polemic, not a textbook.
Companion book is Measurement.

q.t: If you are someone that has kids and their education is important to you, this book gives you some insight

s: Bill Gates's 1995 book on where computers and the internet might take society and business.
w: HN readers recall it as an early classic of software business and an interesting look at what Gates envisioned for the internet, one saying it taught them to value people over companies.
ab: Interesting as a 1995 time capsule.
Visionary and often wrong.
Ties into Microsoft history.

q.t: It made me realize it's not companies I would like to be working at but people I would like to be working with.

s: A collection of Joel Spolsky's essays on software development, management and running a software business.
w: HN readers say they learn something each time they re-read it and love how funny Joel's stories of early Microsoft are.
ab: Essays on teams, hiring and software craft.
Funny and readable.
Written in the 2000s.

q.t: I learn new things every time I read it, but the best part is how insanely funny Joel is

s: A thin aluminium ultrabook from Xiaomi that resembles a MacBook Air at a lower price.
w: HN commenters like its Mac-like design, good battery life and good Linux support at a small price, with one still using theirs ten years on.
ab: Budget MacBook-style ultraportable.
Works well with Ubuntu per owners.
Old model; hard to buy outside China.

q.t: They are suprisingly well supported on linux, in addition to being very good all-around ultraportable at a small price.

s: A 1994 science-fiction novel set in a city of districts that each exist in a different mood or era, following a troubled hero on a strange quest.

ab: For readers wanting offbeat, imaginative sci-fi beyond the usual canon
Author's early sci-fi, distinct from his later thrillers as Michael Marshall
Little-known in the US; HN fans mention repeat re-reads

q.t: Only Forward, One of Us, What You Make It, or Spares from the nineties are all well written

s: Nietzsche's 1882 book of aphorisms and poems, containing the Madman parable and the 'God is dead' passage and the first statement of the eternal recurrence.

ab: For readers curious about Nietzsche's ideas on God, morality and meaning
Aphoristic format; dip in rather than read straight through
Pick a good modern translation (Kaufmann is common)

q.t: The Gay Science by Friedrich Nietzsche, because once I truly understood the full text of aphorism 125

s: A 1992 wordless documentary shot on 70mm film across many countries, showing nature, ritual and human life set to music.
w: HN viewers point to it for people who want dialogue-free cinema, calling it colorful and beautiful, and some find it more compelling than the better-known Koyaanisqatsi.
ab: For viewers who like visual, non-narrative documentaries
No dialogue or plot; the 70mm cinematography is the draw
Often paired with the Qatsi trilogy

q.t: Baraka movie is a colorful vivid beautiful impactful movie without any narrative.

s: Faulkner's 1929 modernist novel about the decline of a Southern family, told through four voices in fragmented, non-linear narration.
w: Listed as a must-read and a book people would re-read for life. It shows up alongside other literary heavyweights, and one HN reader says its first chapter changed how they think.
ab: For readers who enjoy demanding, experimental literary fiction
Stream-of-consciousness opening chapter is notoriously hard going
A cornerstone of American modernism

q.t: Faulkner: The Sound and the Fury

s: Elie Wiesel's short memoir of his time as a teenager in Auschwitz and Buchenwald during the Holocaust.
w: HN readers cite it as a book that showed them how resilient a person can be and helped them understand the world. It is a short, harrowing first-hand account.
ab: For readers wanting a first-hand Holocaust account
Short and quick to read, but emotionally heavy
Often paired with Man's Search for Meaning

q.t: Night by Elie Wiesel. It showed me how resilient a human being can be.

s: Dan Simmons's four-novel space opera series that begins with seven pilgrims telling their stories on the way to the Time Tombs of Hyperion.
w: Repeatedly named as the best sci-fi by HN readers, praised as deeply philosophical and full of ideas. It is a go-to answer in favorite-sci-fi threads.
ab: For fans of literary, idea-heavy space opera
Starts with Hyperion and The Fall of Hyperion; later books are divisive
Structured like the Canterbury Tales

q.t: It is deeply philosophical and caused me to think about life in a way no other science fiction has before or since.

s: The architect of the IBM AS/400 explains its design, including the single-level store, object-based OS and high-level machine interface.

ab: For systems programmers curious about unusual OS architecture
Written by the AS/400's chief architect
Niche and old; used copy prices vary widely

q.t: I highly recommend the expensive book by Frank Soltis who is largely the architect of it

t: Pre-Industrial Societies: Anatomy of the Pre-Modern World
s: A historian's concise analysis of the structure of agrarian pre-modern societies, covering kinship, states, religion, warfare and economy.

Thematic rather than narrative history
Dense academic prose

s: Soft foam earplugs with a 33 dB noise reduction rating.

ab: 33 dB rating
Cheap bulk
Can irritate

s: A casual, illustrated introduction to DNA, genes, proteins and molecular biology for beginners.
w: HN users suggest it as an approachable entry point for programmers or others with little biology background, in threads on protein folding and viruses.
ab: For beginners wanting a readable introduction to molecular biology
Humorous, plain-language explanations
Older edition; check for the latest revision

s: A book on symmetric multiprocessing, caching and memory consistency for kernel programmers.

ab: For systems and kernel programmers learning caches and SMP

Mid-1990s hardware examples

s: A beginner-friendly guide to building dynamic websites with PHP, MySQL and JavaScript.

Covers PHP, MySQL, JavaScript and CSS together
2009 edition; web stack advice has changed

q.t: Try this book. it is phenomenal.

s: A career guide to the unwritten rules of academic science, from publishing to getting credit and getting tenure.

Explains the informal rules of research careers
Earlier editions are dated

t: Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production

Primary source for the five whys
Translated and somewhat dry

t: At Day's Close: Night in Times Past

w: Recommended in sleep and history threads as a great book on our historical relationship with the night and the idea of segmented sleep.
ab: For readers curious about pre-industrial life and sleep
Well-researched social history
Academic in tone

s: A powered 1-in 2-out HDMI splitter for 1080p video that does not enforce HDCP on its outputs.

s: A journalist's tour of healthcare systems around the world, comparing them with the US system.

Short, light read
Humor over rigor

Practical and step-by-step
B2B focus

Niche cult favorite

Mainstream psychiatry disputes its claims

Simple routine you can try in a week
Typical self-help style; little science

Many worked examples
Introductory

Focus on performance and design
Published 2006

Philosophical
Second book by Crawford

Practical OTP

Clever, advanced techniques

Free online

q.t: Eliyahu M. Goldratt has some great books explaining in great detail why this is the case

s: The second book in the Kingkiller Chronicle fantasy series, following Kvothe's studies and travels.
w: HN readers recommend the series for its engrossing storytelling and call the books great fantasy, though one finds the writing and female characters weak.
ab: Read The Name of the Wind first.
Long, immersive fantasy.
Series remains unfinished; some find characters weak.

q.t: The story has been great so far and storytelling is exceptional.

t: How the World Really Works: The Science Behind How We Got Here and Where We're Going
s: Smil's overview of the energy, materials, food and risk systems that underpin modern civilization.
w: HN readers praise it as a sober, data-driven look at how much energy and material the world uses, and a counterweight to rosy green-transition stories.
ab: For readers who want numbers about energy and materials.
Realistic about what decarbonization takes.
Data-heavy and unsentimental.

q.t: one of the best book I've read this year. It gives such a great perspective on how much energy and material we use.

t: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
s: Montaigne's 16th-century personal essays on human nature, friendship, death and customs, across three books.
w: HN readers describe it as like talking to a brilliant, compassionate friend, with pleasant, funny writing that rewards the investment in over 100 chapters.
ab: For readers who like reflective, personal philosophy.
Long; many readers only get through the first book.
Several translations available.

q.t: The best way I can describe Montaigne is it’s like talking to a brilliant, compassionate best friend.

s: Nintendo's hybrid handheld and home video game console, released in 2017, with detachable Joy-Con controllers.
w: HN commenters list it among favorite purchases, noting good hardware quality, and parents use it as a curated, ad-free gaming option for kids. One commenter says it's too large to pocket as a handheld.
ab: For families and casual gamers who want curated, ad-free games
Pair with Ring Fit Adventure for exercise
Succeeded by Switch 2; the original is older hardware

q.t: Nintendo Switch, I'm impressed by the quality of the hardware.

s: A 2012 ARM-based $250 Chromebook.
w: Discussed as a cheap laptop and used as a thin client.
ab: Cheap
ARM
Obsolete

q.t: the A15 dual core + T604 Mali in the Samsung chromebook was getting pretty good

t: Griffin BreakSafe Magnetic USB-C Breakaway Cable
s: A magnetic breakaway USB-C power adapter and cable meant to replace MagSafe on USB-C laptops.
w: Commenters pointed to it as the established third-party MagSafe substitute after Apple dropped the magnetic connector. Caveats: the magnet is weaker than MagSafe and the plug is bulky.
ab: For USB-C laptop owners who miss MagSafe's breakaway protection
Magnetic tip detaches before the laptop gets yanked off a desk
Bulky connector; magnet weaker than MagSafe per reviews

q.t: It's a little plug into the USB-C port, then a break away cable.

t: Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital: The Dynamics of Bubbles and Golden Ages
s: An economic theory of how technological revolutions drive financial bubbles, crashes and later golden ages over roughly fifty-year cycles.
w: Cited in threads on tech bubbles and cycles, including AI hype. Commenters call it eye-opening and note that VCs like Andreessen and Dixon admire her work.
ab: For readers interested in tech bubbles and economic history
Frames bubbles as a recurring phase of technology adoption
Academic and dense

q.t: Years ago I found this book on the topic really eye-opening

s: Beginner-friendly textbook on statistical learning methods with labs in R.
w: Pointed to as the more beginner-friendly companion to Elements of Statistical Learning, though it uses R.
ab: For newcomers to machine learning
Labs use R
Lighter on math than the Elements text

q.t: the latter seems more beginner friendly, except it uses R

t: Money: The True Story of a Made-Up Thing
s: A narrative history of money and its inventions, from clay tokens to credit and crypto, by a Planet Money cohost.
w: Mentioned as an engaging way to understand how money works and why it only works because we all agree to believe in it.
ab: Accessible history of money and finance
Pairs with Debt: The First 5,000 Years
Evidence on HN is a couple of recommendations

q.t: Also would recommend Money: The True Story of a Made-Up Thing

s: A psychiatrist argues that many mental illnesses are metabolic disorders of mitochondria and brain energy, and proposes related treatments.
w: Commenters bring it up in depression and ketogenic diet threads as an interesting reframing of mental health as a metabolic issue. One reader flags uncertainty about how strong the evidence is.
ab: For readers curious about metabolism and mental health links
Covers ketogenic diets and other metabolic treatments
Evidence for its central claims is contested

q.t: For me, by far the most interesting development in mental health is Chris Palmer's work

s: A Manning book introducing Clojure and functional programming through practical examples such as web apps and concurrency.
w: One of the few Clojure books on HN's early lists, named alongside Programming Clojure and The Joy of Clojure. Commenters point to its free first chapter and have used it to learn.
ab: For developers learning Clojure
Practical, example-driven
Written for early Clojure versions; the first edition is old

q.t: provided by the free Chapter 1 of Amit Rathore's book-in-progress, Clojure in Action

t: The Net Delusion: The Dark Side of Internet Freedom
s: A critique of the idea that the internet naturally promotes democracy, showing how authoritarian states use it for surveillance and propaganda.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a corrective to techno-utopianism about the internet and liberation, with historical parallels from communist Europe.
ab: For readers skeptical of tech-driven political change claims
Case studies of censorship and surveillance by states
Written in 2011, before social media's later evolution

q.t: this book could possibly change a bit your utopian view of liberating through radio waves

t: Grace Hopper and the Invention of the Information Age
s: A biography of Grace Hopper that places her work on early compilers and COBOL within the wider history of computing.
w: Recommended as a great book on the early days of computing and her influence. One commenter also points out COBOL was a design-by-committee product, not purely her creation.
ab: For readers of computing history and women in tech
Biography plus context on early programming languages and the Navy
Academic press tone; some sections are dense

q.t: This is an incredible book about her life and contribution

s: A collection of 97 short essays by experienced programmers on craft, teamwork, testing and professional habits, edited by Kevlin Henney.
w: Commenters note the wiki is also a book, and one owner of the paper copy highly recommends it. Another reader says any programmer who wants to be great should read it.
ab: For programmers wanting quick bites of practical wisdom
Short essays by many authors on code, bugs, and customers
Uneven; many pieces are brief and opinionated

q.t: I have an actual paper copy, and I would highly recommend it.

s: Encyclopedic 1944 reference of knots with illustrations, descriptions and uses.
w: Called a wonderful book to have, an encyclopedic tome of knots that no website replaces.
ab: For knot-tying hobbyists and sailors
Encyclopedic
Beautiful hand-lettered book

q.t: the Ashley Book of Knots[1] is a wonderful book to have.

t: Self-Made Man: One Woman's Year Disguised as a Man
s: A journalist's account of living as a man for eighteen months and what she learned about male friendship, dating and work.
w: Cited in dating and gender threads for its firsthand observations of how men and women are treated differently. Commenters point to its sections on dating.
ab: For readers curious about gender dynamics from firsthand experience
Covers dating, friendships and work
One person's experience, not a study

q.t: has quite a few interesting things to say

t: Value-Based Fees: How to Charge and Get What You're Worth
s: A guide for consultants on pricing by the value delivered to a client instead of billing by the hour.
w: The standard answer on HN when freelancers and consultants ask how to stop selling hours. Commenters like its focus on value and relationship over hourly rates.
ab: For freelancers, consultants and agency owners
Explains how to set prices tied to client outcomes
Written for general consultants, not software specifically

q.t: There is an awesome book about that.

s: A narrative history of mathematics from Egypt and Greece onward, explaining ideas and their uses for general readers.
w: HN commenters recommend it as an entry point to math that teaches fundamentals through the story of how people discovered them.
ab: For adults wanting a gentle path back into math
Story-driven rather than problem-driven
Dover paperback; written in 1967

q.t: A good entry point are one of these books which start from the very beginning of math in Egypt/Greece

t: How to Hide an Empire: A History of the Greater United States
s: A history of the United States' overseas territories and the lesser-known story of American empire beyond the 50 states.
w: Recommended whenever the Philippines, territories, or 'is the US an empire' comes up: it fills a gap most American history classes leave out.
ab: For readers wanting the neglected side of US history
Covers territories, colonies and military bases
Argumentative but well-regarded narrative

q.t: It is indeed an empire. Two good books:

s: A height-adjustable rolling hospital over-bed table with lockable wheels, popular as a cheap standing desk.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a roughly $50 standing-desk alternative that is sturdy enough for a laptop and adjusts from sitting to standing height. They note it is not very rigid.
ab: For anyone wanting a cheap sit-stand setup for a laptop
Adjustable height with lockable wheels
Not rigid enough for heavy leaning or large monitors

q.t: is sturdy enough for a laptop, and has lockable wheels

s: A Kindle Single arguing that restrictive housing and land-use rules in productive cities hold back economic growth and cost the wider economy.
w: HN commenters recommend it to explain why housing is expensive in tech hubs and what constrained supply does to the broader economy. Their usual answer to San Francisco's housing is simply to build up.
ab: For readers interested in housing, zoning and urban economics
Short Kindle Single format
Policy argument; economists debate some conclusions

q.t: explains the nationwide economic consequences of constraining housing supply (and thus rising prices)

s: An edited volume by 25 experts on the largest threats to humanity, from asteroids to AI.
w: Recommended as the best book on the subject, and noted as the book that influenced Elon Musk's public concerns about AI.
ab: Edited essays on existential risks
Wide range of threats
Academic and from 2008

q.t: the best book that I've found on this subject is _Global Catastrophic Risks_, edited by Nick Bostrom and Milan M. Cirkovic

s: A scholarly history of wargames, role-playing games and fantasy gaming leading up to Dungeons & Dragons.
w: Recommended for anyone interested in the history of D&D and tabletop games, called encyclopedic.
ab: Deep research into D&D origins
Covers wargaming and Little Wars
Very long and scholarly

q.t: I highly recommend Jon Peterson's encyclopedic Playing at the World

t: Deep Time: How Humanity Communicates Across Millennia
s: A physicist's look at how to communicate warnings and knowledge across tens of thousands of years, including the nuclear waste marker problem.
w: The recommendation whenever nuclear waste warnings or long-term messaging come up. Commenters note it has a chapter on WIPP and the 10,000-year marker problem.
ab: For readers interested in long-term communication
Includes a chapter on nuclear waste warning messages
Short and speculative

q.t: For anyone interested in things like this, I'd recommend "Deep Time" by Gregory Benford

s: A book of C code puzzles with explanations, designed to teach the language's subtleties through predicting output.
w: Recommended as a fun way to learn C, even without a compiler, and for testing your pointer knowledge. Commenters call it a small, enjoyable book.
ab: For learners who like puzzles and testing their C knowledge
Teaches pointers and precedence by working out outputs
Based on older C standards

q.t: You can effectively learn C using it without a compiler.

s: A concise Dover textbook on real analysis for a first course.
w: Recommended as a clear, easy-to-follow first analysis text, used in a university real analysis course. Another commenter suggests it as a gentler alternative to Spivak.
ab: For self-study of real analysis
Inexpensive Dover edition
Terse in places; practice problems needed

q.t: I found it very clear and easy to follow.

by: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
s: A quantitative text on active portfolio management, risk models and generating alpha.
w: Called the bible of quantitative portfolio management by people interested in quant finance. Commenters note you need undergraduate math.
ab: For quants and programmers entering quantitative finance
Covers alpha, risk models and portfolio construction
Heavy math and technical

q.t: A big part of algorithmic trading and stat arb is portfolio management, including deriving alpha, building risk models, etc.

s: A short manifesto about overcoming the instinct to avoid fear and discomfort, and stepping outside your comfort zone.
w: Recommended as a short book about facing fears and expanding your comfort zone, often as a free Kindle read.
ab: For readers who want a push to take risks
Very short and punchy
Light on research

q.t: A great book for facing your fears and expanding your comfort zone is the Flinch:

s: ACM conference proceedings from the second History of Programming Languages conference (1993), with first-hand papers from the designers of major languages.
w: Recommended as primary-source reading on how languages came to be, written by the people who made them rather than by later historians.
ab: For readers curious about where languages like C++ and Smalltalk came from.
Papers by the original language designers, from the 1993 conference.
Academic proceedings, so expect a dense, uneven read.

q.t: The book with papers from the second conference (in the 90s) is quite good

s: A systems-programming guide to the Unix API: file I/O, processes, signals, threads, interprocess communication and networking, for C programmers.
w: It turns up in HN lists of C and Unix learning resources and of systems reading for people who want to understand the OS interface, alongside other kernel and architecture books.
ab: For C programmers who want to learn the Unix system interface
Covers processes, signals, IPC and sockets
Written in 2004; Stevens' APUE is a common alternative

t: Serious Python: Black-Belt Advice on Deployment, Scalability, Testing, and More
s: A No Starch Press book of advanced Python topics including packaging, testing, performance, and project structure.
w: HN suggests it as a short overview of higher-level Python concepts for intermediate and advanced programmers, though one reader found High Performance Python deeper.
ab: For intermediate Python developers going beyond basics
Short book covering testing, packaging and performance
Published 2018; less depth than High Performance Python

q.t: Serious Python is a short, quick overview of some higher-level concepts I wasn't aware of before.

t: Visual Differential Geometry and Forms: A Mathematical Drama in Five Acts
s: A geometric, visual introduction to differential geometry and differential forms by the author of Visual Complex Analysis.
w: HN math fans point to it when they want a visual rather than abstract treatment of differential geometry, and list it among books valued for how they are written.
ab: For readers who want geometric intuition, not just formulas
Companion in spirit to Needham's Visual Complex Analysis
Large, demanding book

q.t: If you'd like more of such a visual perspective on differential geometry, I recommend Tristan Needham's book

t: American Prison: A Reporter's Undercover Journey into the Business of Punishment
s: Journalist Shane Bauer's account of working undercover as a guard in a private Louisiana prison, with the history of private incarceration.
w: HN threads about prisons and prison labor point to it as a vivid look at the brutality, corruption and apathy inside private prisons, highly recommended for anyone interested.
ab: For readers interested in criminal justice and incarceration
First-person undercover reporting plus history
Disturbing subject matter

q.t: I'm currently reading American Prison by Shane Bauer and I highly recommend it to anyone interested in this topic.

s: A pop-science book about creativity.
w: Recommended as a pop-science read, though the author later faced fabrication issues.
ab: Pop science
Readable
Fabricated quotes

q.t: It's a pop-science book, to be sure, but still a really good read.

s: A novel following two friends who become video game designers, tracing their creative partnership and friendship over three decades.
w: HN readers call it the best read of their year for its immersive writing and its portrait of game development and complicated human relationships.
ab: For readers who like character-driven literary fiction
Set in the video game industry
Emotional, long-spanning story

q.t: The narration is very immersive and the author makes you very invested in the story.

s: Chapman's relationship guide describing five ways people give and receive love and how mismatches cause conflict.
w: HN readers, including self-described geeky low-social-skill folks, say it helped them understand how they and their partners express and receive love.
ab: For couples and anyone working on relationships
Simple framework that is easy to apply
Framework is popular rather than research-backed

q.t: Very eye-opening with regards to oneself ways of expressing love, and more importantly receiving it.

s: A light 14-inch Linux laptop from System76 that ships with Pop!_OS and open firmware, weighing about 1 kg.
w: Linux users like it as a very light, well-supported laptop where the purchase funds Pop!_OS development. One long-term owner reports good battery life and no complaints after two years.
ab: For developers who want Linux working out of the box
Very light, around 1 kg
One owner finds the build a bit cheap-feeling

q.t: the best and lightest laptop I have ever owned

s: The 1999 sci-fi action film about a hacker who learns his reality is a computer simulation.
w: HN commenters list it among favorite movies and hacker films, loving how its ideas parallel our world and echo Buddhist concepts.
ab: Landmark cyberpunk action film.
Often on lists of hacker movies.
Sequels get less praise.

q.t: I love how everything has a parallel with our own world

s: A Pragmatic Programmers introduction to Clojure and its Lisp, JVM and concurrency features.
w: Early Clojure learners called Halloway's book excellent when Clojure 1.0 had little documentation.
ab: For programmers new to Clojure
Pragmatic Programmers style
Written for early Clojure

q.t: Holloway book is excellent, and only $22 from a monstrously large online seller!

s: A resource-trading and building board game for three to four players, the gateway modern board game.
w: HN commenters repeatedly name it as a favorite board game, with expansions like Cities and Knights, and house rules like the penny rule.
ab: Gateway strategy game with trading.
Expansions available.
Best with three to four players.

q.t: Settlers of Catan and it's variants are a delight.

t: Lost in Math: How Beauty Leads Physics Astray
s: A physicist argues that the pursuit of mathematical beauty has misled theoretical physics.
w: Cited as the contrarian counterpoint on beauty in physics. One commenter finds the tone off-putting.
ab: For physics watchers
Skeptical of string theory
Opinionated tone

s: A small, light 10-inch Windows tablet-laptop from Microsoft with a detachable keyboard.
w: HN users recommend it as the smallest laptop that can run dev tools with WSL, and as a note-taking and PDF reading machine. Commenters advise getting the 8GB model, and note it isn't great on a lap.
ab: For people wanting a very small second computer
Windows with WSL, stylus support
Cramped keyboard; get the 8GB RAM model

q.t: buying a Surface Go. Using WSL you can tool up, like on any other machine.

s: A book of artisan sourdough bread recipes and technique from San Francisco's Tartine Bakery, with detailed photos and step-by-step instruction.
w: Named in cooking-for-hackers and bread-baking threads as the book to start with, usually alongside The Bread Baker's Apprentice and Italian Baker.
ab: For home bakers ready to try naturally leavened sourdough
Process-heavy; long timelines and patience required
Get the first book in the series

q.t: I can recommend two books: Tartine I and Italian Baker.

s: A textbook introducing quantum computing through linear algebra and computer science concepts, with minimal physics.
w: Readers love that it assumes CS and math rather than physics, and says it ties quantum ideas back to classical computing and automata.
ab: For programmers who want quantum computing without physics
Needs comfortable linear algebra and complex numbers
Covers algorithms, cryptography and programming languages

q.t: it's almost entirely self-contained and you can immediately start to make connections with classical computing

s: A sweeping comparison of East and West across 20,000 years of history, arguing geography shapes who dominates.
w: Recommended in threads about civilizational competition and disruption cycles as a book on the patterns of social development.
ab: For fans of big-picture history
Long, data-driven
Deterministic thesis is debated

q.t: You might enjoy the book "Why the West Rules -- For Now"

s: A phonics-based workbook for teaching children to read, built on regular spelling patterns by a leading mid-century linguist.
w: HN parents and educators recommend it as a simple, pattern-based way to teach kids to read, in contrast to whole-language methods criticized in the Sold a Story discussion.
ab: For parents teaching a young child to read at home
Teaches reading through regular spelling patterns, not guessing
Dated look; check reviews of original vs newer edition
