s: A self-help workbook teaching cognitive behavioral therapy techniques for depression and anxiety, with exercises and self-tests.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a practical CBT self-help guide, and one says their therapist assigned it as homework. It is a shorter, more usable version of Feeling Good.
ab: For people dealing with low mood or anxiety who want structured CBT
Workbook-style with exercises and checklists
Not a replacement for professional care

q.t: It is possible to learn it from a book on your own. I recommend The Feeling Good Handbook by David D. Burns.

t: Dumbing Us Down: The Hidden Curriculum of Compulsory Schooling
s: A former New York teacher of the year argues that compulsory schooling teaches conformity and dependence, in a collection of essays and speeches.
w: HN commenters name it as Gatto's best-known work and the one to start with in threads on schooling, homeschooling and education reform.
ab: For parents and educators questioning conventional schooling
Short essays and speeches
One-sided polemic; claims about history of schooling are disputed

q.t: this is his most well known work and I highly recommend it (and his others)

t: Mirror Worlds: or the Day Software Puts the Universe in a Shoebox
s: Gelernter's 1991 vision of software models of real institutions and cities, from the inventor of Linda tuple spaces.
w: Cited as a visionary idea behind digital models of cities and as related reading on simulation and tuple spaces.
ab: Early vision of digital twins
By the creator of Linda coordination
Predictions are 1990s speculation

s: A comprehensive reference to Ruby on Rails 3 that goes deep into each framework component and its idioms.
w: Recommended as the thorough, somewhat dry book to read after the basics. One reader went through it cover to cover and applied what they learned right away.
ab: For developers who already know Rails basics and want depth
Covers the framework's components in a reference-style layout
Targets Rails 3, so it is badly out of date today

q.t: It's a reference of sorts and it's very complete (afaik).

t: Audio-Technica ATH-M50 Professional Studio Monitor Headphones
s: Closed-back wired over-ear studio monitor headphones with detachable cables and a neutral-leaning, punchy sound.
w: The default price-to-performance headphone recommendation on HN. Closed-back seals block office chatter even at low volume, and commenters say it sounds good across genres.
ab: For office, studio and travel listening on a budget
Closed-back design isolates noise passively
Wired only; the original model is now succeeded by newer versions

q.t: nothing hits the price:performance ratio as sweetly, and it is great-sounding no matter what genre I throw at it.

t: Syntech USB-C to USB-A Adapter, Thunderbolt 3 Compatible
s: A tiny USB-C to USB-A female adapter that lets you plug older USB devices into a USB-C port.
w: The cheap, tiny fix for modern laptops without USB-A ports. Commenters keep one attached to each cable or in the laptop bag instead of using a bulky dongle.
ab: For USB-C laptops used with older USB-A devices
Compact adapter you can leave on a cable
Data-only use; do not rely on it for charging

q.t: just buy a bunch of these[1] and keep them attached to your USB cables all the time.

s: A short, accessible introduction to algorithms by a co-author of CLRS, with minimal math.
w: Recommended as an approachable prequel to CLRS for people without a technical background.
ab: For beginners before reading CLRS
Light math and readable explanations
Less depth than a full textbook

t: Monetizing Innovation: How Smart Companies Design the Product Around the Price
s: A guide to pricing software and products, arguing you should settle willingness to pay before building.
w: Recommended as the go-to book on pricing for founders.
ab: For founders and PMs setting pricing for products.
Covers research on willingness to pay before building.
Corporate case-study style.

q.t: The book Monetizing Innovation is a book all about pricing [0]. It's a great read.

t: The First Six Books of the Elements of Euclid
s: A reprint of Oliver Byrne's 1847 edition of Euclid with colored diagrams in place of letters.
w: Recommended as a beautiful physical edition of a famous visual Euclid.
ab: For lovers of math and design.
Full-color visual proofs.
Covers only six books.

q.t: lovely and wonderful, I highly recommend the modern reprint

s: A psychologist critiques claims of innate brain differences between men and women.
w: Recommended as a systematic takedown of neurosexism, though one calls it a little boring.
ab: For readers interested in gender and science.
Critiques popular neuroscience claims.
Contested.

q.t: It is a fantastically interesting book.

s: Philosophical essay by Josef Pieper arguing that leisure is the foundation of culture and that a world of total work loses it.
w: HN commenters bring it up in debates about overwork and the cult of busyness, as the philosophical case for leisure. A few list it among books that changed how they see society.
ab: For readers thinking about work, rest, and culture
Short, philosophical essay
Catholic and classical in outlook; not self-help

t: Complications: A Surgeon's Notes on an Imperfect Science
s: Essays by surgeon Atul Gawande on mistakes, uncertainty and judgment in medical practice, drawn from his residency years.
w: HN readers give it as a gift and list it among year-end reads for its candid look at how medicine actually works. It also gets cited in debates about hospital care.
ab: For anyone curious how doctors really decide
Essay collection; easy to read in pieces
US-centric hospital system, written in the early 2000s

q.t: Fascinating look at life in the medical profession.

t: Craft GraphQL APIs in Elixir with Absinthe
s: A Pragmatic Programmers book by the creators of Absinthe on building GraphQL APIs with Elixir and Phoenix.

ab: For Elixir and Phoenix developers building GraphQL APIs
Written by Absinthe's authors
Narrow audience: Elixir and Absinthe only

t: The Elements of Computing Systems, Second Edition
s: The Nand2Tetris textbook, which guides you through building a full computer from logic gates up to a compiler, operating system and applications.

ab: For programmers wanting to understand a computer end to end
Project-based, with free online course materials
Second edition updated in 2021

q.t: I would highly recommend you work through nand2tetris

s: A TV drama series following computer makers and startup founders through the 1980s PC era and the early 1990s internet boom.
w: HN recommends it as a great, underrated drama about entrepreneurship and relationships, and a go-to when asked for tech fiction set in the early computing era.
ab: For people who like tech-industry drama
Four seasons; the show grows stronger over time
Fictionalized history

q.t: Not a movie but Halt and Catch Fire was really great.

s: Plutarch's paired biographies of famous Greeks and Romans, such as Alexander and Caesar, comparing their characters and fortunes.
w: HN readers call it an essential book on politics and human nature, saying its stories help you build a mental model of how empires rise and fall.
ab: For readers of classical history and biography
Pairs each Greek with a Roman
Many translations; Oxford World's Classics editions praised

q.t: the stories told between the two alone allow to you build a mental model of the nature of mankind

s: A classic bedtime picture book in which a rabbit says goodnight to everything in his room.
w: HN parents report reading it hundreds of times and it shows up in children's favorites lists.
ab: Bedtime picture book for toddlers.
Rhythmic and calming.
Parents warn you will read it a lot.

q.t: I think I read "Goodnight Moon" to our son every evening for three years

t: In the Plex: How Google Thinks, Works, and Shapes Our Lives
s: Steven Levy's inside account of Google's history, culture, engineering and business decisions, based on extensive access to its people.
w: Recommended for readers who want the inside story of Google's early days and decisions, and cited as a source for details about the company's strategy.
ab: For readers interested in Google's history and culture
Based on interviews with insiders
Ends around 2011

q.t: If you like this article, you would probably enjoy Stephen Levy's book In The Plex

s: Essays by the author of The Mythical Man-Month on design process across disciplines, with case studies including the design of his own house.

Essays and case studies from across architecture and engineering

t: The Man from the Future: The Visionary Life of John von Neumann
s: A biography of John von Neumann covering his life and the lasting impact of his work on computing, game theory and science.

Covers life and legacy
Recent biography with strong reviews

t: Programming Ruby 1.9: The Pragmatic Programmers' Guide
s: The 'Pickaxe' book, a thorough tutorial and reference to the Ruby language and its standard library, covering Ruby 1.9.

ab: For programmers learning Ruby properly
Both tutorial and library reference
Covers Ruby 1.9; later editions exist

q.t: a full examination of Ruby and its standard libraries, as well as for a reference later on

t: Designing with the Mind in Mind: Simple Guide to Understanding User Interface Design Guidelines
s: A guide that explains user interface design rules through human perception and cognition.

Some examples are from older interfaces

q.t: it's a great overview of basic design principles, with clever illustrated examples.

t: The Structure of Magic: A Book About Language and Therapy
s: The founding NLP text, analyzing the language patterns of therapists to model how people construct and change their inner views.
w: A small group of commenters rate it highly and recommend it to programmers interested in analyzing mental models through language. Others find it strange and it is tied to the NLP field.
ab: For readers curious about language and mental models
Founding text of neuro-linguistic programming
NLP's scientific standing is weak; the book is dated

q.t: One of the best reads I've ever done

t: Conspiracy: Peter Thiel, Hulk Hogan, Gawker, and the Anatomy of Intrigue
s: An account of the secretly financed lawsuit that bankrupted Gawker, told through Peter Thiel's long campaign against the site.
w: Called the definitive and very well written account of the Thiel-Gawker saga. Commenters note the author clearly admires Thiel, so the end speculation reads slanted.
ab: For readers interested in media, tech billionaires and lawsuits
Narrative and fast to read
Author sympathetic to Thiel; speculative ending

q.t: Conspiracy by Ryan Holiday is the definitive account of this story. It's very well written and full of intrigue.

s: A Manning book that teaches math useful to programmers, such as linear algebra, calculus and graphics, using Python code.
w: The suggestion for programmers who feel they lack math. Recommenders point to it for a hands-on way in, though one buyer found they needed to firm up their algebra first.
ab: For working programmers who want practical math with code
Python-based examples across several topics
May need basic algebra first

q.t: I also highly recommend Math for Programmers from Manning

s: Ram Dass's 1971 book on spirituality and meditation, including illustrated pages and practical teachings.
w: Named as a life-changing book by some, though one admits it's on the hippy side. It's cited as a major spiritual text.
ab: For readers curious about meditation and spirituality
Unusual illustrated layout
Hippie-era style; may not suit everyone

q.t: for me the book that affected me the most was Ram Dass' Be Here Now.

s: A humorous collection of dot-com failures drawn from the fuckedcompany.com website, with short case notes on what went wrong.
w: HN points to it as the printed list of failed dot-com startups, useful when people ask for a repository of failed companies and ideas.
ab: For readers interested in the dot-com bubble and failed startups
Short irreverent entries on collapsed companies
Humor-driven and dated, from 2002; used copies cost pennies

s: A Dover introduction to graph theory for readers with only high school algebra.
w: Recommended as the cheap, friendly Dover intro for hobbyists.
ab: For beginners to graph theory
Cheap paperback
Light on advanced topics

q.t: I like the cheap Dover intro

by: Bernard R. Gelbaum, John M. H. Olmsted
s: A Dover collection of carefully worked counterexamples that show why the hypotheses of theorems in real analysis matter.
w: Recommended for learning math by seeing where intuition fails, such as when the order of integration matters. One reader calls it a must-have; another notes it contains an error in the Weierstrass function.
ab: For math students working through real analysis
Cheap Dover paperback of worked pathological examples
Some examples are involved; one reader reports an error

q.t: I find they are often useful for understanding the purpose of the technical assumptions that accompany many theorems.

t: Garbage Collection: Algorithms for Automatic Dynamic Memory Management
s: The standard academic text on garbage collection algorithms, covering tracing, reference counting and their variants.
w: Called excellent and fully recommended, and described as one of the most widely accepted academic books on GC algorithms. It is the pointer people give when asked where to learn how collectors work.
ab: For language implementers and runtime engineers
Covers classic GC algorithms in depth
A later handbook edition has newer material

q.t: it's excellent[0]. Fully recommended to all.

s: Knuth's study of chapter 3, verse 16 of each Bible book, with calligraphy and commentary.
w: Mentioned as Knuth's non-computer book, one commenter calling it their favorite Knuth book. It comes up as evidence of his Christian faith.
ab: For Knuth fans curious about his other work
Features calligraphy for 3:16 of each book
Religious subject, nothing about computing

q.t: My favorite book from Knuth isn't computer-related at all.

t: Fumbling the Future: How Xerox Invented, Then Ignored, the First Personal Computer
by: Douglas K. Smith, Robert C. Alexander
s: A history of how Xerox PARC created the Alto and the ideas behind the modern PC, and why Xerox failed to commercialize them.
w: HN commenters cite it as the definitive account of Xerox PARC and why the GUI did not start at Apple. It comes up whenever a company is accused of failing to productize its own research.
ab: For readers interested in computing history and corporate strategy
Clarifies what PARC invented versus what Apple borrowed
Often available cheaply used

q.t: Seriously, that book is a must read for any person that reads this site.

s: A comprehensive guide to the JavaScript language and its browser APIs, by a well-known JavaScript author.
w: Recommended by commenters who rate Zakas's books highly for learning JavaScript the language properly.
ab: For learners who want thorough JavaScript fundamentals
Earlier editions predate modern ES6+
Reference-sized, not a quick read

q.t: I can highly recommend books written by Nicholas Zakas.

t: The Baby Owner's Manual: Operating Instructions, Trouble-Shooting Tips, and Advice on First-Year Maintenance
s: A humorous guide to a baby's first year, written like a car manual.
w: A fun gift for new dads who think in technical terms. One parent says it is not the best but is not just a joke either.
ab: For new parents with a geeky sense of humor
Lighthearted; not a thorough medical guide
Quick, easy read

q.t: Lots of simple things, covered in a lighthearted 'like a car manual' kind of way.

s: An explanation of Harry Browne's Permanent Portfolio, an equal split between stocks, long-term bonds, gold and cash designed to survive any economic climate.
w: Cited by commenters as a sensible capital-preservation approach with low volatility and steady returns. One says it makes sense because four weakly correlated assets keep the portfolio consistent.
ab: For investors who want a simple, low-volatility strategy
Explains the four-asset allocation and why it works
Low stock allocation means it is not an income generator

q.t: capital preservation (wrt inflation) is more important than chasing higher returns - which frankly are not under your control.

t: Against Empathy: The Case for Rational Compassion
s: A psychologist argues empathy is a poor moral guide and that reasoned compassion leads to better decisions.
w: Cited by commenters for its contrarian case that empathy biases judgment and that compassion works better. People point to it when discussing empathy at work and in public debate.
ab: For readers curious about moral psychology
Argues for rational compassion over emotional empathy
Provocative title; the argument is more nuanced than it sounds

q.t: Really liked the point Paul Bloom made with his book about Rational Compasion

t: Programming the Universe: A Quantum Computer Scientist Takes on the Cosmos
s: Seth Lloyd argues that the universe is a quantum computer and explains computation, information and quantum theory.
w: Said to help understand quantum computing and used to illustrate how improbable random text is. It appears in physics reading threads.
ab: For readers into quantum computing and information
Popular science from a leading researcher
Speculative thesis

q.t: Programming the Universe by Seth Lloyd really helped me to understand this stuff.

t: The Hungry Brain: Outsmarting the Instincts That Make Us Overeat
s: A neuroscientist explains how brain circuits drive appetite and why modern food environments lead to overeating.
w: Recommended in obesity threads as an explanation of why willpower alone fails and appetite is wired into the brain.
ab: For anyone curious about the neuroscience of appetite.
Backs up the case that weight is physiological.
Popular-science level.

q.t: It's by a neuroscientist, who explains the deep ways that the appetite mechanism is wired into just about every area of our brain

s: A printed collection of Warren Buffett's annual Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters from 1965 on.
w: HN's paper-version pointer for the shareholder letters, for readers who prefer print to the free web archive.
ab: For investing and business readers
Decades of primary-source commentary
Free online; this is the printed edition

q.t: I am currently reading the collection of Warren Buffets' Annual Letters to the Shareholders

t: Rare Earth: Why Complex Life Is Uncommon in the Universe
s: Two scientists argue that microbial life may be common but complex animal life is rare because Earth's conditions are unusually special.
w: Referenced in HN threads on alien life and the Fermi paradox, usually for its argument that complex life needs many unlikely conditions such as a large Moon and Jupiter.
ab: For readers interested in astrobiology and the Fermi paradox
Argues microbial life may be common, complex life rare
Published in 2000; the argument has been debated since

q.t: The conclusion they come to is that complex, multicellular life is likely extremely rare in the universe.

s: The standard university textbook on cell biology, covering DNA, proteins, signalling and the machinery of living cells.
w: Recommended to programmers and biohackers as the gold standard for cell biology, readable without much prior biology.
ab: For serious self-study of cell and molecular biology
Huge and expensive; a reference as much as a read
Older editions are cheaper but out of date

q.t: the gold standard for cellular biology

s: A comprehensive reference on real-time computer graphics, covering shading, lighting, GPUs and rendering techniques.
w: Named as the standard reference for real-time graphics, usually recommended alongside free ray tracing resources and Physically Based Rendering.
ab: For graphics programmers and game developers
Reference-style; dense
Covers modern rendering techniques

q.t: is one of the standard references here

s: David Brin argues that pervasive surveillance is coming and that society should aim for mutual transparency rather than secrecy.
w: Brought up in privacy and surveillance threads for its argument that the real choice is who gets to watch whom. Commenters say it gets more relevant every year.
ab: For readers thinking about privacy, surveillance and technology
Argues for reciprocal transparency over hiding
Written in 1998; its optimism is debated

q.t: David Brin's Transparent Society gets more relevant every day.

s: A reference for compiler optimization and code generation, covering intermediate representations, data-flow analysis and register allocation.
w: Recommended by tptacek as a heavy, backend-focused compiler book, and cited for its description of multi-IR compiler architectures. Suited to people past the Dragon Book basics.
ab: For readers who want compiler backends and optimization
In-depth coverage of IRs, data-flow analysis and code generation
Dense and from 1997; SSA coverage is limited

q.t: This is pretty heavy on the backend and codegen, which is where my head is at these days.

s: A psychologist's guide to people without a conscience, estimating that about 4% of the population are sociopaths and how to spot them.
w: Recommended in threads about difficult bosses and psychopaths at work as an interesting read on conscience. The 4% figure gets quoted.
ab: For readers curious about antisocial personalities
Case studies and advice on dealing with sociopaths
Pop-psychology; its prevalence claim is debated

q.t: I found the book, _The_Sociopath_Next_Door_[1], to be an interesting read.

t: How to Solve It: Modern Heuristics
s: A textbook on heuristic and evolutionary methods for hard optimization problems, framed after Polya's How to Solve It.
w: One commenter calls it the single best technical book they have read, and others suggest it for developing logical skills. Brought up as a rare heuristics book.
ab: For readers curious about heuristics and optimization
Covers search, evolutionary algorithms and constraints
Not Polya's How to Solve It; a different book

q.t: single best technical book I have ever read

s: A contest-oriented algorithms text covering data structures, graph algorithms, dynamic programming and geometry with practice problems for ICPC-style competitions.
w: Suggested for interview prep and for anyone starting competitive programming; commenters name it the go-to book for building contest skills.
ab: For ICPC and interview-style problem solving
Lots of worked problems across many algorithm topics
Terse style; assumes you can already code

q.t: this is a good book for preparation

t: Chapter Zero: Fundamental Notions of Abstract Mathematics
s: A textbook for the transition to proof-based math.
w: HN readers recommend it for foundations.
ab: Students entering proof math
Accessible
Textbook

q.t: but it does so in an easily understood way

t: This Is Your Brain on Music: The Science of a Human Obsession
s: A neuroscientist and former record producer explains how the brain processes music, covering rhythm, pitch, memory, emotion and why we love certain songs.
w: HN points to it for anyone wanting to understand music and the brain. It comes up when music taste, emotion and the age when musical interest peaks are discussed.
ab: For music lovers curious about the neuroscience behind listening
Accessible writing, no technical background needed
Some findings have been challenged by later research

q.t: For those wanting to understand better brains and music

t: Le Ton beau de Marot: In Praise of the Music of Language
s: Hofstadter's long exploration of translation, using many English versions of one French poem to show what is gained and lost between languages.
w: HN commenters recommend it for the problem of translating poetry and wordplay, calling it an intellectual delight.
ab: For language lovers and translators
Centers on one French poem and its translations
Long and idiosyncratic; assumes interest in wordplay

q.t: A book that deals with this very challenge.

t: Crazy Like Us: The Globalization of the American Psyche
s: Journalist Ethan Watters shows through case studies how Western ideas of mental illness have been exported and have reshaped how other cultures experience it.
w: HN commenters cite it when discussing culture and mental illness, with one saying it changed their thinking about how conditions spread socially.
ab: For readers curious how culture shapes mental illness
Case-study driven, journalistic
Not a clinical guide

q.t: My thinking about mental illness changed a lot after reading a book called Crazy Like Us

t: The Machinery of Freedom: Guide to a Radical Capitalism
s: A libertarian argument for how law, police, roads and defense could be provided without a state.
w: Recommended as a thought experiment about how core government functions could work privately, even by people who aren't convinced.
ab: For readers curious about anarcho-capitalism
Provocative, readable economic reasoning
You may well disagree; that is the point

q.t: it gives you a new way of thinking about these services

s: Ben Fry's O'Reilly guide to acquiring, parsing and visualizing data using the Processing environment.
w: Recommended as a friendly, visually beautiful way to start with data visualization and Processing, with the caveat that the code samples contain typos a programmer can fix.
ab: For programmers new to data visualization
Uses the Processing language throughout
Written in 2008; code has typos and has aged

q.t: is a good easy way to jump into processing

s: A broad textbook on the mathematics used in engineering: ODEs, linear algebra, vector calculus, Fourier analysis, PDEs and complex analysis.
w: Named as an excellent applied-math text and a book that sparked some readers' interest in math. It's mentioned as a staple reference.
ab: For engineering and physics students
Covers a wide range of applied topics
Big, expensive textbook

q.t: I think Kreyszig's Advanced Engineering Mathematics is an excellent text in applied math.

s: Apple's expandable workstation tower, sold in several generations from the 2008 model to the Apple silicon version.
w: HN users mention long-lived 2008 models still used as main machines and a recent workstation purchase they love. Others mention old models as hobby servers.
ab: For professionals needing a powerful Mac workstation
Different generations vary widely
Expensive; older models are obsolete

q.t: This year I spent $15,000 on a Mac Pro and love it.

t: A Practical Guide to Linux Commands, Editors, and Shell Programming
s: Broad reference and tutorial on Linux command-line tools, vi and emacs editors, and shell scripting.
w: Recommended to people learning the command line and sysadmin basics as a solid single volume.
ab: For beginners to intermediate Linux users
Covers commands, editors and shell scripting
Edition is dated; check for newer printing

s: History of the AK-47 and the assault rifle, tracing how this weapon changed warfare and politics around the world.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a great introduction to the Kalashnikov and the impact of assault rifles, read as a story of technology shifting power.
ab: For readers of military and technology history
Covers the AK-47, M16 and their makers
Narrative nonfiction, not a technical manual

q.t: gives a great introduction to the history and impact of the Kalashnikov in particular and assault rifles in general

t: Secure Coding in C and C++
s: Guide to avoiding security flaws in C and C++, including buffer overflows and integer errors.
w: Recommended for C/C++ developers; nearly half is devoted to integer overflow and signedness bugs most developers ignore.
ab: For C and C++ developers
Heavy on integer and memory bugs
Edition is older

q.t: nearly half the book is dedicated to integer underflow/overflow (and signed/unsigned) issues

s: A detachable boom microphone for compatible V-MODA headphones, also usable with other headphones via adapters.
w: Recommended for calls: one commenter says it is much better than a throat mic and closer to podcast quality.
ab: For adding a mic to wired headphones
Works with ATH-M50x using an adapter
Check connector compatibility

q.t: Someone on hacker news recommended this mic before and it's much better than this sample

t: Chaos Monkeys: Obscene Fortune and Random Failure in Silicon Valley
s: A memoir by a former Facebook ad product manager about his startup, Twitter acquisition and work at Facebook.
w: Recommended as an entertaining look at startup funding, acquisition and Facebook culture.
ab: For readers curious about Silicon Valley
Memoir with ad tech details
Some opinionated passages

q.t: It's an really entertaining read and he includes a bunch of asides on how the Silicon Valley M&A pipelines work

t: Mathematical Methods for Physics and Engineering
s: A large textbook of the applied mathematics used in physics and engineering.
w: HN math learners suggest it for applied math in physics and engineering, as a bigger alternative to Boas.
ab: For physics and engineering students
Big, comprehensive
Heavy to carry and read

q.t: I'd also recommend Riley, Hobson and Bence, which has all the benefits and disadvantages of being bigger

s: Hofstadter's research group's papers on computer models of analogy-making and creativity.
w: HN readers recommend it to hackers interested in aesthetics and cognitive science, while warning it is not an easy read.
ab: For readers into AI and cognitive science
Dense research essays
Not an easy read

q.t: I recommend it to any hacker interested in aesthetics or cognitive science, but it is not an easy read

s: A guide for teenagers who want to leave school and educate themselves.
w: HN commenters recommend it to teenagers who hate school.
ab: For teens and parents exploring unschooling
Argues for self-directed learning
Strongly opinionated

q.t: I recommend taking a look at a book called The Teenage Liberation Handbook

by: Albert Paul Malvino and Jerald A. Brown
s: An introductory text building a simple computer (SAP-1) from digital logic.
w: HN readers recommend it as a classic reference for understanding CPU design.
ab: For hobbyists building CPUs
Teaches SAP-1
Older text

q.t: It's a great reference and lets you dive a little deeper into the design as well.

t: Genome: The Autobiography of a Species in 23 Chapters
s: A popular-science tour of the human genome that uses one notable gene from each of the 23 chromosome pairs to tell a story about heredity, disease and behavior.
w: Commenters call it a good, accessible read on genetics and a phenomenal pick for anyone curious about the field; it also gets quoted as a source on the nature-versus-nurture debate.
ab: For curious non-biologists who want genetics explained through stories
One chapter per chromosome, each built around a single gene
Published 2000; the science has moved on since

q.t: is a phenomenal book for those interested in the space

t: It's Not How Good You Are, It's How Good You Want to Be
s: A short, illustrated book of provocative advice on creativity, risk and ambition by a former advertising creative director at Saatchi & Saatchi.
w: HN readers recommend it as a quick self-improvement book that suits entrepreneurs and creatives alike, and keep going back to it for its blunt lines like experience being lazy.
ab: For creatives and founders who want a quick motivational push
Very short, visual, and easy to reread
Advertising-industry tone; advice is aphoristic rather than systematic

q.t: is a good self-improvement book for lots of different people, entrepreneurs included

t: See No Evil: The True Story of a Ground Soldier in the CIA's War on Terrorism
s: A memoir by a former CIA case officer about his years in Middle East field operations and how the agency lost its human intelligence capacity.
w: HN readers call it one of their favorites on intelligence work, and note it inspired the film Syriana. It shows what case officers actually do, which is recruit spies.
ab: For readers interested in spycraft and the CIA
Firsthand account by a field case officer
Single author's viewpoint on events in the 1990s

q.t: His book about his experiences in the CIA, See No Evil, is one of my favorites

s: A Springer text covering nonparametric methods such as density estimation, regression, the bootstrap and wavelets, aimed at readers with a calculus-level math background.
w: Offered in HN threads on statistical learning as a rigorous but accessible look at what is under the hood in statistics, and an alternative explanation of the bootstrap.
ab: For readers who want rigorous but readable statistics
Companion to Wasserman's All of Statistics
Needs solid calculus and probability

q.t: really opened my eyes to the inner workings of statistics in a rigorous yet accessible way

s: A textbook on the psychology of rational thinking, probability, decision theory and judgment biases.
w: Recommended on HN by readers who finished Kahneman and want a more complete academic treatment of decision-making.
ab: For readers who want a rigorous survey of judgment and decisions
Covers decision theory and cognitive biases
Textbook format

q.t: (I say this as someone who has read Thinking, Fast and Slow and other Kahneman books.)

t: Resonate: Present Visual Stories That Transform Audiences
s: A guide to building presentations around story structure and audience transformation.
w: Recommended for people who want to improve their slides and hold attention; one commenter calls it among three kickass presentation books.
ab: For anyone giving talks or pitches
Story-structure approach
Slide-heavy with design focus

q.t: Three kickass books I found very helpful in improving my slide-foo and hold the attention of my audience:

t: The Smartest Kids in the World: And How They Got That Way
s: A journalist follows American exchange students in Finland, Poland and South Korea to see what makes their schools work.
w: Cited as one of the more referenced books on why top countries' schools succeed, and for how teaching prestige affects education.
ab: For readers interested in education policy
Narrative journalism
2014 data and anecdotes

q.t: this is one of the more referenced books

s: A book on the philosophy of object-oriented design, thinking in behavior and responsibilities rather than data.
w: Recommended for people who want to understand OOP as behavior decomposition, often alongside Alan Kay's views.
ab: For OOP practitioners wanting the original ideas
Philosophical rather than practical
Dense in places

s: A short pocket reference of commands and tips for penetration testers and red teamers.
w: Recommended as a handy short reference to keep around, though some call its content dated.
ab: For pentesters and sysadmins
Quick command reference
Content is dated, not a tutorial

q.t: i recommend having a copy

t: AppleDesign: The Work of the Apple Industrial Design Group
s: A 1997 photographic book documenting products and prototypes from Apple's industrial design group.
w: HN gadget fans point to it for photos of unreleased Apple prototypes and early phone concepts. It is out of print and pricey.
ab: For Apple and industrial design fans
Many prototype photos from the 80s and 90s
Out of print; used copies are expensive

q.t: that shows a ton of concepts and a few 'communication device' concepts

s: A compact book on how SQL indexes work and how to write queries that use them well.
w: HN's go-to for database indexing; one commenter says it explains in detail how SQL indexes work and how to use them for faster queries.
ab: For developers writing SQL
Short and focused on indexing
Not a general SQL tutorial

q.t: He goes into great detail to explain how exactly SQL indices work and how to leverage this to write queries.

t: How to Read a Financial Report: Wringing Vital Signs Out of the Numbers
s: A plain-English guide to reading balance sheets, income statements and cash-flow statements.
w: HN recommends it to learn financial statements, including how companies manage their losses and presentation.
ab: For non-finance people who read company reports
Accounting basics, clearly explained
Basic; not a fraud-detection manual

q.t: I recommend How to Read a Financial Report by John Tracey.

s: A broad guide to building a game engine in C++, covering architecture, rendering, audio and tools.
w: Offered as a better pick than Game Programming Patterns for game development and as a guided way to learn engine internals. A reader notes the C++ is older.
ab: For people building a game engine
Uses DirectX and C++
Older C++ style

q.t: A much better books about game development would be Game Coding Complete

t: Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences
by: Guido W. Imbens, Donald B. Rubin
s: A graduate-level textbook on the potential-outcomes framework for causal inference, from randomized experiments to observational studies.
w: Named as a core reference from Rubin, who invented many observational-data methods, and called an excellent statistics textbook in causal inference threads.
ab: For statisticians and data scientists doing causal work
Rigorous, mathematical treatment
Dense and expensive; not a gentle intro

q.t: is another excellent textbook for statistics

t: Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems: Queueing Theory in Action
s: A textbook applying queueing theory to computer systems performance.
w: Highly recommended as a practical queueing theory book, one commenter calls it a secret superweapon for back-of-the-napkin estimates.
ab: For systems engineers
Practical and rigorous
Math-heavy

q.t: Queueing theory is one of my favourite secret superweapons.

s: A romantic comedy about a socially awkward genetics professor who designs a questionnaire to find a wife.
w: HN readers recommend it as an easy, charming novel, one finishing it in a single night, and some saw themselves in the main character.
ab: For readers who like light romantic comedy
Quick, easy read
Has sequels

q.t: The Rosie Project[7] was so completely charming I ended up reading it straight through in one night.

s: First book of Greg Egan's Orthogonal trilogy, set in a universe with different physics, following aliens who race to save their world.
w: Hard-sci-fi readers on HN pick it as a standout of Egan's work and one of the best science fiction reads of the year, for its inventive alternative physics.
ab: For readers who love hard science fiction
Starts the Orthogonal trilogy
Physics-heavy; slow and cerebral

q.t: A multi-generational hard sci-fi story.

s: A widely used undergraduate textbook on discrete math, including logic, proofs, sets, combinatorics and graph theory.
w: Programmers call it the most interesting math book they've read, suited to computer science self-study, and compare it with Susanna Epp's alternative.
ab: For self-taught programmers revisiting math
Covers graphs, combinatorics, logic and proofs
Big textbook; some find math textbooks poorly taught

q.t: The most interesting math book

t: Sandworm: A New Era of Cyberwar and the Hunt for the Kremlin's Most Dangerous Hackers
s: Journalist Andy Greenberg's account of the Russian GRU hacking unit behind NotPetya and the Ukrainian power grid attacks, and the people who tracked it.
w: HN readers turn to it whenever ransomware or Russian state hacking is in the news, and list it among their best non-fiction reads. Described as a gripping, detailed narrative.
ab: For readers who like true-story cybersecurity thrillers
Non-technical enough for general audiences
Covers events up to about 2019

q.t: There's a fantastic book about this group published recently

s: A guide for 'scanners', people with many interests, on how to combine them into a fulfilling career and life instead of picking one path.
w: Recommended on HN for people anxious about too many interests, and for its message that doing a bit of everything is fine. One commenter admits it isn't a great book.
ab: For polymaths and multi-passionate people who feel pulled in many directions
Popularized the 'scanner' term
Self-help style; one HN reader found it uneven

q.t: This book helped me A LOT.

t: Every Tool's a Hammer: Life Is What You Make It
s: Mythbusters host Adam Savage shares stories and lessons from a lifetime of making things, with advice on tools, process and creativity.
w: HN readers recommend it to people who build things, saying it is full of useful information and makes you a better maker. Fans of Savage enjoy the stories too.
ab: For makers, tinkerers and fans of Adam Savage
Mix of memoir and practical maker lessons
Not a programming book, despite coming up in developer threads

q.t: Tons of good information in here, and it tickles the Mythbusters itch.

s: A widely used undergraduate textbook that builds quantum mechanics step by step with worked problems, aimed at junior and senior physics students.
w: HN readers name it among the best textbooks they have read, praising how it breaks a hard subject into digestible chunks with a clear progression. Griffiths' electrodynamics book gets the same praise.
ab: For students and self-learners with calculus and some linear algebra
Clear writing, with problems that reward working through
Undergraduate level; QFT needs other books

q.t: Both books masterfully take exceptionally complex fields and break them down into easily digested chunks

t: How to Do Nothing: Resisting the Attention Economy
s: Artist Jenny Odell argues for reclaiming attention from social media and productivity culture by engaging with place, nature and the physical world.
w: HN readers recommend it as a thoughtful answer to concerns about the attention economy and technology. One calls it thought provoking and timely, while another points others to it for their worries.
ab: For readers uneasy about social media and the attention economy
More essayistic and philosophical than a how-to
Not a literal guide to doing nothing

q.t: About resisting the attention economy and reorienting

t: End Times: Elites, Counter-Elites, and the Path of Political Disintegration
s: Cliodynamics researcher Peter Turchin uses historical data to argue that elite overproduction and popular immiseration drive societies toward political instability.
w: HN readers recommend it as a data-driven way to understand political polarization, rather than just bemoaning it. It is suggested in threads on populism and social decline.
ab: For readers wanting a quantitative, historical model of political instability
Frames current events using past cycles
Predictions are debated; model is contested by historians

q.t: who tries to strike a balance between US-centric commentary and looking at international trends

s: A broad introduction to software architecture covering architectural characteristics, styles such as microservices and layered, and the architect's role.
w: HN readers recommend it to new architects as the best broad overview available. They cite it when asked what to read after being promoted to architect.
ab: For developers moving into architecture roles
Broad survey of styles and trade-offs rather than deep dives
Follow-up book 'The Hard Parts' goes deeper

q.t: is really broad and the best overview I've seen so far.

s: A pragmatic introduction to Elixir and functional programming on the Erlang VM, covering pattern matching, processes and OTP.
w: HN readers recommend it as the first Elixir book, with hands-on exercises, and suggest following it with Programming Phoenix. It is DRM-free on pragprog.com.
ab: For programmers new to Elixir and functional programming
Has exercises and an accompanying video course
Based on Elixir 1.6; newer versions add features

q.t: Programming Elixir[1] has hands-on exercises throughout.

s: A beginner-friendly introduction to SQL using real-world datasets, covering queries, joins, statistics and database design with PostgreSQL.

t: The Creature from Jekyll Island: A Second Look at the Federal Reserve
s: G. Edward Griffin's critical history of the Federal Reserve's origins and its role in money creation.
w: Linked by commenters as a go-to read against central banking and fiat money, often dropped in arguments without elaboration. It is a contested, polemical account.
ab: For readers interested in the Federal Reserve's history and critics
Polemical, with contested claims
Often linked by libertarian and sound-money commenters

s: A tile-drafting board game for two to four players where you collect colored tiles to decorate a palace wall.
w: A frequent pick in HN board game threads because it is easy to learn, beautifully made and has real depth. The spin-off versions are also well liked.
ab: For families and casual groups, 2 to 4 players
Quick to teach with a lot of replay value
Several spin-offs share the same core feel

q.t: It is easy to learn but has a lot of outcomes, moreso when playing with more people.

s: A bedside alarm clock that simulates a sunrise and sunset with colored LED light, with a backup audio alarm.
w: HN commenters who struggle with dark winter mornings say it helps them wake up before the alarm sounds, and some couples swear by it. One says it is brighter than normal lamps but not as bright as true sunlight.
ab: For people who wake up hard, especially in dark winters
Gradual sunrise light plus sunset mode and audio alarm
Not as bright as real sunlight, according to one owner

q.t: I always wake up before the audio alarm starts.

t: From Third World to First: The Singapore Story, 1965-2000
s: Lee Kuan Yew's memoir of how he led Singapore from poor colonial port to a wealthy city-state.
w: Recommended as part memoir, part business book on building a country like a startup. Commenters call it one of the most interesting books they have read.
ab: For readers interested in nation-building and economic development
First-person account by Singapore's founding prime minister
Written by the leader himself, so it is one-sided

q.t: His book on developing Singapore is one of the most interesting books I've ever read.

t: Programming TypeScript: Making Your JavaScript Applications Scale
s: An O'Reilly book on TypeScript.
w: Recommended for learning TypeScript properly.
ab: For JS developers
Thorough
Version dated

q.t: Don't go anywhere, read a book, do it properly :).

t: Empire of the Summer Moon: Quanah Parker and the Rise and Fall of the Comanches
s: A narrative history of the Comanche, the dominant power on the southern plains, told through the life of the last great chief, Quanah Parker.
w: HN readers recommend it as a fascinating account of the Comanche and their final decades, and cite it in debates about relations between Native Americans and settlers.
ab: For readers curious about the American West and Native history
Narrative history built around Quanah Parker's life
Graphic violence; a few commenters argue over its framing

q.t: I highly recommend "Empire of the Summer Moon"[1], a fascinating account of the final decades of the Comanche tribe.

by: Hector Garcia-Molina, Jeffrey D. Ullman et al.
s: A university textbook on relational databases, SQL and the implementation of database management systems.
w: Suggested as a thorough textbook for learning how databases work, both theory and implementation, often alongside online courses.
ab: For learners who want database theory and implementation
Covers relational algebra, SQL and DBMS internals
Textbook-length and academic in tone

q.t: I remember learning that stuff from the book by jeffrey Ullman.

t: The Difference Between God and Larry Ellison: Inside Oracle Corporation
s: An unauthorized biography of Larry Ellison and the history of Oracle, known for its title.
w: Recommended as an inside look at Ellison and Oracle's history. Its title is also a well-known joke, which is how it often comes up.
ab: For readers interested in Oracle and Larry Ellison
Unauthorized, anecdote-heavy biography
Published in 2003; later events not covered

q.t: told me everything I needed to know about Larry Ellison, and the history of Oracle

t: But How Do It Know? The Basic Principles of Computers for Everyone
s: A plain-language explanation of how a computer works, building a simple CPU from logic gates up.
w: Recommended for beginners and non-CS people who want to understand how a CPU works from the gates up.
ab: For beginners curious how computers work internally
Builds a simple CPU step by step
Simplified model, not a modern architecture

q.t: Non-CS majors who want to dig deeper might enjoy

t: Unsettled: What Climate Science Tells Us, What It Doesn't, and Why It Matters
s: A former Obama administration physicist's argument that climate science is less settled than public discussion suggests.
w: Recommended by some as a calmer view on climate science, though other commenters are skeptical.
ab: For readers wanting a skeptical take on climate claims
Highly contested by many climate scientists
Written by a physicist, not a climate scientist

q.t: I found the book Unsettled quite interesting

t: The Difference Engine: Charles Babbage and the Quest to Build the First Computer
s: The story of the project to build Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2 at London's Science Museum, told by the project's curator.
w: Cited when Babbage comes up. One reader found the engineering story and Babbage's design validation compelling; another warns half the book is museum politics.
ab: For readers into early computing history and Babbage
Covers the modern reconstruction of the engine
Heavy on museum bureaucracy

q.t: It gives a lot of color on Babbage, but yes the conclusion was that Babbage design basically worked

t: The Mac Is Not a Typewriter
s: A short guide to typographic basics such as quotes, dashes, and spacing, written for desktop publishers.
w: Mentioned when HN argues about typographic details like spaces after periods and curly quotes. One commenter says it is still useful even though it targets print and Mac users.
ab: For anyone who writes or lays out text
Quick rules on quotes, dashes, spacing
Aimed at print and older Mac software

q.t: may help get them some idea about style

s: University textbook on relational databases covering SQL, query processing, storage, transactions and database design.
w: Recommended for learning relational database theory and implementation, with a note that it is not the newest text.
ab: For students and engineers learning database internals
Covers relational theory and implementation
Edition is older, not up-to-date

q.t: it's probably still the best source for the basics of relational database theory and implementation.

t: How Linux Works: What Every Superuser Should Know
s: A guide to Linux internals, covering boot, devices, networking, shell scripts and system services.
w: Show up on HN reading lists as the book to read after the basics, for admins and devops people who want to understand the system.
ab: For users moving into system administration
Explains how the pieces fit together
Older editions miss systemd-era details

q.t: I recommend the following books to learn more about the work involved on the Ops side

t: Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness
by: Richard H. Thaler, Cass R. Sunstein
s: A behavioral economics book on how default options and choice architecture can steer decisions.
w: Recommended in policy and product-design threads as the standard introduction to nudges.
ab: For anyone designing defaults, policy or products
Accessible behavioral economics
Some findings have not replicated

q.t: If you'd like to learn more, check out Nudge by Cass Sunstein

t: Mindf*ck: Cambridge Analytica and the Plot to Break America
s: A whistleblower's memoir of how Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook data to target voters in Brexit and the 2016 US election.
w: Cited by HN commenters as the insider account of data-driven political targeting; recommended to anyone working with data about people.
ab: For engineers who handle personal data and want the cautionary tale
First-person account by the main whistleblower
Memoir, so one participant's version of events

q.t: should read Christopher Wylie's description

t: Parallel and Concurrent Programming in Haskell
s: O'Reilly guide to multicore and concurrent programming in Haskell, covering parallel strategies, threads, software transactional memory, and asynchronous exceptions.
w: Haskell programmers send people to it for how Haskell handles concurrency, STM, and async exception cancellation. It is the go-to reference on the subject, by a GHC developer.
ab: For Haskell programmers who need parallelism or concurrency
Covers STM, async exceptions, and cancellation in depth
Written in 2013; library details may have changed

q.t: is a great resource for those who want to go deeper into this

t: Effective Haskell: Solving Real-World Problems with Strongly Typed Functional Programming
s: Practical Haskell book for working developers, using real-world projects to teach the language and its ecosystem rather than starting with theory.
w: Readers describe it as a modern, well-written, industry-focused Haskell book. Some call it a great resource, though one commenter did not get on with it and prefers other beginner books.
ab: For programmers who want practical Haskell, not academic math
Published in 2023, so tooling advice is recent
Opinions are mixed; Haskell Programming from First Principles is the usual alternative

q.t: well written, modern (published in 2023)

s: A 15-inch Dell workstation laptop from about 2014, offered with Ubuntu preinstalled and a high-resolution screen.
w: HN developers on Linux praise it as a solid laptop with good hardware support and a high-DPI screen thanks to Dell's work with Canonical.
ab: For developers wanting a Linux-friendly workstation laptop
Ubuntu was available preinstalled
Old hardware, mostly available used

q.t: It works great for software development and 14.04 improved support for high DPI screens.

s: Closed-back wired over-ear studio monitor headphones with detachable cables and folding earcups.
w: A go-to desk and office pair on HN: good sound for the price, durable, and passive isolation without noise cancelling. People swap the stock pads for comfort.
ab: For desk work and casual studio listening on a budget
Closed-back, folding, detachable cable
Stock pads can be uncomfortable; bass is slightly boosted

q.t: I've had Audio-Technica ATH-M50X at work for around 5 years and despite having used them most working days they still look mostly new

t: Foundations of Multidimensional and Metric Data Structures
s: A comprehensive reference on spatial and metric data structures such as quadtrees, R-trees and metric trees.
w: Called the bible of spatial data structures by commenters, and the book recommended for geospatial indexing, nearest-neighbor search and quadtree questions.
ab: For engineers working on geospatial data and spatial indexing
Extensive survey of quadtrees, R-trees and metric trees
Large academic reference, not a quick read

q.t: the bible right now is Samet's Foundations of Multidimensional and Metric Data Structures

t: Free: The Future of a Radical Price
s: Chris Anderson's argument that digital goods push prices toward zero and that businesses can profit from giving things away.
w: Pointed to when people ask how free products make money. Commenters find the historical examples interesting, though it drew heated criticism, and one says they did not agree with it.
ab: For people wondering how free products make money
Historical examples of freemium and free pricing
Controversial; critics challenge its claims

q.t: It includes some interesting historical examples of creative selling.

t: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++: Event-Driven Programming for Embedded Systems
s: A guide to implementing hierarchical state machines in C and C++ for event-driven embedded software, with a complete framework.
w: Praised as the book that explains why and how to use state machines, with an excellent codebase that one reader reuses in server software.
ab: For embedded and event-driven developers
Don't be put off by the UML in the title
One commenter found code built on its approach hard to live with

q.t: the specific codebase described in the book is excellent

t: The Revolt of the Public and the Crisis of Authority in the New Millennium
s: An analysis of how the information age undermined elite authority.
w: Recommended as a book to read for understanding trust and authority.
ab: Information age politics
Political analysis
Gurri's perspective

t: The Endurance: Shackleton's Legendary Antarctic Expedition
s: A narrative of Shackleton's Antarctic expedition illustrated with photographs by expedition photographer Frank Hurley.
w: Mentioned for its photographs of the expedition and as a well-liked account. One commenter enjoyed it and says the author's book on the Bounty is excellent too.
ab: For readers who want the Shackleton story with photos
Features Frank Hurley's expedition photographs
Covers the same events as Lansing's Endurance

q.t: I really enjoyed her book

t: Zen in the Art of Archery
s: A short account of a German philosopher's training in Japanese archery and what it taught him about Zen.
w: Cited on HN when talking about flow, letting go of outcomes, and learning physical skills. Commenters call it a classic.
ab: For readers interested in Zen and the psychology of skill
A short narrative of learning archery
Contested as an account of Zen practice

q.t: what is described in the classic Zen in the Art of Archery

t: Million Dollar Consulting: The Professional's Guide to Growing a Practice
s: Alan Weiss's guide to building a high-fee independent consulting practice, covering marketing, pricing and client relationships.
w: Recommended to freelancers wanting to move up from hourly work, with Weiss called the guru of building a consulting business.
ab: For freelancers and consultants raising rates
Marketing, fees and client relationships
Self-promotional tone in places

q.t: you'll do well to read Alan Weiss, The Guru of building a successful consulting business

t: I Want to Be a Mathematician: An Automathography
s: Paul Halmos's memoir of his life and career as a mathematician, with advice on teaching and doing mathematics.
w: Recommended in math-learning threads as an enjoyable read even for non-mathematicians, and listed as a must-read about the mathematical life.
ab: For readers curious about how mathematicians live and work
Personal memoir with opinions on teaching and writing
Anecdotes center on mid-20th-century mathematics

q.t: I loved reading this book (though I'm no mathematician).

t: The Coming of the Third Reich
s: The first volume of Richard Evans's history of Nazi Germany, covering the roots of Nazism and the seizure of power.
w: Recommended as among the best explanations of the social and political roots of Nazism, covering 1870 to the establishment of Nazi power.
ab: For readers wanting a rigorous history of Nazi Germany's rise
First of a three-volume series
Long and detailed

q.t: The best explanations I've seen of the social and political roots of that period are Richard Evans's

t: The Next 100 Years: A Forecast for the 21st Century
s: A geopolitical forecast of the 21st century by the founder of Stratfor, built on the idea that nations act by geography and national interest.
w: Cited in geopolitics threads as a framework for why states behave as they do, and for its early China warnings. Treat the specific predictions with caution.
ab: For readers who like geopolitical big-picture thinking.
Frames nations as driven by geography and strategic interest.
Specific predictions are speculative and many have aged poorly.

q.t: predicted this, except he believed the implosion of China would be on a truly catastrophic scale

by: Daniel Jurafsky and James H. Martin
s: The standard textbook on natural language processing, computational linguistics and speech recognition.
w: HN readers call it the standard intro to NLP, and say it pairs well with the Stanford NLP course by its author and Chris Manning.
ab: For students and engineers learning NLP
Comprehensive textbook
Early editions predate deep learning; newer drafts are free online

q.t: The standard intro textbook to the field is Jurafsky and Martin

s: Scott Adams's satirical look at bosses, meetings and management fads, including the claim that the least effective workers get promoted to management.
w: Cited on HN for its workplace satire and the Dilbert Principle itself, and listed among books that stuck with people.
ab: For readers who like Dilbert and office humor
Satire rather than management advice
Dated in places

s: A short book on five practices for learning and thinking: understand deeply, fail productively, ask questions, follow the flow of ideas, and change.
w: HN readers call it a clear, practical tutorial for learning and creativity. One notes it's short and repetitive, with an academic bent.
ab: For anyone who wants better habits for learning
Short and easy to read
Somewhat repetitive; academic flavor

q.t: I highly recommend 5 Elements of Effective Thinking

t: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, JavaScript Edition
by: Harold Abelson, Gerald Jay Sussman et al.
s: The 2022 JavaScript adaptation of the classic MIT text on programming abstraction, interpreters and computation, with an open-access online version.
w: HN points to it for people who want SICP without Scheme or Racket. It keeps the classic material and is freely readable online.
ab: For readers who want SICP in JavaScript
Free open-access web version
Original Scheme edition is still the more cited one

q.t: there's last years JavaScript edition

s: A 1977 novel about a self-teaching program that grows into an AI by spreading through the computer networks of its day.
w: HN reading lists for computer fiction bring it up as an early story of AI emerging from the net, predating WarGames. One reader says it left a strong impression.
ab: For fans of vintage computer and AI fiction
1970s technology; very dated details
Hard to find in print

q.t: 1970s depiction of an AI arising from whatever passed for the Internet back then.

t: Clojure Applied: From Practice to Practitioner
s: An intermediate Clojure book on structuring real applications: data modeling, state, processes and design patterns.
w: Recommended as the next step after a Clojure beginner book, especially for Java or OO programmers wondering how to organize Clojure code. One coauthor plugs it in the comments.
ab: For Clojure programmers past the basics
Covers design and organization
Co-author is among the commenters

q.t: is very nice if you are coming from a traditional Java or OO background

t: Docs for Developers: An Engineer's Field Guide to Technical Writing
s: A practical guide for engineers on planning, writing and maintaining technical documentation.
w: Lands at the top whenever HN asks for technical writing books. Commenters like that it treats docs like a product with an audience and a process.
ab: For engineers who need to write good docs
Covers planning, drafting, publishing and maintaining documentation
Aimed at software docs, not general writing

q.t: The subtitle describes the book as "an engineer's field guide to technical writing" and that's exactly what the book is.

s: A programmable LEGO robotics kit with a brick computer, motors and sensors that kids and hobbyists can build and code.
w: HN parents and hobbyists keep suggesting it as a way into robotics and programming for kids, often alongside First LEGO League. Buy extra parts.
ab: For kids around 10 and up who want to build and program robots
Motors, sensors and a programmable brick
Pricey; the original NXT/EV3 lines are retired

q.t: Lego mindstorms is outstanding

s: A short sci-fi novella narrated by a security android that has hacked its own governor module and mostly wants to watch TV.
w: HN calls it a fun, quick read with a voice that is funny and oddly moving. Commenters note the novellas are short enough that you can binge the series.
ab: For sci-fi readers who like short, witty reads
First of a series of novellas
Very short, so you will want the next book

q.t: Martha Wells' Murderbot series is a fun holiday read.

s: Sony's current-generation game console with fast SSD loading, a 4K output and a large exclusive game library.
w: HN's pick for gaming without PC upkeep: plug in and play, strong exclusives, quick loading. One poster uses it as the streaming box for a TV that tracks you.
ab: For gamers who want it to just work, with little maintenance
Fast loading and strong exclusives
Needs separate game purchases and a 4K TV to shine

q.t: If yo don't have enough time, then go with PS5. It's powerful, has good quality exclusive games, and is just plug and play.

s: Microsoft's high-end game console with fast loading, 4K 120Hz output and optional Game Pass subscription.
w: HN owners like Game Pass value, near-instant loading and that things just work. It also doubles as a simple streaming box.
ab: For console gamers who like the Game Pass library
Fast resume and loading; 4K 120Hz support
Game Pass is a subscription, and some lean toward PC instead

q.t: Things Just Work and load times are basically nonexistent

s: Open-ear, wireless bone-conduction headphones that sit in front of the ears so you can hear the surroundings while listening.
w: HN fans use them for walking, hiking and calls while staying aware of traffic and people, with nothing blocking the ears. One deaf-in-one-ear user calls them the best option.
ab: For runners, walkers and office workers who want to hear their surroundings
Open-ear design; Bluetooth with a long-lasting battery
Sound is thinner than regular headphones; bass is limited

q.t: Lets me listen to audiobooks and pod casts while still being aware of my surroundings

s: A marble-powered mechanical computer kit where kids place plastic bits on a board to build logic circuits and solve puzzles.
w: HN parents and teachers recommend it for teaching boolean logic and computing basics to kids, even as young as six, with expansion kits for more complex builds.
ab: For kids around 8 and up curious about how computers work
Plastic board, marbles and parts; puzzle book included
Younger kids may need an adult's help

q.t: Turing Tumble teaches you to build a binary calculator using marbles and bits of plastic.

s: A space exploration mystery game set in a looping solar system, where knowledge is the only thing that carries over between runs.
w: HN players push it hard as a smart, moving puzzle game and say to go in blind. Some call it life-changing and a lesson in exploring.
ab: For players who like exploration and puzzles with no hand-holding
Play it spoiler-free; no combat grind
Some physics-based navigation frustrates certain players

q.t: I can't recommend Outer Wilds enough.

s: A farming-themed worker-placement board game for one to five players with no luck in the main mechanics.
w: A staple in HN board game threads: deep strategy, no dice, and an approachable theme for people who dislike conflict-heavy games. Several say it got them into the hobby.
ab: For strategy gamers who like building an engine
Worker placement with no direct combat
Long and a bit punishing for newcomers

q.t: Agricola got me into board games years ago, and it's always been a joy to go back to it.

s: A 14-inch IBM/Lenovo ThinkPad from 2006 famed for its keyboard and TrackPoint, now a cheap used laptop.
w: HN commenters from the 2000s loved its keyboard and TrackPoint and chose it over Macs, and later users still run it for about $100 as a budget machine.
ab: Cheap secondhand tinkerer laptop.
Excellent keyboard and TrackPoint.
Very old hardware; weak Linux battery life noted.

q.t: The keyboard is just amazing compared to anything else out there.

t: The Rise and Decline of Nations
s: Olson's argument that stable societies accumulate special-interest groups that slow economic growth.
w: Cited by commenters to explain collective action, lobbying and why small organized groups beat large diffuse ones.
ab: For readers interested in political economy
Explains why concentrated interests win
Academic and dense in places

q.t: It explains this phenomenon. Basically, for a group of size n, members only get 1/n of the value they contribute towards any collective goal

s: A signal-blocking pouch for car key fobs and phones that shields against radio relay attacks.
w: Recommended for keeping keyless car keys in to stop relay theft, with one reporting the car would not unlock with the key inside.
ab: Blocks key fob signals
Cheap and simple
Test it works

q.t: With the key in the bag I'm unable to unlock the car even with it right on the door.

s: A line-by-line walkthrough of venture capital term sheets and how valuations are calculated.
w: Listed among the solid books for understanding venture financing, usually next to Venture Deals. Founders turn to it when they need to decode a term sheet.
ab: For founders about to raise venture capital
Explains each clause with examples
Published in 2004, so newer deal norms are missing

q.t: These books on the subject of term sheets are solid

s: A philosopher of physics explains the measurement problem and the main interpretations of quantum mechanics for readers with little math.
w: Recommended as a clear explanation of the measurement problem and collapse theories without invoking consciousness. Commenters keep it on their reading lists for quantum foundations.
ab: For curious readers who want the conceptual side of quantum mechanics
Explains wavefunction collapse and competing interpretations
Conceptual rather than a calculation-based textbook

q.t: There are clearer explanations that rely only on what physicists (mostly) already accept, which David Albert explains well

t: Collapse of an Empire: Lessons for Modern Russia
s: An economist and former Russian prime minister's analysis of why the Soviet Union collapsed.
w: Recommended in threads about the fall of the USSR as an excellent primary source by one of the architects of Russia's economic reforms.
ab: For readers of Soviet and Russian economic history
Insider's account of the oil shock and fiscal crisis
Written from the perspective of a reformer

s: A classic, irreverent guide to running a company by the former head of Avis, on how to stop the corporation from stifling people.
w: Called an outstanding book on running a business and a classic for a reason. Recommended to new engineering managers and in lists of non-tech books for professional growth.
ab: For managers tired of corporate bureaucracy
Short, witty rules on people and organization
Written in 1970; some references are dated

q.t: And outstanding book about running a business.

t: Cooking for Geeks: Real Science, Great Hacks, and Good Food
s: An O'Reilly cookbook explaining the science of cooking with experiments, temperature tricks, and techniques aimed at technical readers.
w: The default answer when HN asks for cooking books for hackers. Commenters say they love it and enjoyed it, drawn to its science and hack-oriented approach.
ab: For tinkerers who want to know why recipes work
Food science, gadgets and kitchen experiments
More technique than a recipe collection

q.t: If you like this stuff, you will love Jeff Potter's "Cooking for Geeks"

s: An inexpensive digital wrist watch with a built-in calculator and data bank, in a retro style.
w: HN's go-to example of the calculator watch: cheap, long-lived, and one commenter wears it daily. Mentioned in smartwatch debates as a no-fuss alternative.
ab: For retro-watch fans who want a cheap calculator watch
Tiny buttons; basic calculator and data bank
Low-cost and simple; not a smartwatch

q.t: Casio's awesome calculator watches can be had for less than US$16.

t: Geometric Algebra for Computer Science: An Object-Oriented Approach to Geometry
by: Leo Dorst, Daniel Fontijne et al.
s: A textbook introducing geometric algebra and its use in computer graphics, robotics and geometry, with companion software.
w: Described as eye-opening and as showing why the cross product is an ugly hack. Readers like the companion program that displays the book's diagrams.
ab: For graphics and robotics programmers wanting better geometry
Includes software to explore the diagrams
Needs linear algebra background

q.t: I found Geometric Algebra for Computer Science (Revised Edition): An Object-Oriented Approach to Geometry to be eye-opening.

t: Xbox 360 Wireless Gaming Receiver for Windows
s: A USB receiver that lets Xbox 360 wireless controllers connect to a Windows PC.
w: The adapter commenters use to hook 360 controllers to PCs for emulators, XBMC and games. One says it worked first try, though USB ports need enough power.
ab: For PC gamers using Xbox 360 wireless controllers
Plug-and-play on Windows
Obsolete as newer controllers use other adapters

q.t: Believe it or not, it worked first try

t: Liars and Outliers: Enabling the Trust That Society Needs to Thrive
s: Bruce Schneier's look at how societies build trust through security systems, morals and institutions, and how defectors exploit it.
w: Recommended in summer reading and as a starting point on trust in society. Commenters say it gives a lot to think about.
ab: For readers interested in trust and security beyond tech
Examines social pressures and cheating
Broad and abstract in places

q.t: Very interesting and gives you a lot to think about. Highly recommended.

t: Objective-C Programming: The Big Nerd Ranch Guide
s: A Big Nerd Ranch beginner guide to Objective-C, the language used for Mac and iOS development.
w: Commenters heard it was a really good intro to Objective-C for iOS beginners and recommend Big Nerd Ranch books in general.
ab: For readers learning Objective-C
Part of the Big Nerd Ranch series
Objective-C has largely been replaced by Swift

q.t: I've heard this is a really good introduction book

s: A multilingual Swiss-style typography textbook, a foundational text of modernist typography and design.
w: Called the book that established modern typography and a beautiful multilingual design book. Recommended alongside Müller-Brockmann's Grid Systems.
ab: For designers into Swiss and modernist typography
Beautiful multilingual layout
Expensive; advanced

q.t: Ruder's Typographie is the book that established modern typography and is the de fact guide to modernist typography

s: Sliding plastic cover that attaches over a laptop or device webcam.
w: Recommended as a cheap physical kill switch for webcams, though one commenter warned a cover can cause screen damage when the lid closes.
ab: Fits laptops, tablets and phones
Slide open for video calls
Closing a laptop with a cover can stress the screen

q.t: This cover fits great over my macbook camera

s: Biography of Oliver Heaviside, the self-taught electrical genius behind much of how Maxwell's equations are used today.
w: Called a must-read for the history and mathematical development of Maxwell's equations and Heaviside's role.
ab: For electrical engineering and physics fans
Biography with some math
Covers Victorian-era science

q.t: Paul J. Nahin's book on Heaviside[1] is a must read.

s: Stainless steel chainmail scrubber for cleaning cast iron without soap.
w: Recommended as a cheap scrubber for cast iron that removes stuck bits without soap.
ab: Stainless steel chainmail
Used without soap
Cheap, about $18

q.t: For $18 it will change your cast iron life.

t: Renormalization Methods: A Guide for Beginners
s: Introductory guide to renormalization methods in physics.
w: Suggested by commenters for learning renormalization, recommended to experts as promising.
ab: For physics students
Beginner-oriented
Requires QFT background

q.t: this book was actually suggested to me here

s: A 27-inch 3840x2160 IPS monitor with a high pixel density of about 163 ppi.
w: Praised as the cheapest sharp, retina-class display for programming work, with one owner liking it more than an Apple Cinema Display.
ab: For text-heavy coding work at high DPI
About $540 at its best price in one thread
Older 60Hz panel; no Thunderbolt or integrated power supply

q.t: I recently purchased a Dell P2715Q[0] and I LOVE it.

t: Causal Inference in Statistics: A Primer
s: A short introduction to causal graphs and the do-calculus, written by Judea Pearl and co-authors for readers with a statistics background.
w: Pointed to as a lighter, newer entry point into Pearl's causality work than his full Causality text.
ab: For statisticians and data scientists new to causal inference
Much lighter than Pearl's Causality
Assumes some statistics background

q.t: is somewhat lighter (at least if you have an statistics background).

s: Reusable earplugs that reduce volume evenly across frequencies so music and speech stay clear.
w: Recommended for concerts and loud events as a cheap way to protect hearing without muffling sound.
ab: For concertgoers and musicians
Cheap compared with custom plugs
Generic fit; custom plugs fit better

q.t: Seriously, if you're a fan of live music, grab a pair and just try it at the next concert you go to.

s: An adjustable single monitor arm, reportedly made by Ergotron, that clamps to a desk.
w: Recommended as a cheaper alternative to Ergotron, since it is reportedly made by the same company.
ab: For anyone mounting a monitor
Cheaper than Ergotron
Check weight limit
